The Sosnowiec Kehilla Commissioner's Reply to the Delegation of the Gemilut-Chesed Fund

Last Sunday the director of the „Joint“[?] [JDC], Mr. Giterman, visited Sosnowiec; having learned of the improper conduct of the kehilla commissioner with regard to the G[emilut] Ch[esed] (interest-free loan) fund, he proposed that a delegation of the fund should approach the commissioner and ask him to explain his tactics so far towards the G.Ch.
The delegation, consisting of Messrs. Giterman, L. Zandl[?] and Ch. Gleitman, was received by the commissioner, who said that „the management of the G.Ch. fund is not loyal towards him“; in passing the commissioner poured out his wrath on the Jewish city councillors, who „are making a hullabaloo over some boy who was murdered“...
It goes without saying that the delegates gave the commissioner a fitting reply, especially to his dismissive remark that „some boy was murdered“; but in the end the delegation did not succeed in getting the commissioner to pay out the subsidy for the G.Ch. fund.
Finally the commissioner declared that if the public is good and pious and pays its „etat“[?] (communal budget dues), kehilla elections will soon take place; if not, there will be no kehilla elections in Sosnowiec even in the year 1938.

A legless cripple falls out of a moving train

On Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a meeting took place at the Artisans' Association in Dąbrowa, which ran a stormy course. A son who poisoned his whole family

In the Witkowski[?] family in Olkusz there is a son, Henryk, 23 years old, whom the family did not love because of his adventurous (rowdy) escapades, and they drove him out of the house.
Henryk picked himself a friend, a certain Maksymilian Gwozdek, who was a bitter enemy of the Witkowski family. The two companions were now united by their common hatred of the Witkowskis. [?] Gwozdek incited his companion against his parents, who had driven him out of the house, and Henryk decided to take revenge on the whole family.
The plan of revenge was a devilish one: the criminal son poured poison into the pots standing on the stove, among them[?] also into a pot of cabbage that was cooking for the midday meal.
Knowing nothing at all, the Witkowski family ate the cabbage at the midday meal. Soon they all began to feel terrible pains; a doctor was called, who applied the first measures to save them, and afterwards they were all taken to hospital.
Only the three brothers could be saved, whereas his old mother died in great agony.

An Impressive Chanukah Celebration

(Under the section banner: “What Is Heard in Upper Silesia?”)
Jewish Youth Is Never Young — Says Rabbi Chameides.
Last Monday evening the Zionist youth organisation “Akiba” in Katowice held a Chanukah evening in the large “Paustanzue”[?] hall, with the participation of Rabbi Chameides and Dr. Feldblum of Kraków.
On the beautifully decorated stage the young Chaim Sperner[?] lights the Chanukah candles in a living menorah, “Maoz Tzur” is sung, and then Rabbi Chameides begins his speech and says — “tsch. pgr.”[?] — that Jewish youth is in fact never young; for just as Bialik lamented, asking where his youth had gone, so the whole of Jewish youth is forced — already at its early age — to begin waging its hard struggle for life.
Turning to the struggle of old with the enemies of the Jews, the esteemed “p-elegent”[?] (speaker) says that the Greeks wanted to destroy us spiritually, and today the war of extermination is waged against our spiritual and physical-material existence. We left Egypt with our property — today the wealth and goods gathered over generations are being robbed from us; and not only that — asks Rabbi Chameides — can the world give us back great spirits such as Spinoza, Heine, Cohen and a long row of other brilliant creators and co-creators of human culture?
With the words that the ancient Jewish people has lived and will go on living, Rabbi Chameides concludes his inspiring lecture, which was distinguished by great rhetorical power and made a colossal impression.
Hot and thunderous applause was the thanks and the expression of recognition of the huge audience.
The well-known Kraków Zionist leader Dr. Feldblum compares in his lecture today's waves of hatred against Jews to volcanic eruptions which spew hot lava and destroy everything around them. In former times, when Jews lived in the ghetto, we were reproached for living in darkness and reaction; [then] part of the Jews in the Renaissance era [sought] to absorb themselves into the wide world — and now has come the brutal push back into the ghetto.
In the staging of “Hannah and Her Seven Sons” Miss Mantefer[?], H[?] Winer and the young Siegreich and Lipschitz excelled; little Gutman also recited nicely.
The Chanukah celebration, which has already become a tradition, passed with great success and ended with the singing of “Hatikvah”.

A Cantor Comes to His Son in a Dream / The Endek Association in Rybnik Dissolved / The Number of Inhabitants in Katowice / Caught Red-Handed… / A Theft in a Restaurant

He is to hold a din-torah with the gabbaim.
Two years ago a small-town Jew came to Königshütte — a Jew of dignified countenance with all the virtues, and a good prayer-leader besides. The Jew soon became famous in Jewish circles as a singer, and for the High Holidays he was engaged by the gabbaim to lead the prayers in the synagogue as cantor (shaliach tzibbur) for a certain fee.
After the holiday the gabbaim regretted the deal and would not pay the prayer-leader the promised fee. The dispute came before the court, and on the strength of the oath the gabbaim gave, the court dismissed the claim of the so-called cantor.
Some time later the cantor died, and the whole affair would have been completely forgotten anyway, were it not for the dreams of the deceased's son, who lives in Gleiwitz.
The first dream was on the night of the first day of Rosh Hashanah. “I have come to you, my child — the father said to the son — you must summon the gabbaim to judgement; they must pay the debt they owe me, thanks to their having sworn falsely.”
The son ignored the dream, and more than that, laughed at the foolish dream. But when the father “appeared” to him a second time — this was on the night of Hoshana Rabbah — he no longer made light of the matter, decided to carry out his father's demand, and right after the holiday summoned the gabbaim to judgement.
The gabbaim, who had already sworn at the time[?] before the court that they owed the cantor nothing, now find themselves in an unfavourable position, so last week they came to Sosnowiec to Rabbi Hager, that he should give them advice.
Rabbi Hager told the delegation that he does not want to get involved in this tangled affair.

Oh, How They Had a Ball

(A stroll on New Year's Eve).

I decided to take a look at whether and when our dear little Jews would celebrate this year in honour of Sylvester [the civil New Year's Eve] and how they would amuse themselves. After all, one hears [?] lately, incessantly, about the bitter crisis, which has eaten itself even deeper into the Jewish bones, so that it is simply impossible to bear any more; now the taxes [podatki], which squeeze and choke the already weak human being [?], poor thing, so that he can barely catch his breath; then again the plain burnt-in troubles of a whole year, in which Jews play first fiddle, so that there is truly nothing to envy them for (on the contrary, be a sport and show me any Jew you like who hasn't got a bundle of troubles) — so I was indeed keen to see how our brethren the Children of Israel would welcome the holy Sylvester holiday; whether this time some little change had come about in the [?] ["P.P." — unclear abbreviation], so that this year Sylvester would no longer be a genuine Jewish holiday as in former years. The "zbór" [Polish: turnout] of Jews at balls would perhaps be smaller.

And I must tell you that my stroll on New Year's Eve did not disappoint me. Everything was "w porządku" [Polish: in order] [?], as God commanded. Our dear little Jews stood at the height of the occasion and saw to it that the Jewish people with "its holidays" should, God forbid, not perish. Tradition remains tradition, so it must be, and no crisis and no other blows will help — a tradition must not only be preserved but even strengthened and broadened. And so, brother Motl, celebrate, let the smoke rise! It's a holiday in the world — so live it up for a day, as long as the soul is within you; don't spoil any holiday, and carouse as much as you can. Well, and so they did carouse and amuse themselves.

Oh, how they had a ball [gebavyet, from Polish bawić się]...

I went into a night club. To tell the truth — a small number of visitors, but on the other hand a majority of Jewish noses. I asked where [?] all the Jewish Sylvester guests were, and I was told that various halls were holding balls and entertainments; well, and the crowd was scattered [?] and dispersed.

So I went off to another café. Here there is already more commotion: the piano chords echo, the weeping pianissimo tones of the fiddle from a longing tango tremble [?], the jazz sounds rush and thunder in every corner; the room is filled with clouds of cigar and papierosy smoke, the feet of dancing couples shuffle, and — in the glow of the spotlight I see the Jewish faces beaming, rejoicing, faces that one rarely sees [?] in a café had turned up today so as not to miss Sylvester. But it does not end here yet. The real "holiday delight" with all the "pitchevkes" [?] [unclear word — trimmings] I saw only at the ball of the Jewish university graduates. Here there was joy and gladness, as it should be. A din, a tumult and such a crush that you couldn't drop a pin on the floor. Here one saw the revelry in its full scope: men and women dressed in [?] and in [?], smokings, ball gowns of every kind, tails, black suits, stiff collars, and faces beamed with delight; liqueur, wine, vodka, cognac (champagne, alas, there was none) flowed like water — lively, merry, carefree, gaiety, humour, drunkenness; they partied to the full, caroused to the full, so that "the whole province nearly shook".

— Oh, how they had a ball.
— To oblivion, to madness.

I was looking — you know for whom? — for a non-Jew. And believe me, I found some. Among the great assembled mass I found 2 people (in words [?]: two!) non-Jews who had wandered in there, poor things, quite innocently, and [?] like Jews they "too" had a ball at the "Jewish" holiday.

I thought to myself that it is no wonder at all why Jews have enemies, when our dear little Jews have the chutzpah to snatch the holidays away from them. Not enough that one snatches from them the "khoinkes" [?] [perhaps Polish choinki — Christmas trees], one also takes away their holidays.

They take away from us — our livelihoods with the couple of guilders, and we inherit Sylvester for ourselves; some amuse themselves in public venues, some at private balls and so-called [?] "kolacje" [Polish: supper parties].

— Oh, how they had a ball...

The Middle Class in Poland

[Poland — economy, the middle class; article.] By L. Szpigelman.
(The difficult situation of the average person in the country. — Where does the cause lie? — Employing too many and too few people.)
At every opportunity, and even with no opportunity at all, people here talk about the middle class (Mittelstand): it complains that things are bad for it, bitter for it, that it is extraordinarily hard to keep up with the current, which flows with tremendous[?] speed. The obligations for today and tomorrow grow[?] in masses[?]. With every day that passes[?] — more and more duties, and that is what one is on account of them[?], because one stays behind yesterday and today.
This element is not in a position to be able to reckon in advance[?] for each day, week or whole[?] month, i.e.[?] it does not know whether in the course of this or that period its income or its expenses will rise. Unfortunately it is not [—], and also[?] lacks the possibility of organizing itself so as to know how it stands, what its actual material situation is[?].
As for keeping people, bookkeepers, who would keep its books, as is necessary nowadays — there can be no talk of it, because at a time when one is constantly thinking how to economize more and more, one cannot bring oneself to enlarge the budget, which is moreover very complicated both in expenses and in various formalities, which must be observed exactly and punctually according to the regulations — if not, a fine is imposed[?] at once; so one considers it superfluous to commit oneself to it, regardless of the fact that nowadays this is a [—] defect both for the business and for the household existence[?] of one's vital interests.
The government takes all measures so that[?] the middle strata of the population should keep books. Thus, for example, the tax rate for these firms is lower, and in addition greater and smaller privileges are granted[?] to them.
And people realized[?] that it is much more convenient this way, and began to engage bookkeepers and correspondents, reckoning that in this way they would pay the tax burdens month by month, pay the pensions[?], and would know where they stand in the world. Unfortunately this turned out to be a utopia: over the slightest trifle the books were disqualified, and they were not taken into account in the tax assessments. That is one thing, but there is another reason: people can tell of [—] who kept books improperly, and afterwards the firms were penalized. The firm, cheerfully[?] knowing that it had provided itself with a person, did not want to know about anything — only that the other should remain responsible for everything; and that is indeed how it was, while those people were not registered[?] with the proper institutions, official and semi-official. The firm argued that this was why it engaged a person — so that he would know the firm's obligations. But the end was that the firm suffered and it was the one that remained responsible for everything. The people, knowing what an important role they play in the books, and also how far they hold the key to the business, left the firm at the first opportunity, knowing that another person would not be able, without[?] them, to approach the books.
Then there is one more reason, and that is that not all enterprises have one and the same expenses, because while one firm had "manipulation" expenses[?] of so-and-so much a month, a second one of the same branch had minimal expenses, keeping no books and employing no staff, so that the latter always remained more competitive.
The reasons enumerated above, both on the part of the authorities and on the part of the employed people, have thus pushed the firms to reduce both the budgets of their businesses and the businesses themselves, so that the middle class today runs almost everywhere miniature enterprises, and a livelihood is not easy to draw from them.
In the European countries it is unimaginable that firms of the middle class should be able to run their businesses almost without people, one may say, as with us in Poland. In all enterprises, however small and modest they may be, different people are put in each branch, who know their job, so that everything is counted as expenses, and only then comes the profit which the business must have. That is how it is for everyone and for each one; it cannot be understood otherwise at all; the authorities take it into account, because everywhere people work under these conditions.
Why go far — even here in Upper Silesia it is, after all, no different. How many saleswomen the average shop[?] has there, how much is spent there on advertising and on the most varied sorts of expenses, which everywhere are matters of course for the average citizen. Here people have no notion of them, or they look like luxurious[?], unattainable phenomena to which one cannot adapt.
One need not look far for the reasons; they are quite simple: there the owner is an entrepreneur, a director, a manager of his business, and therefore he must have people for each branch separately, so that the public, broad society, the great collective, to which the whole country has become accustomed to adapting.
Quite different is it with us in Congress Poland, in former Russia, where the "director" and the cashier, and where the subject[?] and the collector, consist of one and the same person, who is the owner of the business. When these firms want to modernize their enterprises, they run into difficulties, owing to the fact that the great public is not adapted to this system.
Practice has shown us that if firms — of the middle class, of course — want to modernize by committing themselves to greater expenses, the end is that they are driven out of the market, and that is because the great majority consists of the "universal man", who has no choice but to be everything at once.
This proves to us once again that "one swallow does not make a summer": if the great majority runs its businesses under other conditions, then the elements that want to change them[?] must also adapt to them. Incidentally, tradition too plays a great role here, to which, by the way, the whole environment adapts itself excellently.
Which system is better and which we can adapt to, we shall try to elucidate in the second chapter.
Jewish Ritual Slaughter...

The [—] [—] of the [—] State Council (Staatsrat) have submitted a proposal to abolish Jewish ritual slaughter.
(From the chronicle.)
It is, after all, a remarkable thing how Jewish ritual slaughter interests certain "humanitarian" (in this case it would perhaps be more fitting to say — animal, zoological, bestial...) animal-welfare circles more than — let us say — the bloody and bloodless[?], but nonetheless[?], attacks on Jews!..
The customs and manners of the Nuremberg mass-torturers and sadistic scum[?] fly[?] across the borders of that criminal[?] land, and the ban on the slaughter of... cattle and fowl hangs over other countries too, as a problem of human kindness and pity for animals.
The whole problem would be no problem at all, were it not obscured[?] by the beasts in human form, out of false and falsified feelings and — calculations...
As the matter is presented by the interested parties, it is absurd in the highest degree.
It could be understood, and human reason could accept it logically, if the question were put of not eating meat at all, as the vegetarians say — strange[?]...
But where is the practical difference here — what difference does it make to the animal whether it perishes on the altar of the human stomach by a slaughter-knife (chalaf), by an axe, or by electric current...
Even among people who perish by a forced death (not[?] on the "soldierly"[?] battlefield), but on the gallows, by a bullet, or in the electric chair — if one were to ask these condemned to death which death is sweeter to them, they would undoubtedly smile at how [—] foolish people still are to this day!
B.
A Meeting of the Old Year and the New Year.

By David Einhorn.
— One, two, three, four..
On a white[?] field stood the Old Year, counting. A cold autumn wind tousled[?] his long white beard and tore at his clothes.
— Five... come on, faster, to the devil with it — the old man fumed — let me be rid at last of this cursed baggage; who knows whether[?] there, before the clock strikes twelve, something might yet burst in my suitcases, and afterwards they will say I am to blame, and history will put it down to my name.
— Six, seven, eight. O God, how slowly time drags! It seems to me I am not one year old but a whole hundred years. Just look how the Italian is floundering there in the war. He could still do something before the clock strikes twelve — and Hitler, how he is fiddling about there with the bombs.
— Eleven, twelve. Well, at last, thank God! An end to my story. There he comes already, the New Year.
From afar appeared a young man, poor and naked, with a head of black curly[?] hair, red cheeks and burning eyes. He ran like an arrow from a bow to the place where the Old Year stood.
Suddenly the Old Year jumped up and began to shout in a voice not his own:
— Stop. Slowly, you wretch! Stand still! Don't fly like a madman! Watch where you are going — you nearly bumped into the suitcase with the plague-bombs; a fine sight you would have been if they burst under your feet just at the minute when people raise their glasses of wine and greet you with a hurrah!
The New Year stood still as if frozen.
— What are you saying, old man?
— I'm saying you shouldn't jump about[?] among the "baggage"; you could still cause a disaster.
— What baggage?
— What not? — the old man began to [count][?]: currencies, wars, wooden boxes bound with iron — that was my baggage; now it becomes yours. Be so kind, take it and count them over; I will hand everything over to you.
— Look, do you see the black suitcase? Those are glass bombs; inside lie microbes of cholera, plague, spotted typhus. It is enough to drop a few of them over a city for an epidemic to break out.
— Now the black crate. Be careful! Those are gas bombs. A few dozen of them can turn the biggest city into a huge cemetery. Should they burst in your time, you will be recorded as the darkest and bloodiest year in history.
— Nice parcels! — muttered the New Year.
— Now mind[?] the big crates over there for me — those are aeroplanes, innocent machines; but those over there are excellent bombers: when you load the contents of the suitcases onto the steel birds and let them fly, your name will be "Black Year".
The New Year sat down; his knees began to tremble.
— And what is in the iron boxes?
— Better not ask! In them sit the owners of the arms[?] factories — that is a dangerous gang; they do[?] everything they can to set the world on fire. Now mind[?] the bankers and the steel magnates; they lie there in the fine leather trunks. In a word: whichever package you merely touch — there is danger.
— And is that all? — asked the New Year.
— Not yet. Here you have a package of papers. Here you have an exact list of how many hungry there are in the world — don't be frightened, you may yet have more. Here you have a reckoning of how many tons of bread, coffee, sugar, wool and [—][?] were burned. Look it all through carefully. Now farewell, and take the inheritance.
The Old Year laid all the parcels at the New Year's feet and began to walk away.
— Wait! — the young one jumped up — perhaps you could take this inheritance with you! I am ready to come without an inheritance.
— That won't do; I too inherited it from the previous year. True, in my time the parcels have [—] grown, but that is not my fault. Do you see this crate? In it lie the diplomats; try to manage with them as best you can, but don't place any great hopes in them.
— Can one not get rid of this baggage, then? Throw it into the sea, bury them somewhere in a desert? — asked the New Year.
— Try — the old man smiled — if you can do that, you will be recorded as the most beautiful and brightest year in the history of mankind. Meanwhile, farewell, and I wish you the greatest success. But I think many others will still come with such wishes and go away, until one of us manages it. Adieu.
And when the hands of the clocks showed one minute past twelve, there appeared in the streets a young man with a half-grey head, loaded with packs, crates and cages. He walked bent double, and in his head one thought hammered[?]: how does one get rid of this cursed baggage?
And in millions, millions of human heads the very same thought hammered[?]. Tired, they threw themselves into their beds, but not all had yet fallen asleep[?]; and those who wanted it, too, were not united among themselves nor persevering[?] enough. And when they rose in the morning to work, the New Year was already bent[?], grey, his young face ploughed with furrows of worry, and on his back had grown a large hump from the burden..
Twenty-Five Years of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” — Yehuda Yafet

[Jubilee of the paper — congratulatory essay; Zagłębie — the press.]
Yehuda Yafet.
Twenty-five years of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung”.
And again I look at the masthead of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” on the last issue of the past year: twenty-fifth volume. [?], this year the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” enters its twenty-sixth year.
Unbelievable! Is[?] a quarter of a century not too serious (Polish poważne) for our young, life-filled paper? One feels like shrugging: what? Twenty-five years old?
No — the earnestness, the composure and the solidity of the paper harmonize perfectly with the age of a quarter century. Always, when I open the paper, even if one does not know of its venerable age, one also feels that it has many years of serious work behind it. A kind of dignity, a [uncertain word], acquired only through years of experience. How quiet and sure is the path of an experienced, serious person.
Twenty-five years of publishing a weekly in a provincial town, without interruption, amid the greatest difficulties —
And such a weekly — solidity itself, full of decency and piety toward the printed Jewish word, clean, courageous and honest —
Twenty-five years of standing guard over such a Jewish centre as Zagłębie, reacting to all Jewish phenomena, and reacting with dignity, as dictated by honest journalistic responsibility, never [selling?] its journalistic conscience, but serving it faithfully and earnestly —
Twenty-five years of guiding, by word and script, the communal Jewish life of Zagłębie —
the head bows[?] with great reverence.
•
And always, when I open the paper, I seem to see from between the lines the solid, earnest mind of its editor, the esteemed and dear comrade L. Szpigelman.
Words of praise in the columns of a newspaper amount to “praising a man to his face” (shivḥo be-fanav), so I must content myself with “a part of his praise”... It is perhaps not in the modest tone of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” to praise itself. [Sooner?] or later, though, I cannot hold back — the truth one may say and must say — even to one's own... editor.
Does he at least know, the quiet, solid, all-too-modest comrade, what work he has done?
Well yes, with us one is not used to appreciating such work. Thanks and recognition seldom fall to the journalist's lot. We are all “unknown soldiers”, brick-carriers of the great edifice called Jewish public opinion. The only thanks is the awareness: twenty-five years of hard and toilsome work, honestly carrying out the mission.
Do you think many journalists can boast of that? — there with you in the provinces one may think so...
And the good-natured Jewish humour of comrade Szaja Lewkowicz, which holds so much of Będzin's genial Jewish folk humour? And the same earnest attitude to the printed word?
Every issue of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” bears witness to it.
• • •
And one longs all the more for the quiet, simple and honest milieu when one finds oneself in the cauldron of the big city, on whose journalistic bottom there is so much... well, why speak slander?
Every issue of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” brings me a greeting from that genial, simple Będzin honesty.
And I always see the Jews of Będzin, the “amkha” (common folk), which has no equal in any town for its good nature and warm-heartedness; the yearning[?] Będzin intellectual, the yearning Będzin Hasidic Jew, as they sit over their “Zaglembier Tsaytung”, reading the news and the local journalistic articles, feeling that they have before them their friend, who argues out with them all the problems that interest them, takes up their grievances, stands guard over their common interests — and together with those Jews one feels a reverence for this sincere friend.
Do you have many such oases in the great and desolate desert all around? Perhaps it is called foolishness[?], the decent Jews of Zagłębie. How desolate is the desert of the public Jewish word, how many demons and [evil?] spirits dance about there!
• • •
Twenty-five years of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” — a modest, uncelebrated holiday. How modest are the 25 years of activity, of hard and responsible work.
Twenty-five years of Zagłębie Jewish history, written with the help of the editors, are preserved in these pages.
Perhaps at the fiftieth jubilee the times will be better, spirits more cheerful, and society's attitude to such work will be as it should be, and then Jewish Zagłębie will celebrate the true holiday.
This is my blessing, and also the blessing of all the readers.
“Z Nowym Rokiem” [Polish: “Happy New Year!”]. (A monologue)

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton for the civil New Year; municipality, kehilla, taxes.] (A monologue)
First let me introduce myself to you: Getzil son of Yankl, unemployed, without a piece of coal at home, so I would rather knock about the streets. I heard that our Jewish public figures, especially the “elected” city councillors [“Ratmener”] of the “Jewish Koło” [Koło Żydowskie — the Jewish caucus in the city council], are getting ready to greet all their “lords” very warmly and heartily in honour of the New Year, to thank them for the great favours the Jews of Będzin have enjoyed from them until now, and to “express the hope” that in future too they will do only good — so I addressed [?] these “fighters for Jewish honour” in the following words:
— Hear me out, gentlemen! Why should each of you run, like a lackey, to make the distinction, and outbid one another in flattering phrases? Better hire me wholesale [“in hurt” — Polish hurtem], and I will sing the “Ma yofis” song in perfect time, so that an unemployed Jew will earn something too, as the verse says: “that thy brother may live with thee”... Well, whether they hire me or not — I have no time to wait, “Nowy Rok” [Polish: the New Year] is already behind the door and I am setting off on my way; I can only give you, in brief, my [“fershrut” — reading uncertain; apparently: plan].
First of all I dashed over to our first master-of-the-house [?], in whose hands lie the municipal assets together with the deficit. I addressed him with this speech of greeting:
— Honoured Sir! You have been here only a short time, but your favours to Jewish Będzin are already quite great. All the charitable [?] things, such as a building for a school, sports grounds and gardens for children to play in, you hand over to that district which is almost “Judenrein” [free of Jews]; don’t take to heart what evil tongues say, that you need [?] to be at peace with the P.P.S. [Polish Socialist Party] and therefore push your whole “savings capital” into the rayon [district] of the street workers. The “Koło” told me explicitly that this is why you don’t set up any sports ground in the Jewish district — so that Jews, God forbid, should not overexert themselves and, heaven forbid, break a leg... And what, playgrounds for children? — Jewish children must learn Torah and not play.
By the way, there I met the tone-setter of the city council, and the chief matchmaker of the “Łaźnik” [?] flirting with “Pani Doktorowa” [Mrs. Doctor], and I wished him to become, with good luck, a Sejm deputy, God willing, in... a hundred and twenty years’ time.
After that I went in to the “hearty” director of the power station [elektrownia] and congratulated him on his great “success”: that by today’s New Year the power station is almost “Judenrein”; even a single Jewish bill-collector [inkasent], who used to run about the whole town for a whole month, is superfluous too — truly a pity for a Jew to have to run about the streets and work hard in the frost, when he could better travel to Palestine and enjoy the warmth in the middle of Shevat. And what more shall I wish you, [“harenyu” — my dear?]? — May all the good be fulfilled for you too that all Israel wishes you for your kindnesses and your good heart..
From there I ran to the head of the tax office (believe me [?], what a walk! but did I have a choice?). When I came in, everything went dark before my eyes! None of the “old acquaintances” is there. All of them have melted away [?], scattered to other places; oy, I had nobody to greet. Suddenly I catch sight of the head; I bowed deeply and said: I know that the world stands on three things: money, money and money; I know that for our state to be strong one needs money — and what shall I wish you? — That you fulfil your duty honestly. May we be in your eyes like.. cows that are milked, and not like cows that are slaughtered.. Believe me: a slaughtered cow can no longer be milked. Do widzenia [Polish: goodbye] — —
Having got through the several visits to the righteous gentiles, I remembered that we have, thank God, our own Jewish “self-government”; and although our New Year was already three and a half months earlier, our Rosh Hashana is only for “who shall live and who shall die” [printed “mi yikhit u-mi yamit”], whereas for paying the budget [etat] and for losing the subsidies not collected, the gentile New Year is what counts. So I give the head of the kehilla my broad “sholem aleykhem” and deliver my sermon: — Panie Prezesie [Mr. Chairman]! What shall I wish you? That I and my like don’t have a few pieces of coal to warm our bones? Well then [“veyns” — Polish więc?], since that is so, what [“she” — Polish że] can I wish you?..
So much for the congratulations [“vinshevanyes”] for all our Jewish institutions; as for the “Kokh-lefl” [the humour column “Der Kokh-lefl”], the permanent jester of the editorial staff will no doubt compile them in his own style [?]. As for me, you understand me: I had to hurry to get a ticket to the “Sylvester ball” for my grown-up daughter. “Sweet Daddy,” — she ordered me — “you bring me a ticket to the ball, and a match I’ll find there myself.”
Overheard by
Knaknisl [“Nutcracker”].
Heard and Seen.

[By Ben Amotz.]
The kehilla platform...
At a budget session of the Będzin kehilla council.
On the right sit the parnassim of "Agudah"; on the left, the national "Front"; in the middle, the non-partisans, or more precisely the "farkhene" [?], those who still stand at the crossroads and cast "glances" at whoever offers better concessions...
But our task this time is not to delve into some "lofty matters", or, as the vice-president calls it, "gemoynekhts" [?]. We only want to state that, although we are already on the eve of kehilla elections and the kehilla councils of the neighbouring towns hardly exist any more on the bright side, ours, the Będzin kehilla council, is still "in the spheres" [?], in the same "golden age" as at the beginning; no sign of old age can be seen in it, of nullity, of good-for-nothingness, but it is full of "verdins" [?]. Momentum, and, as the yekke says:
— "Donnerwetter!"
And what didn't we hear at the budget session?
— Historical treatises, the power of the "tsaytn" [?] international, Bible lessons, education exams and territorial-psychological, Agudist-national research, etc. [?]
— "To whom does the kehilla president belong?"
In plain language:
— "Who made him?"
— An interesting analysis.
And very interesting on this question was the "personal" (osobiste) statement of the honoured president himself. "I don't deny," he said, "that I was born on a platform-wagon harnessed by the Tsḥy" [?], but when I arrived at a certain station I said: stop! I'm no longer riding in the 'Tsḥy team' [?]..." Clear, sincere words; but the side with which the president has fallen out has this complaint against him: why did the president, with whom they are very close in-laws, take on to the platform, without their consent, several passengers they did not want, for example a few shochtim, a three-quarter rabbi and plain errand-runners, who graze at the kehilla trough...
And therefore we declare our solidarity with the Agudah faction and together with them we express our recognition to the esteemed president, thanks to whom it has become clear to us that besides a kehilla wagon, a "mkoḥe" [?], the Będzin kehilla also possesses
— a kehilla platform...

The "secret" has been revealed...
— A dim-witted question.
— What reasons caused the Sosnowiec kehilla cashier ("kosiser") suddenly to fall out with Rabbi Schwarz and to create a rabbinate?
After all it was clear to everyone how hot were the friendship and love that reigned between Rabbi Schwarz and the kehilla cashier; like a devoted father the cashier acted towards Rabbi Schwarz, and even stood on guard so that not one single oven, God forbid, should be koshered for Passover by another rabbi; he "forbade" the marriages that another rabbi had performed. So what happened? That the great protector should do Rabbi Schwarz in "Turkish fashion" [?], seat several of the kley-koydesh (religious functionaries) in the kehilla premises and give them the title:
— Rabbinate!
— And a real "Ma nishtana"?!
This hard question was asked by the non-partisan side of the Sosnowiec kehilla, those who stand at a distance and waited for an answer.
And the answer was given in "Saki" [?] by a member of the kehilla nominees, who lifted a little the backstage curtain of the commissarial kehilla administration. By the light "of the lifted curtain" we saw how a session takes place at which the commissioner "kert" [?] wants a well-known young man, a member of the shochtim family, to be taken on as a Sosnowiec shochet (concerning this candidate, negotiations about the post took place at the time before the commissarial kehilla. Why did they want to remove a big "goren" [?]...).
But Rabbi Schwarz will not agree to this conception. "I cannot," he shouted, "in my old age give my consent that such a young man should already become a Sosnowiec shochet."
— "But such is my will," thundered the commissioner's voice, "how dare you resist me?!"
— "True indeed, it is true, Panie Prezesie. That you were my right hand, protected me from all evil, handed me the registration books, all the ovens to kosher, all the weddings, took me with you everywhere you delivered your 'spirit-rich' sermons; but what you demand of me, that I give my consent, that I cannot, I will not, as a rabbi of many years, take upon myself such a kashrut responsibility. No, my lord commissioner."
And then the same happened as with King Ahasuerus when Vashti refused to obey the king's command: "and the commissioner was very wroth"; the commissioner became very angry and asked his counsellors what to do?
And the counsellors answered that Rabbi Schwarz had not only rebelled against the king himself, but had insulted all the nominees, and one must [?] take revenge on him.
And the revenge is almost the same as in the Scroll of Esther; the only difference is that in Persia and Media a command went out "that every man should bear rule in his own house", and in Sosnowiec it was decided
— to found a rabbinate...
— The "secret" has been revealed...
Mendele Moykher Sforim

[Częstochowa — literature and language; essay, chapter 1.] P. Blumenkranc (Częstochowa).
A. Mendele and Yiddish.
A people's attitude to its own language is, as is known, a consequence of the spiritual state of that people in the given period.
When a people finds itself at a low ebb, and especially when it is politically oppressed, it is for the most part dominated by a feeling of inferiority; it stops believing in its own strength, in its own creative power, and begins in every field to imitate the stronger one.
The Russians, in their time of spiritual lowliness, yearned [?] for French. The criterion of refinement, of social maturity, was the French language. One was not a complete person, by the notion of the day, in this language [sic; presumably "without this language"], in which one had to "parlez" in the salons. The Germans, too, once held their own language cheap. Connoisseurs considered it a hard, inelastic language fit for the masses, because tenderness and subtle nuances — so they held — were possessed only by French. And even people who stood at the head of the German state created in French...
We Jews, plagued and tormented, driven from one country to another, learned to change languages often. Alongside Hebrew, which became the liturgical language, we created in Greek and spoke Aramaic, created in Arabic and spoke Spaniolish [Ladino], and so on continually, in parallel with changing countries.
The Jews, adapting quickly to those around them, were dazzled by the glitter of the foreign and wrote, in their gallop of imitation (sometimes also for the sake of usefulness), even musar books in foreign tongues — such books that pious Jews of today go to immerse themselves in the mikveh before approaching them...
* * *
But if the process of imitation has lasted among Jews for thousands of years, it grew much stronger in the Haskalah period. The "Ḥovat Ḥivavot" [sic; i.e. Ḥovot ha-Levavot] was written in Arabic for popularisation, the Guide for the Perplexed was written in Arabic so that it would be understood by certain circles, and Maimonides rejoiced on learning that his book was being translated into Hebrew. In a word: the vernacular was used for reasons of convenience or utility. The maskilim, on the other hand, believed that by speaking Russian or by [studying? — printed "lfun"] German in the [?] schools, the Jewish question would be solved.
And hence — the hatred of the folk language, which incidentally was not polished at the time, and hence the disdain for Yiddish, which reached the point of contempt. And even those who wrote Yiddish together with Russian divided their muse: about ideal matters they wrote in Russian, and about plain, everyday ones — in Yiddish.
We see, for example, how the gifted Frug complains about his writing in Yiddish:
"With my last tooth
I have bitten and torn the jargon,
chewed the beloved language of our mothers,
peppered it with caesura, salted it with rhymes,
to make them at least a little soft
and to stifle their smell
of the Vilna market and Tsigabur [?] butcher stalls,
with all kinds of trampled leftovers,
which stinks thirteen miles from the place
wherever even one jargon word glows."
Herein lies Mendele's great deed! Although he too could not leap out of his era and wrote Yiddish for utilitarian purposes, he nevertheless, with his artistic sense, reshaped [?] the folk language and gave it a respectable face.
Mendele even apologises that by starting to write Yiddish he is raising [?] public opinion against himself", but this great folk artist, because of his inner relation to his creative work, began to polish the language and gave it, etc. ["a.m."], an artistic correction.
And out of a language which Frug compares "to an old granny [?] in a torn, gnawed quilted jacket [?], in all sorts of strange colours", there grew, thanks to the Grandfather [Mendele, "der Zeyde"], a language in which generations create joys [?], a language in which both rigorous scholars and subtle poets create, a language in which both an encyclopaedia of European scale and refined lyric poetry are written.
The second chapter, entitled "Mendele and Nature", in the next issue.

Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Vayigash

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the Torah portion of this week. Collected and styled by Yehuda.

Parashat Vayigash

a) "And let not thine anger burn" (Gen. 44:18)
"From here you learn that he spoke harshly to him." Rashi.
As long as Judah thought that he too would be arrested, he did not dare speak harshly to Joseph. Only when Joseph told them "and as for you, go up in peace" and only Benjamin remained, did he begin to speak sternly — because on behalf of someone else one always has more boldness to demand.
Imrei Chen.
• • •
When the congregation says the Shemoneh Esreh it is said quietly, in a whisper, and when the cantor repeats the Shemoneh Esreh it is said aloud. Why is this so?
Because when one comes to ask for oneself one is not bold, one can barely get the request out of one's mouth, therefore one prays in a whisper; whereas the cantor — he after all asks on behalf of the congregation, so he is bold and demands out loud...
Rabbi Yerachmiel Yisrael Yitzchak of Aleksander [Aleksandrów Łódzki].

b) "Cause every man to go out from me" (Gen. 45:1)
Joseph had accounts to settle with his brothers, but he did not want to carry the internal quarrels out before the world; the gentiles need not know what goes on between Joseph and the brothers. This Joseph already understood — unfortunately, today among us it is not understood.
Kinyanei Kim [?].

c) "Doth my father yet live? And his brethren could not answer him" (Gen. 45:3)
"Woe to us from the Day of Judgment. Joseph was the youngest of the tribes, and his brothers could not withstand his rebuke; when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes and rebukes each person according to what he is — how much more so..." Midrash.
"And rebukes each person according to what he is" — I will not be flogged, Rabbi Meir'l of Premishlan [Przemyślany] used to say, for not being as great as Moses our teacher; after all, a Meir cannot be a Moses. I will be flogged only because I was not even a Meir — and a Meir I surely could have been.
• • •
"Many did as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and did not succeed" — because they wanted to I-M-I-T-A-T-E Rabbi Shimon: "they did as Rabbi Shimon". They were not on that level, and they wanted to copy, to imitate...
Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov.

d) "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt" (Gen. 45:4)
In the whole dispute that Joseph conducted with his brothers, he did not merely intend to provoke them a little; he actually wanted to show them that suspicions lead a person astray. After all, their whole hatred of him had fed on suspicions. So he showed them that suspicions can sometimes add up in such a way that a person's supposed guilt becomes clear to everyone. Here they themselves, by their conduct, had given enough material to suspect them of espionage — by entering through ten gates, by entangling themselves in the story of the lost brother. Their "guilt" was clear to every judge, and yet afterwards there was nothing to it at all.
"I am Joseph whom ye sold into Egypt" — because of foolish suspicions you sold me into Egypt, and therefore you too suffered under suspicion of espionage.
Ta'ama de-Kra.

e) "And Benjamin wept upon his neck" (Gen. 45:14)
"For the Tabernacle of Shiloh, which was destined to be in Joseph's portion and to be destroyed in the end." Rashi.
Rabbi Zeira enumerates (in Tractate Ta'anit, folio 20) among his own virtues also this one: "and I did not rejoice at my fellow's stumbling" — I did not rejoice when my fellow stumbled. One asks: is that something to boast about?
But the plain meaning is: "and I did not rejoice" — I did not want any joy "at my fellow's stumbling" — when I knew that my joy rested on my fellow's stumbling, on his failure, such joy I renounced...
So too Benjamin renounced his good fortune — that the Temple was to be built in his portion — because first the Tabernacle of Shiloh, which stands in Joseph's portion, would have to be destroyed...
Rabbi Yitzchak'l of Warka [Warka].

f) "Now let me die, since I have seen thy face" (Gen. 46:30)
If from such a tragic-evil thing — the selling of one's own brother — such good could come out, then there is no longer any absolutely evil thing. "Now let me die" — then death too need not be absolutely bad...
R' Yitzchak Eliyahu Landau.

g) "And Jacob blessed Pharaoh" (Gen. 47:7) [?]
"And what blessing did he bless him with — that the Nile should rise to meet his feet, since Egypt does not drink rain water but the Nile rises and irrigates; and from Jacob's blessing onward Pharaoh would come to the Nile and it would rise towards him and irrigate the land." Rashi.
From where does Rashi derive from the verse that this is how Jacob blessed Pharaoh? How is this hinted at in the verse? But Rashi's intention is different:
As is known, Pharaoh regarded himself as a god because the Nile came to him — after Jacob's blessing. So says the Midrash.
This is what Rashi means: "What blessing did he bless him with?" — what kind of blessing did Jacob give Pharaoh? "That the Nile should rise" etc. Pharaoh after all considered himself a complete god, and what can one wish a god?..
To this Rashi answers: "and from Jacob's blessing onward Pharaoh would come to the Nile" — the fact that Pharaoh began to consider himself a god dated only from Jacob's blessing. Before that he did not consider himself a god, and so Jacob could then wish him what he was not [yet] [?].
Bekhor Shor.

On your victory in the match "Tenant" vs. "Landlord" (gospodarz)!

Khatskele Klbunik is giving tongue again

Well, lads, how do I look, eh? [?] After the [—], did anything [—] me? Nothing!
Oy, [listen?]: I ate, I stuffed myself, I ate [—], [—] and [—] like lords (panie), like all the rich men.. Money they don't send to Podzamcze [?], but if, God forbid, a sickness befalls them, they send it as a kapore (scapegoat) [?] into Podzamcze lane.
You think I've already [croaked?] — [—] may I be sick! I got out of bed because I had [?] to see to the coal action. Straight from bed I went to the kehilla, [—] from the [?] of the president (prezes) about the coal action for our lads.
I went straight in to the president, Reb Lewer [?], and said thus:
— Reb Lewer, what, will one be buying a bit of coal [for us]?
The president stroked his belly and asked me:
— What's your name?
— Khatskele Klbunik is my name, on the "Vshimne" [?] that's what they call me; I am the representative of all the Będzin lads, so I've come to register them for the coal action.
The president heard me out and finally said thus:
— A gabbai (meaning: a gabbai) of a beys-medresh has to come, or a president of an association.
So I got nervous and said thus:
— Reb Lewer, don't bang a teakettle (don't talk nonsense), don't take me for [—] [?]; I understand all these tricks; I'm no gabbai and no president of an association, I represent Podzamcze lane, and basta.
Do you think Reb Lewer was frightened [—] [?] at what he had done? He pressed a button and in came a fellow with a pair of healthy "spoons" (hands) and gave me a [shove?] down — may a calamity come upon all the rich men together with the kehilla [?].
In short, from the kehilla we'll get [—] with radishes [i.e. nothing; ?]; we really must already go over to our own coal action; I'm taking myself to the [tools?] [?].

A little letter from Zakopane

Dearest Shimshe Gerile!
You did quite well, Shimshele my crown, not to come to Zakopane for Sylvester, because I made merry the whole night, and the Gemara says: one does not mix one celebration with another...
Listen, Shimsheletshku, things got rather lively on the Sylvester holiday: it was [—] [?], and who do you think celebrated holy Sylvester? Imagine (wyobraź sobie) — there was all in all one gentile, the caretaker (woźny) of the hall; the rest — the very cream (śmietanka) of Podzamcze street. When it struck 12 at night the lamps were turned down, not for one minute as the gentiles do, but for a whole hour.
I thought of you, Shimshele my crown, in that darkness. The wails and the cries went up to the heart of heaven; people fell like flies, one on top of another, like cut stalks, and as they say, many got engaged [?]. [Hoping] to hear the [pleasant?] [?] from you ever and always.
From me, your faithful
Beyle Gendl, Villa "Gustawa" [?].

The Bastard (68) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishkovski

[Serial novel — instalment 68]
“Leon!” she cries out inwardly. “My poor child!”
“Balbina,” she runs up to Balbina, “we must help him, we must save him. I am sure that without you he cannot live. For all [?] that has happened, I am to blame; I committed a crime against him by separating you, and so made him unhappy, and now I must commit a crime again in order to bring you together and see him happy. Yes, Balbina, it seems such is my fate — always to remain a criminal...”
“What do you intend to do?” asks Balbina, frightened, starting up from her place.
“Balbina, Leon must not know at all that the child is not his; he must not know that his child was born dead, do you hear? It is his child, his...”
“But...” asks Balbina, and does not finish her question.
“Nothing... do you hear, Balbina! That is how it must be. True, it is very sad, but often in life one gives the sick man a bitter medicine so that he may get well. Yes, it is a bitter medicine, very bitter, but he will be happy, and that is needed even more [?]! Balbina, I beg you, rely on me; I will always be with you, and if I was able to do evil, I will be able to make everything good. You must go to Warsaw now; I will give you his address, and you must bring him to Berlin. My sister will travel with you, because, as I have already told you, I must not show myself in Poland.
“You will tell your mother that you have to go to Warsaw for a few days. Will you do it? Yes, Balbina? You will do it for Leon, who loves you, who pines after your every step. You will do it, Balbina, I implore you...”
“Look how you look! Balbina, what has happened?” Max asked her when she came into the house.
“Max! The curse is pursuing me,” Balbina burst into tears, “the curse of my husband's [?] youth [?].”
“But, my dear, what has happened?” he asks, alarmed at hearing her words.
“Max, I have to go to Warsaw for a few days, and when I come back I will tell you everything.”
“Has something bad happened to your relatives in Poland?”
“Don't ask me now; later, when I come back...”
“Perhaps I should go with you?” he asks.
“No, I will go alone; you stay at home and look after the child.”
“But calm yourself, my dear, everything will be all right,” and he kissed her beautiful, curly blond head.
And the next day Max accompanied Balbina to the [?] station, from where she left for Warsaw together with Louise Morgenstern, Matilda's sister.
And Balbina did not sense that at that very moment, as her train moved off, the train from Warsaw pulled in at the platform opposite, and in it sat three of her acquaintances — Leon, and Moshele with his mother.
Chapter 23.
The great steamer “Helvetia” glided with the greatest speed over the waters of the ocean, hurrying to reach New York harbour sooner.
On the command bridge stood the ship's captain, John Aslen [?], holding in his gold-adorned mouth his pipe, from which smoke drew out in long, winding blue strings.
Three more days remained before the ship would drop anchor in New York harbour, where his faithful Ruth would surely be waiting for him with his little Charlie — so he reckoned, looking at the mile-gauge, which shows how many miles the ship has already covered.
On the second-class deck the passengers lay in the deck chairs, warming themselves in the rays of the sun, which caressed their bodies, worn out by seasickness.
“How do you feel today, Rachel?” Moshele asks her; he had not suffered so badly from seasickness.
“Today I already feel very well,” she answers with a smile, stroking his white, delicate hand, which rested on the armrest of the long deck chair.
“And you, Mamenyu, do you feel better today?” he asks Helen, whose face bore witness that the illness had exhausted her.
“Today I no longer feel bad,” she answers in a weak voice.
“Perhaps you will allow me to go for half an hour to our Warsaw acquaintance and see how he is doing?” he asks again. “He suffered very much from seasickness, I was told.”
“Go, go, Moritz [?],” says Rachel, “and if he does not feel bad, bring him here to us.”
In truth, however, Moshele did not go to Leon on account of his illness; rather, all this time he had not had the opportunity to speak with him about the woman in the picture which he had shown her [?] in the railway carriage — and it was not the woman who concerned him, but his father, who had been, and perhaps still is, her husband, about whom he wanted to learn every detail of his life; and that was the most important thing that interested him.

Protest of the Będzin Kehilla Council Against the Legislative Council in the Land of Israel

[Będzin — kehilla.]
Kehilla budget at the council plenum. — Sharp incident between the chairman and the president of the board. — The session is adjourned.
On Sunday afternoon the kehilla council in Będzin held a session. On the agenda — the kehilla budget for 1936. Present — almost the entire board with the president at its head, all the councillors (except the Revisionist councillor, who, probably to stay on good terms with both sides — the “Agudah” and the National faction — did not come to the session) and a “rich gallery.”
The session lasted 4 hours, but the agenda was never reached. The several hours were frittered away [?] on speeches, mutual quips [?] (connoisseurs call it “word play” [?]) and discussions on socio-economic problems.
—
The session opens with a report by the president, Mr. G. [?] Landner, on the general Jewish situation then and now, the dream of conquering the kehillot and the sad reality, and the disregard of the Będzin kehilla board for the council.
“Sain” [?] — says Mr. Landner — the board has committed an evil deed, which is the first case in Poland. The board sent the supplementary budget for 1935 for approval without the council's consent, thanks to which 5 new officials were “smuggled in”...
Then councillor Ryński [?] (Agudah) and others present a protest against the decree of the Legislative Council in the Land of Israel. The protest is adopted unanimously.
President Rubinlicht contents himself [?] with the exchange of letters between the board and the former president of the council, Mr. Kurland, and rejects Mr. Landner's accusation against the board. Mr. L. does not want to remain in debt, and he “upholds” the accusation. On this ground a sharp incident arises between the two presidents, from which the Agudah faction derives much delight...
On this question councillors Herszlewicz and Rozynkier [?] speak; the latter accuses Mr. Rubinlicht that, although he was elected by the Zionists, he betrays Zionist interests in the kehilla.
To this Mr. Rubinlicht replies that he was elected from the Economic National list, which had a common platform, and on this “platform” he travelled as far as a certain station...
Councillor Kornfeld addresses the board with an interpellation: has the board reacted in any way to the Endek anti-Jewish outbreaks that have taken place in the Zagłębie area? To this Mr. Rubinlicht declares that he will give an answer on the matter at the next session.
Only after two and a half hours of killing time does the chairman declare the session open; he speaks out in favour of carrying out cuts in the budget and at the same time reducing the staff establishment. Enough already — says Mr. Landner — of playing at fictitious budgets which in the end are later cut by the authorities.
Councillor Kornfeld is against Mr. Landner's proposal. From the staff cuts — says Mr. K. — the poor masses will not benefit in any case, only the well-to-do taxpayers. The board has no initiative whatsoever in the face of the great want and misery that reign in the Jewish street, and protects only the interests of the bourgeoisie.
After the “heated” discussion on all the questions that stand at the summit of the world, they finally get down to the actual question, the budget — but here the National faction brings in a motion that, since the councillors are already exhausted, the session should be adjourned.
Councillor Ryński brings in a motion to adopt the budget en bloc. The motion fails; instead the first motion is adopted and the session is adjourned.
A Sosnowiec Halutz Killed in the Land of Israel

[Sosnowiec — Land of Israel, aliyah.]
Already the fifth victim from Zagłębie.
Last week we received news that on the road from Tel Aviv to Jaffa the 21-year-old Szmul (Shmuel) Steinfeld of Sosnowiec, brother of the president of the Sosnowiec “Mizrachi,” Mr. Icchak (Yitzhak) Steinfeld, was killed. For certain reasons we did not bring the news in the last issue.
The terrible accident happened under the following circumstances: Steinfeld was riding a bicycle from Tel Aviv to Jaffa, where he worked in a manufactured-goods (textile) shop. On the way he collided with a cart, received a heavy blow from it and fell. In an unconscious state he was at once taken to the “Hadassah” hospital, where he died an hour later.
This is already the fifth victim among the Zagłębie olim (immigrants to the Land of Israel).
A Cantor Hired for the Beth Midrash

[Zagłębie — beth midrash, cantorate.]
These days the beth midrash committee held a session at which the question of hiring a cantor (hazzan) was also dealt with. Mr. S. Fürstenberg also took part in the session and proposed that Mr. Baum be engaged as cantor.
Mr. Fürstenberg's proposal was accepted by the committee.
“Let the Cantor Shorten the Prayers, or Let the Cholent Be Taken Out an Hour Later”...

[Będzin — synagogue.] The question must be decided by the Będzin synagogue committee.
We have already written many times about the lawlessness prevailing in the Będzin synagogue, but what happened last Sabbath during prayers absolutely must not be tolerated, and the so-called synagogue committee must give thought to the question and take proper measures so that such a thing does not recur.
The first scandal broke out before the Shema, when a member of the committee carried out an “eviction” (eksmisja) of a young man who had dared to stand on the bimah.
The second scandal — during the Torah reading one of the worshippers quarrelled with the gabbai, because the latter did not want to honour his son with a “fat” aliyah. But the “most interesting” thing happened at the Kedushah of Musaf.
In honour of Shabbat Hanukkah the cantor wanted to draw out the Kedushah, but as soon as he began to sing he was at once interrupted by the “hungry” worshippers, who, watches in hand, showed the cantor that “it is already late”...
This behaviour aroused great agitation among the worshippers and an ugly scandal broke out.
As we are informed, the synagogue committee, in connection with the latest scandal, is to take up the question “whether the cantor should shorten [the prayers], or the cholent should be taken out an hour later than until now”...
If Not a Merger, Let There at Least Be Friendly Relations Between the Merchants’ Associations.

[Merchants — organisation.] So demands the Central Merchants’ Union.
As we have already written, a few weeks ago a Main Council was created in Warsaw, in which are represented delegates of the merchants’ and small traders’ central bodies and presidents of the merchants’ associations in the provinces; among others also the president of the Sosnowiec Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Association, Mr. Józef Safer, who also holds the post of secretary.
The main task of the council is to create mergers of the merchants’ and small traders’ associations in the provinces, which are being called upon to do so.
At the Sunday [?] meeting of the board of the merchants’ association, the council’s call was discussed, which proposes creating the merger, or if not, that there should at least prevail friendly relations between the two associations.
In connection with this a commission was elected, which is to undertake the realisation of the project.
Cheaper Tram Tickets.

[Sosnowiec — transport.] Since Wednesday the fare for tram tickets on the stretch from Sosnowiec to Dąbrowa and Czeladź has become cheaper. Instead of 65 it now costs only 55 groszy. The fare on the city line has also become cheaper, so that from Huta Milowice to “Akshpi” [?] Street in Sosnowiec one can ride for 20 groszy.

Czeladź Women “See” a Dead Man Strolling in the Street.

[Czeladź — rumours.] Among the inhabitants of Czeladź a rumour has lately spread that one of the Czeladź residents who died not long ago takes a stroll every day late at night along the empty and barely lit [?] Parkowa Street.
Of course, first of all nobody believed this foolish rumour as devoutly as the women. And of course women were soon found who had even seen the dead man strolling with their own eyes in the middle of the night.
One can well imagine that, as far as I know [?], nobody in Czeladź any longer dares to walk along the said Parkowa Street late in the evening. As for the women, there is nothing to say. Not one of them dares to go out alone at all onto that “dead” street, unless it is one who still knows nothing at all about the whole story of the dead man...
There were even some “bold” women who took up position and waited together for the dead man, and they “saw” him and afterwards even told the town exact details about him: that the dead man is dressed like a living person, wears trousers and boots...

A strong “revival” in the “divorce season”

[Będzin — rabbinate and family life.] We thought the crisis had already gripped almost all branches. It turns out that there are still plenty of “seasonal articles” on which not only does the crisis have no influence at all, but on the contrary — production keeps growing.
Thus, for example, a strong “revival” now prevails in the “divorce (get) season”. The rabbinical court (beit din) of the Będzin rabbinate was full this week of “interested parties” from Zagłębie. Among the “interested parties” was a gang of wild [?] youths from Sosnowiec, who tried to force the rabbinate by violence to grant a divorce free of charge to a couple from their “[—]” [?].
In the course of the week 7 couples received a get (divorce). Among them was a “faithful husband” who, for the favour of giving his wife a divorce, took 50 zł. as “odstępne” (compensation money) from her. Otherwise he did not want to give it to her, and threatened that he would go back to his Będzin mistress (kochanka).
Anti-Jewish Outrages

[Page banner:] "Life in Kielce" — Friday, 8 Tevet 5696 — piątek 3 stycznia 1936 [Friday, 3 January 1936].
There is no end to the Endek attacks on the Jewish shops in Kielce. These incessant acts of terror are taking on a catastrophic character. Hardly two or three days go by without a stink bomb being thrown in, or the windows being smashed, in one Jewish shop or another.
On Saturday night a stink bomb was again thrown into the largest delicatessen shop, that of Mr. Hirszel Mincz. Because of the suffocating smell a large part of the goods, worth over [—] thousand zł., was destroyed.
This is already the second act of terror against Mincz's shop. Some months ago a stink bomb was thrown into it. At that time the hooligan was arrested, but what became of him nobody knows. In any case, nothing was heard of his having been punished.
The same evening, on Piotrkowska Street, the vice-president of the Kielce branch of "Halutz Ba'al Melakha", Mr. Yehoshua Wagszajn[?], was attacked by Endek hooligans. The hooligans struck him over the head with an iron bar and wounded him badly.
On Monday, at 9 in the evening, the large shop-window pane of the drapery (manufaktura) shop of the well-known firm Jakub Balicki was again smashed. Balicki's son and his neighbour Mr. Motl Kager[?] immediately ran out into the street, seized the thrower and handed him over to the police. According to them, this is the 21-year-old pupil of the local commercial school, a certain Bus, who was taken to the police station. A search was made at his parents' home and at his father Kazimierz's a revolver was found, for which he had no permit. After a short interrogation at the police, young Bus was released.
A Jewish delegation headed by Rabbi R' Rapaport this week visited the Kielce starosta, Mr. Porębalski[?], and informed him about the events, which have caused great damage, particularly to the grocery (colonial goods), fruit and sugar shops.
The starosta declared to the Jewish delegation that he had issued the appropriate orders and that measures had been taken so that these regrettable incidents should not recur, and that the guilty would in any case be severely punished.
This week there was also an urgent consultation of a number of Jewish public figures, at which it was decided that a delegation should present itself to the Kielce voivode, Dr. Dziadosz, to whom they will hand a detailed memorandum on the security situation of the Kielce Jews.
Kielce Mohalim Refuse to Circumcise a Jewish Child

We have been informed of an unheard-of fact that occurred here in our town through the local mohalim (circumcisers), who did not want to circumcise a Jewish child; and had it not been for the energetic intervention of the local rabbi, Rabbi Rapaport, with a visiting mohel who happened to be staying in Kielce, the child would not have been circumcised.
The facts are as follows: at the home of a certain Aharon Rajzman of Masłów[?], a village near Kielce, a brit was to take place last Sabbath. The father came to Kielce for this purpose and began running around to the mohalim, asking them to travel out with him on the Sabbath to the brit, but none of them wanted to go with him, wriggling out with various excuses. Especially since the father is a Jew, a poor man, and was not able to give any "honorarium"...
The father, at his wits' end, turned to the local rabbi, Rabbi Rapaport, with the request that he prevail upon the mohalim so that one of them would after all travel out with him to circumcise the child.
Even the "official" mohel, who already takes money for circumcising, did not want to go, and did not care at all that a Jewish child would not be circumcised on time.
Finally, on Friday afternoon, the rabbi learned that a visiting mohel happened to be staying in Kielce, R' Reuven Rotszyld of Wierzbnik. The rabbi himself went to R' Yudl Rotszyld's home and told him to have his son travel with the father to the village for the Sabbath.
The mohel obeyed the rabbi and went out to the village for the Sabbath, in order to circumcise the child on time, at 8 days.
The unheard-of conduct of the Kielce mohalim, who did not want to circumcise a Jewish child on time, has caused great indignation in local religious circles.

Lazar Kahan's 50th Jubilee

[Press — jubilee.] The Yiddish literary family is celebrating today, Friday, the 50th jubilee of the editor and writer Mr. Lazar Kahan. The jubilarian began his first journalistic work in the year 1985 [sic] as a contributor to the first Yiddish newspaper in Poland, "Der Veg" ["The Way"]. When "Der Veg" closed down he worked on "Undzer Lebn" ["Our Life"] and "Fraytog" ["Friday"], until at the end of 1907 he was engaged as editor of the "Lodzer Togblat" ["Łódź Daily"]. Later he founded "Undzer Ekspres" ["Our Express"], where to this day he plays the most active role both as editor and as publicist.
The jubilarian also has a rich public activity behind him: he serves as a parnas [community board member], in the Łódź and now in the Warsaw kehilla; he was very active in the revival of the Yiddish theatre, and in this field Mr. Kahan published a whole series of books and weeklies.
Together with the entire Jewish and journalistic family we greet you, esteemed friend, jubilarian, and we wish you length of days.
An Open Letter

[Będzin — polemic; open letter.] To the initiators of the Mendele Committee in Będzin
The Jewish world is now celebrating the 100th anniversary of the creator of modern Yiddish literature and culture — Mendele Moykher Sforim. It is a holiday of all Yiddish-loving and freedom-striving elements of the Jewish people; the holiday must be a mighty popular demonstration for Yiddish, for Yiddish literature and culture, a holiday among all the Jewish masses, among all strata of the Jewish population, a holiday of all people who love the Jewish people — that is how we understood it. But what are the initiators of the Będzin Mendele Committee doing? Instead of inviting all the groups and cultural institutions that stand on the ground of the Yiddish language and culture, instead of making the jubilee a popular holiday, the initiators have made it a party undertaking. Therefore we ask:
1) Why did you not invite all the cultural institutions that have a positive attitude to the Yiddish language, literature and culture?
2) From whom and with whom did you learn the "story" that Mendele Moykher Sforim was a socialist and Marxist, and that a celebration in his honour must be "in a revolutionary socialist Marxist spirit"? Does this correspond to the works and the world-view of Mendele Moykher Sforim? Are Mendele's works not, after all, popular? Was he not a poet of all strata of the Jewish population, except for the small handful of rich urban tax-paying householders?
3) Do the League [for Labour Palestine], Poale Zion and all the others who take part in the committee know that they are being used by the "Bund" as an object in the struggle against Poale Zion (Ts. S.) [Zionist-Socialists], the League and all other closely allied organisations of Labour Palestine? That the "Bund" means [?] nothing by the whole celebration but to fight against us and to pursue its petty politics?
4) Do the initiators want to make a Mendele academy into a Bundist undertaking?
5) Finally: do the initiators want to be the ones who disturb the Mendele celebrations in our town? Will you allow it that through your politics yet another Mendele committee should be created? If not, then [?] call a conference once more, where all groups of cultural institutions shall be represented, which have a positive attitude to Yiddish literature. What do you say to that? We hold that this is a popular matter. Let the Jewish public of Będzin know who is the disturber of unity in the Mendele celebration. We demand a clear answer from you.
With comradely greetings,
Culture and School Union "Shul-Kult",

Lecture by editor P. Bernstein of Holland.

The Zionist organizations of all trends in Katowice held last Thursday, in the kehilla hall, a lecture by the delegate of the Zionist Executive, editor Bernstein, on the topic "The political, economic and organizational problems in the process of building Eretz Israel".
The chairman, Dr. Rappaport [?], welcomed the guest, explaining that this time the lecture would not be tied to any fund-raising campaign, but devoted exclusively to the discussion of the above-mentioned problems.
Then editor Bernstein began his lecture, in which he dealt mainly with the importance of founding the Zionist territorial federations, in accordance with the resolution of the 19th Zionist Congress; what matters here is not only the organizational link between the separate factions but precisely full harmonious cooperation.
The world reckons with public opinion, despite its weakening in some countries, and that is our greatest strength today. In this connection the speaker mentioned the recent resignation of the English foreign minister Hoare under the pressure of public opinion.
Editor Bernstein touched on the dangers threatening the Zionist movement from separatist tendencies, such as the founding of a separate General Zionist Progressive federation, a separate faction in the KKL for "Maccabi", and the constant mutual distrust among the factions. All this may lead to undesirable results.
The lecturer discussed a further series of important Zionist political and economic problems and ended his lecture. [word unclear] The large audience warmly applauded editor Bernstein and sang "Hatikvah".
Aroy.
