The Middle Class in Poland

L. Szpigelman.
(Yes, economise — but carefully. — The hardship of the middle-class system. — Reduced incomes and increased expenses.)
If we speak of the middle class — only of that category of people who do not live in great „luxury“ (raskosh) — then it has already been said. That their prospects are far[?] from brilliant; their incomes suffice only to keep body and soul together. Fortunes[?] are out of the question; one only wants[?] to manage — at least in a time of crisis — to get by with what one needs, and with that one is already content.
It goes without saying that under such conditions every firm is keenly interested in making the most far-reaching economies, because it often happens that, thanks to a well-calculated economy, the firm stays on its feet. But at the same time one must not forget that making economies is not so easy either: just as it is dangerous for a business to have too many expenses, so it is harmful to want to economise too much. Suppose one removes a person [an employee] or saves on some other significant expense, and afterwards it turns out that by this very act one has touched off the ruin of the business and everything begins to limp — then surely we cannot, in such a case, agree that taking such steps is not risky; certainly they are no less harmful than having too many expenses, too many people. With reductions one must be very, very careful; one must[?] know exactly what one may touch and what must remain guarded with the greatest care.
And yet one is often compelled to make economies in various enterprises, not so much because one supposedly has too many people who do not contribute to the business — no, not that; on the contrary, one needs them, as the saying goes, like a blind man needs an eye — but one simply cannot afford the expense, because the neighbour opposite, who is in the same line of business, insists[?] on being cheaper, since he has smaller expenses, and in the present[?] times one must reckon with that very seriously.
But if we are not to fool ourselves, we must come to the conclusion that this very economy „does not make the merchant's soup any fatter“, and it is highly doubtful whether he gains anything by it. Yes, he saves in one place and in another he suffers a greater loss, because there supervision is lacking and an enormous damage arises, which, however, is not noticed at once.
It is an established fact that the middle class in Poland pays the largest proportion of taxes; the rate (stawka) is immediately higher, and then he often pays what is not his due[?] or what he has already paid once: here he does not have the receipt, and here he cannot defend himself properly. In any case he must first of all pay, if he does not want to be exposed to unpleasantness.
The situation of the citizens who belong to our middle class is very, very serious and highly complicated. At every opportunity our politicians and economists have pointed out that their situation is hopeless and that every tomorrow is veiled in darker colours.
Do we not see a great camp of fallen shadows who go hungry in silence, a large percentage of whom stretch out their hands for a piece of bread? Is this contingent not recruited entirely from the middle class, which formerly maintained itself with dignity? Were these people not broken only because, when they were drowning[?], no one stretched out a hand to save them? Do we not see the very same picture now too? We notice the same pictures even now, only with the difference that today one no longer stops at them: it has become an everyday phenomenon, and like every everyday thing they have grown tiresome and nobody pays attention to them any more.
Can we not point to many firms that lived quite well, and people earned from[?] them, and within a couple of weeks they were broken and collapsed? Is this not a sad reality that takes on ever more terrible forms? May we pass by this terrible phenomenon with indifference?
Yes, the worst of it is that we see no way out that might improve our situation; on the contrary, it gets worse and worse — not because the times are more dangerous, for after all we are used to going with the stream and suffering when there is a necessity — but even that is too little: one keeps inciting against the Jew, making him loathsome in the eyes of the Christian population so that they should not cross any Jewish threshold — and this happens at a time when the situation is becoming harder of itself, when incomes shrink and expenses grow.
Things are getting ever harder for the middle class, because money is becoming dearer, he is more heavily burdened with taxes, the social responsibility has widened — for collecting all kinds of donations for necessary purposes has long ceased to be a [rare] guest in the Jewish home, where one feels for the lonely and the fallen; and then all kinds of commercial premises — i.e. shops, warehouses, workshops — are also leaving tenant protection, so that if such an average family saves a few percent on its private flat, it will have plenty to say and sing about the landlord where it keeps its business premises: knowing that the tenant makes his living there, he will nevertheless[?] want to raise the rent, and if not — he will throw the „divorce“ at his feet and demand that he clear out. For now one does not yet hear of it, but further on this will become an entirely normal, self-evident thing.
As we see, then, the situation of the middle class threatens to become even more dangerous because expenses grow at a time when incomes keep shrinking. And here the question arises: what does one do? How does one crawl out of this blind alley[?]? Making reductions in the enterprise means shrinking it, and once it is shrunk — how will it be possible to draw a livelihood from it? It is on these questions that one must dwell more consciously and consider them from all sides. It goes without saying that one of the most important roles here is played by calculation: one must know where the world stands, how earnings look[?], and then one knows how to manage and in what way to make the reductions and to adjust the enterprise. Besides that there is one more condition which one must remember at every opportunity: to be competitive.
The Campaign Must Be Brought to a Victorious End! (The Million Campaign in Zagłębie)

[Zagłębie — fundraising and relief; editorial.] It is already 5 months since the "Cekabe" [CEKABE, Centrala Kas Bezprocentowych — the Central Office of Interest-Free Loan Funds] [?] began to carry out the Million Campaign in Zagłębie — strictly speaking in Sosnowiec and Będzin. It was reckoned that the campaign should last no longer than a month in each town.
It cannot be denied: work began intensively and quite substantial sums came in, which gave still more courage to the committees created especially for this purpose to carry on the most necessary [?] work, so that it seemed [?] that both Sosnowiec and Będzin would exceed the assigned quota. Yet, to our regret, to this very day the campaign has not been completed in either town, and the required sum has not been collected.
At the first moment it evidently got off to a flying start. People began to work energetically and proper work was done which made itself felt, but it went on too long and evidently got put on the "long bench" [shelved indefinitely], and so the assigned sums cannot [?] be collected, either in Sosnowiec or in Będzin.
Things have cooled off on both sides [?] and taken on a chronic character, which is so dangerous for this important campaign, on which thousands upon thousands of oppressed Jewish families depend.
The campaign must therefore be completed in any case [?] both in Sosnowiec and in Będzin. But the Jewish population — those who can give — have not fulfilled their obligations to this day. Many of the better-situated have at best given groszy, and the rest has not yet been paid in. It goes without saying that without this the total cannot be drawn up.
It is therefore required that the necessary campaign be completed as quickly as possible and brought to an end. There are, however, disruptive elements, consisting of those who neither give nor refuse. These are in fact the worst, because with them one does not know at all what to do; therefore it is important to hear clear words from them, so that one may know how to draw up the total.
We believe, however, that every Jew knows how necessary it is to take part in this important campaign, from which our fallen sisters and brothers — who not long ago were themselves among the givers — will benefit in large measure.
We have much confidence in, and faith in, those who can still come to help, that they will know how to appreciate properly the Million Campaign that has been created, and will want not only to finish the campaign as quickly as possible, but also that it should have the proper success, as befits the Jewry of Zagłębie.
We hope that the concluding work will come to an end as quickly as possible — and not merely for form's sake, but in a victorious and honourable manner; we shall gladly publish the names of the donors in the columns of our pages.
Selekt.
The Bagel Seller (A Little Picture from Modrzejowska [?] Street)

[Literature — sketch/short story; Sosnowiec [?].] A small attic room; the ceiling hangs over one's head, the walls are damp, and big, black, dirty drops of water hang on them like tears on the black face of an unhappy, hungry beggar. Shadows dance about the walls, casting fear; they chase one another about, creeping even [?] up to the mute [?] ceiling.
Somewhere, on a three-legged table covered with a holey oilcloth [?], burns a yellow tallow candle, spreading around it a dim, half-mysterious glow.
In a corner stands a cradle. There a tiny child is sleeping and talking in its dream with longed-for little angels with silver wings. Now they weave a garland of flowers for it, baskets full of chocolate and sweets.
It is late at night. The hands of the big old-fashioned wall clock with its half-worn, yellowed dial move on mercilessly, as if one hand were chasing the other.
Not far from the cradle, on a crooked [?] chair, sits a young woman; her eyes, sunk in a deep black frame, have long since lost their youthful lustre, and various hardships have inscribed themselves in wrinkles on the woman's forehead...
The woman is sewing a little shirt for her child. For long weeks she stinted herself on food in order to achieve it — a new little shirt for her child. There, it [?] is now talking unintelligible words in its sleep... Every day she put aside a few groszy from the day's earnings. She got by on a piece of dry bread until she had bought the piece of linen.
The clock is already striking eleven; her husband is still not here.
Various pictures pass before her eyes: there he stands, her Avremele, in the street with a basket of bagels the whole day, shouting in a hoarse voice:
— Fresh bagels! Buy, Jews!
She hardly [?] sees him a whole day. From six in the morning, winter and summer alike, he drags himself through the streets with the warm bagels, coming back only at twelve at night, exhausted, broken.
Sometimes he grows tired from shouting; something stabs him in the left side, his shoulders ache as if breaking, and he feels in his whole body a kind of heaviness, as though he had been stuffed with lead.
And sometimes he coughs hard and spits out a clot of blood as he does. A shudder runs through him, a sudden fear. The blood lying there on the bare stones, mixed with mud, casts an incomprehensible dread upon him.
Dirt cheap! A bargain
The words now run out of his mouth by themselves, but after every word he feels a stab in his heart. Standing like this by the gateway, he thinks about Chanele, who works, poor thing, hard and bitterly, and yet has not a pair of stockings for her feet. He stands as if chained to his spot; he cannot move his half-frozen feet. Now an elderly Jew passes by and buys several bagels from him.
A little spark appeared in Avremele's eyes; now he again feels a stab in his left side, he is short of breath, he wants to shout, but soon he feels easier.
— Jews, only at my stand! The best bagels!
And Jews do indeed buy; now he has only a few bagels left in all. He takes the little money-pouch out of his pocket and starts counting; his face shines — nicely taken, eighty groszy more than yesterday. He becomes quite another man; he has reached his goal.
In the little room a perfect stillness reigns. Chanele is still awake; it is already half past eleven and her Avremele is still not here. The ticking of the clock pierces her brain like sharp nails. Various thoughts awaken in her head and gnaw without ceasing; she grows uneasy. Every day at this hour he is already asleep, and today he lingers so long in the street, without having eaten even a bite. An indescribable fear seizes her; she feels as though a hidden thought were gnawing out the marrow of her bones. Hundreds of cries and screams for help stay stuck in her throat, as if they had frozen.
She is afraid to cry out — the child might still wake up. The shadows on the walls begin to dance wildly. On the stairs she hears heavy footsteps! She runs quickly to the door. Her Avreml is here.
— Where have you been so long?
He did not answer; he felt as if someone were digging inside his heart with sharp, pointed nails. He sat down, set down the empty basket, took out of it a pair of new stockings and gave them to Chanele.
— Here, this is for you — he barely stammered out, as though his tongue had stuck to his palate.
Chanele was happy. She did not know what to do for joy and gratitude, and as she embraced her husband's pale head, two big tears like pearls appeared in her eyes and slowly slid down her pale cheeks...
Z. A.
Mendele Moykher Sforim

P. Blumenkranz (Częstochowa).
2.א [section mark as printed]
The dismissive attitude of Jews toward nature has deep roots in the Jewish outlook on life.
The Jews, having received the monotheistic faith in the desert — a faith that harmonised with, and perhaps was even a product of, the whole monotonous surroundings — strove along the entire long road of their existence to extend this idea over the whole area of their life.
The commandment "Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image", which was created at the outset as a means of protection against the surrounding polytheistic current, took on, in the long exile — where Jews had no possibility of outward self-expression — bizarre forms.
Disregard for the outward reigned both among the enlightened, who concentrated their spiritual interest on purely abstract matters, and among the masses, who lived in cramped conditions and were sunk in worry, darkness and torments, consoling themselves with "Rachmana liba bo'i" ["the Merciful One wants the heart"].
We must remember that if among other peoples religion was the first impulse toward plastic art, among Jews it was the opposite.
The Greeks and Romans, through their personification of the world's forces, strove to represent the gods[?] as beautifully as possible, and this was a great factor in the colossal development of sculpture.
The Christians, in turn, believing in the incarnation of God in His son on earth, took up painting and sculpture as a matter of course, for purely religious aims, reaching mighty artistic heights in those fields.
The Jews, however, having based their world-view from the start on abstraction, became, in time, owing to their [?] conditions, so sharpened and intensified that "one forfeits one's life if one interrupts one's study in order to admire a tree"..
* * *
And strangely: after long hundreds of years a Jew comes from tiny Kapulye and actually apologises in these words: "Gentlemen, I confess, I have a weakness, which I have had since childhood — not to be thought of Jews — which in their language is called love of nature, that is, everything that grows, that sprouts, that lives, that is found in the world. It draws me, draws me — may it not be said of you."
And Mendele describes nature to us with pathos. His books are stuffed with the most wonderful descriptions of nature; he is in love with every little blade of grass, every ear of grain, every rustle.
And the grandfather tells us at every opportunity about the splendours of nature.
And the grandfather delights in the yellow-golden [?] strips of wheat and the dull-greenish[?] tall-grown maize; in the green valley, the walnut trees, the clear little stream in which the rays of the sun dip[?] and cover it with sparkling golden spangles — and we, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, with him...
Mendele for our generation.
Mendele's great significance for us was appreciated long ago. Already in 1910 Mendele's journey through Poland was a triumphal journey. Thousands of Jews greeted him in every town; he saw with his own eyes the effect of his works.
But his importance was not only for the older generation, [but] for the young[?] as well, as A. Reisen tells of his father, who allowed [him] to read "Di Klyatshe" ["The Mare"] on Friday night.
After all, Mendele created the foundation for everything that followed. He had to begin from Genesis in all areas: to create the language, which had been neglected as fit "for servant girls"; to create the nusach [style] (in Bialik's term); to establish certain generally valid rules which, before him, neither Yiddish nor Hebrew literature possessed; and to give literature realistic subject matter. Already in 1859 Mendele comes out in his little book "Mishpat Shalom" against the melitzah [florid rhetoric], against linguistic acrobatics, and already then Mendele writes that (Hebrew) writers should not use [empty] phrases and should write about the life of the people.
But Mendele's work has for us an even greater significance, a cultural-historical one: the reflection of the Jewish way of life of a whole era.
If everything from the first half of the 19th century that relates to Jewish life in Russia were to disappear, and Mendele's works were to remain, we would be able to form a clear notion of the Jewish life of that time — remarks David Frischmann in his enthusiastic essay on Mendele.
Mendele, with his synthetic-artistic sense, painted for us individuals in whom the collective of that time is mirrored. His types, such as Binyomin, Senderl, Fishke and others, are symbols of Jewish life, like the later Menachem-Mendl and Tevye.
And therefore, when we, in all Jewish communities, celebrate the hundredth birthday of Mendele, we stand with reverence and love before the memory of the creator and builder of today's richly branched Yiddish literature, which we cannot imagine without the pioneering, many-years-long artistic work of our great grandfather — Mendele Moykher Sforim.
The Zagłębie Victims in Tel Aviv.

[Tel Aviv — Eretz Israel; road accidents; immigrants from Zagłębie.]
(For the attention of the Tel Aviv municipality.)
The case that occurred recently with a young man from Sosnowiec, who was killed in Tel Aviv, is not the first. Unfortunately, already a considerable number of names of Zagłębie Jews who lost their life or their health in motor accidents in Tel Aviv and its vicinity.
We do not want to record this as though a fate pursues the people of Zagłębie in Eretz Israel, or — what is more likely — that Zagłębie Jews are no exception in this respect. In any case, however one takes it, even the bare number of Zagłębie people killed is a cruel and frightening [?] figure.
* * *
One of the causes — or the only cause — of the large number of motor accidents is the not sounding of horns. To avoid street noise, the cars there are not permitted to sound their horns when they notice a passer-by from a distance while driving.
Such a system does indeed exist in some European cities too. In those cities, however, street traffic is properly regulated. Crossing the street is permitted only at certain points where a policeman stands, directs the traffic and lets the pedestrians through; in Tel Aviv, on the other hand, sounding the horn is also forbidden, but the proper safety measures have not been adopted.
It is possible that this system suits the immigrants (olim) from the Western countries, who are already used to it. One must, however, reckon with the large number of immigrants from Poland, who are not used to it, which is why the number of motor accidents is so considerable.
Even if the Polish immigrants should get used to it in time — one surely cannot carry out experiments at the risk of human lives.
* * *
In the highly motorised European countries, where the proper safety measures have even been adopted, the number of motor accidents is not small either. The number of "motor victims" occupies one of the first places in the mortality statistics.
In Eretz Israel, on the other hand, the number is apparently much greater. If one considers, for example, that Sosnowiec is surely not much smaller than Tel Aviv, and nevertheless, God forbid, not as many accidents happen here as have happened there to Sosnowiec Jews alone, who after all form only a small part of the general population there.
* * *
The latest accident was caused by a cart; the other Zagłębie people mentioned were killed in motor accidents. In view of such grave tragedies, which are a result of heavy motorisation, we seriously [?] doubt the "blessing of civilisation", in whose supposed name so many victims are falling in hot Africa.
* * *
Feeling especially stricken by this sad [?] state of affairs, it is our right and duty to demand of the Tel Aviv municipality the regulation of street traffic in general and of wheeled traffic in particular, in order to prevent in future such cases — that people who leave their homes inspired by the idea of building a home for the whole people in their new land should not meet such a cruel death.
To those who will perhaps [?] regard our appeal as naive — we must explain:
When one stands at the fresh grave of a young friend, with a weight on one's heart — one must speak one's mind a little.
P. Leiner.
Our Panorama

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — satirical feuilleton: kehilla, gabbaim and the Chevra Kadisha.]
(Nothing new under the sun. — The Purim miracle in Old Sosnowiec. — An appointed gabbai on a droshky. — Thus shall be done by the Commissioner. — "Lesr Makhnikes"[?] in Będzin. — A political kiddush. — A split in the Będzin Chevra Kadisha. — A custom abolished.)
"There is nothing new under the sun" — says King Solomon; there is no news under the sun: what happened thousands of years ago happens today too — the same decrees, the same Hamans, even the same honour that Mordecai the Righteous had in the days of Ahasuerus is given in our times as well.
The only difference is that in the days of the kingdom of Persia and Media Haman had to lead the horse on which Mordecai rode through the streets and shout: "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honour"; whereas the Mordecai of the twentieth century, in the reign of the Commissioner, is no more than a gabbai, rides in a droshky, and on the coachbox sits not Haman but a plain droshky driver...
The "miracle" happened in Old Sosnowiec. For several weeks a revolt has been raging in the local beit midrash against the gabbaim. The scoffers of the generation even say that the revolt was inspired by the adversary [tsar] who is close to the commissarial kehilla administration and who set himself the goal of uprooting the "wicked ones" of the former dozór [synagogue board]. But be that as it may, the struggle flared up and grew worse from day to day, and the kehilla Commissioner appointed a gabbai. Why not? If the "new" Sosnowiec has an appointed kehilla administration, why should not an appointed gabbai rule in the beit midrash of Old Sosnowiec?
And the appointed gabbai soon convinced his holy flock that he is worthy of that mantle and that he has earned the right to run the beit midrash. He has exactly the same qualities as the late King Ahasuerus; it is only a pity that the story is not immortalised in a special Megillah, in which the following sentence would have had to appear:
"And the gabbai made a great feast — the commissarial gabbai made a great banquet for all his princes and servants, for his subjects; but since the gabbai does not possess such fine palaces as King Ahasuerus had, the feast took place in a tavern"...
And when the appointee and his "creator of servants" [sic] had already reached the higher level of:
— "Brandy talks and oats walk", they all climbed into a droshky harnessed with 2 horses and drove through the streets of Sosnowiec; and when the droshky with the "princes" reached Małachowskiego Street... the gabbai cried out:
— "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the Commissioner delights to honour"...
———
Sosnowiec has plenty to sing and tell about the appointees, and Będzin — about the "9-ers". Heaven and earth and — the "9-ers". As soon as one sees in the street a young Hasidic man with a hunched shoulder, sidelocks over his ears and trousers over his boots, people point at him:
— There goes one of the "9-ers"...
The "9-ers" became famous after the quiet upheaval that took place several weeks ago. The camp split into two camps; one camp, the 100-percent "9-ers", abandoned the position and moved over to Mandoszewer[?] Street, where they changed their name, etc.
— "The Pipkes"...
And in that lane wondrous tales are spread about the young Hasidic men, who, according to their behaviour, are called — "Lamdetnikes"[?].
In an old "Frankish"[?] building, in the attic, is the "shtibl". The way up is by a ladder "whose top reaches to heaven"; no ordinary flesh and blood may — better said, can — enter that "Holy of Holies", because, as soon as the full quorum is present, the ladder is pulled up and the "Lamdetnikes" are isolated from the sinful world...
— Happy are you, Sosnowiec, that you have merited appointees, and blessed are you, Będzin, with the "9-ers"...
———
Besides the "Lamdetnikes", Będzin has a "political Chevra Kadisha", which wanted to hold a "political kiddush"...
As is known, "kiddushes" take place on this Sabbath of the weekly portion Vayechi at all the Chevra Kadishas in Poland. Very well — when times were normal, when Chevra Kadisha people occupied themselves with the dead, and diplomats — with politics, such a "kiddush" was celebrated with awe and love [printed "brekhilu verotimu"], followed by a little bottle of brandy — why not, but all within the limits of their competence.
Today, however, when all existence depends on politics, even the "kiddush" of the Będzin Chevra Kadisha has acquired a political undertone.
— How so?
When the "kiddush" question became topical, one of the gabbaim, who belongs to the "Aguda" [Agudat Israel], made a proposal that this year the Chevra Kadisha should pray in the Great Synagogue and that all the rabbinical judges [morei hora'ah] be invited. This "innocent" proposal, however, did not find favour with all the gabbaim, seeing that with this "let all the morei hora'ah be invited" the side to which the proposer belongs is out to achieve an important position in the synagogue... Since this is a political step forward, a strategic chess move in the direction of the Będzin rabbinate question, some of them did not give their consent.
As we write these lines the matter has not yet been decided. It is not out of the question that because of politics the "kiddush" will not take place at all, since the committee of the Chevra has split into 3 camps: 1) a kiddush with the rabbinate, 2) a kiddush without the rabbinate, and 3) that no "kiddush" take place at all...
But according to the information we have received from the "front", the majority is in favour of the Chevra not praying in the Great Synagogue but in the beit midrash, and of the "kiddush" taking place without the morei hora'ah.
But be that as it may, the little Jewish world in Będzin is in uproar, and all because of politics, which has already "infected"[?] even the non-partisan "institution of the dead"; and the upshot may be that the custom of Parshat Vayechi — the traditional "kiddush" of the Będzin Chevra Kadisha — will be abolished...
Ben Amotz.
The Notables of the Town Have the Floor...

(What causes brought about the closing of the outpatient clinic in Dąbrowa?)
The one and only Jewish social institution, the outpatient clinic (ambulatorium) of the "Bikur Cholim" society in Dąbrowa, where the destitute part of the Jewish population received help — has been closed.
— Who is to blame for this? What causes brought it about?
We shall try to give an objective answer to these questions and, on the basis of the material in our possession, to clarify who bears the responsibility for this public scandal.
In its time the "Bikur Cholim" society understood the demand of the hour and decided to open an outpatient clinic for poor Jewish sick people. It goes without saying that carrying out this decision ran into great difficulties in such a "philanthropic place" as Dąbrowa, but after great efforts, [?] in time, the board of the above-mentioned society succeeded in realising the decision.
The clinic had — as we are informed — an income of 90 zł. a month; the expenditure, apart from the medicines, was 109 zł.
Praise must also be given to the doctors, Messrs. Mittelman and Shmirel [?], who throughout the whole time the clinic was in operation served without expecting any reward, entirely free of charge.
How useful the institution was for the poor Jewish masses is shown by the following figures: in the course of its 11 months of existence the clinic gave help to over 1,100 sick people. These round figures are living testimony to how much benefit the clinic brought and how necessary it is that the institution be revived. A wrong crying to heaven has been done here, one that must not be passed over in silence.
The first to bear the great responsibility are the well-to-do part of Dąbrowa. On them lay the sacred duty to help ensure that such an institution, the panacea, even if in miniature, should not be closed in the present hard and bitter time.
We would also have to blame the magistrate (town council), because such an institution, where poor sick people receive help, must absolutely be subsidised; the best example can be given by the magistrates of the neighbouring towns, where all institutions engaged in social aid are subsidised in the municipal budgets. But, as I am informed, the subsidy was not granted for other reasons. The letter that the board of "Bikur Cholim" sent to the magistrate about a subsidy — at the plenary session of the town council there was nobody who would take the trouble to have the letter read; but that already belongs to the past. It is something that can no longer be put right; the main thing now is only that Jewish society in Dąbrowa should hear the call of the great camp of poor sick people:
— Reopen the clinic!
We must apply all our forces to save the institution from ruin, because with good will on the part of the Dąbrowa notables there is a possibility of maintaining this important and necessary institution; it is not yet too late. Remember that the responsibility is a very great one. All forces must be mobilised for the benefit of the institution, for the benefit of the great number of poor Jewish sick. Some with money, some with work; the wealthy must make the beginning, and after them the whole town. So:
— The notables of the town have the floor!
B. Rechnitz.
How Was the Cinema Born?

[Science and technology — history of the cinema.] ("Interesting news") by Z. Hager, Vienna.
There is today not a single village in the whole civilised world that does not possess its own cinema. Even uncultivated peoples, who possess no modern facilities whatsoever, pass their time at the cinema.
At the Prague fair one could now see a quite faithful picture of how the cinema began and what troubles it went through until it reached its present level. No invention has made such a stir in the whole world as precisely the cinema.
Who invented the cinema? And how was it born? Edison answers this best[?] in his work "Troubles of an Inventor", which has just come out in print.
Louis Lumière, a small photographer from Besançon [printed "Bezankan"], not far from Lyon, found out that photographing does not require ten minutes, as was then believed; he improved the camera so much that in a single moment he could take in everything that was[?] in his field. This invention was the first step towards the cinema. In the year 1886 he exhibited the photographic camera at the Lyon fair. But nobody wanted to buy it. Every photographer and every dealer thought it was not necessary: when one already goes to the photographer, it may as well last another ten minutes...
But Lumière did not lose heart; he passes his time with his snapshot photographs. Having nothing to do in his small town, he goes around all the streets and amuses himself by taking pictures of people and animals in various positions in which they happen to find themselves at particular moments. Several years pass until it occurs to Lumière to travel to Paris and look for merchants for his invention. In Paris he sees in a shop Edison's invention, the "Kinetoscope", into which one can peep and see various little pictures that turn this way and that.
Lumière writes to Edison about his invention, and before long the two of them create an apparatus that moves the pictures on a large scale, so that Lumière can take with his snapshot camera all sorts of momentary situations, which can be joined into a whole picture with a content.
Edison writes that the first time he saw the pictures move — that was on 22 June 1894 — he himself could not believe he was not dreaming; both inventors burst into tears of joy.
In the first days of the year 1895 — forty years ago — they brought the apparatus to sell at a fair. In a restaurant they hired a hall in order to show their cinema apparatus.
Lumière himself turned the strips with the pictures by hand. There were eleven strips of seventeen metres. The whole show lasted twenty minutes, but taking out and putting in the strips lasted more[?] than half an hour. So the audience ran off.
The show was not a success. They had expenses of thirty francs, and their income was all in all thirty-three francs; they could not find even a single person who would take an interest in the cinema.
Lumière took the whole affair to heart[?] and gave up any further work. Edison himself later took it over and improved it more and more, until it became the greatest work of his life.
A Living Greeting from the Land of Israel.

[Palestine — immigrants from Zagłębie and Silesia.] Association of Zagłębie and Silesian olim (immigrants). — Senator Dr. Dawidsohn promises his assistance. — The contact with the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
(From our correspondent.)
Among the olim from Zagłębie who have already settled earlier and have been living in Eretz Israel for some time, and especially among those who arrive here with every ship, various questions have come up that need a solution for the benefit of the Zagłębie olim — above all at the present moment, when every oleh needs help in getting settled.
In this connection a group of olim from Zagłębie took the initiative to create an association of Zagłębie and Silesian olim. With the help of a series of notices in the local press, and also through special invitations, a meeting was called at the premises of the Polish Zionists (Nahalat Binyamin Street 1), in which about 200 people from Zagłębie and Upper Silesia took part.
The meeting is opened by Mr. Binyamin Fishl (Dagli[?], Sosnowiec), who invites to the presidium Messrs. Yaakov Glicksman (Sosnowiec), Meir Leml Sendishev[?] (Będzin) and Zeev Friedman (Königshütte).
After the introductory speech by Mr. Fishl, who pointed out the importance of founding the association, a discussion took place, in which the Polish Senator Dr. Dawidsohn also took part; he promised to take an active part and to work together for the benefit of the Zagłębie olim.
Then the decision was adopted to be in constant contact with the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", where various news items, reports and communiqués of the Zagłębie and Silesian association in Eretz Israel will be published, so as to be able to accomplish things jointly[?] for the benefit of the Zagłębie olim, which is very urgent at the present moment.
Finally a board was elected, consisting of: Binyamin Fishl (chairman), Meir Leml Sendishev[?], Fishl Batshe[?] (Sosnowiec), Zeev Friedman, Yaakov Glicksman, Meir Hirsh Jungster and Chaim Welner (Będzin).
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayechi)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayechi
—o—
a) "And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt" (Gen. 47:28)
1.
"Why is this section 'closed'? — Because once our father Jacob died, the eyes and hearts of Israel were 'closed' by the distress of the servitude, for [the Egyptians] began to enslave them." Rashi.
One asks: surely the servitude did not begin with Jacob's death? Rashi himself (Va'era, 6:16) says that the servitude began only with the death of Levi, the last of the tribes —
But the taste of servitude they already felt with Jacob's death, for, as the verse relates, they had to come to Pharaoh for permission to carry Jacob up [for burial], and with that they already felt the taste of exile. Where there is shtadlanut [intercession with the ruler] — it already smacks of servitude. Orach Chayim.
2.
"...Another explanation: he wished to reveal the End to his sons, and it was closed off from him." Rashi.
Because if one knows the End — the fixed date when the exile ends — one easily gets through the bad time, and the exile is no longer an exile... Therefore the End is not known; for if it were, there would be no exile at all. Sfat Emet.
• •
When Jacob wished to reveal the End, he saw what troubles the Jews would then have to endure, and a great sadness fell upon him — and "the Divine Presence does not rest amid sadness"; therefore the Shechinah departed from him. Rabbi Moshe of Kobrin.
• •
"From the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools and children" (Bava Batra 8 [sic]).
For the Shechinah does not rest upon one who is sad, and not to be sad in exile — only a fool or a child can manage that... Imrei Chen.
—o—
b) "And the days of Israel drew near to die" (ibid., 29)
With a great man, only his days die. "And the days of Israel drew near to die" — but he himself lives forever, his spirit remains forever: "Jacob did not die." Siftei Da'at.
—o—
c) "Bury me not, I pray, in Egypt" (ibid., 29)
"For the dead outside the Land will come to life only through the pain of rolling through underground tunnels." Rashi.
With this the "Gore'a bi-Yehuda" [?] explains, by way of jest, the Torat Kohanim, which says that the sections on usury and the Exodus from Egypt are stated together because in the merit of not taking interest the Jews will go out of exile.
For of usurers it is said that they will not rise at the resurrection of the dead. So what use is it to them to go from exile to the Land of Israel in order to be spared the rolling through tunnels, if they will not rise at the resurrection anyway...
—o—
d) "These are my sons, whom God has given me here" (Gen. 48:9)
Joseph's children, like the children of the Egyptian king, were probably dressed in Egyptian fashion, and when Jacob saw them he asked: "Who are these?" — who are these little Egyptians?
Joseph answered: "These are my sons, whom God has given me here" — my children, who were born here in Egypt and, unfortunately, must dress like Egyptians. Dvash ve-Chalav.
—o—
e) "And let my name be named in them, and the name of my fathers" (48:16)
If they dress like Egyptians — let them at least bear Jewish names. That may perhaps save them from assimilation. Kehilat Yitzchak.
—o—
f) "With my sword and with my bow" (ibid., 22)
"That is, his wisdom and his prayer." Rashi.
"Whoever scrutinizes his prayer — his merits are scrutinized" —
Why should any punishment come to one who scrutinizes his prayer? Because prayer is not a thing that depends on the brain. Prayer comes from the heart and needs no "scrutiny", no calculated reflection, but heartfelt enthusiasm.
Rabbi Avraham Moshe of Przysucha.
• •
Prayer is likened to a sword ("with my sword and with my bow"), because it must cut deep [?] into a person like a sword...
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
—o—
g) "Am I in the place of God?" (50:19)
Joseph was displeased that they humbled themselves so before him and said "Behold, we are your servants." So he asked: "Am I in the place of God?" — am I then instead of God? Before a human being one does not abase oneself like that. A man must not become a slave of a man... Leket Amarim.
Today's Jewish Fortunes.

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; poem.]
I.
Chaim Leyzer Pieterke
keeps a little shop of [?].
His goods he used to bring
from Warsaw and from Chmielnik,
from Kraków and from Katowice,
from Łódź, from Częstochowa
he used to carry them as luggage [by rail],
afterwards by motor-car [?] ["samokhode", Polish samochód].
From the motor-car [?] he switched
to the carters — —
today he buys right in his own town...
fortunes turn around — —
Gone are the times, laments Chaim Leyzer,
of taking in hundreds of zlotys.
Today from just 20 zlotys
one also makes a "takings" [?],
but the bad thing is that even 20
come in very seldom — —
How [?] does one make a living today?
And how [?] does one hold out today??
II.
Reyzl with the blue lips
used to, years ago,
keep a shop of dry goods
and travel to the fairs — —
white Częstochowa linen,
plush and "taldingi" [?] —
Reyzl used to sell more
than two other shopkeepers.
From every market day she saved
and made herself a capital,
for with 7 daughters
she was burdened with a family — —
and the business was enough
to marry off the children,
to give each child a dowry
and set aside for each separately —
Today — says Reyzl — I'm badly off
and it's bitter as death,
she toils a whole week
and hasn't even enough for bread.
Of the Sabbath she has no sign,
only a little "sikhl" [?],
and that too she buys largely on credit,
she takes in only "on the little book" [on credit] — —

M. Grynszpun.

If God made a fool of me [?] and men ruined me, what can I expect from the devil already.

Our Demands to the "Joint"

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satire — Sosnowiec, kehilla, the "Joint".]
At the conference that took place last week in Sosnowiec with the participation of the "Joint" [JDC] director Mr. Giterman, we put forward the following demands:
Since many people, poor things, are hanging around dying for a "prezes" [?] (president's) seat, new associations should be created.
They should stop tormenting the Sosnowiec rich men about money for the Million Campaign for the poor, because it causes them, poor things, great distress, and they might even look bad because of it.
To relieve the commissarial kehilla administration completely of its heavy burden of helping the needy who have never traded in coffee, the "Joint" should take the mission upon itself.
To give back the 25 guldens [zlotys] that the commissarial administration gave for the 150 halutzim [pioneers] for Passover,
The "Joint" should, at its own expense, put up the tombstone for the [?] victim, so that the councillors' "Koło" [caucus] should not, with its hullabaloo, cause any distress to Mr. President [pan prezes].
To fix an annual subsidy for the Bałuty hooligan, so that he can keep his blackmail sheet going.
About a Jewish Theatre Building in Sosnowiec.

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satire — Sosnowiec, kehilla and culture.]
As we learn, a confidential meeting of the commissarial kehilla administration and national activists took place in Sosnowiec in recent days, about building in Sosnowiec a building of its own for a Jewish theatre.
At the consultation — as we are informed — the following opinions were expressed:
Pan Ignacy: On this question I am in agreement; I reckon the thing won't be so hard to carry out, but one thing I demand: that the performances take place in Polish, so that the kehilla officials and some of the Jewish shtadlonim [intercessors] can "enjoy themselves" ["cieszyć się"]...
Judenstaatler [?] [Jewish State Party man]: I think that the theatre's premises one should [?] have built in advance [?] [in mock German], I mean to say, that the theatre performance should take place in Hebrew, because whether one plays in Yiddish or in Hebrew, nobody will come. So let the theatre at least ["chociażby"] die a national death. I have finished ["skończyłem"] — Shalom!
Head of the kehilla: Gentlemen! As a European and a disseminator of religion I put forward this view: what does one need a theatre for? Why not — if the Almighty helps, we shall, bli neder, have a theatre too; it only depends [?] on whether the Jews of Sosnowiec will be [?] worthy of it and understand that one really has to pay (only not in instalments..). The main thing is only: 1) that the parokhet [ark curtain] should not be of shaatnez, for you know I don't budge from the Chatam Sofer..' 2) in the theatre there must be a separate "women's gallery" under the supervision of my "editor", who is quite [?] an expert in the laws of mixtures... 3) historical plays should be performed, because firstly I too want for once to belong to great history, and secondly, when one plays a piece with a king, such as "Ahasuerus", "Samson the Hero", "The Two Kuni-Lemls" [Goldfaden], the audience must say the blessing: "Blessed be He who has given of His glory to flesh and blood"... 4) in a play in which a commissar appears who delivers a sermon, the audience should say the "Rabbis' Kaddish".
If this is done, the kehilla will support the campaign and will give money.
A Sermon in the Sosnowiec Synagogue.

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satire — Sosnowiec, kehilla.]
In honour of "Zot Hanukkat" [the last day of Hanukkah], "he" came to the town synagogue, where he gave a sermon about heroism [?] in... a salaried post ["etat"].
At the end of the sermon he turned to the women in these words:
— Dear women! To you I turn with the great request to help me out of the great kehilla distress [?]. I know, after all, that all the power lies in your hands; with a single smile you compel the strongest men to fall at your feet; even Alexander the Great you conquered; therefore, righteous women, have pity not so much on me as on my seat, which I strove for 18 years; prevail on your husbands to open their purses, wipe away the filth your husbands have made, and a redeemer shall come to Zion, and let us say Amen.
The Będzin Kehilla Council Turns to YIVO

[Humour ("Der Kokh-Lefl") — Będzin, kehilla council.]
In connection with the new "play on words" between the president of the kehilla board and the president of the council, the Agudah kehilla faction has turned to the Jewish Scientific Institute ("YIVO") in Wilno with the following queries:
1) Whether "nieścisłość" [inaccuracy] coincides with "kłamstwo" [a lie]...
3) [sic; should be 2] Whether one may compare the word "ordynacja" [statute/regulations] with "ordynarne" [vulgar].. and
3) Whether it is permitted to climb [?] onto a platform [flat cart] — apart from horses [?] — also for kehilla representatives?
The query asks for an immediate answer, so as to know how to conduct oneself at the further sessions on the new kehilla budget..
Who Is Fighting?

[Humour ("Der Kokh-Lefl") — the Italo-Abyssinian war.]
A sensational report from the Abyssinian front.

The local oil merchant Parasal [?], who has business connections with Abyssinia, has received a little letter from an acquaintance of his [printed "zeygem", read "zeynem"], an Abyssinian merchant, in which he writes:

Don't believe the newspapers; here in Abyssinia no war at all is taking place between the Abyssinians and the Italians — there is only a war going on between the correspondents. The correspondents who side with Italy wreak devastation in the Abyssinian army and drive it from all its positions, and those who side with Abyssinia — make ash and mud of the Italians.

As for the prices of oil, you should apply to my partner in London.
The Bastard (69)

[Serialized novel — "The Bastard"; installment 69.]
Adw. [advocate] S. Geliszkowski [?].
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy (illui)

"How are you, Panie [Mr.] Grin?" Moshele asked him as he came into his cabin.
"Thank you, Mr. Rabiner. Today I want to try going out of my cabin a little and take a look at God's little world, which I have not yet managed [?] to see."
"Do you feel well already?"
"I am very weak, I can barely stand on my feet. Please, sit down, Mr. Rabiner, and tell me how your wife and your mother are, and how they feel?"
Thank you, today they no longer feel badly.
For a while both were silent. The silence was broken by Moshele, who asked him to show the photograph of the woman he had shown [?] in the train carriage.
Leon walks with weak steps to the night-table and hands him Balbina's picture.
"Mr. Rabiner," he says, "I do not want to be insincere with you, for that would mean being false in soul toward a person of your sphere; but still I have a great suspicion that the woman is known to you. I noticed it from your great astonishment in the carriage when you caught sight of the picture. Isn't that so, Mr. Rabiner?"
"You are right, your suspicion is well founded, but in quite another respect. The woman would not interest me at all, were she not the wife of my father" [printed "paster", read "foter"].
"What?" Leon asks in amazement. "Naum Rozen is your father, Mr. Rabiner?"
"Yes, my friend [printed "freygt", read "freynt"], Naum Rozen is the one who brought me into the world. Do you know him?"
"No, I have never seen him. I know him only as much as his wife — that is, Balbina — told me about him."
May I perhaps know what she told you about him? he asks. "You will forgive me, Panie Grin, for putting these questions to you; you must understand that he is, after all, my father. True, he did not behave toward me like a father, but God forgives people their sins, and therefore we too must do the same. So I beg you, tell me what you know about my father. Perhaps you know where he is and why they parted?"
"As she told me, she left her husband because she did not want to deceive him in her feelings. She was 18 years old when she met him. She had come to Warsaw from a small shtetl; lonely and poor she was. He took her on as a clerk-typist in his office. She was inexperienced then, and his wealth impressed her. A greater happiness than wealth she did not know; the feeling of love was foreign to her, and when that feeling came, she saw herself a poor woman in his golden cage, from which she tore herself away with all her strength, left him and came over to me. But our happiness, too, did not last long: she left me too, and I do not know where she went. I searched all of Warsaw, I was at her parents', and there too I found no trace. True, she did not treat me right, leaving me without so much as a goodbye, for which she is not worthy of my sacred love; but unfortunately I must confess that to this day she is engraved in my heart, because she was the first woman I loved; she was the first woman who awakened in me the feelings of a man. I was still young and innocent when I met her on my life's path."
"And since she came over to you she has not seen him again?" asks Moshele.
"No; as far as I know, he left Poland."
"Yes, yes. So it is in life, young man. Very often a person builds his happiness on another's misfortune."
"I believe, Mr. Rabiner, that you do not mean me by that," says Leon.
"God forbid, it is not you I mean, but rather your lady friend, who wanted to build her happiness on the ruins of the grief, suffering and tears of my unhappy mother. My mother suffered very much, and I believe that to this day her wounds have not healed; very early [?], quite young, she lost in her life that which is dear to us — family happiness. There is not yet in the world such a remedy as could heal my mother's wounds."
And again they both fell silent, sitting with lowered heads, sunk in their thoughts, which were different for each of them.
Leon in his thoughts called Balbina, called [?] her in his strong longing for her. And Moshele?
Moshele was thinking about the misfortune of his mother and his father. Now, sitting lost in thought, he tried to awaken in himself the feeling of longing for his father. But he did not feel that feeling within him; the feeling was foreign to him.
And at the same time, while the two men sat in the cabin sunk in their thoughts, Balbina sat in Mamilran's [?] room with Luiza [Louise], who had returned from Warsaw only yesterday.

The Local Kehilla Is "Looking for" a Gaon to Rule Whether Yechezkele May Become a Poultry Slaughterer...

[Będzin — Kehilla and shechita.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 15 Tevet 5696 — Friday 10 January 1936.)
Będzin
The local kehilla is "looking for" a gaon to rule whether Yechezkele may become a poultry slaughterer...
The story of Yechezkele the shochet is, it seems, well known in our town, and no wonder, since the gmina [the Jewish community] together with the rabbinate waged a bitter fight against him and declared the meat of his slaughtering forbidden dozens of times, o.ch.[?]. Finally the kehilla board, seeing that the fight was damaging the kehilla treasury, decided to settle the dispute peacefully, and the shochet R' Yechezkele was engaged as an official "without portfolio".
Now, when R' Yechezkele must, for formal reasons, appear in the new kehilla budget, the idea arose of taking him on as a poultry slaughterer; but since he was at the time disqualified by the rabbinate, it was decided to turn to a gaon who should give his opinion on the matter.
The Conference on Uniting the Merchants' Associations — Without Result

[Będzin — Merchants.]
As we have already written, in connection with the present situation of the merchants a project was put forward that the split between the local "big" and "small" merchants should finally end and that at long last a united merchants' association should be created.
At Sunday's conference in the premises of the Merchants' Association the project was supposed to be realized, but because of the statement of the delegates of the Small Traders' Association that the association must reach an agreement on this with its headquarters (the "Centrale"), the union was not created.
Craftsmen's Representatives in All Government Institutions

[Będzin — Craftsmen.]
In connection with the circular (okólnik) of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, according to which representatives of every guild (cech) are to be represented in all public and government institutions, an extraordinary meeting of all the guild boards took place on Sunday at the Craftsmen's Association (Pargudska[?] 4). After Mr. A. Klajman reported on the importance of the circular, the following were elected — from the tailors' guild: ratman M. Hans"[?], starszy (guild master) A. Klajman, M. Kajzer and M. Rapszyk[?].
From the shoemakers' guild: starszy Y. Tuchszniejder, deputy starszy Ogarnik[?] and A. Berger.
From the shoe-upper stitchers: deputy starszy A. Uflinger[?], Sh. Gliksman, N. Sfarsin[?] and Y. Szwajcer.
From the locksmiths: ratman Grosman, Sh. Grajcer and M. Flesner.
Finally the assembled were informed that whoever wishes to receive a loan from the government credit must submit a declaration at the municipal treasury.
Commercial Agents Organize

[Zagłębie — Commercial agents.]
Under the chairmanship of Mr. M. Lewin a meeting of the commercial agents in Zagłębie took place on Sunday in the premises of the Merchants' Association.
After Mr. M. Lewin's lecture on the necessity of creating an association of commercial agents, a discussion developed in which the delegates of the Commercial Agents' Association in Katowice also took part; they tried to weaken the initiative that a separate association of commercial agents should be created in Zagłębie, but the majority of those assembled were for creating such an association.
As we are informed, the number of enrolled members is still not large. It is to be expected, however, that those not yet decided[?] will take stock of the present situation and enrol as members of the above-mentioned association.
Beit HaMidrash Worshippers Against Cantor Boim

[Będzin — Kehilla and beit midrash.]
A group of 60 worshippers has sent the kehilla board a request to annul the decision of the beit midrash committee that Mr. Boim be taken on as cantor in the beit midrash.
Wanted to Betroth Her "z pomocą" ["with help"?]...

[Będzin — Rabbinical court.]
An interesting[?] din Torah took place before the local beit din. A young man, who had not managed "to win the heart" of his sweetheart, summoned her to court with the claim that she should return to him what it had cost him as a "gentleman". After the pleadings before the rabbinate the young man wanted to betroth her [by kiddushin]. But the girl, too, is not one of the "suckers" (frajerki) and prevented her "bridegroom" from carrying out his plan.
The useful work of „TOZ“ at the Będzin Talmud Torah

For several weeks now the society „TOZ“ [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population] has again begun the feeding campaign at the „Talmud Torah“ in Będzin.
Because of the apathy of the broad Jewish public towards „TOZ“, no more than 80 children (out of a number of over 300) benefit from the campaign; they receive every day a roll, cheese and, those who need it, cod-liver oil.
„TOZ“ carries out great and praiseworthy work in the field of hygiene. In this field very much has been done at the Talmud Torah, where the hygienist specially employed by „TOZ“ sees to it that the children keep themselves clean.
— Since Tuesday a quartz lamp has already been operating for the Talmud Torah children who are qualified [for it] by a doctor.
The society „TOZ“ has a broad programme for improving the state of health of the Jewish masses, and of the poorest children in particular; this, however, depends on the attitude of the Jewish public, which unfortunately does not have the understanding to appreciate this useful Jewish institution.
Sosnowiec — The post office is open all day

Sosnowiec
The post office is open all day.
From the 4th of this month the local post office is open from 8 in the morning until 8 in the evening without a lunch break.
Registered remittances can be handed in from 7 in the morning until 21 and[?] deliveries; on the other hand from 21 until 7 in the morning for an additional fee of 70 groszy.
In connection with this, one will no longer [see] at the local post office the „shankes[?]“ (queues/crowding[?]) there have been until now.
A [tax] appeals commission is to operate in Sosnowiec

This week a meeting of the trade section took place at the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec. At the meeting the question was discussed that tax appeals should no longer, as until now, be dealt with in Kielce, but in Sosnowiec.
The rapporteur of the section took the floor on the question and explained that in the nearest future the matter is to be settled in the form of a decree of the Ministry of Commerce.
5-złoty communal-tax sums are collected through distraints

This week we had the opportunity to hear the laments of local payers of the communal tax (etat), well-known poor people, from whom the head of the kehilla demanded, through the Urząd Skarbowy (tax office), communal-tax debts of... 5 złoty.
From one of the [—] the bailiff took a piece of furniture for the 5 złoty...
— The „for with a strong hand... will I rule over you“ [Ezekiel 20:33] is truly being realised...
„The dog deserves the stick“...

The blackmailer already well known in Sosnowiec, who is supported by the commissarial kehilla administration in publishing his gossip sheet, recently attacked with his [—] tongue a well-known nationalist (Zionist) activist, whom the scoundrel[?] insulted with the most disgusting abuse.
For this vile performance several young men, friends of the insulted man, took revenge, and carried out the „verdict“ on the above-mentioned.
Inspection of shops and workshops on the [Christian] holidays

On Sunday and Monday the Labour Inspectorate in Sosnowiec carried out a check in a number of shops and workshops in the Zagłębie area.
During the check, which lasted almost a whole day, reports were drawn up against the owners in whose shops the commercial employees were present at the time.
Propaganda for the Free-Loan Fund in Pogoń

(S. G.) For 2 years now the struggle around the local gemilut chesed (free-loan) fund has been going on in Pogoń, as a result of which it has been brought down to a very low level; only thanks to a few individuals headed by Mr. S. Altman has it been possible to maintain the institution to this day.
Last Sunday the annual general meeting took place with the participation of the „Joint“ director, Mr. Giterman. The chairman, Mr. S. Altman, opens the meeting, and after the deceased board member Sh. Shmulevitsh is honoured, H. A.[?] welcomes Mr. Dir. Giterman and Mr. Wendel.
Mr. Wendel is elected chairman, Mr. M. Glidman secretary, and Messrs. B. Pilcer and B. Wożnica[?] to the presidium.
After the activity report for the year 1934 by Mr. Y. S. Horowitz, a very sharp discussion takes place, in which Messrs. G. [—] Shayer, Sh. Blum, M. Glidman, Prodalski and Horowitz take part.
Then Dir. Giterman delivers a lecture, emphasising the importance of a free-loan fund at the present moment, and appeals to those assembled to tear out the quarrels which may cause the downfall of the fund in Pogoń.
After the lecture the old board is elected, together with a recruitment committee consisting of: Altman, Shayer, Perleger[?], Blum, Glidman and Prodalski.
After the meeting a session of the recruitment committee takes place with the participation of Mr. Giterman, and it is decided to conduct a broad recruitment campaign. Among other things also, that every Sabbath before the Torah reading Messrs. Blum, Shayer and Glidman are to speak about the importance of the free-loan fund.
Propaganda for the “Beis Yaakov” school.

The committee of the local school named “Beis Yaakov” is preparing a large campaign to recruit members and a fund-raising campaign for the enlargement of the school premises. As is reported, some 400 girls study at the school, but almost the same number [more] are registered, for whom there is no room in the present premises.
Protest meeting against the Legislative Council. / A theft in the “Mizrachi” synagogue.

Next week a mass meeting against the Legislative Council [in Palestine] will take place in our town. The meeting is being organised by the Zionist youth organisations.
—o—
A theft in the “Mizrachi” synagogue.
On the night from Monday to Tuesday thieves got[?] into the “Mizrachi” synagogue on Modrzejowska Street, where they broke open a drawer and took... a tallis with tefillin.
Dąbrowa: An interesting jubilee academy. / A railway accident. / 6-hour working day at “Flora”. / 6 months' prison for giving a bribe

An interesting jubilee academy.
This evening, Saturday night, a festive academy in honour of the 20th jubilee of “Hashomer Hatzair” in Dąbrowa will take place in the “Yegus”[?] hall, with the participation of Mr. Asher Sheinfeld (Palestine), member of the supreme leadership and member of the executive of the “Kibbutz Artzi”, who will lecture on the topic “Hashomer Hatzair in the year 1916 and today”. Also a rich artistic part.
—o—
A railway accident.
At the local railway station a wagon of coal overturned, as a result of which the [—] rail traffic was held up for several hours.
—o—
6-hour working day at “Flora”.
The mine workers have for a long time been waging a struggle for the introduction of a 6-hour working day. The management of the “Flora” coal mine has introduced the [shorter] working time and at the same time reduced the wage, which amounts to no more than [pay] for 6 hours of work...
—o—
6 months' prison for giving a bribe
In the little shop of Hersh Meir Gersten a policeman drew up a report for not having a price list. Gersten gave the policeman one złoty and a packet of “tobacco” so that he would destroy the report. The policeman took it and brought a charge against Gersten, who was sentenced for it to pay 100 zł. and to 6 months in prison.
A Kielce resident becomes a great millionaire.

In Australia the millionaire Krisztof Szpachen [?], owner of gold and diamond mines, recently died. The fortune of the deceased is estimated at several million pounds sterling.
The news of the death of Szpachen, who came from Poland, spread throughout the whole country and especially in Kielce, where (on Piotrkowska Street) Mr. Gustaw Szpachen lives, the owner of a dye-works, who considers himself a very close relative of the deceased millionaire.
For this reason the Kielce Szpachen travelled to Warsaw and visited the Foreign Ministry. The Ministry immediately made inquiries at the Polish consulate in London, from where an answer arrived that the Australian government is looking for the heirs, who live in Poland. Mr. Szpachen of Kielce is, as he states, a nephew (brother's son) of the deceased millionaire.
A village head goes home from a New Year's Eve ball without trousers, many ladies without blouses, and the orchestra players — without instruments...

For several months a dangerous band of thieves and safe-breakers operated in the Kielce voivodeship, carrying out many daring burglaries and thefts in homes and shops. In the city of Kielce alone several families were simply left destitute [?], and this gang of thieves could not be discovered.
This week, after lengthy observation, the Kielce police finally liquidated this gang (szajka). Almost all members of the band have already been arrested, and together with them several dozen receivers of stolen goods were also detained, from whom many of the stolen objects were confiscated.
Mass searches were carried out in various towns and townlets as well as in many villages of the Kielce and Łódź voivodeships, where much of the stolen property and clothing was discovered.
In the village of Umianowice, Pińczów county, the police established that many of the inhabitants were parading in holiday clothes originating from the said thefts, and because of this many of the pretty local peasant girls and lads had their festivities spoiled.
Among other things, the police also confiscated from the sołtys (village head) of Umianowice a new suit and a hat, just when he was wearing both and getting ready to go to church. The suit and hat had been stolen from a certain Mr. Bieliński in Kielce.
In the same village the police burst into a dance hall where a New Year's Eve (Sylvester) celebration was taking place and ordered many of those present to take off at once the clothes that came from the local thefts. Some elegant peasant girls and lads [?] simply had nothing to go home in, and everyday clothes had to be brought for them.
From some of the orchestra, too, the instruments were taken away, as they came from thefts.
All these things the police confiscated; it arrested, as is known, all the dangerous thieves and burglars, detained all suspicious persons, and thus finally liquidated the dangerous gang of bandits.
What is new in the People's Bank affair?

As is known, a delegation headed by Rabbi Rapaport intervened recently [?] in Warsaw with the director of the "Joint", Mr. Schweitzer, in the matter of the Kielce People's Bank (Folksbank). As a result of the intervention, the director of the "Foundation" for Poland, Dr. Flaum, ordered the material and the list of members to be handed over to Rabbi Rapaport and President Goldman, who together with a special commission are to assess the possibilities of collecting money from the members.
Meanwhile, however, the liquidators published in a Kielce paper an announcement whose content caused great agitation among the entire Jewish public.
This week the committee held a lengthy meeting together with the council and the "Commission of 5" of the People's Bank. It was decided to work jointly in the interests of the members of the People's Bank.
100 zł fine for not signing the marriage and birth certificates.

We inform our esteemed readers that those who in 1935 had marriage and birth certificates drawn up and have not yet signed the certificates must report by Wednesday, the 15th of this month, at the Magistrate (municipality) together with the witnesses they named, in order to sign the certificates. Those who do not sign the certificates by Wednesday will be punished with a fine of 100 zł or with 2 weeks' arrest. Let the Jewish population of Kielce remember this well.
When coming to the Magistrate one must bring the Magistrate receipt, on which the number of the certificate appears.
—o—
Protest meeting against the Legislative Council.
In the coming days a large protest meeting will take place against the Legislative Council [in Mandatory Palestine]. The meeting will be organised by all the Zionist groupings together with the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel].
Recitation evening of Dr. Gustaw Werner at the Zionist Club.

Today, Friday evening, at 8 o'clock [?], the famous reciter Dr. Gustaw Werner, formerly an actor of Reinhardt's theatre in Berlin, will appear with recitations at the Zionist Club. On the programme: recitations from world-famous men of letters and writers.
Success of the campaign for the Jewish library.

The collection campaign for the Jewish library in Kielce, conducted by the special committee chaired by President Mitzenmacher, is showing very good results. The Jewish public in Kielce responded very warmly and supported the campaign. So far a sum of 600 zł has already been collected. The campaign is being continued.
In addition, the committee has set itself the task of carrying out a broad drive to recruit new readers. In connection with this, a large purchase of the newest publications in Yiddish, Hebrew and Polish literature will be made in the coming days.
Taking part in the campaign for the library are the members of the committee and representatives of all political organisations in Kielce.
Meeting of the Homeowners' Bank.

Next Sunday, the 12th of this month, the continuation of the general meeting of the Homeowners' Bank in Kielce takes place. This meeting will decide on the further existence of the bank.
It is the duty of all members of the bank to come to the meeting without fail, so that no unpleasant surprises can occur, as happened recently with another Jewish cooperative bank. About this [?] those who want to fish in troubled waters should also think carefully..
About 200 prisoners released from the Kielce prison

[Kielce — amnesty; prisoners.] As a result of the amnesty, about 200 prisoners were released from the Kielce prison, among them up to 50 political prisoners.
—o—
[Zionist Club — culture; Mendele evening.] A lecture by Gross-Zimmermann at the Zionist Club.
In the coming days a Mendele evening will take place at the Zionist Club. With a lecture on the life and work of Mendele Mokher Sforim (recitations[?]) will appear the well-known literary critic and famous journalist, contributor to "Haynt", Mr. Gross Zimmermann.
—o—
[Local — antisemitism; stink bomb.] Locals tried to throw a stink bomb into a Jewish shop.
On Wednesday towards evening unknown local hooligans tried to throw a stink bomb into the [stone?] shop of Mr. Rubinsztejn on Czysta Street. Fortunately the bomb, instead of into the shop, fell onto the pavement.

How capable swindlers „took in“ several radio-set firms

On 30 December („grudzień“) the Christians Bazyli Kuszec[?] and Feliks Naganda, both of Sosnowiec[?], came into the firm Retman—Berkowicz[?] to buy a radio set on instalments. Kuszec[?] was the buyer, and Naganda came as the „expert“.
The above-mentioned firm, after acquainting itself with the buyer's material situation and receiving the appropriate undertakings, handed over the set and at the same time suggested to Naganda that he too buy a set on the same terms, but Naganda „declined“. Poor Patients, or Political Patients?

[Dąbrowa — municipality and community.] (A reply to the trustee of the Jewish outpatient clinic in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza])
It is one of the frequent phenomena that certain persons suddenly take it upon themselves to defend public matters and speak with fiery enthusiasm about the importance and rightness of this or that thing, but in truth the whole matter concerns them exactly as much as what happens on the far side of the Sambatyon; they are really after an ulterior motive, which needs to occupy altogether a few lines, and the whole public matter serves him as no more than an accompaniment to the tune itself.
It all depends, however, on how it is done. One must do it subtly and smoothly; if not, one immediately sees plainly the writer's ulterior motive in all its nakedness, and the accompaniment comes out as a screeching cacophony.
Just such an impression is made by the writing of the above-mentioned. One immediately sees the real intention, as he wants to tell the public that since he left the magistrate [town council] "the Divine Presence has departed from there", and so he begins to pick on the Dąbrowa magistrate, and right away he takes a leap up onto the councillor's [Ratman's] bench...
But let us answer first things first and last things last.
As regards the accusation that the Dąbrowa magistrate does not subsidise the "Bikur Cholim", where help is given to poor patients, I state that to this day all poor patients, without distinction of faith, receive medical help from the magistrate.
But if the writer holds that, if a separate Jewish outpatient clinic exists, the magistrate ought to have given the "institution" a subsidy — with which I agree with all my heart, and I stand on the same position — one would like to ask him: why did the writer not make the effort, when he was a councillor as recently as the last few years, to have the Bikur Cholim subsidised, especially since at that time no Jewish patients received any support — after all, the Bikur Cholim does not exist only since today?...
And as regards, further, the letter from the board of the "Bikur Cholim" to the magistrate, I learn of it only from the writer, and I was not informed about it at all; the board of the "Bikur Cholim" can confirm this.
For the future I advise that the writer send a letter to the magistrate about creating an outpatient clinic for political patients, and if he informs me about it, I will see to it that the letter is laid before the plenum...
Respectfully,
Councillor Abraham Neifeld.

On the initiative of the Zion[ist][?] representatives in the Katowice kehilla, a meeting of the council and of the board took place last Thursday, which unanimously adopted the following protest resolution:
