When One Finds Oneself in a Time of Distress — In Będzin no union came about between the merchants' and small traders' associations

In Będzin no union came about between the merchants' and the small traders' associations.
A few weeks ago we reported with satisfaction that in Warsaw a union had at last come about between the merchants' and the small traders' central bodies. A main council was created there, on which the president of the Sosnowiec Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, Mr. Safer[?], is also represented.
As a further consequence of putting [the union] into effect, a conference took place in Będzin last week between the small traders' and the merchants' associations, whose aim was unification, strengthening, consolidation[?], and above all finding a way out: how to exist, how to stay standing on one's feet, which have already grown so weak and weary that they no longer have anything to hold on to. An urgent rescue is therefore needed both for those who have just collapsed and for those who are "sure candidates" (sic) to be classed before long in the same[?] category.
Unfortunately, and to our greatest regret, the conference ended in nothing. The answer of the small traders' delegates (printed "relegates") was that they must inquire in Warsaw how they should act on the question. At the given moment.
We do not know whether the answer was a matter-of-fact one, a well-founded one, a considered one, or perhaps an evasive one given merely to discharge an obligation. It goes without saying that we do not wish to accuse anyone here of any ulterior motives. And yet it is not at all[?] appropriate, for once one comes to such a conference one must not go away with nothing. The matter is, after all, serious enough, weighty enough and painful[?] enough, and one must strive with every possible means to find a radical solution.
Must[?] one then first begin painting pictures of the prevailing gloomy situation of this middle class? Do we not see[?] the "pictures of beauty" at every step, in the most vivid colours? Why sink into this pessimistic mood, when it will certainly bring no benefit and the already overstrained nerves will not grow any stronger either?
Today is, after all, no time for threadbare phrases or for playing at "high politics". At a moment that is catastrophic one cannot get by with evasive answers or by dragging things out. That is too dangerous a game, and one must without any doubt give an account of what may come of this delay — and, who knows, perhaps it is recklessness of the highest degree? No — one must by no means make light of the most topical question, which must stand at the very top of the most urgent agenda.
It is, after all, nonsense today to distinguish between merchants and small traders. Do the two of them not have today one and the same interests? Are they not oppressed together, fettered together? Do both not suffer from one and the same blows? Do they not need one and the same deliverance? Can both not be helped together[?]?
We know, after all, that the one differs from the other in almost nothing, except that one is squeezed in a larger dose and the other in a smaller one. But it is a fact that both have the same sorrows and joys, and one must reckon with that and classify them in one category.
The fact that there are merchants holding trade patents [licences] of different categories does not change the situation at all, just as there is no difference between a merchant who keeps books and one who is exempt from that same work.
We no longer have today the merchants with the great aspirations of former times, and if such do exist, they are in the most minimal number, and they manage better without an association, because their employees look after them in the very best way.
The same is true of our manufacturers. If they are industrialists with their own chimneys and boilers and the whole clattering apparatus, then what do they need the association for? On the contrary, it is the association that surely needs them. What remains, then, is no more than the handful of petty manufacturers, who quite often employ (printed "confirm") in their enterprise, which is called "manufacturing", no more than their own[?] household members. So what is the difference — we ask — between that "manufacturer" and the small trader?
It is, upon my life, high time to stop playing with fantasies and illusions, which never bring us any benefit but, on the contrary, lead us to the abyss.
We must adopt every possible means in order to achieve unity in our ranks. We must do it immediately, that is, as long as there are still members in both the small traders' and the merchants' associations, for later there will be nothing and no one to unite with. This we must take well to heart.
With good will an understanding can without doubt be found. Moreover, one must not forget that there is no other way out, because time does not stand still, and the further it goes, the worse and more catastrophic the situation becomes.
We must bear well in mind that the middle class, consisting of the members of the above-mentioned associations, finds itself in a time of distress, and we must find a common understanding so as to be able to save ourselves while it is perhaps not yet too late.
R. Les.
Zagłębie Local Economy. For the Attention of the Town Councillors.

For more than one occasion we have already written about the sanitary situation in Zagłębie, which nevertheless is not being improved. True, we were answered that in Będzin and in Sosnowiec it must for the time being go on just like this because of the carrying-out of the sewerage (canalisation) work. It goes without saying that while the pipes are being laid in the ground there must be disorder, so that traffic in the streets is disrupted.
But one must not forget that the work was carried out long ago throughout the towns of Zagłębie, and yet the situation is no better. On the contrary: the later it gets, the longer it goes on, the more dangerous and the worse the condition becomes.
People have never fallen in the streets as often as in the last year, and it is really no wonder at all, since there are pits not only across the width of the streets but also on the pavements themselves. True, this is justified by the fact that the sewerage has not yet been carried out everywhere. But we know that in the town centres the pipes are already laid and the whole connection has already been joined — so why is no care taken that the streets be repaired? Why is it not taken into account that the citizens cannot walk through the streets as carefully as outside the town[?]? Besides, our magistrates [municipal authorities] ought to see to it that not only the sanitary condition be in order, but also that the roadway and the pavements be level, and not one stone higher than normal and the next one torn out — and then one falls and breaks one's neck when one does not notice it. Moreover, it is now winter, when it happens[?] that overnight a burst of snow comes pouring down and covers all the uneven places, so that the accidents immediately multiply and the public begins to walk through the streets as if over barricades[?]. And when a frost sets in and it becomes slippery, it is downright frightening to walk in the street; especially the fair sex, with their high narrow little heels, are afraid even to set foot.
The streets are particularly badly neglected. The properties[?] ("sisye") that belong to the house-owners — these must keep everything in line with the regulations so as not to be fined. On the squares and houses that belong to the town, on the other hand, the sanitary condition is taken lightly and the work is quite considerably neglected.
One must therefore not go on neglecting the towns of Zagłębie like this; their streets must be cleaned regularly[?] and carefully. But cleaning is still the least of it compared with the torn-out and sunken stones, which — the above having been forgotten[?] — [lie] not only across the width of the streets but also on the pavements themselves.
First of all one must see to it that the streets are paved. The citizens pay for the aesthetics of the town — they may at least have what concerns not only aesthetics but also health, and the danger of not becoming a cripple when going out into the street.
The ławnicy [aldermen of the municipal board] and the town councillors must take a keen interest in having the matter solved radically as quickly as possible; that is their sacred duty.
Selekt.
The Get (Divorce).

[Feuilleton — humorous story; life insurance and matchmaking.] A tale that happened not in Eishishok [Ejszyszki] and not in Honolulu, but here among us, and retold by Y. Oberzhanek [?].
— What's new?
— What should be new?
— What's new on the domestic-peace front?
— Better not ask, dear friend, it's bitter — I'm getting divorced.
— Why are you so astonished — how come, you ask, that I, Zelig Leizer, a father of grown-up children, am getting divorced, and from my Miriam Rachel at that? Such a good woman, such a housewife — to tear a mother from her children and children from their mother? You laugh? Perhaps I would laugh too, if the folly [?] weren't mine. You're lucky that you didn't insure your life and that you have no dealings with matchmakers.
Ah, you hear — the matchmakers! Because of the matchmaker I now have to divorce my Miriam Rachel.
— What happened?
You'll hear right away.
You know today's fashions; a new fashion has come out — insuring your life. Jews, "gornikes" [?], run around with briefcases from house to house and talk the wives into having their husbands take out policies, and wives need nothing more; and as you see [?] a man today — he has a policy in his pocket.
Sarah Leah the shopkeeper has a policy, and Breindl Frimet the pharmacist's wife [?] has a policy — so why shouldn't my Miriam Rachel have a policy? So she started eating me alive and nagging: Zelig Leizer, look, all the wives have policies. Why shouldn't I have one? A person is not noodle-groats after all. Even noodle-groats can get spilled... Cars race through the streets, you like to jump off the tram while it's moving, lately one hears of railway disasters, you [groan?] when you get a stitch in your side... who knows what can happen to such a broken vessel as you; listen to me and let yourself be insured. In the hundred-thousandth case, let me have a policy in my pocket.
And when a wife wants something — does anything help? And isn't she right? What is a person, after all? A person is like a soup pot: he boils and boils until he boils out. And what would really become of my Miriam Rachel if I, just like that, "unintentionally" [niechcący], boiled out? After all, I'm a played-out gramophone; I already have [rheumatism?] in my legs, I sneeze [?] with musical accompaniment, I sleep when she wants [?] to be awake... Well, it goes without saying that I had to take out a policy for my Miriam Rachel.
But that's not what I meant to tell you; the trouble is actually the matchmaker. God keep you from having to do with matchmakers when your wife has a policy in her pocket.
Hear a story:
As you know, I have a grown-up son, Velvele, a precious child — not like today's "ville-frantslekh" [?] with their short jackets [marynarki] and wide trousers, who [carouse?] whole days at the billiard table and "shoot" with the "sticks" and "eggs" [?], who don't know how to earn a broken penny, whose whole work consists of running around with girls and [—] [?]. My Velvele, may he be healthy and strong, is a successful child: he doesn't kick "goals" [bramki], doesn't play billiards, doesn't run after girls — a decent, solid young man. So what if he's a bit of a cripple, that he drags one foot a little and has a spot on his head like the moon every [?] month, and stammers a little? Nonsense. On the other hand he is modest [skromny], he doesn't belong to today's young people who will pick themselves a painted doll [lalka] and then tell their father "mazel tov"; my son knows that he has a father, may he live to a hundred and twenty, who understands a thing or two about such matters.
Recently my Miriam Rachel says to me: Zelig Leizer, what will be the end of it? We have to give some thought to Velvele. Are brides lacking [?] in Zagłębie today? It seems this "merchandise" is plentiful here — one need only whistle once. If there's a pair of trousers [?] — nowadays that's a groom!
So I turned to Itche Ber, the matchmaker, and asked him:
— Do you have something decent for my son, for my Velvele?
— Whether I have decent things? asks Itche Ber. I have a [?] of little etrogs, one by one, each prettier than the next [?]. What do you want — pedigree or money? Or both together, pedigree with money? Here, look — he shows me his book of records — here, he says, you can pick whatever your heart desires.
I began to [leaf?] [?] through the book of records — and really quite up-to-date stuff: brides aged 20 and aged 30 with apartments but without dowries, and brides with dowries but without apartments.
In the midst of it a notice caught my eye: a young widow with her own furnished apartment of three rooms and a kitchen, and besides the apartment the young widow also has a dowry of three thousand dollars, and she is looking for a young, healthy bachelor.
That's it, I say, that's what I like. A young widow, her own furnished apartment, and such a [dowry?] [?] on top of it — it's just what I'd have wished for my Velvele; he'll finally know what life is...
The next morning I took my Velvele; I put on my Sabbath kapote, Velvele put on a clean collar, polished his gaiters [kamasze] to a shine and [spruced up?] [?] — I and my son, together with the matchmaker Reb Itche Ber, so he would show us the young widow.
Imagine my surprise: the matchmaker leads us to the very house where I live.
Ah, very good, I say, in my own house, a neighbour even — here I'll be able to get the right information. But who can she be, I wonder, this young widow? I've lived in this house for ten years already, and I don't remember any of the neighbours having died.
But my surprise grew even greater when the matchmaker led us to my own apartment.
What's the matter with you? I asked the matchmaker, astonished. Why, I live here myself; you must be mistaken, Reb Itche Ber.
I'm not mistaken at all, the matchmaker answered in a confident tone.
Here is the young widow, said the matchmaker, pointing at my Miriam Rachel.
When my Miriam Rachel saw the matchmaker and the "groom" with the "in-law", she fainted. Neighbours, men and women, came running, they poured cold water, pressed her temples, and with great difficulty brought her round.
How do you come, Miriam Rachel, into Itche Ber's notebook? What sort of young widow are you? Have I died already, that you're looking for grooms?
Forgive me, Miriam Rachel began to sob, pouring out tears. It was a year ago today, when you, may it not happen today, lay sick with angina [tonsillitis]... I thought... the doctor... I wanted to "secure myself" [zabezpieczyć]...
Only now did the whole story become clear to me: a year ago today, when I was sick with angina, my Miriam Rachel remembered that she has a policy for three thousand dollars, an apartment of three rooms with a kitchen, with furniture — so why shouldn't she think about a decent match? And why not, indeed, with a "healthy" bachelor? So she wanted to "secure herself" in good time in Itche Ber's notebook.
That is how the matchmaker brought me into my own home and paired my son with his own mother. Because of the policy my Miriam Rachel became a "young widow" who, while I'm still alive, is looking for a young and healthy bachelor... And now I'm divorcing her. Rather than her wanting to become a young widow, I'd better remain a young divorcé.
May they be unthinkable — the agents with their policies!..
Will the voice of the tormented Jewish merchant be heard?

[Poland — economy; Jewish merchants and antisemitism.]
The idea of creating a Supreme Council of all Jewish economic organizations in Poland was launched a long time ago.
However, it ran into various obstacles of an organizational and also a political character.
To a certain extent the Supreme Council was held back by the recently deceased deputy Wiślicki, who was the de facto leader and the uncrowned king of Jewish merchantry in Poland, and to whose voice the authoritative circles used to listen with great interest.
After his death a void[?], an emptiness, was created in the merchants' ranks, from which[?] some evil[?], cold winds blow; and in order to fill this emptiness, and since it is impossible to find a person who would be able even partly to replace the late Wiślicki — the organizations, for which creating the Supreme Council is a matter of first-class importance, had to give up many of their ambitions so that the Supreme Council could be created.
We have three kinds of merchant organizations: the Central Merchants' Association with its branches, the Small Traders' Association with its branches, and independent merchant organizations which for certain reasons are not affiliated to the Central Merchants' Association.
On 24 November, thanks to the initiative of the Central Merchants' Association, a Supreme Council of Jewish Merchantry was created, and its executive includes representatives of the Central Merchants' Association, the Small Traders' Association and the more important independent merchant organizations, as well as the chairman, Mr. Józef Safer of Sosnowiec.
Thus a body was created which represents the whole organized Jewish merchantry in Poland.
In the earlier fragmentation of the merchant organizations there were frequent cases where one organization would obstruct another, and consequently the whole Jewish merchantry suffered.
Now an instrument has been created, a telephone, a loudspeaker, through which the entire Jewish merchant community will be able to voice its pain.
And there is much to voice, and even more to cry out about...
At the last meeting of the Supreme Council's executive, the question of the recent antisemitic outbreaks and of the boycott campaign against the Jewish merchant was dealt with in utmost seriousness.
The reports brought by the representatives of many towns aroused the greatest alarm and concern.
It became clear that the recent antisemitic outbreaks, directed by a well-organized hand, may undermine the existence of thousands of Jewish merchants and perhaps of the whole Jewish merchantry.
It also became clear that the struggle against us, waged on the economic plane, stops at no means whatsoever.
It is worth mentioning that the plan of the antisemitic students, who used to stand in front of Jewish shops so as not to let in any Christian customer, has now been taken over by ordinary hooligans, whom the Christian trader pays for every customer they bring him.
A new line of livelihood has been created for these "naganiacze" (touts), and one can easily imagine with what self-sacrifice the "naganiacze" tear customers away from the Jewish shops in order to get the few groszy from the Christian shopkeeper.
In recent days a larger[?] delegation of the Supreme Council visited the Minister of Commerce and the Minister of the Interior to present the ruin which the antisemitic outbreaks are bringing upon all Jewry in general and upon the Jewish merchant in particular.
Let us hope that the voice of the whole Jewish merchantry, expressed through the loudspeaker that bears the name "Supreme Council of Jewish Merchantry", will be heard and will have the proper effect.
M. Szuf.
A few words

[Będzin — housing; the tenants' association.]
On the "Remedy for the Plague".
(A reply to Mr. R. Let).
In the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" Mr. R. Let criticized the Będzin Tenants' Association, saying that all its work consists only of sending out the collector after the monthly dues.
As president of the Będzin Tenants' Association I do not hold it against Mr. R. Let that he characterizes the activity of the Tenants' Association in this way. It only annoys me why Mr. Let attributes to us the blame for the appearance of the decree on tenant protection. Our association has in fact existed for about 2 months, and it was created at a moment when it was seen that a danger threatened the tenants from the organized moves of the rich landlords. We fully agree with Mr. R. Let's remarks about the "benefits" that come to the tenant from the new decree, but we in no way agree with the author's remarks about the activity of our association. Instead of rebuking the association, Mr. R. Let should have rebuked the tenants at large, who have such an indifferent attitude to their own vital interests and to the newly arisen Tenants' Association. It is a disgrace to say that after distributing thousands of communiqués about the founding of the association, a total of 33 members signed up, already including the initiators. A still greater disgrace is that the collector, who was sent out to collect the monthly dues, brought back a whole 2 (two) złotys! Is it possible under such conditions to conduct an activity befitting such an institution? At the present moment we exist thanks to the hospitality of the Small Traders' Association, which places its premises and staff at our disposal without any payment.
As regards our activity, we would advise Mr. R. Let to acquaint himself with the copies of a series of our representations to various government and municipal institutions on various matters. It is especially worth noting that thanks to our representation to the Minister of Finance, the distraints for the premises tax on tenants have been stopped; tenants are exempted from this tax from 1 January 1936.
M. Landa.

Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec — weekly feuilleton; kehilla.] By Ben Amotz.

The power of forgetting...
Nature has endowed man with various powers and qualities, but the greatest role in human existence, in human energy, courage, enterprise — is played by the power of forgetting. This power makes man forget about the end, and only pushes him into the arms of the human lust for wealth, prosperity and earthly honour. And this is — in everyone's opinion — a very great plus for mankind, for were it not for forgetting, absolutely nothing would ever have been created, nothing would have been built and nothing would have existed.
The power of forgetting also plays a great role in public life. For example, when a communal worker gives his „word of honour“ that he will not accept the mandate offered to him, that he renounces his personal honour, we nevertheless see that it does not take long before the man in question has „forgotten“ what he said yesterday... Or another case: a communal worker who is insulted and smeared in a very ugly way decides to take revenge on the one who humiliated him; but then the power of forgetting intervenes, and not only does the insulted man forget everything, he even holds out his hand and begs forgiveness...
— And what are we getting at[?]? Here before us lies the latest number of the kehilla commissioner's „organ“, in which 2 (read: two) Sosnowiec personalities have been immortalised. Not only in praises and eulogies — but with... photographs, so that the „great Jewish world“ may indeed appreciate the greatness (at least through the photographs) that Sosnowiec possesses..
More photographs of a number of Sosnowiec communal activists wanted to be immortalised in this blackmail sheet, but unfortunately these are good-for-nothing people: not one of them has risen to the rank of a director, nor to the rank of a house-owner. They are not even Zionist representatives, and above all, the power of forgetting is poorly developed in them. They therefore remember to keep away from that scoundrel at every step, not to be found within his four cubits, and thanks to that the poor things have not been granted the „honour“ of having their photographs appear in this blackmail sheet.
And the same, God forbid, would have happened to the national activist, had the power of forgetting not been so strongly developed in him — in the Zionist activist, that is; for then he would surely have remembered that moment when he simply turned worlds upside down, running to his party comrades with a [—]itsaki[?], saying that deeds must be done: „To root out[?] the blister[?] that has settled on the body of Jewish society in Sosnowiec, that it is the commandment of the hour to teach this rascal[?] (quoted verbatim) a chapter in decent conduct, to hand him — this dissolute[?] lawless youth — over to legal responsibility for his base lies about the finest and best of Jewish Sosnowiec“.
But that was said a few months ago, in the year 1935, and the photographs, after all, appeared in the year 1936...
And with the Zionist activist an even greater „miracle“ happened, thanks to which he was granted [—] „honour“. — Not only has he forgotten what he himself said, but also — what was said to him... And it was said to him not by just anyone, but by none other than the self-appointed[?] head of the kehilla (the financier of the „revolver sheet“), who gave the Zionist representative the same honour that he himself received through the photograph...
And therefore we say that the greatest role in a creature of flesh and blood is played by — the power of forgetting..

When the bells ring — it's a holiday...
„Nie możemy dłużej milczeć“ „We can no longer keep silent“! — under such noisy headings begins the appeal that has been distributed in Sosnowiec in recent days and is signed by „a group of non-partisan householders in Sosnowiec“.
At the first moment we were simply all but sure that the appeal bore a character concerning all of Jewry — presumably (so we thought) a call to all of Israel about[?] voicing a general protest against the decrees, pain and suffering that pour onto Jewish heads in the Diaspora, and against[?] the Legislative Council in Eretz Israel in particular — so we thought; but after reading the first lines of the „jednodniówka“ [one-off leaflet] it only then became clear that the „group of non-partisan householders“ are taking up the injury[?] done to the „important personality, well-known communal worker, great philanthropist, who faithfully attends to communal needs“, and above all: „the kehilla receives a full 100 per cent“, and every Jew in Sosnowiec „has from time to time a spiritual delight from the sermons about kosher feet[?], Hanukkah candles“ etc., etc.
We do not wish this time to pour a bitter drop into the great cup of joy which the „non-partisan householders“ have offered to the kehilla commissioner — may it do him good! — but from the praises and eulogies we gather something else: we understand that if the „important personality“, who has such „colossal merits“ (not from the kehilla[?] and pump-bellies[?]...) for the Sosnowiec kehilla, must actually come to need the approval of Reb Leizer Paganier[?], then something in the commissioner's little world is not quite right — as the saying goes:
— „When the bells ring — it's a holiday“...
“Correct sources” for the history of the Mysłowice Jews in the light of “Polonia”

[Silesia — antisemitic press; history of the Jews of Mysłowice.]
The Christian-Democratic (Chadecja) “Polonia” [the Katowice daily], which considers itself a very important paper on Jewish affairs and which is read with considerable relish by nationalist Jews, does not yield in its antisemitism to the “Karta Polska” [?].
In the New Year issue of this paper we find a piece of “history” of the Jewish population of Mysłowice, and here is what the Polish reader has learned:
“It is not known exactly from what time Jews first settled in Mysłowice. It is only known that in the year 1511 Jews were not tolerated; until the year 1500 [sic] Jews had absolutely no right to live in the town or to engage in trade. Only around the year 1560 do we find Jews in the town engaged in trade. One of the first Jews was a certain Aharon Moshe, a leaseholder (arendator), who was hated by these burghers, and yet the youth of Mysłowice always spent their time at his place (!).
At the end of the 16th century 6 Jewish families, 62 souls in all, were expelled from the town without the right to return. The cause was the accusation that the Jews had murdered a Christian child. In connection with this many Jews were also killed. The expelled Jews, disregarding the ban, came back nonetheless, built themselves little houses, and even tried to settle in the centre of the town.”
With great joy the author further relates that at that time, until the year 1600, Jews were not allowed to lend money, to sell land, were not admitted to public offices, and were also forbidden to adorn themselves with golden belts and [ornaments — doubtful word], but had to wear special garments and yellow garments or berets, and the author quotes further:
Only at the end of the 17th century were Jews given municipal rights; the local clergy was then very indignant at this state of affairs. In particular, the provost (proboszcz) of the time, the priest Surotka [?], protested strongly against giving the Jews these rights.
After Silesia was joined to Prussia, the Jews became loyal Prussian citizens and denounced the Christians. Such a denunciation took place at that time in the case of the Christian Juriczek [?], who was sentenced to death for high treason. The informer was a certain Moshe [printed “Kshe”] Izakowicz, who at that time handed many Christians over to the Prussians. Some time later Izakowicz was killed in his own house with axes and his family was beaten bloody. From that moment anti-Jewish excesses began in Silesia, which were, however, soon suppressed by detachments of the Prussian military.
Continuing its “historical” account of how the pogroms, the [—] [?] and the excesses developed, “Polonia” joyfully arrives at the conclusion that the Jews are leaving Mysłowice more and more.
At present Mysłowice counts in all 300 Jews. The greater part of them moved to the nearest towns, Katowice and Chorzów. Many Jews moved to Zagłębie, and many even to Palestine, where they took with them quite large capital. In November (listopad) of this year two more Jewish businesses in Mysłowice were liquidated. With every day the number of Jews in Mysłowice grows smaller. In time there will surely be no Jews there at all; they will move only to where they expect better business.
The author of this “historical” sketch, who is so overjoyed that Mysłowice will soon be “free of Jews”, ought however to be consistent and thorough and to prevail upon the owners of “Polonia” not to accept any advertisements from Jews (as, for example, the advertisement of a Jewish lawyer [?], which is printed on the very same page on which the inflammatory article is printed). That could, after all, have the effect that the Jewish merchants would emigrate from Katowice too...
(Sh. —G.)
Zagłębie olim create a relief fund of 1,000 pounds

[Palestine — immigrants from Zagłębie and Silesia.]
For olim (immigrants) from Zagłębie and Silesia.
(From our correspondent.)
As we already wrote in the previous issue of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung”, an association of olim from Zagłębie and Upper Silesia has been founded in Tel Aviv.
The committee, which was elected, held a consultation with the participation of various Zionist activists from Zagłębie.
The consultation took place in the Café Gdański [?] under the chairmanship of Mr. Binyamin Fishel (Sosnowiec), who greeted those present and pointed out the importance of immediately creating a fund called “Quick Help” with a capital of 1,000 pounds, which is to be raised from well-to-do olim in Palestine (Eretz Israel) and also from Zagłębie capitalists abroad. The purpose of the relief fund is to help the Jews of Zagłębie, the middle class and artisans, to establish themselves in Palestine, and also those who already live in the country and are in need of material help.
It was also decided to get in touch with the Jewish Agency and to call on it to allot a large area of Keren Kayemet land in the vicinity of the city for intensive farming, with small loans repayable over a number of years, for the Zagłębie olim.
Mr. Fishel also pointed to the possibility of realizing the plan with the help of those present, and proposed co-opting onto the committee Messrs. Avraham Hampel (Będzin) and Yitzhak Meir Stark (Sosnowiec).
Mr. Hampel, thanking them for the honour, declared that he will take an active part in the above-mentioned campaign.
Also taking part in the discussion were Messrs. Friedman, Chaim Welner [?], Meir Jungster and others, who expressed their thanks to Mr. Fishel for his energetic activity. After the adoption of a number of proposals, the consultation was closed with the singing of “Hatikvah”.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shemot)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemot
—o—
a) "I have surely seen the affliction of My people" (Ex. 3:7)
"It does not say 'I have seen' but 'seeing I have seen' — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: You see one sight and I see two sights. You see them coming to Mount Sinai and receiving My Torah, and I see them receiving My Torah, and this is 'seeing' — 'I have seen' — that is the deed of the Golden Calf, as it is said: 'I have seen this people'." Midrash Rabbah.
Why, then, did Moses, the chief of the prophets, who saw everything through a clear glass, see no more than one sight — the receiving of the Torah — and not the deed of the Calf?
Because — Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev answered — the tzaddik who sees the sins [?] of Jews in truth sees nothing; he is no seer... Moses saw in the Jews only their virtue [?], the receiving of the Torah, but not the deed of the Calf.
• • •
Once a maggid came to Olyka [?] to preach, and he spoke about the neglect of Torah, about the lack of piety among Jews, etc. [?];
the Baal Shem Tov, who happened to be there, rebuked him:
"You dare to speak ill of Jews? A Jew runs around the market a whole day, and towards evening he catches himself: Oh dear, I almost missed praying Minchah! — and he runs into the house, snatches a Minchah, and sometimes does not even know [?] what he is saying — and a commotion is heard in heaven..."
—o—
b) "Unto a good land and a large" (ibid., 3:8)
God first enumerated to Moses the economic virtues of the Land of Israel: "a land flowing with milk and honey", "a good land and a large"; but when Moses later passed God's words on to the elders of Israel, he spoke of the land's economic virtues at the end.
Because Moses was speaking to the elders, to the righteous, and for them "flowing with milk and honey" is not the main thing... Whereas God delivered [the message] to all Jews, and for the ordinary Jew "flowing with milk and honey" plays a great role...
—o—
c) "Jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment" (ibid., 3:22)
God commanded that the Jewish women should borrow from the Egyptian women their finery, gold and silver vessels and clothes; yet further on, in the portion Bo, where the verse lists what they borrowed, jewels of silver and jewels of gold are mentioned, but no clothes.
Apparently it is easier for women to lend out [?] gold and silver objects than clothes...
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
d) "But they will not believe me" (4:1)
"Me" — me they will not believe; they will not believe that I, who was brought up in Pharaoh's house, who dress like an Egyptian — that I will bring them the redemption. The people trusts only one of its own [?], a man dressed like them.
Netziv.
—o—
e) "The God of Israel", "the God of the Hebrews" (5:1)
When Moses said to Pharaoh "Thus saith the Lord, God of Israel", Pharaoh asked: "Who is the Lord, that I should hearken unto His voice?" — he knew of no such god at all; and only later, when Moses spoke to him in the name of "the God of the Hebrews", he no longer asked him [?] "who is the God of the Hebrews" —
because the God of the Jews was known then as "the God of the Hebrews", the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who were called "Hebrews"; of Him Pharaoh had heard, whereas "the God of Israel" was something new to him.
Rosh.
—o—
f) "And the officers of the children of Israel were beaten" (ibid., 5:14)
"Va-yuku" with a shuruk [?], meaning that the officers of the children of Israel were beaten because they had tormented the Jews too little.
And that is why they are mentioned in the Torah: because a Jew must be able to take blows for the sake of another Jew...
Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasów.
—o—
g) "And Moses was content to dwell with the man" (2:21)
"When Moses said to Jethro: Give me Zipporah your daughter as a wife, Jethro said to him: I give her to you on condition that the first son to be born shall be for idolatry, and from then on for the sake of Heaven."
Mekhilta, portion Yitro.
How could Moses agree that one of his sons should belong to idolatry?
Because he knew that in his offspring there was bound to be something [?] bad from the blood [?] of the mother's stock [?], and rather than have a mixture of good and bad in all the children, he preferred that the children be divided — the good ones solely to God and the bad ones solely to idolatry...
Imrei No'am [?].
The “Division”

(After La Fontaine)
What is mine is mine and what is yours is mine — a wicked man
(Avot ch. 5)
A cow, a little sheep and a goat
Made a pact, “one hand”, with the lion,
That there should be no more quarrel between them,
But all should live in peace and contentment.
Whatever prey any of them finds,
Be it [?] or merely poultry [drób],
Be the meal poor or rich —
It must be shared out equally.
Now it so happens that a ram [baran]
Strays onto a meadow [łąka] where there is a swamp,
And can no longer get out of there.
Just then, grazing there beforehand,
Was the little sheep, the partner of the four.
Its joy was very great,
It at once sent off a courier [sztafeta]
And thereupon called the whole company.
The lion, as is known,
Was there at once with the “cutting” and the “uncovering” [circumcision terms — i.e. ready to carve],
And as the chief in-law,
He cut the victim into four.
And solemnly His Majesty declared:
The first part comes to me as is proper,
For that I need bring no proofs,
I am, after all, king over all the beasts;
The second part too is for me alone
As a partner of us four;
The third part belongs to me as well,

The Bastard (70) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishkovski

[Serial novel — instalment 70] By Adv. S. Gelishkovski.

Broken, full of despair, they came back from there, where they no longer found Leon. As they were told, he had left for America, where he had been engaged as a film artist; but they do not believe it. Leon an artist? How, when could he have become that? they asked themselves, but they got no answer to the question.

Very broken was Matilda by the news that Balbina and Luiza had brought from Warsaw [?].
"Yes, yes," she sighed, "I shall never see my child again."
And at that, rivers of tears poured from her eyes.

"Why won't you see him?" asks Luiza. "Is America today what it once was? Today one travels there and comes back from there in ten days. Today it is, as it were, within arm's reach. He could have travelled to America and come back; and secondly, you may [?], Matilda, also travel freely [?] to him, if you want to see him."
"What are you saying, Luiza! I should travel to him in America? I have no worth at all for him. His feelings for his mother have been stifled by his feelings for Balbina. Only she can give me back my son. Only she can reawaken in him his feelings for me, of that I am sure."
Balbina had sat the whole time sunk in her thoughts, listening to the conversation of the two sisters. These last few days she has been going about like a madwoman. She has neglected the household at Max's home, which she had run in exemplary fashion, something Max used to be delighted with; she has neglected her child, neglected him, Max himself — and not because of anyone else but because of Leon, whom she had all but forgotten.
Time, which is the best doctor, had already healed her of the wounds of her unhappy love for Leon, and now everything had broken open anew. Everything had torn apart anew in her heart, where the wounds had already been completely healed.

She had already grown used to Max, who is a full twenty years older than she — she could have been his daughter. True, he cannot be Leon's rival; Leon is handsomer, younger than he; but all her experiences had made her so tired that she was content with her present life. In the time she has been with Max she has had peace of mind, and she would already have agreed to live out her years in this way with the man who is more to her than a father, more even than a husband — for what is a husband, if he is not at the same time also a woman's companion in life? And that, after all, happens very often in life. Max is a devoted friend to her and also her life's companion; she is to him like the apple of his eye. And what does the world say? If you don't have what you want, you must want what you have — and for her that is Max, who loves her, who can secure her future and the future of her and his child.

But otherwise is man's fate: man plans and God laughs.
Balbina, who had already begun to persuade herself [?] that she had completely forgotten Leon, that all the threads that had ever bound them were already completely torn, had felt from the moment she met Matilda that she had made a great mistake about her feelings for Leon, whom she loves even now; and learning from her how Leon had suffered and still suffers, and all because of her, she was seized by a strong longing for the man who had awakened in her a woman's passionate love. Yes, she also loves Max, but differently, not like him, like Leon, whom she will perhaps never forget. "Ah, how good it would be if I could live with both of them" — the foolish, empty thought ran [?] through her mind — "how good it would be if they would both agree to it."
"Balbina," Luiza interrupts her thoughts, "I believe you will not refuse Matilda's proposal and will travel with her to America to search for Leon."
"What are you saying, Luiza! How can I do that? What will Max say to that? I would shatter his life completely, and how can I do that? He is so good [?] to me."
"And Leon? Don't you know that Leon is suffering and will go on suffering for a long time?"
Matilda tried [?] to awaken her feelings for Leon. "Is he not worth it, for what he has done for you, that you should throw everything away and run to the one who is pining with longing for you, Balbina? If there is still a spark of pity for me in you, though I have not deserved it, if even one spark of your former love has remained in you, then you must not be so indifferent to his tragic life. There, with him, is your place; there, with him, is where you must be, because he loves you even now."

A hysterical cry mingled with sobbing tore through the quiet atmosphere of Matilda's room. It was Balbina weeping and sobbing, she who had been silent the whole time:
"The curse pursues me; a quiet, calm life is not destined for me."

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Meeting of the Local City Council

[Head of the local page; Będzin — City council.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 22 Tevet 5696 — piątek 17 stycznia 1936 [Friday, 17 January 1936].)
Będzin
Meeting of the local city council.
Jewish proposals and amendments rejected.
Tuesday's city council meeting dragged on until 1 a.m. At the meeting the Jewish tragedy again revealed itself in all its nakedness: our fragmentation, and the non-Jewish „front“ on the smallest question that concerns Jews. During the debates about lean and fat meat there is still a difference of opinion among the non-Jewish groupings, but when it comes to getting milk from the „milch cow“, everyone agrees on it, both from the left and from the right.
A great part of the blame is borne by the Jewish councillors themselves. Unity is lacking; agenda questions are not dealt with beforehand, before the meeting; because of this such disorientation prevails that Jewish councillors vote against Jewish proposals...
———
President [mayor] Iwidarczyk[?] opens the meeting with a New Year speech, in which he points to the work of the city administration so far, among other things the road to the Małobądz and Gzichów[?] area, etc.
Councillor Błażejewicz delivers the report of the audit commission, which during its inspection of the market halls and the slaughterhouse found certain irregularities concerning the payments for trading on the premises of the halls, and arrears owed by the holders of the „budki“ [stalls] at the market. The commission came forward with a proposal that the traders pay for 2 months „z góry“ [in advance].
The president does not agree with the proposal, which could — he says — lead to the traders, who are poor people, having to give up trading at the market.
Councillor Goldsztajn proposes that, following the example of the government, the magistrate too should cancel the old debts of the market traders; to this the president replies that the proposal will be considered with the new budget.
A longer discussion develops over the municipal tax on turnover and on patents [trade licences]. On the part of the Jewish councillors the following amendments and proposals are submitted: 1) from Councillor Goldsztajn, that 7th and 8th category industrial patents be free of the levy; 2) from Councillor Montag[?], that 16 per cent be taken from turnover and 20 per cent from patents; and 3) from Councillor Jakubowicz, to exempt from the tax the small traders who hold category 4 and 5.
Councillor Solski is for passing over all the proposals to the order of the day.
President: Our task is not to reduce the tax revenues, because we would thereby bring about an economic crisis.
Alderman [ławnik] Rubinlicht strongly defends the reduction proposal and among other things says: If you, Mr. President, are afraid of economic suicide, then first examine the „hearts“[?] of those from whom you want to take the tax.
But all the arguments have no effect, and with the votes of the „Workers' Club“ and the Sanacja the Jewish proposals are rejected.
The same fate befell the statute of the tax on immovable property, of which the municipal surcharge amounts to 85 per cent.
Alderman Rubinlicht speaks out against the high tax and proposes that it be fixed at 53[?] per cent, as in Dąbrowa.
Councillor Montag[?] describes the situation of most house-owners, who have become impoverished and now have smaller incomes, because rents have become cheaper.
Councillor Grinwald also speaks for the proposal. Against it speak the „left“ councillors, one of whom permitted himself to shout out such a piece of „wisdom“: „What[?] the Jews possess is only from the workers, because the Jews do not work.“
All amendments are rejected and the same rate as until now is adopted at once.
Because of the late hour the meeting is broken off.
From the Commercial Agents.

[Będzin — Economic organisations.]
From the Commercial Agents.
In the premises of the Merchants' Association the first meeting took place of the newly founded section of commercial agents.
Mr. M. Lewin in his introduction points to the permanently abnormal situation of the commercial agents, who always find themselves between hammer and anvil; and this — says Mr. L. — is precisely what compelled the founding of the section, and it is to be hoped that every agent will understand what situation he is in and will enrol in the section.
———
After the introduction a discussion develops, during which various proposals surface, among others to have a permanent fund to lend to agents without means for buying patents [trade licences], and still various very[?] important proposals; but unfortunately all these proposals were not adopted, pending a larger number of members. Finally a temporary board is elected, consisting of: Lewin, Fajner and Hajgsztok[?].
It was also decided that from the moment a larger number of members have enrolled, the association should become independent, and not, as until now, attached to the Merchants' Association.

Sosnowiec: Suicide of a Jewish Doctor

[Sosnowiec — suicide; medicine.] Jewish Sosnowiec is under the heavy impression of the mysterious suicide committed by the beloved 32-year-old Jewish doctor Oskar Weger [Yiddish וועגער].
On Sunday towards evening Dr. Weger travelled to Katowice, where he rented a room at the Hotel "Monopol". He told the hotel staff to wake him at 8 o'clock in the morning.
When the servants began knocking at the door at the appointed hour and no answer came from inside, they broke the door open and saw that Dr. Weger was lying dead on the bed.
The doctor who was called established that Dr. Weger had committed suicide by injecting himself with a sizeable dose of morphine.
On Monday the body was brought to Sosnowiec, and the next day at noon the funeral took place from the Jewish hospital.
At the open grave eulogies were delivered: in the name of the Jewish hospital and the medical staff — the hospital's director Dr. Weinzieher, [who said] that Dr. Weger had fallen a victim owing to his gentleness[?]; in the name of the Doctors' Association — Dr. Selaris-sa[?]. The eulogies pointed to the great work of Dr. Weger, who had made a name for himself among doctors and done much for Jewish society.
What was the cause of the suicide?
Various versions about the terrible suicide have been circulating. But according to authoritative information, Dr. Weger fell a victim to his profession because of the great measure of gentleness and humanity he possessed.
Some [—] time ago Dr. Weger, on the recommendation of the well-known surgeon and chief head of the hospital, Dr. Jankowski, was taken on in a post in the pavilion[?] for tuberculosis patients of the municipal hospital at Pogoń[?], where the following case occurred. A young Christian woman, gravely ill with tuberculosis, on whom Dr. Weger had performed an "odma" [artificial pneumothorax] — died.
This incident, which happened last Saturday, was however exploited as incitement against Dr. Weger, [claiming] that he was to blame for the patient's death. The accusation made a heavy impression on the doctor, and he could not free himself from the terrible nervous strain.
The next afternoon he went to the hospital at Pogoń to see Dr. Jankowski and pour out his bitter heart to him, but fate willed that the car in which Dr. Jankowski had left in the morning broke down on the way, so that Dr. Jankowski was set to return only at noon, as Dr. Weger had thought.
Coming back home, he told his wife that he was going to a patient. His wife, seeing that he was very agitated, began to press[?] him not to go, but he explained to her that he had to go because the patient was waiting for him, and that he would be back in an hour.
When several hours had passed, the wife began telephoning acquaintances and the hospital, but everywhere she was answered that he was not there.
Only the next day was the tragedy learned of — that he had committed suicide at the Hotel "Monopol" in Katowice.
Dr. Jankowski, wishing to rehabilitate the honour of the victim, spared[?] no effort and money to have an autopsy performed on the [deceased] patient.
The autopsy, which took place on the day of the funeral, was carried out by a group of specialist doctors, and it turned out that Dr. Weger had performed the "odma" in the best order, and that the patient had been hopeless, because her lungs were already completely decayed[?].
Dr. Weger was the only son of his parents; his father is a doctor in Włodzimierz Wołyński [Vladimir-Volynsk].
The medical staff of the Jewish hospital has decided to commemorate the tragically deceased Dr. Weger with a marble plaque, which will be placed in one of the hospital rooms.

[Kehilla — community tax ("etat").] The commissarial president of the kehilla has sent out to all payers of the community tax ["etat"] "wezwania" [summonses/demands] concerning the kehilla tax.

On Saturday night a heavy downpour (sleet-rain) swept over Zagłębie, accompanied by lightning and thunder, just as in summer. In Koszelew [?] the wind tore off part of the roofs of the houses there.
In [—] a thunderbolt struck a barn (stodoła), where a fire broke out. Everything that was in the barn went up in smoke.
Further Acts of Terror against the Jewish Shops in Kielce

[Kielce — antisemitism.] The acts of terror by the "gart-people" [?] against the Jewish shops in Kielce do not stop. After a "pause" of several days, stink bombs were again thrown into the shop of Mr. Zomer on the Bazaar Square, into the bakery of Mr. Hasser on Ra-Maszadska [?] Street and, this Wednesday towards evening, into the fruit shop of Mr. Silberstein on Duża [?] Street. Luckily the bomb, instead of falling into the shop, fell onto the pavement and did Mr. Silberstein no great damage.
A delegation of the Jewish merchants and small traders recently presented itself to the chief of the security office of the Kielce voivodeship, gave him the details of the acts of terror carried out against the Jewish shops in Kielce and asked him to take energetic measures to secure the life and property of the Jewish population.
The chief of the security office received the delegation very cordially, listened attentively to the account of all the acts of terror, which, as he himself declared, are quite well known to him, and declared to the delegation that the necessary orders had been issued so that such unheard-of deeds will not be repeated any more. The chief promised that within a few days the activity of the terror gang would be liquidated.
Rumours are also going round town that this week, in connection with the acts of terror against the Jewish shops, arrests have been made of the bomb-throwers and their instigators, among them several Endek "bigwigs".
As reported, today, Friday, a kehilla delegation headed by Rabbi Rapaport will present itself to the Kielce voivode, Dr. Dziadosz, and ask him to issue the sharpest orders against the wild hooligan excesses, by whose shameful deeds they [bdil h"l — reading uncertain] and ruin the Jewish merchants.
The Jewish population believes that the visit to the Kielce voivode will have the proper effect.
The 20th Yahrzeit of the Chęciny Rebbe of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — Hasidism.] This Monday, 18 Tevet, fell the 20th yahrzeit of the Chęciny Rebbe, R' Chaim Shmuel Horowitz of blessed memory, whose ohel [tomb] is in the Kielce cemetery.
For the yahrzeit a great crowd of several hundred Hasidim and many rabbis and rebbes of the Chęciny dynasty came to Kielce.
The throng in the ohel was great, and from the content of the [kvitlekh? — word missing in print] one could recognise the Jewish troubles and want. The main theme of all the laments was the terrible Jewish want, the dreadful poverty now prevailing among Jews, the intensified antisemitism and the latest sharpened boycott campaign against Jews.
A LOPP Committee Founded at the Jewish Boot-Upper Makers' Guild

[Kielce — organisations.] Last Saturday, the 11th of this month, under the chairmanship of the president of the LOPP [Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] committee, Mr. Polit, with the participation of the board members Messrs. Kuszjuszegowski [?] and Wieczorek, as well as representatives of the starosty and the Chamber of Crafts, an organising meeting of the Jewish cholewka [boot-upper] makers was held in the LOPP premises concerning the organisation of a LOPP committee.
After hearing the reports of the chairman, Mr. Grangasman [?], and of instructor Sobel, as well as the speech of the representative of the starosty, Captain Serkang [?], it was resolved to organise a LOPP committee at the guild of the Jewish cholewka makers in Kielce.
At the said meeting a board and an audit committee were also elected.
At the meeting 36 members signed declarations.
The creation of a new LOPP committee is the result of the planned work which the district LOPP committee conducts among the Jewish population, which it wishes to draw into cooperation in building the state's defence.
This is already the third guild of Jewish craftsmen at which LOPP committees have been organised.
It is to be hoped that the work of the new committee will develop properly, that all members of the guild will unite around the committee's work, and that such LOPP committees will also be created at the other Jewish guilds.

A Great Recruitment Campaign for the Jewish Library

[Kielce — culture.] As was already reported in the last issue of our paper, the collection campaign for the Jewish library in Kielce has been concluded with great success. With the money collected a large number of the newest books in Polish, Hebrew and Yiddish will be bought.

It is therefore to be hoped that the Jewish public in Kielce, which responded so warmly to and supported the collection campaign, will also, with still greater interest, help in the campaign to recruit new members, who will secure the library a normal existence.

Dąbrowa

Hooligan attack outside the Zionist premises.
On Saturday night a group of young people walking along Sobieski Street was attacked by several drunken brawlers (awanturnicy), who threw themselves on the young people and beat them.
About this attack we have received the following communiqué from the Dąbrowa Zionist Organisation:
On Saturday 18 January at about 11 p.m., when members of the Zionist Organisation began to leave the premises, a band of hooligans suddenly ran up — among them was also the well-known feldsher (medical orderly) Karo[?]-lewski — and threw themselves on the Zionists going home. As a result the chairman, Dr. Icchak Sztajnberg, was knocked to the ground. His face was battered[?], his glasses smashed and his hat stolen; Messrs. Icchak Bernsztajn and Mordechai Rozenblum, who ran up to rescue chairman Sztajnberg, were attacked with revolvers to the cry of the above-mentioned: „I'll shoot you all“. Besides this, Michał Winer and Natan Stuszegowski were beaten up. The latter had his clothes slashed with a razor and his shoulder scratched till it bled.
The police drew up a report on this incident and sent it to the public prosecutor's office.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — A Big Erets-Israel Mass Meeting.

[Upper Silesia — Zionism; Mizrachi.]
(Y. S.)[?] Last Sunday evening[?] the Katowice Mizrachi organization held a mass meeting in the kehilla hall devoted to Erets-Israel problems.
Mr. Gros opened the meeting and greeted the distinguished speakers: Rabbi Chamejes [probably Dr. Kalman Chameides, rabbi of Katowice], Dr. Hirszfeld (Bielsko-Biała) and the rabbi of Andrychów. Having explained the purpose of the meeting, he gave the floor to Rabbi Chamejes, who on this occasion gave a short speech, supporting with a number of very interesting arguments the Mizrachi ideals and the religious-national education of Jewish youth, and quoting, among others, the opinions and views of Jewish religious scholars on the purpose of our life in exile. Rabbi Chamejes closed with a "welcome" (brukhim ha-baim) to the next two speakers.
Rabbi Dr. Hirszfeld said, among other things, that the Jewish situation today[?] is much worse and more tragic than in the dark Middle Ages. Then Jews had a free, open world to wander and emigrate to; persecuted in one country, they were taken in by another. Moreover, the Jewish people was then united, there was one authority in all questions of Jewish life, and the Jewish family too was firmly united in one aspiration — not like today, when the soul is torn and opinions are divided. Even Jewish suffering then had a meaning, a purpose.
The Andrychów rabbi said that the Jewish people is always hated because it is the embodiment of freedom and democracy and a living protest against all kinds of dictators; the world no longer wants to accept the old "Thou shalt not kill", and above all it wants nothing spiritual from us — therefore it grabs with both hands and squeezes out our material possessions.
All the speakers in their addresses called on the audience to support the Keren Erets-Israel.
The large audience applauded the rabbis warmly.
The meeting closed with the singing of "Hatikvah".
Later a banquet was held in the Mizrachi premises.
