A World of "We Are All Holy"... The People and Its Benefactors, Then and Now.

The people and its "benefactors", then and now.
How can such a situation end, in which everyone — that is, everyone at the top of the "shpeyger"[?], at the top of the helm, at the top of the seats — is a great man, a genius, a saint, an upright man, in short holiness itself, while all those who have no claws and no elbows stay on the sidelines and are decried, torn down or hushed up — relegated to the lower ranks?...
Say what you will — before the ruinous war it was not like this. Then one knew: this one is a fine man and that one — a scoundrel; this one — a gentleman and that one — a boor; this one — a hard toiler and that one — an idler, a parasite; this one a scholar and that one an ignoramus; this one a talent and that one a graphomaniac, a plagiarist. Now, however, it has become a generation of the Tower of Babel, chaos, the categories completely mixed up, impossible to sort out who is this and who is that; all of them are the cream of the world, "we are all holy", as the money-bag Korah once said... All of them save the world, all of them are world benefactors, redeemers, "messiahs" — not a degree less...
And if one wanted to penetrate to the core to find out what the shouters and noisemakers have accomplished, not for themselves but for the community, one would discover to one's surprise — nothing! Absolutely nothing — pure bluff!
And if one overcame the feeling of disgust and took a look behind the curtain, behind the scenes of all the "city benefactors", world benefactors, "messiahs" and "liberators", one would see — little people, intriguers, careerists, who wrap impurity in a cloak of holiness — to blind the eyes.
In the past too there were communal workers, people's representatives and, in particularly evil times — shtadlanim (intercessors), who loved the people without tricks, were devoted to it to their last breath and truly sacrificed themselves for it. The people has not forgotten its true great men and faithful communal leaders.
They were crystal-pure souls of chosen people, whose life was truly a holy life and to whom it never even occurred to consider themselves saints; on the contrary, they were always dissatisfied with themselves and held that they had never done their duty towards God and the people. Those were the exalted souls of whom I. L. Peretz dreamed in his "Folkstimlekhe geshikhtn" (Folk-style Stories).
Even in the last several decades there were great public workers who adorned Jewish Zagłębie with colossal institutions, and even today there still go about among us former communal leaders of the above-mentioned type, heads bowed like the dethroned, with a deep pain in their hearts, watching the froth of the modern public bluffing and its sad results..
Once Jews had God in their hearts and lived their lives in a living Judaism. They sought no one's kosher certificate for their Torah, believed in the eternal survival of the nation, believed in the ingathering of the exiles and in redemption through the Messiah — and they built themselves a magnificent, original cultural edifice, maintaining it all by themselves without any support from any side, neither from foreign lands nor from foreign states.
But all that was once, when there were individual holy men[?]; today there are no individual holy men — today everyone is holy, "we are all holy" — all "representatives", all gabbaim, all city benefactors, who have taken the whole Jewish world on lease and "do NOT graze among the sheep" — and so today we have destruction, chaos along the whole line: in public life as in the whole of culture — in the fields of Jewish schooling, Jewish literature and press, Jewish art, Jewish theatre and Jewish science.
This was brought about only by the self-crowned rulers over all these fields, who fundamentally hate the people and now dance self-satisfied on the ruins of the people and its spiritual values.
A. J. Goldszmidt.
The Amended Decree on Tenant Protection

Disputes between landlords and tenants. — Base rent. — Divided apartments. — How the reduction is applied. — How an overpaid sum is reclaimed.
Our recent observation proved accurate: that the amended decree on tenant protection gives landlords many times greater concessions than tenants, and that even from the rent reduction the tenants will not experience any significant relief.
We based this assertion on the state of affairs that most tenants, having withheld or even accumulated rent debts, or court-ordered evictions, will not have the „boldness“ to demand a rent reduction; that at best only the better-situated, and hence punctually paying, tenants can count on such a reduction — but in many cases their rent has already been reduced voluntarily, so that under the present reduction they no longer come into consideration; and that many landlords will try, by various means, often not particularly ethical, or by all sorts of quibbles and tricks, to influence the remaining tenants to renounce the reduction or to agree to a compromise.
Barely a month has passed since the said decree came into force, and the mass of disputes that have arisen on this ground in the meantime between tenants and landlords fully confirm the correctness of our forecast.
On the present occasion we shall therefore clarify some such points of contention that have arisen.
—
The rent reduction is calculated not according to the present current rent, but according to the base level of June 1914 or according to the assessment of the „shirs-amt“[?] (probably the tax office).
But what if the situation of June 1914 cannot be established and no assessment by the „shirs-amt“[?] has been made either? Since the same tenant has already lived in the apartment for many years and has paid the same sum of rent throughout that whole time, the reduction must be calculated according to the last sum actually paid.
—
Apartments partitioned off from larger dwellings are not subject to the provisions of the tenant-protection decree if the lease was concluded after 1 grudzień [December] 1935.
If, however, such an apartment was rented before 1 December 1935, it is indeed subject to the tenant-protection decree and consequently also to the provisions on reducing rent.
Commercial and industrial premises, except those occupied by enterprises that buy [?] or 7th, alternatively 4th category patents, are not subject to the rent reduction. If, however, the private dwellings of the proprietors are located next to the business premises, the rent for those dwellings must indeed be reduced.
If the base rent for such business and residential premises has not been set separately, the tenants concerned may apply to the court to have the rent of the dwelling set separately, and accordingly they will then be allowed to reduce the relevant sum of rent.
The same rule can also apply to cases where a commercial (4th category) or a workshop (8th or 7th category) premises adjoins the private dwelling. In such cases too the rent can be set separately; then the dwelling will be reduced by 15 percent and the business premises by 10 percent.
It should be remembered in this connection that the work premises of the free professions (offices and consulting rooms of doctors, lawyers, dentists, feldshers, midwives), premises of professional unions, of social, educational and cultural institutions are regarded as private dwellings; they are subject to a rent reduction, and the reduction is calculated according to the number of rooms occupied.
—
If before 1 December 1935 a tenant paid rent in advance for a certain period, he has the right to reclaim the overpaid sum.
In such a case he must send the landlord a registered letter (polecony) asking him to refund the amount or to credit the sum against future rent.
Y. Infeld.
At the “Green Table”

[Feuilleton — court sketches.] (Chekhovian court sketches.)
I have decided: newspaper reports must be not only about celebrations, meetings, sessions and other “-ungs”... but one must sometimes also benefit the public with what goes on “at the green table”. There, where our Jews (and perhaps even more so, our Jewesses) display “practical genius” in accusing one another, and meanwhile one hears such a Polish that the one God in heaven should have mercy.
No sooner thought — than done. From today we begin, and — without warning [?]. Jews will supply the material. As you know, the portion Mishpatim is the hardest in the whole “Chumash”, and that is surely why Jews study it all year round...
———
The trial is between two women over... a string of corals. The plaintiff — let us call her Pesa Klamka — a small, dried-up woman with an elongated “tsukers” [?] face and big black, quickly darting eyes. The defendant — let her be called Bella Klapnavist [?] — a medium-sized, plumpish woman, a face with puffed-out cheeks from which peep red and white spots of unprofessionally smeared paint and powder. The black hair on her head, cut short and freshly crimped, spreads around her the smell of smoking iron curlers [?] and cheap hair-water.
The two women stand facing each other like warring camps, ready for battle at any minute.
The judge reads the indictment. Pani Bella is accused of having, on the day of Yom Kippur, taken from around the neck of Pesa Klamka’s 5-year-old little daughter a string of corals, which she then no longer wanted to give back.
The defendant does not deny that she did it, but — the corals are hers, and it was her very own “własność” [property] that she took.
She speaks quite genteelly, with “obce wyrazy” [foreign words], as befits a “better-class woman”... Her words even sound soft, but perfectly calm, so that one can count every word of hers exactly. She does not get nervous; on the contrary, while she speaks she nods her crimped head, each time throwing a “sympatyczny” [charming] smile now at the judge, now again at the public.
— “Owszem” [indeed], she did take the corals, but — they are hers, after all — “proszę Wysokiego Sądu” [if the High Court please]! Surely no one will suspect that she — pointing at herself with her little finger — would want to take corals “niesłusznie” [wrongfully] from such a one as that — and she gives a turn of the finger — from which a big coloured stone set in a golden ring peeps out — towards the plaintiff. So she insists on telling “pan sędzia” [Mr. Judge] how the corals came to her. Her “szwagier” [brother-in-law], who “uważa” [esteems] her greatly, wanted to buy her a “pamiątka” [keepsake]; so he took her to a jeweller’s shop and wanted —
— “Do rzeczy, proszę” [to the point, please], comes the voice of the judge.
— Excuse me — I must tell it exactly: the “szwagier” wanted to buy “jakiś kryształ” [some crystal], but she does not “fancy” crystals, so he wanted to buy some nice “bransoletka” [bracelet], but that was not “według gustu” [to her taste]. So they began to look at other things — —
— “Proszę mówić o koralach” [please speak about the corals] — the judge cuts in again — the rest does not interest us!
— “Przepraszam Wysokiego Sądu” [I beg the High Court’s pardon], we will indeed come to that too. But she wants pan sędzia to know as well what a “delicate szwagier” she has. Well then, she had already “nalegała” [insisted] that the brother-in-law should buy the “pamiątka” a second time, but suddenly the “kupiec” [merchant] took out of a little cabinet... “a śliczny medalionik” [a lovely little medallion].
— Well [?], “jeszcze nie o koralach!” [still not about the corals!] — asks the judge, already a little angrily.
— Right away, right away, not long now — Pani Bella answers calmly. “Więc” [so], the medallion would have been fine, but it was too small — so the brother-in-law considered — so they could not find anything there and had to leave.
— So you did not buy the corals in a shop after all? — asks the judge sharply, trying to “catch” her out.
— “Ależ, co też pan sędzia mówi!” [Why, what is Mr. Judge saying!] — she takes offence; they only did not buy in that particular shop.
— Then why did you have to tell us all that? — the judge is now getting angry.
— “Najmocniej przepraszam” [I most humbly apologise] — Pani Bella answers again — in court, she considers, one must tell “szczerą prawdę” [the honest truth]. Well then, they went to another shop, and there they really saw “cudne rzeczy” [wonderful things].
— “Krótko, korale gdzie były kupione!” [In short, where were the corals bought!] — the judge interrupts her.
— “Trudno” [it can’t be helped]; I wanted to tell “szczegółowo” [in detail] how things went there, but pan sędzia evidently (“widocznie”) has no time, so I must finish [?]. “Otóż” [well then], there the brother-in-law bought the corals and really wanted to make a mark on them so as to be able to “przysięgać” [swear] that these are the very same ones.
— What does the plaintiff have to say on the matter? — asks the judge, turning his gaze to the other Jewess, who all this time has been tossing about, unable to stand still in one place.
— “Już skończyła?” [Has she finished already?] [?] — she pipes up. (Pan sędzia should not believe a single word of hers) “Jaka mi ważna” [?] [look how important she is]! One can already [have one’s fill] of such “słodkie cukierki” [sweet candies]!... I will tell it, and the High Court will know whose corals they are.
— Good, tell it, but briefly — the judge reminds her.
— What? Why was the other one allowed to babble [?] so much! Let the High Court hear me out too! — she pleads with tears in her eyes. — Well then, 20 years ago I was in service in Konin with a very rich merchant who dealt in grain, and —
— “To nas nie interesuje” [that does not interest us] — the judge cuts her off at once.
— Why ever not? Let everything be known! He was a thoroughly honest man and treated her like his own child. His wife, too, always bought her whatever she needed — an apron, a dress; if only she could afford that today.
— “O korale!” [About the corals!] — the judge does not let her indulge in memories of the former “happy” times.
— “Zaraz, zaraz, pamiętam też o tym” [just a moment, I remember that too]. The corals [?], if pan sędzia really wants to know everything, were indeed bought for me by the “pan gospodarz” [master of the house] in Katowice; I have a mark on them too, and here it is! — she points to a notch in one coral. She has witnesses as well. Thereupon she at once names about a dozen of them.
Pani Bella is not silent either; she too names so many witnesses that the judge therefore adjourns the trial.
Hada—es.
Fundamental changes in the turnover-tax law. New turnover-tax “rates” (stawki).

Under a decree of the President of the State of 14 January 1936, the law on the turnover tax has been partly amended.
The changes concern first and foremost the “rates” (stawki), which have been increased relatively sharply.
From now on, therefore, the following new “rates” will apply:
1) One and two-tenths per cent (1.2%) will be paid by commercial enterprises, “skup” (wholesale-buying) enterprises and suppliers — that keep commercial books, as well as publishers of books printed in Poland.
2) One and a half per cent (1.5%) will be paid by industrial enterprises (factories, workshops) of the sixth, seventh and eighth category.
3) One and seven-tenths per cent (1.7%) will be paid by commercial enterprises, “skup” enterprises and suppliers — that do not keep commercial books.
The same 1.7% rate will have to be paid by banks, exchange offices and short-term credit institutions that keep commercial books, with the exception of gross earnings from transactions in foreign currencies, foreign exchange, foreign cheques and all kinds of securities.
4) One and nine-tenths per cent (1.9%) will be paid by industrial enterprises of the first five categories that keep commercial books.
5) Two and a half per cent (2.5%) will have to be paid by forwarding and transport enterprises.
6) Six per cent (6%) will be paid by commission enterprises and commercial agents (cat. 11).
7) On all other turnovers subject to turnover tax, three per cent (3%) will have to be paid.
The above-mentioned rates for commercial enterprises will apply only if the goods are resold in an unprocessed state. If, however, such a commercial enterprise sells goods after processing them, the “rate” will be one and nine-tenths per cent (1.9%).
The “rates” will apply at the above-mentioned level until the year 1939. From 1939 on they will be reduced by one tenth.
As we see, then, the “rates” have been raised quite considerably, but in return the surcharge taxes in force until now have been abolished. The 25-per-cent surcharge for the benefit of municipal self-government has been abolished, as has the 15-per-cent “dodatek” (supplement), as well as the property levy (danina majątkowa) for the years 1936 and 1937.
The municipal self-governments will receive directly from the State 17% of the revenue from turnover tax and, in addition, 30% of the trade licences (patents). On the other hand, the taxpayer will not have to pay more than the amount of the tax calculated according to the above-mentioned, newly introduced “rates”.
Further changes provided for by the decree:
Commercial enterprises of the 1st and 2nd category, as well as industrial enterprises of the first five categories that keep commercial books, have until now had to pay the monthly “advances” (zaliczki) by the 15th of the following month; this deadline has been moved to the 25th.
The quarterly “advances” for those who keep no books will now have to be paid a month earlier: the first advance, instead of by 15 July, will have to be paid by 15 June, the second — by 15 August, the third — by 15 October and the fourth — by 15 February.
Newly established enterprises that keep no commercial books are obliged to pay the “advances” every quarter. The amount of these payments is set by the tax office after three months have elapsed since the enterprise was opened. This assessment by the tax office must be made after a prior examination of the amount of turnover achieved by the enterprise.
The Minister of Finance is also given the right to fix a lump-sum (ryczałt) tax for smaller enterprises, as well as to introduce the “consolidated” (scalony) tax on a number of goods and to issue ordinances that will regulate the said tax questions exhaustively.
The new rates will be calculated on turnovers made in the period beginning 1 January 1936.
G. Adv. Y. Warszawski.
On the Tip of the Pen.

Little has changed.
Mendele could not bear to watch how the nag [“di klyatshe”, Mendele’s “The Mare”] was tormented, how she was whipped, how she was tortured and robbed of the last bit of her health. Mendele could not endure the suffering of the poor, emaciated Jewish nag, how they rode on her and made her a laughing-stock.
It is all the same whether the marrow was sucked from her bones by the bully, the rich man — the strongman, or by some lowly person; it does not matter what the bloodsucker and whipper of the nag is called — what matters is that he sat there and did his sorry piece of work.
To Mendele, and later to all of us, it seemed that the Jewish nag, the tormented and persecuted Jewish masses, would now at last throw off all the invited and uninvited “benefactors” and providers, the whole gang of the meat-tax (taksa) people, who live at the community’s expense and suck the marrow out of the Jews’ bones. It could well have seemed so to us, especially since for a few decades now people here have been talking about the emancipation of the common man and about the political maturity of our masses.
They talk about it, and even very nicely, but it is nothing more than lip-service, because — —
It is enough to take a look at our own four cubits, to see the ruin in our ranks, the despair and dejection in every corner of Jewish life, for the picture of Mendele’s nag to come alive again before one’s eyes. The Jewish masses are tormented from all sides, and our own bosses and “public workers” push them further down.
From Mendele to the present day is quite a long way. But his nag lives on to this day, and her whippers too. The difference is only in the somewhat altered form.
B. S.
From the Film World.

Hollywood talks about Kiepura
The famous Polish singer Jan Kiepura is now staying in Hollywood, where he is working on his film “Give Me the Night” [Give Us This Night]. He has got on well with his director, with his partner Gladys Swarthout and even with the extras. Everyone has the best opinion of Kiepura. People admire his modesty and directness. He is on everyone’s lips; everywhere people talk about him. The newspapers write whole articles devoted to the Polish singer, and the illustrated magazines show his photographs and stills from his first American film.
Carole Lombard in new roles
Carole Lombard is no new face in film. She already has behind her a gallery of types and characters that made her famous in motion pictures. Not long ago she played one of the leading roles in the film “The Living Pledge” [Now and Forever]. Alongside her played Gary Cooper and the tiny star — the wonder-girl Shirley Temple. After she had finished that film, a catastrophe happened: walking in the street, she fell under a moving automobile and afterwards lay ill [“am”?] for a long time in hospital.
When she finally recovers and comes back to the film studio, she gets the leading role in the film “Hands on the Table” [Hands Across the Table]. The film is a success and Carole Lombard is engaged for a second film, in which she plays the leading role of a woman who steals [?]... the newest dress models in the Paris fashion houses.
A Stroll Through the Sosnowiec Institutions.

[Sosnowiec — institutions and welfare; the old-age home; a visit report.] By Ben Amotz.

"Moshav Zkenim" [Old-Age Home].
Far from the city's noise, from the bustle of the street, from the stock-exchange of "bargains", lies the institution in which the "bikhes"[?] of old age rests.
As soon as we appear[?] in the long corridor leading into the large, spacious rooms, a certain stir arises. People look at us — worn out, faces of long, wearying years, bent under the burden of hard life, dim, submissive eyes that look at everything with suspicion and fear.
Several of them greet us with the question of what we have come for. With them, with these old people who have almost finished playing the role of "Rekhor"[?] and "Abram", the fear of "the man with the briefcase" has nevertheless been preserved...
Many of them still remember him — the man with the yellow stripe on his cap and the briefcase under his arm; he reminds them of a home of their own, a little shop, a workshop that they once ran. They too once had a connection with the life that roars in the streets, and when later there came a series of "shpeyerg"[?], struggles, and in the end — the two-storey house at Chmielna 7 — the "Moshav Zkenim".
— How do you live here, granny? How does the help look that the Sosnowiec municipal providers[?] give you? — we ask them.
— Nothing to complain about — I get an answer from the "chief spokeswoman", and all nod their heads in agreement — we lack nothing, "we can't eat as much as they give us". They treat us
[...] good, quite
— What else, granny? Say it, don't be afraid.
— After all, we are already in our old age, we need some "treat". Once — says the old woman — when Sabbath or a holiday came, ladies from the town used to come here and bring us a little fruit, sweets and other "treats", but for some time now nobody comes here, and "whoever has money buys for himself, and whoever has none must do without".
And at that moment I "envy" the old people, in whom the concepts of the old world still glow[?], of the time when "all Israel are responsible for one another" was not an empty phrase; but who nowadays has any interest in such "foolishness".
———
It is lunchtime.
The old men and women, 32 in number, gather in the specially large dining hall (between us, none of the "Sosnowiec restaurants has such a dining hall), and sit around the long, laid tables — an original picture; it gives the impression that one is in a boarding-house for the old only... with the difference that in other boarding-houses the owner "casts an eye" on guests who have a bigger appetite, while here the "boarding-house keeper", Mr. Frywer[?], takes great pleasure in his "guests" leaving no leftovers...
———
— How does the institution's income from the Jewish public look?
To this question we receive from the director, Mr. Frywer[?], very sad figures: were it not for the self-sacrifice of the founders — G. Safer, Ch. Y. Zajonc, M. Rajner, Sh. Fachser[?] and others, the handful of communal workers who built the institution and still work today in the old way, not for honour, not for publicity — the institution would long ago have been closed, and the 32 old men and women would have had to drift about in attics and damp cellar rooms.
— To this day — says Mr. F. — we have no more than [?] 200 members who pay monthly pledges. At the beginning, when the institution was opened, the management accepted members who paid no less than 2 złoty a month, even though the members were able to pay much more. But when their "businesses" began to shrink, they did like those passengers who, wishing to lighten "the loads on the sinking ship, first of all threw tallit and tefillin into the sea..." The "vine"[?] rich men too, among them "fine" Jews, made their first economy at the expense of the 32 old people and reduced the monthly payment to 1 złoty. Among the "economisers" there are such that, by their wealth in houses alone, it comes to twenty groszy per house for the old-age home...
———
Today humanity has an interest in practical and worldly matters; for example, the "modern" world has a taste for sport, dancing, card-playing and the like, and the pious trust that their prayer "Cast us not off in the time of old age" will be heard; consequently the whole burden falls on "amkho" [the common people]...
———
— How much does the subsidy from the Magistrat [municipality] amount to? — we ask.
— If our old people received food only for the subsidy we receive for them from the Magistrat, we would be playing the role of the "Chesed shel Emes" society [burial society], because from the Magistrat we receive about 15 groszy a day per old person... This sum was won only last year, for the first time, through the struggle of our town councillors, among whom are also those who only a short time ago "revealed themselves" with their photographs..
Among the "half-savage" peoples of old the young used to hang their old people and learn to shoot at them, or simply chop off their heads; today, after all, we live in a progressive century, when "morals" and "ethics" reach the highest level — so civilised society indeed takes care of the old people, and they receive for their livelihood... 15 groszy a day...
There were times when Jewish youth threw itself into the arms of philanthropic activity, took an active part, organised various events, itself acted for the benefit of this or that society — after all, the Krawiec brothers and others staged a series of plays for the benefit of the old-age home and thereby strengthened its source of income.
But "new times, new songs": most of the youth is immersed[?] head and all in politics, and the "non-partisan" satisfy their "pleasure" at a bloody boxing match.
———
We visit all the rooms on the upper floor, the men's and women's prayer rooms, the office — and did not see what we "wanted". We did not see there the "tablets" [memorial plaques] which are already found in almost every "tal u-matar"[?] institution and on which the names of the management are engraved in golden letters (for the presidents the honour is allotted in the form of large photographs..). The "tablets" have become so popular that they are already found in the batei midrash, and every gabbai who helped replace the beit-midrash stove[?] is immortalised for generations...
And here, on the walls of the splendid building of the old-age home in Sosnowiec, there is not a single memorial plaque at all, except in the front building, where in passing the names of the "first brigade" are mentioned — those who erected the building.
And to this we receive from the director the following answer:
— Our management does not chase after this cheap honour; the best memorial plaque for them — for the management, that is — would be that the Jewish public in Sosnowiec should remember on every occasion that on Chmielna Street, number 7, there is a warm home for old people, who receive from the local Magistrat 15 gr. a day...
Jews in Czech Industry

[World — Jews of Czechoslovakia; economy and industry; report from Prague.]
By Dr. F. Lagstein, Prague.
At the current fair in Tel Aviv, Czechoslovakia will play quite a large role. As I learn from the highest Czech economic circles, Czech industry wants to show the world with all its strength that it can today compete with the greatest industrial countries of the whole world, and that Czechia alone is sufficient today: it is to satisfy all needs in goods that one may only require [?] — no other country is needed any more.
It is hard today to say exactly how large the percentage of Jews in Czech industry is. In recent times no exact figures have therefore been published. — This much is certain: more than half of the Czech factories are in Jewish hands, at the very least they are under Jewish influence, and individual branches are almost all one hundred percent Jewish.
If one takes a walk over the Prague fairground, which is open all year round, one sees that, for example, the Czech textile industry is almost entirely in Jewish hands. Brünn [Brno] fabrics became known in the four corners of the world, and even earlier, before even England began to flood the world with textile goods, Jewish firms from Czechia supplied their fabrics — and still supply them to this day — precisely to England. It is enough to cast a glance at the statistical figures the Prague fair has now published to get an idea of the great Czech export. Thus, for example, Czech textile goods were supplied to the whole world last year for no less than half a billion dollars — a sum no other country has reached.
Not much less was the export of Gablonz [Jablonec nad Nisou] fancy goods. What is manufactured there (mostly by Jewish firms) is widespread even among the savage tribes. Not only civilized women — half-savage Negro women too admire themselves in Gablonz beads and wear Gablonz jewellery, which no country in the world can imitate.
The Japanese tried to imitate it; they even named a place where they made it "Gablonz", so that they could say "genuine Gablonz things". But they too did not succeed. Everywhere people look for things from Gablonz in Bohemia and not from "Gablonz" in Japan.
Porcelain and glass from the Karlsbad [Karlovy Vary] region are also shipped all over the world. Jewish manufacturers have created qualities in this branch that are known everywhere today. The modern porcelain and glass of Czechia are seen today not only in cheaper workmanship but also in a production bought by very rich lords [?] and even imperial courts.
Recently rich Jewish industrialists have set up large linen factories in the Trautenau [Trutnov] region, which manufacture everything from the cheapest to the finest article; naturally, for example, things are manufactured there in such workmanship that the factories today succeed [in ranking] among the largest and finest in the world.
[In] metal [?], toys, mother-of-pearl and more and more, production has now begun here in such qualities that these industries now compete with the largest factories of world industry.
It goes without saying that everywhere there are Jews involved, helping to develop Czech industry into one of the greatest economic centres in the whole world.
News from Częstochowa

(From our correspondent A. Wrocławski.)

On making the slaughter fee cheaper.
In connection with the order of the voivodeship on making the ritual-slaughter fee cheaper (for large cattle 5 zł. per head), the kehilla board of Częstochowa has decided to turn to the supervisory authority with an appeal, in which the board will show with figures that if the slaughter fee is reduced, this item of the budget will produce a deficit.
The board has also decided to remark to the authority in the above-mentioned appeal that if the authority does not take the board's position into account, it will be forced to give up the slaughter.
The board's proposal was also accepted by the council, with the exception of the last part, which speaks of resigning from the slaughter.
The council took the position that this argument should not be used, because according to the regulations it [the slaughter] belongs to the kehilla.

From the Culture Union.
The Culture Union, which has aroused great interest among all strata of the local Jewish population, has already set about intensive work.
The drama circle has been reorganised and is preparing for a big evening. The work of the drama circle is led by the dentist A. Perec.
The singing and music section has also set to work. The singing lessons will be conducted by Professor J. Weintraub.
In general the Culture Union shows a great deal of will to activate the youth and to revive cultural work here in our town.
Finally we wish to note that the beloved communal worker, the advocate Dr. Leon Asz, and Dr. Tarbeczka [?] have been drawn into the committee.

A Mendele committee formed.
In connection with the Mendele academy [commemorative evening for Mendele Moykher Sforim], which takes place today, the 24th, in the Fire Brigade hall, a Mendele committee has been formed, to which belong Messrs. dentist A. Perec, M. Asz, P. Blumenkranc, Sz. Frank, Sz. Fejgenbaum, Perkal, Klarman, Eichenwald and Gliksman.
Taking part in the academy will be the editor of the "Literarishe Bleter", Nachman Meisel, and the well-known reciter Jacques Lewi. Apart from the Warsaw guests there will be a special vocal part performed by local forces.
The academy has aroused strong interest among the local Jewish population.

From the Chamber Theatre.
The Chamber Theatre is now staging a very pleasant American comedy entitled "Roxy" by Barry Conners.
The comedy depicts life in a middle-class household in a smaller American town, where the lady of the house, an impostor, torments her husband with her caprices.
The comedy is very well constructed, contains [printed "termagt", apparently a misprint for "farmagt"] many scenes that provoke merriment, and is brilliantly played by the actors.
Of the ensemble the following distinguished themselves very successfully: the well-known [?] Irena Tomaszewska as Roxy — this actress created a fine figure of a young naive girl, in some scenes simply moving with her naivety; as well as the actor St. Kozakowski [?], who rendered with understanding the role of an American merchant and loving father.
Direction by Bancza [?] — pleasing [?]; scenery — capable [?].

An interesting boxing match.
Nordia (Sosnowiec) — Maccabi (Częstochowa) 11:3.
On Sunday, in Maccabi's own premises, an interesting boxing match took place between "Nordia" of Sosnowiec and "Maccabi" of Częstochowa, which after a fairly interesting and fine contest ended with a high score of 11:3 in favour of the local Maccabi, although in truth "Nordia" did not deserve such a heavy defeat.
For "Nordia" the points were won by Danger [?] and Abraham. Feldbaum, who had "unershirn" [?], was awarded a defeat by the referee.
Fasak [?] behaved very unsportingly, leaving the ring in the middle of the bout.
On the whole "Nordia" left a very sympathetic impression.
For "Maccabi" the points were won by Kohat [?], Windman, Diament, Kliwiner, Granek and Kantor.
Oyneg Shabbes — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'era)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on the portion of this week.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Va'era
—o—
a) "And God spoke unto Moses" (6:2)
"He spoke with him in judgement, because he had spoken harshly, saying 'Why hast Thou dealt ill with this people.'" Rashi.
"Spoke" — the Master of the Universe said: "with him [is] justice" — Moses is right, Moses is worthy of being the Jewish leader, because "he had spoken harshly, saying: why hast Thou dealt ill with this people." Because he stood up for the Jews against God, as it were, and demanded justice for them from Him, although he knew that he would be punished for it and not be let into the Land of Israel.
Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany.
• • •
Rabbi Levi Yitzhak of Berdychiv once heard a poor, sick Jew consoling himself: "Whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good" — everything is for the best... Rabbi Levi Yitzhak said to him:
— Don't[?] make the Master of the Universe so right. True, "evil does not come forth from Him"; nothing bad issues from God, blessed be He, and even the bad that God does yields good. But when a doctor prescribes a bitter medicine to a patient — even though it keeps him alive — if the patient cries out that it is too bitter and he cannot get it down[?], the doctor prescribes him a milder one... Therefore one must cry out if the medicine is bitter.
• • •
Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Lyady used to say:
— According to Rabbi Levi Yitzhak of Berdychiv, the Master of the Universe has not yet fulfilled His obligation towards a single Jew...
—o—
b) "But they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit" (ibid., 9)
"Impatience of spirit" refers to Moses. Moses was impatient for the redemption; he would storm at God, he stormed — to make the distinction — at Pharaoh... He was without patience, and that is precisely why he was the true redeemer. Imrei Hen.
—o—
c) "And gave them a charge unto the children of Israel" (ibid., 13)
"He charged them to lead them gently and to bear with them." Rashi.
Rabbi Israel Salanter, as is known, left Russia, where he was born and brought up and spent most of his years. He went to the western countries, where he worked for Judaism in his own manner: with kind words, with friendliness he drew to Judaism people who were far from it. He spent a number of years in Memel, Frankfurt, Berlin, Paris, Königsberg.
He was asked:
— If it is to bring Jews back to repentance, why did he leave Russia, where the great majority of the Jews are, and go off to the Western European countries, where there are so few Jews? In Russia there is surely much more to accomplish.
He answered:
— I will tell you a parable. A horse breaks loose from its rider and gallops downhill. Who dares then to stop the horse — and not with force, but with kindness! But once the horse has come down the hill, one can more quickly approach it and bridle it.
The moral: Russian Jewry has set off at a gallop downhill, and so there is no possibility of stopping it; Western European Jewry, which has already reached the bottom of the hill, is easier to harness again, with kind words, into the yoke of Torah and commandments.
—o—
d) "These are that Aaron and Moses... These are they that spoke to Pharaoh... these are that Moses and Aaron" (ibid., 26-27)
First Aaron is listed before Moses, and when speaking to Pharaoh, Moses is mentioned before Aaron — because earlier, when Pharaoh had to be spoken to kindly, Aaron went first, since Aaron was "a lover of peace and a pursuer of peace", genial and good, and could more readily speak words of entreaty; later, however, when harsh words had to be spoken to Pharaoh, Moses went first — he who was bold and stern even towards God ("Why hast Thou dealt ill?!") when it was a matter of Jewish redemption. Ateret Tsvi.
—o—
e) "See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh" (7:1)
This is the eternal Jewish fate: to become a god to the Pharaohs, to give them new teachings, new Torahs, and to be "rewarded" for it with... blood. Yoreh u-Malkosh.
• • •
It is told that when the court priest of Count Czartoryski was persuading the famous Yehezkel Hoge to convert, he painted for him what a career he could make with his brilliant talent: he could become a bishop and even a cardinal and even[?] a pope. History, after all, knows of two Jews who became popes.
But Yehezkel Hoge shrugged his shoulders: it was all too little for him... he wanted a higher price[?] for his apostasy. At that the priest grew angry:
— Then what would you want? To become a god, perhaps?
— Why not? — Yehezkel shrugged[?] — after all, a Jew once did become a god..
—o—
f) "Only let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more" (8:25)
How then did Pharaoh mock them[?]
Rather, Pharaoh practised diplomacy with them: he answered Moses and Aaron "I will let you go" — and "you" could mean: you, Moses and Aaron, I will send out. Moses understood the diplomatic excuse and said: "Only let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully with us[?] any more in not letting the people go" — don't joke with us, and don't say later and don't say that by the word "you" you meant only Moses and Aaron and not the whole people. This diplomacy of a solemn promise and a false interpretation afterwards frightened Moses more than giving no promise at all.. Kehilat Yitzhak.

The Bastard. (71)
A gripping tragic novel about a prodigy

All the gabbaim, in tall shiny top hats, with their eldest member at their head, stood not far from the entrance, beside a small table on which lay a long, rounded [object — reading uncertain] with an embroidered [?] Star of David in the middle.

On the bimah, not far from the Holy Ark, in his long black cantor's gown, stood Binyomindl, the cantor of the synagogue, his face turned towards the entrance, waiting for the moment the new rabbi of the synagogue would appear.

On both sides stood, Torah scrolls in their hands, the two eldest shammosim, they too in long black gowns, with pointed caps on their heads.

The women's gallery too was full of women, who had come to take a look and to hear a few words from the new rabbi.

It did not take long, and on the threshold of the synagogue, accompanied by two gabbaim, appeared the newly arrived rabbi, who was none other than our well-known Moishele.

The cantor and the choir sang festive prayers, and the rabbi appeared on the beautifully decorated bimah, where he began to preach about [?] the importance of his taking over the rabbinic chair of the synagogue on West[er] Avenue.

Long, very long he spoke, his words penetrating the souls of his listeners.

All were enchanted hearing the words of Moishele, which poured from his mouth like pearls. He moved his listeners to tears with his speech, and they saw in Moishele an important spiritual force.

And before long Moishele became great and popular in the big city of New York as well. Every Sabbath the synagogue was packed full with people who came to hear the rabbi's sermon. He enjoyed great trust not only among the worshippers of the synagogue where he was rabbi — people came from other synagogues too to hear him, and everyone felt relief on leaving the synagogue after the rabbi's sermon.

And so it is no wonder that people flocked to him from all sides, asked him for advice and sought help. Men and women would come to him, confide in him their deepest hidden secrets, telling him the [the] most terrible tragedies of their family life, and for each of them he found a remedy, showed each what to do next and how to go on living.

Many were those who sought help from him. Here, in the great abyss, in the great city of millions of people, he saw the tragedy of human life, learned of things that made one shudder; only here, in the modest room of his reception office, were the tragedies of life revealed to him in their true colours.

"Believe me, Rabbi, I am not guilty; he, my husband, himself pushed me onto this path," says a woman of about thirty. "My husband was always busy with his business, never had a free minute for me; when he came home I was already asleep, and when he left I was asleep too. Alone, by myself, I lived, although I had a husband. The Sabbath was no Sabbath, the holiday was no holiday, and when he did have a [—]-day free from his business, he would fall down like a dead man and sleep through a whole day and night.

"I began to cry that I could not live like this, that I was lonely as a stone; so he gave me — the way one gives a crying child a toy — a toy, and told me to play with the toy.

"He brought a friend of his into the house, who is rich and has plenty of time, and showed me that in his company I would not be bored. But the acquaintance took advantage of the moment and betrayed his friend, my husband. At first it was very sad for me and I felt like a fallen woman; I wanted to commit suicide, for I loved my husband; but I felt a foetus under [?] my heart and did not know whose it was, my husband's or his friend's. Had I been sure that it was the friend's, I would have strangled it alive; but I was not sure, and because of the foetus I had to live and choke in my sufferings. Often, when I saw how my husband cuddles [?] the child and kisses it, blood would pour from my heart like water.

"I hate my husband's friend, I cannot look at him, but I am afraid that if I resist [?] his desire, he will reveal the terrible secret to my husband, and that would kill him. How bitter my life is, Rabbi" — and the woman wiped the tears from her eyes.

And she left contented, happy: at last she had found a person who listened to her, to whom she had confessed, and he took it upon himself to separate [?] her from her husband's friend and give her back her husband, who would forgive her everything.

"Rabbi," weeps a young woman before him, "I can no longer bear my sufferings; I had to commit such a crime, because I love my husband too much; though he is ill, there are no people in the world like him. May God only not take him from me."

The First Meeting of the Appointed Supervisory Board of the “Sz. Fürstenberg” Gymnasium

[Będzin — education, the Jewish gymnasium.]
No embezzlements [defraudations] were committed in the school; it was only that the finances were badly managed.
As our readers know, a parents' meeting was called a few months ago at the “Sz. Fürstenberg” Gymnasium [Szymon Fürstenberg]. At that meeting those assembled, at Mr. Fürstenberg's wish, proposed a list of several persons as the parents' representatives on the above-mentioned supervisory board, and Mr. F. [printed: S.] declared that he would take the proposed candidates into account.
Besides this, at that meeting — which for certain reasons did not bring the desired result — the director, Dr. Einhorn, publicly declared that within 30 days a second parents' meeting would be called. Unfortunately several months have already passed, and the director's solemnly promised word of honour has not been fulfilled. But as we learn (despite the strict warning that the course of the meeting must, for heaven's sake, be concealed from public opinion..), last Thursday the first session took place of the supervisory board appointed by the Merchants' Association, to which the new appointees, those “elected” by the parents, were also invited. Of the candidates put forward[?] at that[?] time, not even a single one was invited...
The session is opened by the chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, who greets the existing and the freshly announced appointees of the supervisory board and points out the importance and usefulness of joint work for the good of the gymnasium.
Mr. F. [S.] at the same time declares that all the complaints about abuses in the school do not at all correspond to reality, that they are mere lies; on the other hand he states that the management had been bad, which the board must avoid in the future.
Director Einhorn speaks of the school's high level, thanks to which the school has attained category A. Mr. Einhorn speaks out against calling a parents' meeting, so as not to permit the “interference” of the parents; this — he says — could also cause some nationalism to be brought in among the children.
Of all the appointees (among whom there were “patented[?] democrats”) none protested against this procedure, except Mr. Z. Berkowicz, who protested against the parents not being given the possibility of freely electing their representatives, whereby the parents' rights were violated. As a sign of protest Mr. B. resigns from his post as an appointed member of the supervisory board.
President[?] Rubinlicht speaks out against calling a second parents' meeting, because at the first meeting there were only Zionists and Mizrachists [members of Mizrachi]... (a harmful element, to be sure...). He also denies the complaints that any abuses whatsoever occurred in the school.
Then several commissions were elected, and with this the first session was closed.

Kielce woman pays several hundred zł. for diamond earrings of the "Queen of Sheba"...

When the Kielce woman Sheyndl Feuerstein (Piotrkowska 64) was strolling this week along Sienkiewicza Street, she was stopped by an unknown person who began speaking to her in a foreign language. Since [?] the stranger could not make himself understood to Mrs. Feuerstein, he became very agitated and went away. At that same moment some young man came up to Mrs. Feuerstein and began explaining to her what the stranger had wanted of her. Mrs. Feuerstein answered that she had not understood his language. The young man introduced himself to the woman as the son of the well-known local jeweller Shloyme Koner and explained to her that the stranger with whom she had spoken earlier had wanted to sell "diamond" earrings which come from Abyssinia and the famous [?] "treasure" of the "Queen of Sheba", and which had been forced to be sold in Poland so as to be able to continue the war with Italy...
The young man added that half an hour earlier the same foreigner had been at his father's shop wanting to sell the earrings. His father had indeed wanted to buy them, but he was "afraid" they came from a theft, because it is hard to believe that the earrings really come from the treasure of the Queen of Sheba.
From the young man's words [misprinted "yungegman"] Mrs. Feuerstein was "sure" that it was an "honest" deal and that one could go ahead with it quite boldly. She therefore proposed that the two of them, i.e. she together with "Koner", buy the "bargain" in partnership. Mrs. Feuerstein gave the young "Koner" 62 zł. and asked him to complete the "deal".
Half an hour later the young man brought Mrs. Feuerstein only one earring, saying that a little more money had to be added, for the "Abyssinian" guest had regretted the "transaction" and had to be paid extra, since one is really buying a "kosher bargain".
Mrs. Feuerstein then gave her partner 3 gold rings and 31 metres of linen and waited several hours for Mr. "Koner", and when he still did not come, Mrs. Feuerstein went to the shop of Mr. Shloyme Koner and asked his son for the earrings. Shloyme Koner was alarmed and astonished by the strange [?] story and explained to the woman that she had, unfortunately, fallen victim to a cunning swindler who had passed himself off as his son...
The same swindlers had been at Mr. Shloyme Koner's that same evening and had tried to cheat him too, and when he caught on and wanted to detain them, they quickly fled from the shop, and on Sienkiewicza Street they found themselves a real sucker.
Mrs. Feuerstein reported this "transaction", which cost her over 200 zł., to the police, who are conducting an investigation. Whether the "Abyssinian" swindlers will be caught is a big question. Apparently they are already in... Addis Ababa [?]..
Terror gang uncovered in Kielce.

In the last issue of our paper we already reported on the arrests carried out by the Kielce police authorities among the Endek hooligans in Kielce. The arrests caused an understandable sensation in town and at the same time a hope that the acts of terror against the Jewish shops would at last cease.
The Kielce investigation office issued a special communiqué to the press about the arrests. It states, among other things, that about 40 men were detained, among them the chief leaders of the Endek youth in Kielce, such as the former [?] deputy and correspondent of "Orędownik" Henryk Przybylski, the organisation leader Duda, Kazimierz Warwid [?], Zdeb, Michalski, Kęsa [?] and others. Some of those arrested have already been convicted by various courts for knifings, thefts and similar "good deeds".
In Kielce the "material" for the stink bombs was prepared in a field behind the town. The liquid was poured into small bottles which were thrown into Jewish shops. The gang had a list of many Jewish shops in Kielce into which they wanted to throw the bombs.
At the investigation office the detainees denied having any connection with the bomb attacks. A large part of them were released. Among those released was Zdeb, but on the same day, in the evening hours, a bomb was thrown into the grocery ["colonial"] shop of Leyb Zilbershteyn on Lange Gas [Długa St.?], and as was established on the basis of witness statements, the bottle was thrown by the said Zdeb, who was therefore arrested a second time.
As we learn, as a result of the investigation only 6 persons remained under arrest. The rest were released, among them Przybylski, Warwid and others. Some of them, however, must report to the police station until the date of their trial. This trial is apparently to reveal many sensational details about the hooligan activity of the Endek terror gang.
— Meanwhile the acts of terror against Jewish shops in town have stopped. It is to be hoped that an end has now been put to the unheard-of hooligan deeds of the terror gang.

Kielce Jew finds 600 zł. in a railway compartment

The Kielce resident Mr. Józef Mendel, travelling this week by train from Warsaw to Kielce, found in a compartment past Radom a lady's handbag containing a sum of over 600 zł. Mendel reported this at the railway station in Radom to the police and to the station master. Upon the inquiry among the passengers in the carriages as to which of them had lost a handbag with money, a certain lady at once came forward — the wife of the ministry official Jackowicz — who explained that when she went over to another compartment to an acquaintance of hers she had forgotten to take the money with her. After giving the proper identifying marks Mrs. Jackowicz received the money back. Mrs. Jackiewicz [sic] warmly thanked Mr. Mendel and declared that, notwithstanding all the wild lies of the antisemites that Jews are swindlers, thieves etc., only "now" had she become convinced that Jews are honest people.

An all-Polish collection drive to honour the memory of Marshal Piłsudski

[Poland — Piłsudski memorial fund.]
(Sh.) Unceasing growth of the P.K.O.

At the annual press conference of the P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank], its president Mr. Gruber reviewed the activity of the P.K.O. in the year 1935. In all fields of the P.K.O.'s work significant progress was recorded, which is proof of the trust of the broadest strata of society in this institution. The total of deposits grew to 679.3 million zł and the number of savings books to 1,906.000. Cheque turnover reached the record sum of 27,5 billion zł. The cashless share of turnover grew from 63 per cent in 1930 to 76.4 per cent in 1935. Favourable too is the insurance activity (119 thousand active policies) and the credit activity (the portfolio of securities amounted to 670 million zł). Thanks to very cautious and careful [?] management, the cash reserve (pogotowie kasowe) amounted on average to 27 per cent of the capital entrusted to the P.K.O., and the impressive economic results are clearly illustrated by the balance surplus of 7 563.958 zł. Favourable, too, is the development of the P.K.O. bank in the Land of Israel, where, besides the branch in Tel Aviv, an agency was opened in Haifa. Answering questions, president Gruber gave explanations about the consolidation of state loans and also announced the planned opening of a P.K.O. branch for cheque turnover in Łódź.
Impressive Mendele academy in Będzin.

On Friday a festive academy in honour of the 100th birthday of Mendele Mocher Sforim took place in the premises of the Craftsmen's Association.
Before a packed hall the impressive academy was opened by Mr. Poliwoda [?], who called on those assembled to honour the great writer by rising. Then Mr. Tzvi gave a lecture on Mendele's life and work. For an hour and a half the speaker traced the development of Yiddish literature and language [?], pointing out that Mendele laid the cornerstone of a literature meant to reflect the real life-forces of the Jewish masses — and therefore he is a classic. In conclusion the speaker called for creating a protective wall for Yiddish and for helping to spread the Yiddish word and literature.
After the lecture a series of declamations and recitations took place, performed by members of "Frei-Heim" and "Gordonia". In an elevated mood Mr. Poliwoda closed the impressive academy.
