The Modern Course — Various shades of antisemitism. — Wild orgies — How do we react to it here?

[Essay — antisemitism in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.]
Dr. Papuri.
Various shades of antisemitism. — Wild orgies — How do we react to it here?
Years ago, when the antisemites of every direction and current began, like leeches [?], to suck the marrow out of the Jewish body — a body ill-starred enough as it is — people began to shout and weep and plead that someone take our part, that we not be allowed to be exterminated merely because we, like every living creature, want to live in God's little world.
Since then several years have passed, and it is, after all, a rule that a few years, and even several decades, play almost no significant role in history — and yet how different it is. In our present era. It seems [it is] [?] only a few short, counted years, and what a change has come about in them. How different and how much harder the Jewish situation is today, wherever we may be. Everywhere we are persecuted, and our only sin consists in wanting, and having, to live together with all other living creatures.
The antisemitic course has become fashionable, just like any other fashion. The only difference is that all fashions change with lightning speed, while the "antisemitic course progresses, and each one wants to outdo the other. It has become a kind of race, as if it were a matter of winning a prize. Just as inventors want to perfect their newest inventions as quickly as possible and make the world happy, so the antisemites in every corner of the world strain to accomplish [?] their "holy" mission.
And one cannot say that their work is easy. Ordinarily citizens live together amicably; one trades and deals with the other like simple, naive people. Nationality plays no role in this case. As is known [?], these are [?] people and citizens, and as such one bears the obligation. So one must in [?] time get into the human soul and begin to incite and arouse hatred. That the Jew — this one here, to whom no soil and no country belongs [?], the one who all his life is a wanderer — is your bloodthirsty enemy, he wants to exterminate you — so they persuade him — and therefore you must see to driving him out in good time, to make him loathsome in the eyes of your neighbours, in the eyes of your sisters and brothers. Once the beginning has been made and something of the agitation has stuck, it is easier to go on further and further. The main thing is the first step; after that it goes like a psalm. Once one sets out on this road, the Jew is a sorcerer, a devil, and it is not hard to believe that he has horns, and, needless to say, he must have human blood to bake matzos for Passover. Once one sets out on this road, the greatest absurdities are quite normal phenomena, handed down with the greatest simplicity from generation to generation and from parents to children.
In the Middle Ages the mission was carried out in a crude way by underworld people in religious garb. Today we live in an age of renaissance and modern technology, so for the "holy" work modern means are used. Thus antisemitic newspapers have been fruitful and multiplied throughout the country, distributed in hundreds of thousands every single day across town and village. And it is, after all, a rule that the most powerful factor is the printed word, which the population treats with due regard — so much so that the town, and still more the village, believes that everything the newspaper writes is truth and justice.
All sorts of individuals have realised that antisemitism is a commodity, and the more one incites and agitates, the more "the public takes it" — so much so that each wants to outdo the other, and it has become a race for antisemitic lies, which are poured onto Jewish heads every single day.
One should therefore not wonder at all that antisemitism finds itself, so to speak, in a period of bloom and keeps on progressing, in constant upswing.
* * *
Take, for example, Zagłębie and Upper Silesia. It seems we have always lived here harmoniously; relations between non-Jews and Jews were the friendliest, the best, and even today our neighbours know that Jews want nothing more than to live and let live — so much so that they gladly do business with Jews and see in them honest citizens and devoted friends.
But that they will by no means let us get away with, and with the most violent means they incite and stir up with all their might.
However strong the printed word may be, and however much they wanted to poison the hearts of the masses, they nevertheless [?] realised that the process is too long, and that it also needed "a hand to be lent" [?].
With acts of violence they set about sowing hatred and enmity in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, if only to shed blood.
We can record the bomb at the Pogoń beth midrash [Pogoń, Sosnowiec], which cost the life of an innocent boy; then comes the bomb at the Katowice synagogue and a series of other acts of violence in Upper Silesia and Zagłębie.
But as it turns out, they do not stop at all this; they keep on pondering and devising how to get rid of us more quickly. Thus the chronicle has recorded "brilliant" ideas of photographing every Christian who visits a Jewish shop.
That is a Sosnowiec invention, but Dąbrowa [Górnicza] does not lag behind either. There they fall with their fists upon every passing Jew whenever an opportunity offers, and afterwards they abuse the victims in the most disgusting way.
It is interesting that everywhere they "work" intensively, and always according to a certain method of Jew-destruction. When the commercial employees in Katowice considered the question of extending shop hours on the eve of the holidays, they came to the decision that the hours must not be extended — not because they do not want to or cannot work longer, but they argued that it must not happen solely so that the Jews should not be able to exploit the employees too much.
Będzin, too, does not lag behind in the antisemitic agitation: when a Jewish citizen walks by — whether a man or a decently dressed woman — a hooligan springs up as if from under the ground and splashes them with a liquid that burns. The same has now begun to be used in Sosnowiec as well.
That is how far Jew-hatred reaches. At every opportunity they keep trembling lest the Jew too derive some benefit, together with the whole population, from this or that submitted project — in which case it must at once be postponed. On this road people are willing even [bodaj] to have one eye put out, as long as the other loses two.
Once, here, people would have jumped out of their skin on hearing of the aforementioned outrages; they would have turned worlds upside down — and today people have become indifferent to everything, as if Jewish victims were not being lain in wait for.
True, efforts are made [?] when Jewish delegations go [?] to this or that authority about attacks on innocent citizens, and they even receive satisfactory answers — but that is far too little in contrast with the hooligans' systematic work of destruction. One sees [?], after all, that we are dealing here with lawless gangs whose aim is that Jewish blood be shed.
All attention must be devoted to getting the situation under control, so that the orgies plotted by all sorts of individuals — who stop at nothing, not even the cruellest thing that can happen — are not allowed to be carried out.
Our representatives must be vigilant and form for themselves a clear picture of the tense prevailing situation in which the Jewry of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia finds itself.
When You Have a Stubborn Wife... (Monologue of a Jew with a Bundle)

[Humorous feuilleton — monologue.] By Y. Oberżanek [?].
(Monologue of a Jew with a bundle)

Mne[?], what a world it has become — may it come to an end!
Life is no life, people are no people, businesses are no businesses, children are no children, men are no men and wives are no wives.
Wives, so to speak[?]! Today's wives! You call these wives? In the old days a Jewish woman was a delight to look at; she would "pour out"[?] a dozen boys for you, like bears, and on top of it she was healthy and strong as an oak, and had no complaints against anybody. And today's "menzhatkelekh" [little married women, from Polish mężatki] — may I not sin with my words! At first they don't want to, and later, when they do want to, they can't... And if, God forbid, they get a "zrazhenie"[?], they have "pshepises" [Polish przepisy — doctor's prescriptions]. They walk "pshepisove" [przepisowo — by prescription], drink "pshepisove", eat "pshepisove" — everywhere with the "pshepis", and since every doctor has his own "pshepises", one [does][?] exactly the opposite of the other: one has a "pshepis" to lie whole days on the couch [kozetka], to nibble lemons and to take drops, and the other has a "pshepis" that she must walk more, she needs "exercise"; one eats nothing at all and the other chops away with all her molars working overtime... one eats only "gn-bigli"[?] and another eats "slodytshes" [słodycze — sweets] — [—] according to the doctor's "pshepis".
In the old days a Jewish woman knew that she was no more than a Jewish woman and that the husband wore the trousers; she knew the meaning of "and he shall rule over thee", i.e. that when the husband says "midday" — when it is Shabbat she must send the cholent to the baker...
And today? Husband, shmusband! The husband dances to the tune the wife plays; but the worst of all is a stubborn wife. If by chance you get a stubborn wife, you had better provide yourself in good time with a "wygodny" [comfortable] plot on the Czeladź road [apparently an allusion to the cemetery].
I am saying this about my Khantshe, may she be well: quite a decent Jewish woman, only stubborn! And perhaps you think her stubbornness consists in outlandish things? God forbid! Her stubbornness consists in this, that she wants to copy everything I do: if I once come home at 1 at night, she comes home the next day at 3 at night; I play "telephone"[?], she plays poker; I smoke one "Erga", she smokes 3 "Dames" [Damskie cigarettes?]; I go into the shtibl for melave malke [printed "malkhe malke"], she goes into the "club" for "malkhes melekh"; I travel to "Him, may he live" [the Rebbe], "he" comes to "Her, may she live"; I have my little beard trimmed, she has the nape of her neck shaved, and so on.
So I complain to her: Khantshele, if you do everything I do, then do everything just like me — I take no money from you, so don't you take any from me either.
She answers: Not that! I will copy everything after you, only not that — that is what you are my husband for, until a hundred and twenty years.
Why am I telling you this? To show what women's stubbornness can lead to. Hear a story:
A year ago I took my old father to live with me. What does my Khantshele do? She takes in her mother — my mother-in-law, that is! We gave her a separate room, and all was fine and good. I took care of my father and my wife "pilnoveh"-ed [Polish pilnować — looked after] her mother.
I brought my father a new velvet hat — my wife brought her mother a brand-new "kupke" [bonnet] with flowers and with "stenges"[?].
I bought my father a tobacco box — my wife bought her mother a big leather "saketke"[?] [handbag, saszetka?] with a powder compact [puderniczka] and with all the other ladies' "kosl"[?] utensils.
All this would not have bothered me, were it not for the latest story; you may hear it:
As you already know, my old father had his own room and my wife's old mother — her own room. The old man lay on his bed and groaned, and my wife's old mother lay on her bed and groaned.
Next morning my old father asks my wife's old mother: Makhuteneste [co-mother-in-law], did you groan?
— Yes — answered my wife's old mother — hee, hee, hee... it's "smutne" [sad], one cannot shut an eye... it's somehow so not "wygodne" [comfortable]...
— And you, makhuteneste [printed "makhutentete"], are still quite... khi... khi... a fine Jewish woman...
— And you, makhuten... hee... hee... hee... are also still quite a "zhvaver" [żwawy — sprightly] fellow...
— Believe me, makhuteneste, that you... could still be quite a fine bride.. khi... khi... khi...
— Hee... hee... hee... I would not want to swear that you, makhuten, couldn't still make a... hee... hee... hee...
What came of these "declarations of love" and "mutual compliments", you can already understand by yourselves.
A few days later in comes Yosele the matchmaker — Good morning, Reb Hirsh Leyzer! — he says to me.
— I have come to you — he says — to propose a match.
— A match? Probably for my eldest daughter, I thought to myself — who is the groom, somebody decent?
— Heh, heh — answered the matchmaker — I should only have such luck. Not one of today's gang of dandies; a "stały" [steady] man, no rake, no dancer, doesn't run around whole nights, a settled man, a calm one, a fine family —
— he takes entirely after you.
— And how is he for a living?
— As for a living. He is provided for — answered the matchmaker — he is provided for for his whole life; his wife will have a merry life with him.
— And how much dowry does such a groom ask for?
— Nothing! He doesn't ask a single groszy from you; he is not one of today's grooms who chase after the dowry; he likes the bride, and may it be in good luck!
— Khantshele! Khantshele! — I called my wife — come in here, just hear what luck. A groom, a "stały" man, a living, and he wants no dowry.
— Let's hear then, who is the groom? — I became curious.
— A relative of yours, a very close relative — the matchmaker smiled under his moustache.
— A close relative of mine? Who is this relative of mine? — says [?].
— The groom is... the groom is...
— the matchmaker barely stammered out — your... your father, may he live and be well!
— What I dreamt this night and that night, may it fall on the heads of my enemies! You are mad. Or are you only now intending to go mad? What does it mean? My father a groom? A Jew, no evil eye, eighty years old?
— And who is the bride? — my missus burst out laughing.
— The bride? The bride... the bride is...
— the matchmaker answered — your... your... your mother...
— My mother? — my missus let out a shriek, as if she had been doused with a bucket of cold water.
In short, why should I go on at length — my father, in good luck, became a groom with my wife's mother — my mother-in-law, that is.
Here began a fresh "weddings" — my wife's stubbornness: I made my father a "wyprawa" [trousseau] and my wife made her mother a "wyprawa". I bought my father bride-gifts and my wife bought her mother groom-gifts.
And now?
Now, in the "honeymoon", the old father doesn't groan on his bed and my wife's old mother doesn't groan on her bed; my father "pilnoveh"-s [looks after] my wife's mother — my mother-in-law, that is, and my wife's mother — my mother-in-law, that is — "pilnoveh"-s my father — the father has taken the mother, and all this — because of my wife's stubbornness!
Why Did the Merger of the Two Merchants' Associations in Będzin Not Come About?

(A clarification from the Będzin Small Traders' Association.)
In the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ No. 2 there was a notice that, because of the position of the representatives of the Będzin Small Traders' Association, the planned merger of the Będzin merchants' organizations did not come about.
In No. 3 Mr. R. Les again wrote at length about this matter and again laid the entire blame on the position of our delegates.
We therefore consider it our duty to clarify this matter in order to avoid misunderstandings.
The matter of merging the merchants' organizations has already been touched upon[?] more than once in the columns of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“. Of a union in the form of merging our association with the Merchants' Association („Sokhrim-Fareyn“), for example, there can be no talk as long as the Warsaw central bodies are not united; from the social-Jewish standpoint, too, such a merger is not desirable, for reasons that cannot be explained in this place. The notice that in Warsaw both central bodies have united is not entirely in accordance with the truth, because only a Main Council was created, whose task is to consolidate the position of both central bodies during appearances of principle vis-à-vis vis-à-vis the outside. The organizational work, on the other hand, is carried out, as hitherto, by each of the two central bodies separately.
The matter of a merger of the Będzin merchants' organizations has [?] quite a different background. The plan, as we know, was put forward precisely by the secretaries of the associations, and that for the sake of raising the income. Since the senior [official][?] in the Merchants' Association was interested in having the Merchants' Association become the initiator of the plan. The speaker, however, at the first conference, did not present the matter correctly and simply produced a mishmash of plans. We therefore proposed that the secretaries, the true initiators of the plan, should work out the principles in writing, and only then would we be able to take a position on it. Our proposal, however, was rejected, and the question of merging was again put forward, which can cause Jewish merchantry, and first and foremost the small traders, considerable damage, which we have already mentioned above — so we decided to ask the opinion of our central body, which is, incidentally, the only one competent to decide this matter.
Let the gentlemen who see in our conduct a harm to the whole of Jewry (first and foremost Mr. R. Les) acquaint themselves more closely with this matter, and they will find out what our sincere position looks like.
The Board of the Small Traders' Association in Będzin.
Radio Corner.

[Sosnowiec — radio.] The new radio station in Sosnowiec.
A very important place in the history of Polish radiophony is held by the day of 15 January.
A year ago, on that day, the ceremonial opening of the radio station in Toruń took place, and this year, on the same date, a radio station began operating in Sosnowiec, from which the Katowice radio station will regularly broadcast programmes devoted to the Dąbrowa region.
When Polish Radio decided to set the radio branch in Sosnowiec in motion, it reckoned above all on the Dąbrowa region having a point of support from which it could broadcast programmes of its own local content.
Here one relied on the fact that the folklore of the Dąbrowa region has not yet been exploited: that new cultural values are multiplying there; therefore the Sosnowiec radio programme lets all of Poland and beyond know what the Dąbrowa region is and how great its importance is for the whole country.
For this purpose the management of the district power station [?] of the Dąbrowa region in Sosnowiec has handed over splendidly furnished premises on Będzińska Street. This studio room is of very great importance; it is located here, where the city's most important traffic arteries cross. But both the floor and the walls have been hung [?] with a material that dampens the noise of the street, regulates the acoustic properties of the room and adapts them to the character and requirements of the various kinds of broadcasts. Truth be told [?], one cannot yet stage there everything one would wish, and so one makes do only with vocal and musical broadcasts by soloists and smaller groups. But this is only temporary, and for the time being nothing more is needed.
The Sosnowiec radio branch has well-installed microphones and microphone amplifiers, located in an adjoining room where the city amplifier station is installed. The latter in turn is connected with the studio by a system of electro-optical signalling, as in all other radio stations. From this amplifier station the broadcasts travel through a suitable cable to the city telephone exchange and to the main amplifier station of the Silesian radio station. In addition to all this there are nicely furnished waiting rooms for lecturers, artists and ordinary interested visitors.
In the same premises there is a permanent radio-technical advice office, which has a great deal to do there [?]. All radio listeners in Sosnowiec and the vicinity who need any advice concerning radio receive the best guidance there.
Paris Is Bubbling.

[France — economy; Paris fair.] From our correspondent Jakub Berger.
In the midst of the boiling tumult of Paris, in the midst of the great and small events playing out in this noisiest of world cities, a whole city is now being built here which is to encompass [?] the economic life of all France and her colonies.
French industry is still young; it does not occupy the great place in the family of economies, but it will not be long before it grows into one of the largest industries in Europe.
Signs of this can already be seen today, and the Paris fair, which will be held on a grand scale from 10 May to 2 June of this year, will show how far French industry is already able today to supply the world with its products.
The Paris fair is being built in a park covering an area of 410 square metres. 8200 firms will display France's industries. At the building fair one will not only show with what modern materials one can build today, but houses and little houses of the most varied types will be exhibited, so that one can see [?] what a building of the most varied materials looks like.
Quite a large space there will be taken up by the food industries. Half a million bottles of drink will be exhibited there, from the simplest to the finest kinds.
Expensive French perfumes and cosmetic articles will be on view in new varieties, and people will [?] literally gape open-mouthed at the novelties...
To this are added the various articles of Paris fashion and many other assorted articles, which one will [?] see there in full splendour, as only Paris can...
Since almost all countries grant reductions on the railways, on passports and visas, it is expected that thousands upon thousands of people will gather from everywhere to look and to shop in Paris.
Our Panorama

(The Krimilover shtibl and... Berek Joselewicz. — When the gabbaim travel to the rebbe, the Hasidim must[?] fast[?]. — At "Hakhnoses Kalo" there is rejoicing[?]... a split. — Scuffles[?] over "the bride with the stomach" — uprising in Ząbkowice. — The revolutionaries found a separate "kingdom".)
The Krimilover "shtibl" in Będzin is like a keg of gunpowder that any[?] minute could blow up. The cowards left the "shtibl" long ago and settled[?] in a quieter position, and those who remained truly live in constant fear: any moment now, any moment...
The one to blame for this — so people say — is none other than Berek Joselewicz. Never mind that the great Jewish hero has been dead for about 160 years: his fighting spirit still lives on, and since the Krimilover "shtibl" is located on Berek Joselewicz Street, its[?] "followers", the Krimilover Hasidim, are naturally[?] of a warlike disposition too, and at every opportunity they are ready to tear one another apart... But luckily there exists a "League of Nations" that does not allow any new world war, and the Krimilover "shtibl" has such refined gabbaim, well versed[?] in the laws of diplomacy. Thanks to them, the quarrels are settled peacefully.
But — of what case are these words said? When was this said? When the gabbaim are on the spot and in their own honoured persons hand out the honours, the aliyot, as you know[?]; but when the gabbaim travel to the rebbe for Shabbat and their functions are carried out by "foreign" hands, the situation becomes very serious, and between a "yes" and a "no" the factions compete with each other and slaps echo through Berek Joselewicz lane...
And precisely for that reason a "mortal" battle was fought in the relocated[?] "shtibl". Because the distributor of aliyot allowed himself a caprice and gave no honourable[?] aliyah to a worshipper whose wife's sister-in-law had given birth to a baby boy...
Well, was the man entitled to the aliyah supposed to keep silent? How could that be? Even the greatest "peace-chaser" would have lost his temper at such an injustice — so he answered measure for measure[?] and honoured the "distributor" with a "slap-aliyah", for which one is exempt from a blessing...
According to the "latest reports", the gabbaim are trying to restore the peace, and the main foundation of the planned peace is that the "shtibl" should no longer be located on Joselewicz lane...
—
In the neighbouring lane, on Rybna Street, a "world-[?]" incident also took place, which will no doubt cause a sensation in the "scientific world".
In that lane there has existed for many years a society "Hakhnoses Kalo" [dowering of brides]. The society also has a minyan; the wits of the generation even say that "the [—][?] was created" for the sake of the "snuff-box", that is, the minyan was only for appearances, while the core, the content, was that after the prayers every member of the society should say "Al ken berakh" over a big goblet. But that is beside the point; and anyway, whose business is it that Jews make Kiddush over a bigger goblet, enjoy the "holiness of Shabbat" and at the same time fulfil "how does one dance before the bride"?...
But Satan, may his name be blotted out, did not rest until he succeeded in having his accusation accepted by the Heavenly Court, and "the bride was split"...
Well, so be it — split is split; are there few splits in Jewish life? The trouble, however, is that the "parts" of the "bride" were not divided fairly: one side grabbed "the bride with the stomach"... and the other side was left only with the World to Come, with the "bride's soul"...
And, as we are informed, the side that possesses "the bride with the stomach" is growing stronger; things have gone so far that members are joining not only from the bride's camp — even synagogue worshippers are declaring themselves members of "the bride with the stomach"...
It is truly an injustice crying to heaven, and from this place[?] we appeal to the world's conscience to take up the wrong done to the injured side, so that the equal rights of the "Hakhnoses Kalo" society in Będzin may be restored...
—
Nor should one pass over to the order of the day the rebellion that broke out in Ząbkowice; in our opinion the proper precautions must be taken so that the "fire", God forbid, does not spread to the neighbouring towns, where the disciples still have a certain measure of respect for their rebbe.
— What actually happened there? —
What happened is something that would not have occurred in any big city; such a thing can only happen in a "metropolis" like Ząbkowice. A group of Agudah young men fell, during the Musaf prayer, into such religious ecstasy that they grabbed the wet towels and "honoured" the Musaf prayer-leader with them... who is no lesser flesh-and-blood than the rebbe of the throwers themselves.
It goes without saying that this "gift" was the signal for the "rebellion", and only after "Oseh shalom" did the general attack begin between the two sides, the throwers and the "thrown-at"; and according to the official reports from the "Ząbkowice front", the revolutionary side had to abandon its battle position, and the youngsters intend to proclaim their own "republic" and open a separate "shtibl"...
Ben Amotz.
Thanks to the „Zaglembier Tsaytung"

[Będzin — Hasidim; press satire.]
Thanks to the „Zaglembier Tsaytung" the „9-ers" Hasidim in Będzin have won a name in the wide world.
A few weeks ago we reported in „Our Panorama" the course of the upheaval among the „9-ers" in Będzin. The New York „Forverts" picked up the story and added the following „delicacies":
Będzin, a Jewish town in Poland lying on the German border, grew envious of neighbouring Germany. Why should Germany have a dictator and Będzin not? So the town thought it over and also set over itself a dictator by the name of Reb Anshel...
And just as every dictator likes to create a party around himself, to create followers who will jump „kadosh" for him, so too the Będzin dictator Reb Anshel created followers around himself who would carry out his orders.
The Będzin dictator fixed on one thing — that the Jews of Będzin should strictly keep their Jewishness, and whoever would not keep „Jewishness" was not to be allowed to wait until he received his punishment in the next world; rather he must be punished at once in this world for his sins, so that he would be deterred[?] even a tenth[?] time from sinning again.
For this purpose the Będzin dictator founded a party which he named „the party of the Nines". He divided all his party men into groups of nine persons; that is precisely why he named the party „the Nines party" and every party member — „the Niner".
What were the „Niners" supposed to do? First, the dictator of the Nines party demanded that everyone belonging to the party of Niners should study as little as possible and dance and sing as much as possible in the Ger shtibl. And one must dance so long that the sweat pours down and the cheeks turn red. This very dancing is a very great mitzvah, said the dictator, and in the next world one will receive for it a world full of Paradise.
But that is not all. The second task of the „Niners" was — to go about the town and spy in the houses whether the Jews of Będzin keep their Jewishness as they should.
Above all the „Niners" had to check how the „kest-children" [young couples boarding with the in-laws] behave after the wedding. They went from house to house and measured with a belt whether between the beds of husband and wife there was a space of an ell. They also watched whether the young wives wear wigs on their heads, whether, God forbid, a little of their own hair shows from under the wigs; and also whether the women go about in dresses with long sleeves, buttoned up to the neck.
But all that is still nothing. To know how the kest-children behave at night, patrols went round the alleys and peered through the chinks of the shutters, and also through the keyholes, to see how things stand with piety among the young Hasidic men of Będzin.
So the dictator Reb Anshel commanded, and so his followers did.
Whoever seeks[?] sins finds them. And indeed the night-watchmen kept finding sinners. The dictator Reb Anshel punished every sinner either with wine — that is, the sinner had to buy ten bottles of wine for Reb Anshel and his men — or with lashes. If one had no money to buy wine, one had to let oneself, begging your pardon, be laid on the table and catch the real lashes from Reb Anshel and his men. And Reb Anshel did not give lashes with belts, as ordinary Hasidim do; he gave salted lashes — that is, he ordered leather straps to be soaked in salt, and with these very salted straps he had the sinners whipped, so they[?] would feel the taste.
Sometimes Reb Anshel would also order his men to burst into young men's houses, take the food out of the kitchens and bring it into the Ger shtibl, so that a little feast could be held.
The young Hasidic men of Będzin suffered the greatest troubles from Reb Anshel the dictator and kept silent; they were afraid to speak, for they trembled before the salted lashes.
When Reb Anshel saw that his dictatorship was a success, he began to devise all sorts of new decrees against the young Hasidic men of the town. Whomever he wished he sent off to the Rebbe for several weeks, with the stern order that he must not dare come home before the appointed time; on others he imposed heavy levies, so that with that money he could make feasts for his men. People had to sell their tallis and tefillin or their Sabbath kapote when Reb Anshel the dictator demanded money. He also began to meddle in the private lives of his own men and issued them dates — how long they must not come home to their wives but sleep in the Hasidim's shtibl. He behaved like a real dictator.
That was already too much. On a certain day the young Hasidic men of Będzin revolted.
The leader of the revolt was Hershel Shochet. When the dictator Reb Anshel was standing in the Ger shtibl issuing his orders, Hershel Shochet and his men burst into the shtibl and fell upon the dictator.
In the shtibl a mighty war broke out between the revolutionaries and the dictator's loyal followers. They beat each other and tore at sidelocks, until the revolutionaries won and drove out the „Anshelists".
Then they laid the dictator Reb Anshel with great honour on the table and gave him the real lashes.
Reb Anshel the dictator screamed „gevalt" that they should whip him dry, not with the salted lashes, but the revolutionaries did not listen and dealt out salted ones as many as would go in, and more.
Now the young men of Będzin have breathed freely again and are enjoying[?] the freedom they fought for.
How[?] about doing the same already with the dictator of neighbouring Germany, which lies next to Będzin!...
News from Częstochowa

(From our correspondent A. Wrocławski).

On the cantorial question.

As is known, the kehilla only recently received word from Cantor Mr. Badasz that he is staying in South Africa. So the matter of a cantor for the town synagogue (Stadt-Schul) has become topical.

Work has turned up for the Częstochowa choir-singers... from all around [?], every Sabbath they have the pleasure of the trial cantors.

This Sabbath the well-known cantor and composer Kamieniecki, until recently cantor in Piotrków, is coming.

From the Mendele academy.

On Friday a grandiose Mendele academy took place in the Firemen's Hall.

The lecture on Mendele was delivered by the well-known literary critic, editor of the "Literarishe Bleter", Mr. N. [?] Mayzel. The well-known artist Mr. Jacques Levi recited from Mendele's works.

Local forces also took part in the concert section, such as the laureate of the Kielce voivodeship, Mr. Y. Richter (song) and Mr. Sommerfeld (violin).

The academy made a great impression; hundreds of people went away without tickets.

The council at work on the budget.

The council, as every year, had prepared to deal with the budget over the course of... years [sic] and to unburden its heart of all its grievances and complaints, both justified and unjustified.

The supervisory authority, however, took a different standpoint and sent a letter in which it categorically demands that the kehilla not deal with any personal matters, nor any political affairs, but only take upon itself the duty of drawing up the budget at the proper time, by the 28th of this month, without any scruples; otherwise it will draw the appropriate consequences.

A tragic incident.

On the local railway ramp on Monday a terrible accident befell the young Jewish man Yosef Heisfelner, of blessed memory, who was crushed on the ramp by two shunting wagons.

On the way to the hospital Heisfelner died.

The tragic incident made a depressing impression in the town, as the deceased was greatly loved by the whole Jewish population.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bo
—o—
a) "For I have hardened his heart" (Ex. 10:1)
When speaking to Moses about Pharaoh, the Almighty always stressed "for I have hardened his heart", because when Moses our teacher saw such [?] steadfastness in Pharaoh he took fright: with obstinacy one achieves everything, "chutzpah avails even against Heaven"... So God underlined to him "for I have hardened his heart" — his steadfastness is no natural might that works wonders [?]; only now have I put into him some [?] hardening of the heart... Rabbi Yechiel Meir of Gostynin.
—o—
b) "And that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son" (ibid. 2)
For with them [?], with your son and your son's son, the same will happen: in every generation they will, without knowing it, live through the miracle of the Exodus from Egypt. That is why, in the remembrance of the Exodus, it is said "Remember this day, in which ye came out from the land of Egypt" — for every day of ours in exile is "this day", a repetition of the miracle in Egypt... Panim Yafot.
—o—
c) "Go now ye that are men" (ibid. 11)
When Russia began to care for the souls of the Jews and set about founding schools for their children and the like, R' Moshe Meisels said:
— To Moses' demand "we will go with our young and with our old" Pharaoh answered "go now ye that are men": the old ones may be pious — just leave the children to me. As for them — "come, let us deal wisely" — with them let me be clever: found schools for them, stuff them with wisdom and Haskalah...
* * *
In the days of Nicholas I, when the government began to spread Haskalah among the Jews, Minister Uvarov sent Dr. Lilienthal into the Jewish Pale to spread enlightenment among the Jews.
Arriving in Vilna, he called together all the communal leaders (parnasim) and notables of the town and spoke to them about education and about the great favour the Russian government was doing the Jews by spreading knowledge among them.
A parnas named Chaim Nachman answered him:
— One thing [?] is hard for me. Why does the government want to spread knowledge among the Jews before it has done so among the gentiles? Most Jews are literate, while most Russians do not even know the shape of a letter...
—o—
d) "Speak now in the ears of the people, and let them ask every man of his neighbour" (ibid. 3 [as printed])
For twelve months the borrowed things lay hidden with the Jews, and no Jew informed on another to his Egyptian neighbour that he had not returned the borrowed things but intended to run away with them... That was [—] proof that they had already repaired the trait of informing, because of which the Jews were driven into exile.. Yalkut Shemot, remez 182.
—o—
e) "The man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants, and in the sight of the people" (11:3)
The way of Scripture is to speak in the manner of "not only this but also that": the greater novelty is counted at the end, and here the greatest novelty is that Moses was esteemed "in the sight of the people", in the eyes of his own people — that is a greater thing than "in the sight of Pharaoh's servants"... Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
* * *
"The poor man's wisdom is despised" —
"Misken" means familiarity. Because one is used to him, his wisdom carries no weight... Derush.
* * *
Because Moses was great among the Egyptians, in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants, he was also great "in the sight of the people", in the eyes of the Jews. Jews attach importance only to one who is esteemed in the eyes of the gentiles... Imrei Chen.
—o—
f) "Their kneading troughs being bound up in their clothes" (ibid. 34)
The Be'er Heitev on Orach Chaim §477 writes: it is customary to break off a piece of the afikoman and keep it. On this the Magen Avraham §110 [as printed], s.k. 7, and the Sha'arei Teshuvah write that there is no hint of it [in the sources].
But in truth there is a hint in this verse. On the words "their kneading troughs bound up in their clothes" the Mekhilta writes: "They took the leftovers of the matzah and bitter herbs with them, for they cherished the commandments." Hence it follows that one must leave over a remembrance of the matzah. Divrei Yirmiyahu.
—o—
g) "And the children of Israel did according to the word of Moses; and they asked of the Egyptians" (12:35)
"According to the word of Moses — which he had told them in Egypt: and let them ask every man of his neighbour." Rashi.
What is Rashi adding here? The verse says it explicitly.
But "let them ask every man of his neighbour" means that one Jew should lend to another. It was a special command, that Jews should do kindness to one another, and that is why it says "speak now" — "na" is nothing but an expression of request. One had to ask that one Jew lend to another, but not that they borrow from the gentiles; and when the verse relates the praise "and the children of Israel did according to the word of Moses", it too means only this praise, that "they asked every man of his neighbour" — that one Jew lent to another... The Vilna Gaon.
Meyz's interview with the kehilla leaders.

[Będzin — humour and satire; the kehilla. Opening of the "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle) section.]
"Der Kokh-Lefl" — humour and satire, compiled by Amutzli.

When I saw that there is no other news,
I decided to snatch an interview
with all the kehilla leaders, with the bright minds
who sacrifice all their strength for the community —
with the Zionists, Agudah, the artisans, the P.Z. [Poale Zion] and the non-
party Hasidim,
as the verse says: ringstraked, speckled and grizzled...
and how all of them
were so[?] polite and smiling[?]
and without any [?]
spoke out their thoughts
concerning the gmina [kehilla] and concerning the rabbi
in the holy community of Będzin, in the year 5696.

Says the vice-chairman of the council, R' Nute[?]:
I have never yet regretted my speeches,
for even if we were to win completely
it would still be better that both kehilla bodies
be dissolved,
because in the gmina mill the transmission has broken down
and therefore everyone must resign.

The non-party parnas R' Avraham Yissachar
holds that the business does not pay and "they turned backward"...
He is a Jew, a wit,
a sort of[?] Arthur Schnitzler;
according to his "patientsche"[?]
the whole gmina-"vrientsche"[?] is good for nothing...
It is like a cliché without colours
and like a broken shard;
so it would do no harm at all
to dissolve both — the board together with the council.

R' Shlomo Yitzchak Wider surmises
that, by his reasoning,
the government, speedily in our days,
will chase away the board — may its merit protect us —
then he and the parnas R' Itche Meir
will recite the full Hallel,
and together with R' Eli Ber, "the lion of the company",
the angels will sing praise;
he will drive out of the gmina the evildoers, the "drabes" [louts],
and no one will run to the starosta on the Sabbath any more;
there will be "gladness and joy, light for the Jews";
the Right P.Z. will harness themselves entirely to the Hasidim;
it will be good by all opinions;
parnas Kornfeld[?] will grow sidelocks,
and parnas Herszlewicz will also become loyal
and demonstrate on the 1st of May.

And now, gentlemen, the floor goes to his eminence —
hear what the P.Z. parnas R' Shlomo says,
he, the "lion" of Będzin socialism:
he says the gmina is full of chauvinism;
he hates the intelligentsia,
all the people's "hostile elements";
for him the main thing,
as gossips[?] say, is "Panye" —
the "harmony";
therefore he holds: "naplevas"[?] [roughly Polish: spit on it]!
on the whole chauvinist council.

More interesting, however, is the opinion of the chairman:
as far as he is concerned, gentlemen, he says,
all the talk of the council chairman has no substance;
it truly makes him[?] faint.
As chairman of a [?] gmina
he has first of all in mind
to pay out the pensions to the monopolists of the Torah;
thanks to this he fears no one;
he took the weapons away from the Zionists,
and now they[?] shout "alive and enduring";
the situation is clear to him,
but the starosta will not accept his
resignation.
Ha-Tsofe.
Statement by the chief kehilla commissioners in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — satire; kehilla and rabbinate.]
In connection with a sequestrator having come to Rabbi Hager [one of the rabbis of Sosnowiec] to collect 10 zł. of kehilla dues (etat), we turned to the presidium of the commissarial kehilla board with the question why this had been done.
"We are convinced," the head of the community declared, "that Rabbi Hager will not pay the dues for reasons of principle; we shall then take from him, against the debt, a few holy books that we need — for instance, I need the 'Yoreh De'ah', the laws of the festivals [regalim — also 'feet'; there are no such laws in Yoreh De'ah]... and my colleague the Doctor is starting to study a lesson in 'How does one dance' [after Ketubot 16b, 'how does one dance before the bride'] — before the commissioner."
Khatskele Kalbonik is angry at the small traders.

[Będzin — satire in Galician-Polish dialect; small traders and their associations.]
[?] Yasn[?], I have a new story to tell you. A brand-new story about our "knall-tiers"[?].
Here in Będzin a few merchants are "freyning" (meaning: uniting[?]) — perhaps half a dozen [?], so that every little union has a president, with a bell, with a green [cloth?] on the table; every president [?] "shlogn shimusim"[?]; they grab a teapot and [?] give money.
So I, Khatskele, came and said this:
Let us make of all the stones one stone; you understand — of all the presidents let there be one president, one bell, one green [cloth?], and the "shlogn shimusim" at their best.
Was I right?
Well, the "knall-tiers"[?] were afraid they would go kaput from their little benches [=board seats], so[?] they went [?] and said they have a "geyem mismatn"[?] — a "beheym-rot" [pun: Geheimrat, secret council / "cattle council"].
You know, [?], what a "beheym-rot" is? [?] to know thus [?] ... to know that their wise men themselves know "a plague" [=nothing].
[?] that they run around with their [?] each time in another "melina" [den]; but if I make a [?] of the "beheym-rot" and tell them the story — you know what I'll tell them?
Go to all the devils with your crooked[?] cynicism; [?] ... do you think it is for the good of the small traders? Me, Khatskele, you won't [?]; I already know what you want; [?] live thus, as I know — that's what I'll tell them.
Meanwhile, may you[?] have a good Sabbath and keep well.
Walking

[Humour — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle) page; satirical feuilleton, Będzin and Sosnowiec; followed by two short jokes.]
(A popular medical lecture)

When we manoeuvre[?] with our feet and a policeman does not demand a złoty fine from us for standing, that means we are walking.

Everyone has his own gait. For example, the communal activist Mr. Rechnic goes to the magistrate [town hall] every day, although the president [mayor] needs the "lazhnikes"[?] [perhaps the bath-house, łaźnia] only 2 hours a week.
The town "notables"[?] go to the "Club" every day.
A certain local public figure goes walking every evening with a strange "dove".

How should one walk?
When public figures walk, they must look around to see whether a newspaperman is following them; when haberdashery merchants walk, they must look around to see whether a member of the boycott committee is following them; when a "dove" walks with a strange young man, it should, of course, be none of the husband's concern.

Where should one walk?
People who are interested in politics should go to the "Hachnasat Orchim" [hostel]; people who want to hear empty, threadbare speeches should go to a session of the kehilla council; people who want to stay healthy must not go to the doctors of the "K.K." [probably the sick fund, Kasa Chorych].
Walking is very healthy; that is why the Sosnowiec rich men know how to keep walking when one asks them for a donation.
Above all, one must be very careful when walking on the pavement.
And here we wish to warn (according to the "ferv[?]..." of the local "windows"[?]) the old men and old women of the "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] that when they walk in the street, they should, God forbid, not pester the "nerve-shattered" passers-by.
Yosef.

—o—
A "Devoted" Son-in-law.
A mother-in-law lay on her deathbed and wept. They ask her: why are you crying?
She answers: I am not leaving behind a son who will say Kaddish after me.
The son-in-law calls out: Mother-in-law, I will serve you like your own son.

—o—
Time Difference.
A Będzin bill-discounter [money-lender] has calculated that it pays better to travel to Sosnowiec by taxi than by tram.
How so?
Because on the tram you must pay in advance, while a taxi you pay only later — so you gain time.
The Mamzer (72)

[Serial novel — "The Mamzer" (The Bastard), a thrilling tragic novel about a prodigy; installment 72; set in America.]
By Adv.[?] S. Gelishpavski [S. Gieliszpawski?].
A thrilling tragic novel about an illui [prodigy]

— Fifteen years, fifteen whole years he [my husband] worked as a bookkeeper in his [the employer's] business. He had come to him while still a boy, and when he fell ill with consumption, he used up his savings on his illness. Nothing was left for me but to jump into the water. Helpless, without any means to live, I was left with a sick husband with whom the doctors told me to travel to warm baths; but how could I travel with him when I had not a penny to my soul? Everything I could, I had already sold off myself, and having not a single cent left to keep up our bit of life, I went to his employer, fell at his feet, wept and begged him to lend me a few dollars to save my husband. He heard me out, told me to come a second time, a third time; four times I was in his rich office, four times he looked at me and devoured me with his eyes, four times my eyes shed tears before him and my heart shed blood.
— Quite right[?] — he used to say — a woman must do everything to save a sick husband. And I did not notice when, like a beast, he threw himself on me and began to kiss me. I wept and screamed, begged him not to bathe himself in my blood, but my tears did not help. "A woman must do everything to save her husband," he said, drawing me to him, "my iron safe stays open for you, you can take as much money as you need, only mine you must be, to me you must belong [printed "mut... mutu"], and if your husband's life is dear to you — then choose..."
— I had no way out: on one side stood my loving sick husband, and on the other — betraying him; and I chose the second, I submitted to his bestial desire in order to save my husband.
— Already in the first month, when I was with my husband in California, I felt that I was going to be a mother. I could not bear a child by my husband, because married life with a woman was strictly forbidden to him; I could not have an illegal operation — I could not leave my husband alone for several days. Again I found myself helpless, and disregarding the doctors' prohibition I, as his wife, was obliged [to live with him] in order to dispel the suspicion, which would have killed him had I given birth to the child. He is sure that the child is his, but I, Rabbi, know that my child is a mamzer, a mamzer is my child, Rabbi, and I suffer very hard from it.
— Three years have already passed since I gave birth to the child, three years I have been living such a life, full of suffering and torment. I cannot look my husband, who even today is still not well, in the eyes. How bitter it is for me, Rabbi — she wept.
Once an elderly man of about sixty-five came to him, a member of his synagogue, and asked him to come along with him to his sick wife, who wished to talk with him.
— She is very sick and weak, we fear for her life. Forty-five years we have lived together like two loving doves. Not a widower will I remain if, God forbid, she should die, but an orphan, Rabbi. My wife asks you to come to her; perhaps you will bring her a complete recovery — he said, and as he did so his eyes filled with tears.
When he entered the room where the sick woman lay, he saw at her bedside three young women and two gentlemen.
— These are our children — the sick woman's husband explained, wiping the tears from his face.
— How do you feel, dear Mrs. Gneskin? — he asks the sick woman.
With a contented smile she nodded her head, looked around to see who was in the room, and, turning her head back, closed her eyes.
And Moshele understood that the sick woman did not want to speak in the presence of her husband and children, and he asked them to leave him alone with the sick woman.
— We are alone now, Mrs. Gneskin — he said to the sick woman.
And again she opened her eyes, looked around the room once more, and, taking a small key from under[?] the pillow, she said in a weak voice:
— Please, Rabbi... open the drawer... there is a little box there...
With trembling hands she took out of the little box a not-large written notebook and handed it to Moshele.
— "My Confession" — Moshele saw written in large letters on the first page; he turned[?] the leaf over and began to read:
"I was nineteen years old when I first saw, in the zoological[?] park, David Gneskin, who later became my husband. Right from our first acquaintance we became great friends, and not a single day passed without our meeting.
He was a peddler, very hard-working, and every day he would tell me how much he had earned, and we were very happy. I felt that I loved the modest, honest and good David.
I knew very well that David was a good friend to me, that he was not like other young men who seek to exploit the frequent unawareness of a young girl such as I was.
(To be continued).
The Kehilla Budget at the Council Plenum.

[Będzin — kehilla.]
Pension for M. Lewin struck out. — Agudah parnassim leave the meeting — Pensions for members of the rabbinate reduced.
Sunday's meeting of the kehilla council aroused wide interest. The “gallery” is packed full; only the “benches” of the Revisionist and Left Poale Zion parnassim remain “orphaned”. About the latter “legendary” stories are told, that a few weeks ago the “bench” of the P[oale] Z[ion] parnas was “bought off” by the “Agudah” for a shitse[?] [unclear word; perhaps a trip] to Eretz Israel.
The mood is tense. The telephone does not stop ringing; the interested circles ask how the “sects” are dividing up. The answer is:
— The National Bloc has a majority...
———
— I declare[?] today's meeting open — says the chairman, Mr. G. Landner — and state that it is valid with any number of members. After the minutes of the last meeting are read, Mr. Landner remarks that the minutes do not agree with the true course of the previous meeting, and proceeds[?] to the agenda, to the first item of the budget — pensions for the rabbinate.
Chairman: I take heaven as my witness that the Zionists are not against the person of M. Lewin because he is an Agudah man, but against the tactic of getting in as rabbi in Będzin. Right on the day of the rabbi's passing pressure was applied to force through the candidacy of M. Lewin, and since then various means have been used, and outside forces are being used as well. Mr. Landner quotes a responsum of the Chatam Sofer, which forbids a rabbi who wants to push his way in against the will of the community, and he proposes that the pension for M. Lewin be struck out.
Parnas Rygnski in the name of the minority[?]: One must consider the question seriously, not offhandedly, because it concerns people's lives. As regards the prohibition of the Chatam Sofer, let us — says Mr. Rinski — ask the Chatam Sofer's grandson whether one may strike out a pension for a person on whom public opinion agrees.
We do not wish by this — he says — to settle the question of the rabbis; we are ready to give the guarantee that all we want is that Rabbi[?] M. Lewin should be only a moreh hora'ah [religious decisor].
Parnas Herszlewicz says that if Będzin needs a fourth moreh tzedek, a competition should be announced; but that is not being done — by various combinations they want to settle the rabbinate question in Będzin. The intention is not a moreh tzedek, but a rabbi.
Against striking out the pension speak the parnassim Schönberg and Ehrlich, the latter saying that in their time all were “gar” [probably a misprint for: in favour of] the candidacy of M. Lewin as moreh tzedek.
Dozór [kehilla board] member Hampel appeals to the council to wash off the “stain of shame” from the administration and to strike out the pension.
The vote is taken. Result: 7 for striking it out and 4 against. After the vote the Agudah parnassim leave the meeting.
On the pensions for the rabbinate the chairman proposes reducing them by 15 percent. After a short discussion the proposal of parnas Goldsztajn is adopted, that the reduction should amount to 10 percent.
The emeritus pensions for the rebbetzins Grojbart and Lewin are set at 4000 zł. a year.
The discretionary fund in the amount of 500 zł. is reduced after a discussion to 100 zł.
A lively discussion, which led to stormy moments, took place over the item of 1000 zł. for renting larger kehilla premises. Mr. Landner is against the kehilla allowing itself larger premises in the present hard times, and he submits the following proposals: 1) to take back the kehilla room in which the Bundist[?] library exists, and 2) that a commission be elected to settle the question in general, whether the kehilla is obliged to maintain the library with premises and with the related expenses. The proposals are adopted with the amendment that if the commission finds that the kehilla must maintain the library, premises elsewhere should be rented at the kehilla's expense.
With this the meeting is closed.
The continuation will take place next Sunday.
From the Commercial Agents' Association.

[Zagłębie — trade associations.]
At the last meeting, besides all the members, Messrs. Abamow[?] and Chmielnicki (Katowice) took part. The chairman, Mr. Lewin, welcomes the guests and points to their fruitful work in this field in the Upper Silesian region, on account of which they were invited, so that they should give a talk and lay out the plan of work for the future.
Then Mr. Abakhow[?] speaks on “The present situation of commercial agents, and what next”. The speaker paints the present situation of commercial agents in the blackest colours, and the only salvation is to organise in one strong association. Mr. A. cites several facts from the Poznań region, where non-Jewish merchants approached several Jewish manufacturers in Łódź to dismiss their Jewish travelling salesmen and take on non-Jews in their place. Mr. A. ends his talk with an appeal also to the absent agents of Zagłębie to create a large and strong association, which would be able to remove all stumbling blocks.
The talk is supplemented by Mr. Chmielnicki, who points out the usefulness of such an association in all matters.
Finally it is resolved to protest against the approach of the Poznań Christian merchants and to send the protest to Warsaw.
Correction.

From Mr. S. Fürstenberg, chairman of the supervisory board of the „S. Fürstenberg“ Gymnasium, we have received a correction, which we publish on the basis of the press law.
„The supervisory board of the „S. Fürstenberg“ Gymnasium states that the report of the first meeting of the new supervisory board, which appears in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ No. 4 of 24 January (styczeń) 1936, at the top of page 7, under the title: „The first meeting of the appointed supervisory board of the S. Fürstenberg Gymnasium“, does not correspond in any way whatsoever to reality; nor is the assertion true that the supervisory board supposedly established that no defraudations (embezzlements) and abuses had been committed in the school.“
Sosnowiec — A criminal gang was active on the streets of Zagłębie

and poured a burning substance over the clothes of dozens of Jewish passers-by.
The Jewish population is under the impression of what has happened in the last few days in Sosnowiec and in Będzin.
On the busiest streets of both towns a criminal gang was at work and poured a burning (corrosive) material over the fur garments and coats of many dozens of Jewish passers-by.
The victims, of course, did not notice at all what was going on behind their backs; only when they came home did they suddenly see „hot“ [?] stains on their outer garments. At first everyone thought it was an ordinary „hot“ stain, but when they began to clean it, only then did they see the ruin — the garment was burnt through.
One can easily imagine the tragic scenes that took place in many homes, for among the victims there are many who for months saved grosz by grosz in order to be able to have a garment made for the winter.
We also know of the case of a poor girl, whose relatives had a „pakenem“ [?] coat (palto) made for her. On Saturday night the girl went out into the street and came back with a damaged coat.
In this connection a delegation of the local Jewish councillors' „Koło“ (club) intervened with the competent authority, where the promise was given that a strict investigation would be conducted into it and that the police guard on the main streets would be reinforced.
A public elementary school will be built in Pogoń

and in the town [itself] — „in the time to come“...
Meeting of the town council.
On Monday a meeting of the local town council took place. The main item on the agenda was to allocate 40.000 zł. for building a public elementary school in Pogoń.
On behalf of the Jewish „Koło“ (club) councillor Mr. Aliner took the floor; he described the dire state of the public schools in the town in general, and of the school on Kościelna Street in particular, and appealed to the presidium of the town administration that the so badly needed public school should also be built in the town [centre].
In the reply of the president [?] it was promised that the plan provides that after the school in Pogoń is finished, such a school will be built in the centre of the town.
Whether a shochet belongs to the clergy (kley-koydesh) or not.

The opinion of Professor Schorr will be heard.
As we wrote at the time, the local district court recognized the claim of Mrs. Makower, widow of the well-known shochet R' Yekl of blessed memory, and awarded her the payment of a sum of 2,500 zł.
Against this verdict the commissarial kehilla lodged an appeal, in which it is stressed that a shochet does not belong at all to the „duchowny“ (clergy) category, and therefore the kehilla has no obligation to pay a retirement pension to the surviving family.
The question will be dealt with by the court of appeal in Warsaw; Professor Schorr is to be called as expert.
The appeal also stresses that „the former dozory (kehilla boards), not knowing any Polish, did not understand the difference between the words: „support and pension [?]“...
Under-age hooligans snatch a jar of herring

Into the grocery („colonial goods“) shop of Mr. Yosl Lidowarski on Dęblińska Street, on Monday in the evening hours, several under-age łobuzy (rascals) came in and demanded to be given candles and matches. When Mrs. L. explained that she did not have the requested articles, one of the gang said: „Even without that we will burn you down“. Then they snatched a jar (słoik) of herring and ran away.
General meeting of the Zionist Organization

On Sunday, in its own premises, under the chairmanship of Mr. Buksbaum, the annual general meeting of the Zionist Organization took place.
In the presidium: Messrs. G. Stawski [?], A. Langman, and as secretary Mr. Pfeffer. The memory of the deceased member Ber Zelinger [?] of blessed memory was honoured by rising.
The chairman Dr. S. Meladista [?] gives a report on the general activity. Among other things he emphasizes the great achievements of the Zionist Organization in carrying out the Keren Hayesod campaign, and firm foundations have been laid for further work for the Keren Hayesod.
Director Lejwrowicz reports on the activity of the Jewish councillors' club. Dr. Meladista explains that as the elected representative of the local Jewish population on the audit commission at the magistrate (town hall), whose task besides supervising the finances is also to work out a comprehensive [?] economic plan, he has succeeded in doing a great deal for the Jewish population in Sosnowiec. Further reports are given by: Gitler of the KKL (Jewish National Fund), Gachtman [?] — the Artisans' He-Halutz, and Mr. Brzeski of the treasury.
Then Dr. Meladista gives a longer lecture on the topic „The present situation in Zionism and our further tasks“. Pointing to the great achievements of the Zionist movement, the speaker says that Eretz Israel is our only hope; in the Diaspora it is growing darker and darker; even in our kehillas, which should have been a model of Jewish self-government, the spirit of black reaction has broken in. Against the will of Jewish society unwanted rulers are imposed, who want to rule with a strong hand as in medieval times.
After the discussion and the granting of the absolutorium (discharge of the outgoing board), the following committee was elected: Dr. S. Meladista (chairman), G. Stawski, G. Abramczyk, Director S. Lejwrowicz, Adv. Katz, S. Brzeski, Inusz, Mangel, Mrs. Żarna [?], Feldman, Czarny, Marianka, Gitler, Yaakov and Saks. Deputies: Ledibehm [?], Schlesinger and Pfeffer. Audit commission: Mrs. Stawska, Frenkel and Radwik [?].
With „Hatikvah“ the meeting is closed.
—o—
A theft at the tax office.
In the premises of the tax office, councillor Mr. Kizer [?] had a wallet (portfel) containing 70 zł. stolen.
Will the author of the shameful “Aryan” resolution, Councillor Kosterski, become Vice-President of Kielce?

[Head of the section “Life in Kielce”; Kielce — city council and antisemitism.] “Dos lebn in Kielce” — Life in Kielce. (Friday, 7 Shevat 5696 — piątek 31 stycznia 1936 [Friday, 31 January 1936])
The local vice-president [deputy mayor], Mr Jan Mitshka [Mieczka?], a few days ago sent a letter to the Kielce voivode, Dr Dziadosz [?], in which he announces that he is resigning from his post as vice-president of the city of Kielce.
The reason for the resignation is said to be the various differences of opinion prevailing between him and the other members of the city administration concerning the methods of running the city economy and concerning the guidelines of local self-government.
Rumours are already going round the town that the councillors' “club” intends to push Councillor Kosterski [?], the initiator of the shameful “Aryan” resolution, into the post of vice-president. This demonstration by the councillors' “club” is supposed to be a “satisfaction” for Mr Kosterski, who became so “famous” on account of his antisemitic resolution, which — as was already reported in our paper — was subsequently annulled by the Kielce voivode.
Whether Mr Kosterski's eventual election as vice-president will be confirmed by the supervisory authority is a big question.
Names of other councillors and of ordinary persons are also being mentioned, people who until now have had nothing whatsoever to do with the economy of self-government, but who for various reasons cannot come into consideration.
Sanacja paper demands that the city council be dissolved and a commissioner appointed.

[Kielce — city council and politics; followed by an appeal for the KKL.] The local Sanacja paper “Ekspres Codzienny” has for several days been coming out with unusually sharp articles against the Kielce city council and even against the city president [mayor]; this paper is at pains to show that the vice-president's motives for resigning are correct.
Meanwhile the dispute has sharpened even further because of the tactless conduct of the city council towards the outgoing vice-president.
This happened at Tuesday's city council session, which, incidentally, supplied characteristic curiosities of its own. First of all it took an hour and a half until a quorum was assembled. The one who helped out in this situation was, namely, the Jewish councillor R' Meir Eisenberg, who was called out to the session. The “numerous” Jewish representation was thus destined for the first time to play a certain role in the present city council.
A second[?] curiosity: the vice-president, Mr Metshke [Mieczka?], asked for the floor for a personal statement. Instead of giving him the floor, however, the president, Mr Artwiński, puts it to a vote whether he should be given the floor. The motion fails. Nevertheless the president gives Mr Metshke the floor, and he approaches the rostrum.
At that moment the Sanacja councillor Tomczyk rises and asks for the floor on a point of order.
President Artwiński: Please!
Tomczyk: I request that a 5-minute recess be ordered.
The motion is adopted and a recess is declared.
After the recess it turns out that the councillors have broken the quorum of the session and thus prevented the vice-president's statement.
As we learn, the results of the said dispute are to become known within the next few days.
It is important to add that Mr Metshke is a former major of the Polish army and is known as an experienced economic manager.
—o—
[Boxed appeal:] Jews of Kielce! Buy the little flower today for the benefit of the Keren Kayemet!
Report meeting at the Small Traders' Association.

[Kielce — small trade.] On Sunday a large report meeting was held in the premises of the Small Traders' Association about the recent congress of small traders in Warsaw. The delegates — Fiszman, A. J. Szejnfeld[?], G. Górski, Złota[?] and Zajączkowski — gave a report on all the questions that were discussed and resolved at the congress.
Among other things Mr Górski also conveyed to the assembled the words of Deputy Dr Sommerstein, with which he had addressed the congress: “that Jewish society in Poland should not lose heart because of the intensified antisemitic agitation”.
At the end Mr Górski also reported on the question of reducing rent, which was likewise dealt with at the congress.
The “Abyssinian” diamond merchants arrested.

[Kielce — crime.] The Kielce police have arrested 2 well-known swindlers, Ignacy Ciechanowski[?] of Żyrardów[?] and Edward Zamojski of Warsaw. These are the “Abyssinian merchants” who last week swindled Mrs Feuerstein, selling her “diamond” earrings supposedly originating from the “famous treasure” of the Queen of Sheba... On the arrested swindlers 66 various rings and earrings were found, made of brass, which they sell as gold. Both swindlers were put in prison.
Important general meeting of “Linat Hatzedek”.

[Kielce — welfare and health.] On Sunday, 2 February, at 6 o'clock in the evening, an important general meeting of the “Linat Hatzedek” society in Kielce will take place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla.
Since the doctors' strike has already been settled — the doctors will, beginning from 1 luty [February], again give medical help to poor sick people on certificates of Linat Hatzedek — it is very desirable that the Jewish population of Kielce take part in the meeting en masse, in order to set this very important and highly useful institution anew on its proper level.
Kehilla budget for 1936 approved.
[Kielce — kehilla.] At the session of the kehilla board, which took place this week, the budget for the year 1936 was approved. In the next few days the plenary sessions of the council will begin.
General meeting of the House-Owners' Bank.

[Kielce — economy and banking.] This[?] Sunday a general meeting of the House-Owners' Bank took place. Because of the importance of the meeting, which incidentally had very sensational moments, we shall give a detailed report in the next issue.
Big Dance at the Zionist Club

[Kielce — society, Zionism.]
Tomorrow, Saturday night, a big dance (“dancing”) will take place at the Zionist club [in Kielce]. Admission for members and invited guests.
A Meeting about the “Road Tax”

[Kielce — small trade, municipal taxes.]
On Sunday, 2 February [luty], at 6 in the evening, a joint meeting of all merchants and small traders will take place at the Small Traders' Association concerning the new “road tax”, which the local magistrate [municipality] wants to introduce and which is very irrational. One pays it as many as [?] 4 times a year. At the meeting appropriate material will be worked out, which will be sent to the proper authorities.
Major Lecture by Rabbi Gold

[Kielce — Zionism, Mizrachi.]
On Wednesday, 5 February [luty], the president of the world Mizrachi organization, Rabbi Gold [presumably Rabbi Ze'ev (Wolf) Gold], will be staying in Kielce. The distinguished guest and famous speaker will appear the same day at 8 o'clock in the evening at the Teatr Polski with a public lecture on the present political situation in Zionism in general and in Mizrachi in particular.
Rabbi Gold's visit has aroused great interest in all national Jewish circles in Kielce and the surrounding area.
We greet the honoured Zionist leader with a heartfelt “Barukh ha-ba” (welcome)!
From the Fruit Section of the Jewish Small Traders' Association

[Kielce — small trade, organisation.]
This Monday an organising meeting of the fruit section of the Small Traders' Association took place at the premises of the Small Traders' Association. After a lengthy discussion, in which a number of fruit merchants took part, a commission was elected consisting of: Baumsztejn, Wróbel [?], Rozenblat, Krajzman [?], J. Zylbersztejn and Jasna [?]. The task of the commission is to settle, in an amicable, merchant-like manner, all kinds of disputes among the merchants and to draw up a regulamin (by-laws) for the fruit section.
About the Examinations for Paint Merchants in Kielce

[Kielce — small trade, licensing.]
This week Messrs. J. Górski and H. Piotrowski visited the pharmacy inspector at the Voivodeship Office and discussed with him the planned examinations for paint (dye) merchants. The inspector declared that he will meet the wishes of the merchants as far as possible and will endeavour to find a way (modus) of easing the examinations for the merchants.

Which Documents and Invoices Are Exempt from Stamp Duty?

[Kielce — taxes, trade.]
In view of the mass of written inquiries about stamp duty, we consider it necessary to explain that exempt from stamp duty are all invoices, copies of invoices and all kinds of commercial documents concerning purchase, sale and the like [?] which are issued by a merchant or manufacturer to a buyer, if one of them — either the buyer or the seller — holds a patent (trade licence) or pays turnover tax. If one has only a patent and pays no turnover tax (obrotowe), one likewise need not put stamps on invoices.
In businesses where there is a patent, no stamps are needed on any cash receipts whatsoever, nor on any other documents that arise from a transaction in goods and the taking of money.
If a person who has no patent issues an invoice or receipt to another person who likewise has no patent, stamps must still be affixed — for example, when a private person issues an invoice for an article sold, which a person bought not for trading but for his own use. (H. H.)

The Excesses in Przystajń.
The disturbances that have begun in the small towns of the Częstochowa district are taking on an ever more serious character.
The outbreaks took on a drastic character this Monday in Przystajń. The outbreaks were organized during the market day.
At about half past ten in the morning a hooligan went up to a Jewish stall selling soap [?] and overturned the stall with the soap [?]; as if at a signal, people began to overturn and loot the Jewish stalls.
An indescribable panic arose among the local Jews and those who had come from elsewhere. The police, consisting of 8 men, could not cope, because while they were guarding some of the market stall-keepers [?] so that they could pack up their goods, in other places Jewish property was being overturned and snatched.
After these deeds they set about smashing windowpanes at Jews' homes: at all 27 Jewish families the panes were smashed, even the window frames being torn out.
The hooligans also broke into the dwellings of Lehenhof [?], Feige Mantel and others, and destroyed everything. Several Jews were also badly beaten, among others Y. Szmulewicz and Mrs. Abramowicz.
