When One Sits Down in the Jewish Kehilla

[Article — Będzin, kehilla and culture.] It is still a good thing that once a year it falls to make a budget for the Jewish kehilla affairs; were it not for that, one would not even know whether such an institution exists at all in Jewish life. And yet, when one gathers for such a budget session and looks at the great scale [printed „גרייסן פערנעם“] these people command, one can only burst out laughing and pity the people who have so much feeling for playing — just as children do it; it seems they themselves see it perfectly well, and yet they do not refrain from it.
Here Będzin is making the budget for the current year, and it is ridiculous, upon my life, to listen to all those "debates" over which they haggle [„מ׳טאלקעוועט“] for hours on end, and the end is — self-evidently — that everything stays as it was and nobody moves a hair's breadth forward.
Wanting to give the kehilla premises the appearance of an "urząd" [government office] with departments is also of no great value, because not everything is the rich appearance and the comforts, which incidentally involve very large expenses; the main thing is surely the activity, the achievement, the creation. Simply enlarging the expenses so that everyone may receive respect, so that everyone may think it is something — that makes no sense whatsoever.
After all, Sosnowiec made the same experiment — does any citizen have more reverence now because of the modern premises than formerly, when this did not exist? We know it is exactly the opposite: today people treat the institution with contempt and with an ironic smile, whereas formerly[?] they looked upon a proper representation with respect. What matters, therefore, is the representation on the one side and its good deeds on the other; otherwise it makes no sense and gives the impression of children playing at grown-ups and wanting thereby to exert pressure so that they be shown respect.
Besides, one must not forget one more thing: as said, such pleasures involve relatively large expenses, which are not very desirable at a time when the citizens are constantly busy economising. So where will they take the money for the expenses from? Since of the budget sum[?] in all only 50—60 per cent is collected — is there now really a tendency to raise [the levy on] those who still pay?
And something else: Mr. Langner, who chairs the council sessions on the budget, proposed that, since the "Hazamir" library, which is now in the premises of the Jewish kehilla, belongs to the "Bund", it should be evicted, because it makes no sense — says Mr. Langner — that the kehilla should maintain precisely a Bundist library when it does not do so for other libraries. Actually that would have been a just claim if the situation were as Mr. L. painted it for us. But we know quite otherwise. The older generation regards the library as a communal [town] one and in no way as a party one, because in its time both books and money[?] were collected for it from all people who had any feeling at all for the Jewish book — regardless of which party one belonged to and what sort of stamp one bore at all. So why does Mr. Langner ascribe the library to the Bund? Perhaps because Bundists [„בונדאווצעס“] busy themselves with it and look after it? Then they surely deserve a "yasher koach" for their devoted mission.
We know, after all, that Sosnowiec too had such a library, and since nobody looked after it, it was given its resting place in an attic, and the end was that to this day no trace of the books remains. Is the Sosnowiec carelessness then better than the Będzin understanding for the Jewish book, where there are some four or five thousand books, approximately?
The writer of these lines is far from belonging to the Bundist camp and cannot be suspected of partisanship, so that we treat such a question purely from an honest and non-partisan standpoint, and must protest against[?] the kehilla representatives for their carelessness toward the Jewish book. We hold the opposite view. We think the gmina [community] should have been content that, without dipping[?], as the saying goes, its hand in cold water — that is to say — it does[?] maintain a Jewish library at its own expense. What other plus has it to credit to its account besides its fair bit of poverty and meanness[?]?
We would have understood if it were to finance it, subsidise it, help enlarge it; but we cannot in any way whatsoever understand the unwillingness to carry the burden on its shoulders, although the whole matter lies for it "in the left sidelock" [i.e. is a trifle to it].
The Hazamir library is therefore a communal [town] one and must by all means be housed in the premises of the Jewish community as a non-partisan institution which also belongs to the whole town.
Wanting to evict the Jewish book from the Jewish kehilla because those who busy themselves with and look after the library without expecting any reward are not wanted by this or that faction is an absurdity and a crime.
For the Jewish book — incidentally, there are also many Hebrew books there — one must have understanding, reverence and the greatest respect, gentlemen!
Selekt.
Whom Are We Waiting For? (A Few Words to Our Small Traders' Institutions)

[Zagłębie — economy; traders' and small shopkeepers' associations.]
Not long ago we dealt here with the question of our fragmentation and separateness, and we dwelt on the merchants' institutions — only on the merchants' and the small traders' associations. We showed clearly that the members of both the first and the second association are all impoverished and helpless, and that both institutions must seek [?] radical help for their members as quickly as possible; otherwise they will go off [?] the stage and the ground will give way under their feet.
Our published lines received attention from the board members of the "Small Traders' Association" (Kleinhändler-Verein), who took the floor on this important matter.
It is truly gratifying to see that the institution has shown understanding (printed "farshtendish") and is ready to debate the painful question.
In the article printed by the "Small Traders' Association", the writers argue that, since we are not well acquainted with the question, we must first acquaint ourselves with it from all sides, and then the writer of these lines will himself realise that, for various reasons, there can be no talk here of joint work.
So be it (sile); we will not deny that you are better acquainted than we are with the problem under discussion, but that changes nothing at all in the situation. It may be that when we study the matter more, the tragedy will prove considerably greater and more dangerous, and a quicker [?], more urgent joint effort will be needed. To free oneself from the cooperation will then certainly no longer be possible.
If that is so, why this polemic?
As an argument we pointed out that your central bodies have begun joint work. You say that it is not entirely so, only that Warsaw will control the position taken toward the outside world in public statements of principle.
Be it so; all that matters to us is that in Warsaw, too, they realise that joint work or coordination [?] is needed — sum it up however you like.
The worst thing, however, is that you keep insisting on your own, that it is out of the question to work together because of the secretaries of the said associations. Yes, the arguments are ridiculous and not worth discussing. A union will after all come about in the end — only then, when there will no longer be anything left to unite.
The same thing happened with our financial institutions. Every minyan opened a bank of its own, until everything was fragmented, and no union could be reached because of various "principled" reasons; only when everything had already rotted did people begin talking about union.
Have you learned nothing from all this?
R. Let.
Hamisha Asar BiShvat (Tu BiShvat)

[Land of Israel — holidays; Tu BiShvat. Feature article.]
By Daniel Persky.
Hamisha Asar BiShvat, that is, the fifteenth day of Shevat, is a half-holiday among Jews. One works as on all days, one holds no special ceremonies — it is an ordinary weekday.
Only the children get pleasure from Hamisha Asar BiShvat: in the cheder they study only half a day, and it is also a mitzvah to eat carob, figs and other such fruits from the Land of Israel.
What kind of holiday is Hamisha Asar BiShvat?
It is an old, very old nature festival, dating from the most ancient times of our history. The Jewish tillers of the soil in the Land of Israel celebrated the holiday through their life together with the phenomena of nature in our land.
In the Bible we find no hint of Hamisha Asar BiShvat, but in the Talmud we read: "On the first [misprinted] of Shevat, the fifteenth for the tree; Beit Hillel say on its fifteenth" [so printed; the Mishnah reads: "On the first of Shevat is the New Year for the tree ... Beit Hillel say on its fifteenth"].
As in all disputes, here too the opinion of Beit Hillel was accepted, and the fifteenth day of Shevat was declared the New Year for trees and plants.
The reasoning behind this New Year is quite simple: most of the rains in the Land of Israel end, as is known, before the month of Shevat or in mid-Shevat, and so it is self-evident that the trees which blossom afterwards already belong to the new year.
Around the fifteenth day of Shevat, after the rains had stopped, our forefathers used to go out into the field in olden times and plant new trees. The month from the fifteenth of Shevat to the fifteenth of Adar was a month of planting. The Talmud relates facts about how Tannaim and Amoraim were strict about the custom of planting trees in the period after Hamisha Asar BiShvat. For them it was reckoned a great mitzvah.
In the time of the Second Temple, on Hamisha Asar BiShvat they used to close all the accounts of the tithe of fruits (a tenth part of the fruits for the Levites) and of the poor man's tithe (a tenth part which every tiller of the soil used to give to the poor of his town).
Hamisha Asar BiShvat is regarded as a joyful day. Even when a community has declared a fast for Monday and Thursday, if the fast falls on Hamisha Asar BiShvat one may not fast.
On the night of Hamisha Asar BiShvat there is a custom to gather in the synagogues, eat fruits of the Land of Israel and recite a kind of "Tikkun", that is, selected passages from the Bible and the Talmud that speak of the trees and fruits of the Land of Israel.
Among the Sephardi sages it is the custom to stay awake the whole night of Hamisha Asar BiShvat; one eats fruits of the Land of Israel and studies Torah (especially about the grains and fruits of the Land of Israel) between one fruit and the next.
Connected with the month of Shevat is a superstition that in this month the demons rage fiercely (as it seems[?], the demons are angry when the rains and storms stop). So it is best to be careful and not eat any geese in Shevat, especially on the eighth[?] day of Shevat. The slaughterer who slaughters a goose in Shevat is in danger of dying, unless he eats up the heart of the goose...
Throughout the whole time of exile, in which the Jews were only wandering about, they did not forget the Land of Israel. On the great festivals, such as Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, we recall the historical, national, religious and natural-geographic significance of the Land of Israel. On the small half-holiday of Hamisha Asar BiShvat, Jews longed for the simple earthly pleasures[?] of the Land of Israel by eating the fruits for which the Land of Israel, "a land flowing with milk and honey", has been famous since biblical times.
It has always been a mitzvah, especially for children, to taste on Hamisha Asar BiShvat carob, dates and figs, which come from the land of our origin and our hope.
About carob in particular there are legends going round among us, that in the Land of Israel the goats eat carob, so much of it is there — at a time when here in exile it is a delicacy and an expensive item for us.
The legend has now come true in the Land of Israel. Walking in the Herzl Forest, not far from the new children's village of Ben Shemen and the old historic town of Lod, I indeed saw how thousands of trees were laden with large, sweet and plump carobs, and many [printed: "sil"] fall down to the ground by themselves. However much we, fellows, stuffed our packets[?], it was all nothing compared with the great abundance there. Ah, our Jewish little children in exile would revive a little in the Herzl [printed: "Heutsl"] Forest...
In recent decades a new, beautiful holiday has been introduced in the Land of Israel on Hamisha Asar BiShvat, called Hag ha-Neti'ot: the planting festival. In Jerusalem, Haifa, Tel Aviv and in the other towns the teachers take their pupils out of town; a huge celebration is arranged with a fine programme; speeches are made about the beauty of the nature of the Land of Israel, about the importance of planting many trees in our land, desolate for two thousand years; various dances suited to the occasion are performed; songs are sung about planting and blossoming; a small theatre performance of the life of nature is put on — and only then does the main thing begin: each pupil in turn takes a young sapling, digs a pit himself and with his own hands plants it in the soil of our land. It is done with holiness, with a great many preparations and ceremonies. The child remembers his sapling, hangs his name on it, visits it from time to time, sprinkles it with water, prunes the branches and watches over it like a treasure.
In Tel Aviv children took me to show me "their" little trees, which they had planted several years ago. The trees have already become real "people", grown up beautiful and tall — a delight to look at. They are proud of the fact that they too, with their childish strength, help to cover our beloved fatherland with ever more trees and flowers.
Hamisha Asar BiShvat has thus become an instructive[?] and interesting holiday for our children in the Land of Israel, a holiday that binds them forever to our renewed land, for which they are ready to live and to die.
In the lands of exile too, the National Fund [Keren Kayemet] has revived the great national and patriotic significance of Hamisha Asar BiShvat. In every town great celebrations are prepared, where people tell of the flowering of the Land of Israel and distribute fruits of the Land of Israel in little bags bearing suitable Hebrew inscriptions. Little by little Hamisha Asar BiShvat is becoming a great and beautiful holiday, which brings us closer to the lap of our glorious and fruitful nature, which is [printed: "in" for "is"] ready to receive with love her wandering children from the whole world and to [—] ["begeyen", unclear word] and free them forever.
The zeal to "build" houses

By force of tenants and landlords.

Polish laws have never distinguished themselves by any particularly successful wording. Nevertheless, no piece of legislation published so far has given grounds for so many doubts and differences of opinion as the latest amended decree on the protection of tenants.

The whole periodical legal literature is literally flooded with treatises on the obscure points [lit. "shadow points"] that have arisen, but all these interpretations are in almost every case one-sided, tendentious, viewed[?] in the light of the house-owners' interests. In any case, as long as the Supreme Court does not authoritatively decide the contentious questions that have surfaced[?], they remain finally unresolved.

Building fever.

As soon as the amended decree was published, the landlords pounced on point "c" as on a roast [i.e., a windfall]. The masses of tenants were immediately sent notices to quit their dwellings[?], with demands that they vacate the occupied flats after the set term, the landlords invoking the circumstance that they intend to rebuild or to build new houses.

Where has such a building fever suddenly come over the landlords? Does the said point "c" really give them such an impulse? Analysing the point in question according to the old and the amended wording, one must come to the conclusion that the state of affairs has in fact not changed.

If now, just as before, a landlord who wishes, on setting about building, to get rid of his tenants must prove[?] in court the necessity of the building undertaking, then likewise a landlord will continue to be obliged to pay the tenant monetary compensation, if the court recognises the justification of the landlord's demand and on that basis adjudges[?] him an eviction.

True, the old decree provided in this case for compensation amounting to 3 years' rent, or the obligation to provide the tenant with another suitable flat, whereas under the new decree a landlord must in such a case grant the tenant monetary compensation amounting to 1 year's rent where a dwelling is concerned, or to an amount of 6 months if it is a business premises.

As regards removal costs, the old decree recognised a special reimbursement. Moreover, under the old decree the reimbursement corresponded to the actual expenses of moving at the time, [whereas] the new decree has fixed for it a kind of lump sum [ryczałt] amounting to 1 month's rent.

One must not[?], however, forget that the economic conditions of that time have, compared with today's, changed considerably. It was then easier, and it paid the landlord better, to meet the tenants' larger legal claims than today the reduced ones. It is after all quite incomprehensible that precisely at the present moment, amid the prevailing general economic depression, the landlords, especially the Jewish ones, although[?] a wealth of all sorts of concessions is pouring down on their heads, should throw capital into new building.

No, neither by juridical nor certainly by economic motives can one explain the "zeal" to build that the landlords have all at once displayed. It seems that under the pretended readiness to pull down the present buildings and put up new ones, some landlords aim at nothing more than to instil fear in their tenants, to keep them in check so that they will not only give up reductions [of rent] and repairs, but even be compelled to agree to a rise, or perhaps they even reckon, by means of the said building trick, to get rid of them altogether in a cheap way.

A difficult and responsible task will therefore lie with the courts. With the greatest caution they will have to see to it that under the cloak of economic initiative no speculation or other malicious intentions are hidden, and that even in the case of a genuine readiness to build no eviction be decreed[?] as long as it has not been established with absolute certainty that the present building really must unconditionally be cleared away.

This caution is all the more necessary because, while the old decree still somehow protected the tenant against abuses in such cases, containing the clause that if the landlord does not start building within 6 months he is obliged to pay the former tenant, besides the compensation already received amounting to 3 years' rent, a further supplement in the amount of 6 years'[?] rent, the decree now in force releases the landlord from any obligation towards a tenant who has already moved out.
Radio Corner.

[Radio corner — radio and technology news.]
The success of Polish Radio.
Polish Radio has received a large number of letters from Palestine in which the Jews there tell of the great pleasure they get from listening to Warsaw radio.
In the last two months letters have arrived not only from the Land of Israel but also from Canada, Australia, Brazil, Argentina and from Manchukuo in the Far East. These letters come from various peoples who listen to the broadcasts of the Polish short-wave radio station at Babice. This station is the property of the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs, which has lent it to Polish Radio.
The Babice station works on a wave of 22 metres, or 13,635 kilocycles, with a power of 10 kilowatts in the antenna. It broadcasts programmes 3 times a week: twice at 6 in the afternoon for North America and Europe, once at 10 in the evening for South America and north-east Asia. These times were chosen specially so that when the broadcasts arrive there it is already daytime. In North America the Warsaw radio broadcasts are in practice heard at midday; in Manchuria, Australia and New Zealand — at 6–7 o'clock in the morning. All these broadcasts are heard there quite clearly.
The Babice short-wave radio station is being written about more and more often in the foreign press.

Gramophone records made of glass and sugar.
In Holland they have begun to manufacture gramophone records of glass. Such a record is played with the help of a sapphire needle, but the needle can be used only 60 times. Naturally the glass records do not last long: they break easily, and they can be played no more than 15 times. In England they have begun making records from a sugar mass. But whether the experiments have succeeded or not is not yet known.

A children's competition for the anniversary of Jules Verne's death.
Radio Strasbourg is organising an interesting competition for children. The competition consists in this: in one hundred lines, on 4 pages of a school exercise book, the children must write:
1) Why did Jules Verne's books interest you so much? How was the writer able, back then, to foresee so many inventions?
2) If you feel like it — write briefly — how do you imagine the life of mankind in the year 2,000?
Prizes have been set for this competition, which both French children and foreign children may win.
Grandma Tells Little Stories to Her Grandchildren

...If you'll be [?] quiet, little children, I will tell you a few little stories. The stories may perhaps not suit your little minds; it may be that for you, little children, they will be hard to take in, but tell them I must, so that when you are as old as I am, you too will tell the stories to your grandchildren.
———
...Once there was a hard time for Jews (in exactly which year, I don't remember). The gnawing curse of rebuke had been poured out upon the people of Israel; despair and hopelessness reigned in the Jewish ranks, lawlessness and demoralization — in every field; "kol de-alim gavar" [might makes right] had seized the whole of Jewish life, pimps had taken over the mission of the moral preachers, charlatans had pushed their way to the Jewish printed word, the number of Jewish informers grew from day to day. The remnant of the escaped [?]. The better part of the Jewish people sighed, groaned, but was powerless. So, little children, a hard and bitter time came then upon the whole of Israel.
— Well, Granny dear, what happened in that time?
— Health to your bones, little children, that you are curious to hear what all happened in that period.
In a big city (which city, I don't remember) there lived a Jewish merchant. The townspeople knew him as "an everyday Jew" [an ordinary, respectable Jew]; he conducted fine business, a decent man in society, but none of the inhabitants, not even his closest ones, knew that this man lived through frightening dreams, such dreams in which he saw epochs of Alexander the Great, of tsars [?] and of Nicholases. Many times (mostly it happened in the middle of the night) the people of the house were woken from sleep by his outcries:
— "With a mighty hand will I rule over you" [Ezekiel 20:33]. I will teach you manners, I will root out the recalcitrant, and all the poultry dealers who will not accept my command I will "russify" [?].
— I'm scared, Granny dear — one of the grandchildren spoke up — I won't hear any more about the terrible dreams, I won't be able to sleep at night..
— My little children, don't be afraid. This is, after all, already "a very old little story"; there is nothing to be afraid of; I'm only telling it to you so that it should not be forgotten...
— Well, little children, where were we?
— At the dreams, Granny dear — the grandchildren answered.
— And at that time, little children, the man was crowned as leader of the kehilla in which he lived, and his 18-year-old dream came true.
And just as it is written in the Teitsh-Chumash: "There arose a new king." The new king arose; "and they set over them" — great taxes were laid upon the "people"; "and the children of Israel sighed" — the Jewish inhabitants sighed under the heavy burdens (the kehilla taxes were taken from the men as well as from the women); "and they cried out" — and they shouted, protested. But nothing helped. The entrenched [?] leader struck fear with his threats that "whoever is not loyal to him will be thrown out of his position." These threats he published not only by word of mouth but in writing, in print. For this purpose he took to his aid an ugly scoundrel, a vile outcast, who for a few coins wrote praises, ran through the streets and shouted:
— Long live! Long live the redeemer of the city, long live the modern Messiah!
The leader also possessed a rare sense of smell: he knew precisely what goes on in everyone's home, how much one spends on a summer residence, how many dresses the wife of this or that "etat" [kehilla tax] payer owns, even how many partners someone has in his business — he knew it all.
Where he obtained all these precise details is not clear to me, little children; I don't remember it exactly, only Grandpa dear used to say that he took it from the materials, through the questionnaires that he demanded from every "etat" payer.
Once a young man came to him for a slip [permit] to put up a tombstone.
— A slip you want? If you give such-and-such, you can get a slip from me — said the leader.
— My lord, my master — the young man pleaded — I surely cannot give such a sum as you demand of me.
— Ha, ha, ha — the strongman burst out laughing — me you won't fool. You surely believe that with me, too, you'll manage to tell lies that "you run a small business"? That you have no fortune? No, no, with me an iron discipline reigns.
— Well, Granny dear, what did the young man do?
— He took fright at the words and gave as much as the kehilla strongman demanded of him...
- - - - - - - - - -
— Now go to sleep, little children; God willing [?], next Shabbat I'll tell you a second little story.
Passed on for print by
Ben Amri.
The Will of the Hearts.

[Poland — commemoration of Marshal Piłsudski; the Chief Committee and its fund-raising.] (Sh.) The will to honour the memory of Józef Piłsudski and to hand down [?] his memory to the coming generations is rooted deep in the hearts of the people.
In this field a great task is plainly evident, one that stands before the Chief Committee for Honouring the Memory of Marshal Piłsudski, which — as is known — was created by the President of the State soon after the Marshal's death.
In order to unite the efforts of the whole of society in one pot [?] and to concentrate the will to honour Piłsudski on works that should be worthy of his name and able to outlast generations.
On the Sowiniec, near Kraków, the Marshal's Mound is growing; in Warsaw a monument to Piłsudski will be erected; shortly work will begin on building the sarcophagus on the Wawel, where the Marshal's coffin will rest.
All this is still little. There exist [?] on Polish soil several thousand points closely bound up with the Marshal's work. These points — battlefields from which he emerged victorious, huts in which he lived, etc. — will be immortalised. They will be immortalised by means of movable [?] means — executed monuments of the work and toil that Piłsudski invested in the Polish soil.
Every Polish citizen will want to take part — if only a small part — in honouring the Marshal's memory. One can do so by giving a donation to the fund for honouring the memory of Marshal Piłsudski — a modest sum, suited to individual means, spread [?] over instalments of groszy [?] — and, what must be stressed, given entirely voluntarily; this is the only possible form of contributions (składki) that can be applied among the broad masses of society, who have the best will.
The Chief Committee only recently issued a precise instruction on collecting, and also sent out collection lists to all offices and institutions. As emerges from the instruction, the voivodeship committees do not accept any sums from the collections; rather, these must be transferred [?] directly to the Committee's account at the P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank].
It must also be noted that lately a series of publications, albums, has been issued which were supposedly meant to honour the Marshal's memory, but in practice they were issued not only without approval (aprobata) but also without the knowledge of the Chief Committee.
Citizens must be informed that the only body called upon by the President of the State, on behalf of the whole of Polish society, to honour the memory of Marshal J. Piłsudski is the one whose account at the P.K.O. is No. 1313, and only the donations [?] paid into that account will reach the goal.
Remembering this, let everyone — according to individual means — help the work of the Chief Committee.
Not all voivodeships, not all areas [?] of the Republic have yet organised voivodeship committees. These committees must be created as quickly as possible. Nowhere is there a lack of people of good will, to whom the Marshal's memory is dear and who must energetically organise local committees, without which the campaign is greatly hampered.

When One Eats Dairy... (A Little Feuilleton).

[Satirical feuilleton — the kehilla council (probably Będzin).] (A little feuilleton).
My neighbour Reb Uzer likes [?] to clamber up to the gallery of the city council, to the gallery of the kehilla council, and to listen to the clever speeches of the city fathers.
My neighbour already knows what is meant by a budżet [budget], an "ogólna" [general] debate and a "szczegółowa" [detailed] discussion, the floor on a point of order and the floor not on a point of order, a "wniosek nagły" [urgent motion] and a "wniosek zwyczajny" [ordinary motion], an interpellation and an interpretation.
In a word, my neighbour is as versed in the laws of parliamentarism as in Ashrei.
So Reb Uzer also came to the last session of the kehilla council and could not understand what on earth was happening with the parnassim: when do they have an "ogólna" discussion and when a "szczegółowa" one? After all, with them both look the same: they talk and talk about everything in the world! They begin with the secular kehilla, meanwhile take a dip in the mikveh, cast a glance at the rabbinate, a shove at the officials, a jab at the Jewish schools, a whack at the former kehilla — and whoever wants can repeat once more his own sermon from last week and from a year ago.
— When I eat meat — I know of a norm, of a beginning and an end. You come to the compote — I know that lunch is over. But when I eat dairy, I don't know how and when it ends. I chew and chew so long, until my temples begin to throb from the chewing; then I know that the meal is over...
Among people one eats meat, but our kehilla council gives the impression of a dairy feast. A discussion is carried on so long, until the temples begin to pound from talking; then one knows that the discussion is over.
A Shvartser ["A Black One" — pen name].
From the Film World.

[Cinema — Hollywood; Fred MacMurray.] From a Shoeshine Boy — to a Film Star.
Life is not such an easy thing, especially when one also has various plans and artistic aspirations. A young man comes, for example, to Holly-wood, to the rosy film paradise, and has various plans which were born while still at home, somewhere in a provincial small town. Naturally, the plans have a direct connection with film, with acting in the film studio and in time becoming a film star. But the rosy plans are not always realised, and many a young man and many a young girl must give up the whole business. Sometimes such a [?] story ends tragically — suicide or (for women) the road to shame. Only a few have the luck, after a hard struggle full of sacrifices, to swim up to the surface, where in time all hopes and plans are fulfilled.
One of the few lucky ones is also the young actor Fred MacMurray.
He could tell a great deal about his years of hunger and want in Hollywood: about nights when he slept on a bench in the parks and city gardens, about days of hunger that exhausted and tormented him. He already felt overjoyed when he managed to get a post as a shoeshine boy in one of the quiet streets. He was by now hardly going hungry. But he did not give up the struggle to get into films. In a magazine he reads that a film extra is wanted.
That was just his birth-town [?]. With his passport and birth certificate in hand, he runs, all flustered, to the film studio. He plays as an extra. He finds favour in the eyes of the director, and after a while he gets the leading role in the film "A Woman Who Loves" [The Gilded Lily?]. His partner is none other than the famous star actress Claudette Colbert. The whole press praises the new young actor highly — and his fate is sealed. From now on he is a star. He is already acting together with the actress Carole Lombard in the film "Hands on the Table" [Hands Across the Table]. He will be the partner of Sylvia Sidney; he acts in the film "The Bride Comes Home", as well as in the picture "Thirteen Hours in the Air" [Thirteen Hours by Air].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Beshalach
—o—
a) "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him" (13:9 [sic; should be 13:19])
R' Eliyahu Chaim Meisel [rabbi of Łódź] once asked one of the notables of Łódź to sign up for a certain contribution for a philanthropic purpose. The man declined:
"Who am I, after all? What am I, to stand at the head of such an undertaking?"
R' Eliyahu Chaim answered him:
"When it comes to a mitzvah one must not be humble. On the verse 'And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him' the Gemara (Sotah, folio 13) says that the Jews handed over to Moses our Teacher the mitzvah of carrying Joseph's bones, 'because Joseph's honour is greater with the great than with the small'. The question arises: Moses, the humblest of all men on the face of the earth — he regarded himself as a great man? But when it concerns a mitzvah, even Moses set his humility aside..."
• • •
Rabbi Yehoshua Ber of Brisk [Brześć] and Rabbi Yaakov David of Slutsk [Słuck] were travelling in the same 'boyd' [covered carriage]. On the way they fell out [?] over a point of halakha; R' Yaakov David got angry, left the carriage and sat down beside the coachman.
On entering the town the people were astonished: two rabbis, one in the carriage and one beside the coachman..
They greet the one sitting beside the coachman and ask him:
"Who is the rabbi sitting in the carriage?"
"I am," answers R' Yaakov David, "R' Yehoshua Ber of Brisk, and the one sitting in the carriage is R' Yaakov David of Slutsk, and since it is not fitting that I should sit together with R' Yaakov David, I sat down beside the coachman."
"Don't believe him!" cries R' Yehoshua Ber. "I am Yehoshua Ber and he is Rabbi Yaakov David of Slutsk.."
"Rabbi," R' Yaakov David answers him back, "a pity about your effort... everyone knows your humility.."
—o—
b) "Before Baal-zephon" (14:2)
"It alone remained of all the gods of Egypt." Rashi.
'Baal-zephon' means — as the Yalkut says — the idol of money ("out of the north cometh gold"), and that idol has remained to this day.. All the foolish [?] idols that people once worshipped have been destroyed. No trace of them is left; only the idol of money 'remained of all the gods of Egypt', and it rules with the same power as before.. Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "And behold, the Egyptians marched after them, and they were sore afraid" (ibid., 10)
When even on the road to redemption Pharaoh's shadow [?] still pursues them, they took fright. They became afraid that they [?] might some day take his spirit along with them to the Land of Israel; that is why they were so afraid... Asifat Chachamim.
* *
"They mingled among the nations and learned their works" —
Both sides learn: the gentiles learn good Jewish qualities, and the Jews learn the gentiles' bad qualities.
Like that rabbi who made a match with a rich coachman from a distant town. The wedding was set in a small town between the two towns where the in-laws lived. Travelling to the wedding, the rabbi thought: why should I show off before my in-law? So he took off his rabbinical garb and dressed like an ordinary householder, just so as not to show off before his in-law.)
The coachman, for his part, thought: why should I shame my in-law with my clothes? So he got himself rabbinical garments and dressed like a rabbi.
When they met, the town received the 'rabbi' (in fact the coachman) with great honour and looked askance at the 'coachman' (in fact the rabbi).
So it is with Jews and gentiles in exile. We want to adapt ourselves to them, and they learn good things from us. The world sees them as the 'rabbis', the elite, and us as the coachmen...
—o—
c) [sic; should be d] "For He is highly exalted" (15:1)
The Master of the Universe gives each person more of what he wants. If someone is proud, the Master of the Universe gives him more pride... 'ki ga'oh ga'ah' ['exalted — He exalts']... If someone is wise, He gives him more wisdom: 'He gives wisdom to the wise'. Siftei Da'at.
—o—
d) "And what are we?" (16:7 [?])
Rachel, daughter of R' Yitzchak Meir of Zinkov [Zinków], made a match with a grandson of R' Aharon of Karlin [?]. He was full of pride and looked down on the mother-in-law. But Rachel was a very clever woman and a great scholar, and she said to the in-law:
"Moses said 'And what are we?' The question arises: granted, Moses could say of himself that he was nothing — he was so humble; but how could he include Aaron? Why 'we'?! The answer is that Aaron's greatness comes only from the fact that he is Moses' brother, and if Moses is nothing, Aaron is nothing too... Your importance, too, comes only from lineage, and if you attach no importance to lineage, then you have no importance either... And then again, if we are to measure by that measure, we are both equal."
—o—
e) "He that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack" (ibid., 18)
The Rebbe of Aleksandrów, R' Yerachmiel Yisrael Yitzchak, once said:
"Master of the Universe! You take from one Jew and give to another — 'the Holy One, blessed be He, takes from this one and gives to that one' — but You do not behave well: You take from the righteous man and give to the wicked one, so the righteous man has grievances against You. Aaron Shloyme the shopkeeper
has half a dozen children,
he was really rich as Korah — was,
and, what a wonder!
he opened himself a warehouse [skład]
of millet[?] and paint and flour,
he also sold tomatoes there,
dry goods "on ice"[?] — —
soap and vinegar, honey, tea,
eggs and haroset —
cinnamon, pepper and chocolates,
wine for the Four Cups,
spices, olive oil, salt and sugar,
shoelaces[?], beer
and more such similar
kinds without measure — — —
everyone was busy,
he was short of hands.
If you took a look there today
you would no longer recognise it,
of the goods of former days
there is not a trace today,
because the inspector [probably the tax inspector]
took hard to Aaron Shloyme,
a bit of the shop he gave away on credit,
the rest was auctioned off — — —
and the great Aaron Shloyme
lies today deep in the ground.

[Humour ("Der Kokh-lefl") — Będzin sketch; social life.]
A Będzin tale in two parts.
Part one.
He came in to the fortune-teller on the "Wszymne"[?] and said:
— Dear lady, today a woman will come to you who will want you to tell her a little about her future. The woman has a mark on her right cheek and two gold teeth on the left side of her mouth. The lady is my wife. So I give you ten złoty and ask you to tell the lady the following:
Tell her that the "przyjęcie" [party] she wants to give in honour of Hamisha Asar [Tu BiShvat] — for heaven's sake she should not give it, because one of the guests will be in the first stage of influenza, a second guest will be in the stage of a typhus illness, and she will catch it from them. Then tell her not to go to the tennis court; then tell her not to dismiss the cook, because the next one will be even worse; then tell her not to travel to Zakopane, because a certain[?] death awaits her there from a fall off a mountain; but the main thing — tell her that her "przyjaciel" [friend, admirer] is false and laughs at her. Good day to you, and you know what you have to do.
Part two.
— Do you want to hear, Zygmunt, what a surprise I had today? I was at a fortune-teller's, and she guessed things for me so strangely well.
— Really? — Well, let's hear.
— First of all she warned me not to give the party, because two guests, she said, will be in the first stage of contagious diseases. But I am, after all, the clever Frania, so I found a way: I'll give the party in four weeks' time, when the two guests will already be lying sick.
— And what else did she tell you?
— That I shouldn't go to the tennis court, because I'll break a leg.
— Is that so? Break a leg? — Rubinstein exclaimed — what else did she tell you?
— Yes, that I shouldn't go to Zakopane this winter, because I'll fall off a mountain; and do you know what I'll do, Zygmunt? I'll simply go to Krynica...
— What else did she tell you?
— That I shouldn't dismiss the maid, because the next one will be worse. Do you know what I'll do? I'll dismiss the present maid, take a second one, send her away too and take a third.
Then she told me that my friend [przyjaciel] is really[?] an enemy, so I'll indeed send him to the devil and take up again with Moszkowicz... he is going to Krynica anyway. We'll both travel together...
Frania said no more, but ran into the kitchen with a wild scream: quick, water, water! Zygmunt has collapsed! He's fainting! Quick, water!

The Mamzer. (73)
A gripping tragic novel about a prodigy

"I had full trust in him, but later..."
At that word the woman burst into heavy weeping.
"Why have you broken off your confession?" Rabbi Moshele asked.
"Rabbi, I cannot go on telling about what has been weighing on my heart for decades."
"Be open-hearted and hide no secret from one who shares your suffering."
"Good man, how have I deserved that you should show me [?] so much compassion, so much sympathy and human love? After all, I am a sinner."
"What did you say? A sinner?!"
"It is not I who am guilty, but he, to whom I gave away my heart and my soul."
"Calm yourself, Mrs. Gneskin, I share your suffering. But do not despair because you bore an illegitimate child; such victims I have met very many in my life, I too..."
"Why have you suddenly turned so pale, Rabbi?"
"Nothing," answers Moshele. "I feel very tired and must go now. Good day to you, and may the Blessed Name send you a complete recovery."
Here, in the great city, here in the great abyss of living, writhing souls, he first saw the life of humanity in all its nakedness.
"It may be," he thought to himself, "how right Reb Dovid is: we are all mamzerim; there is only a small percentage of people in the world who are kosher children. And the Gemara is right when it says that if a woman sins even in thought while living with her husband, or when it is the other way round, the children too can be reckoned as not kosher" — so he thought, sitting in his room, about the various tragedies of family life that had become well known to him and that he hears every day in his study, when people come to him to ask for help and advice.
He too has lately been very worried about Rachel, who goes about sad, and he does not know what is wrong with her; he has never even asked her. Several times he has wanted to ask her the reason for her sad mood, but he did not do it. He does not know why. He loves her as a man should love a woman, he is devoted to her with all his body and soul — and is that not enough? — he would ask himself, but at once his heart gave a tremor within him. Before his eyes there began to appear the pictures of the tragedies of the women who had confessed before him, who had revealed to him the deeply hidden feelings of a woman, who longs not only for the passionate feelings of a man but also for his friendship, for his attachment to the woman as to a friend.
His responsible office had torn him away from her entirely, and it may be that this is the reason for her melancholy.
"Rachel, what is the matter with you?" he asks, coming into her room. "You have been somehow sad lately; perhaps there is a reason which I may not know, even as your husband and friend?"
"Moses," she comes up to him and puts her arms around his neck, "I may not know, you say — on the contrary, you must know it, because you are my husband, my friend. Four months we have been in New York, four months have already passed since you took up your high post as rabbi. Soon I am to become a mother, and that frightens me very much."
"But why, my dear? What frightens you so? God will help, you will get through it all in peace."
"Yes, my dearest, but just imagine: if already now, when we have not yet been married a year, you neglect me so, what will it be like later, and especially when I am already the mother of a child? Moses, I love you with my whole being, I have sacrificed everything for you, but you must not forget that a woman is not an object that one can put wherever one wishes, that one can regard as a thing which serves to calm the passions with which nature has endowed a man. No, Moses, a woman too is a human being like all human beings; she too has her desires, which one must not belittle and neglect, because one can lose her. A woman — if she does not find in her husband his attachment to her as to a friend, if he regards his wife only as one who must serve him in order to satisfy his human passions — such a woman begins to be unable to bear the man, she begins to be unable to tolerate his passionate feelings and comes to hate him; she must then begin to seek that to which her young heart is drawn and for which it yearns. And who is to blame for that? I believe you will be honest and tell me that the woman is less to blame in this than the man — isn't that so, Moses?"
Moshele sat the whole time with lowered head, listening to the words of his wife, which seemed to scald every limb of him...
"But I believe, my dearest," she said with a good-natured smile, "that my friend will not neglect me, true?"
"You are right, my dear, a woman is not an object and one must not neglect her. From today on we will go walking more often, spend more time together, so that you should not be bored. I promise you that, my dear."
"Above all, Moses, you must take more care of me now, because..." — and she did not finish the sentence.
(To be continued).
The kehilla budget at the plenary session of the council.

On Monday the kehilla council of Będzin held a session, at which it was decided to continue [the debate on] the kehilla budget.
The chairman, Mr. Landner, opens the session with the statement that the session is taking place on the second date and is valid with any number of members present.
At the first budget section, the synagogue, the chairman proposes to reduce the pension of the cantor by 5 percent. After a short discussion it is approved [?] that the reduction be 3 percent. In the course of the proceedings [?], on this section the parnas Kornfeld takes the floor and accuses the parnasim of the national camp of being "demagogues". In the reply of the parnas Herszlepicz (as printed; perhaps Herszlewicz) an incident arises between the speaker and the parnas Rubinlicht because of Herszlepicz's statement that "political corruption exists in the kehilla".
On the motion of the parnas Goldsztajn the synagogue (shul) section is adopted en bloc. Also adopted unchanged are the beth-midrash section and the pensions for the shochtim and the ne'emanim [supervisors]; a discussion arises only around the pension of 3000 zł. for the ne'eman Chajcman. The chairman, Mr. Landner, is against the kehilla giving 3000 zł. a year to an official who performs no function whatsoever, only so that he "shall not move his tongue" [lo yecheratz, Ex. 11:7]... and he expresses his wish that the kehilla administration come to an understanding with the rabbinate on this, so that Chajcman should work as a shochet.
The pension of the controller, Mr. Wekselman, is reduced by 10 percent. It is also decided that the cleaning of the poultry slaughterhouse be handed over to the "Kibbutz".
A longer discussion takes place over the expenditure of 1200 zł. for the investigator of clandestine slaughter. Mr. Landner speaks in favour of striking out the item, arguing that since all the "left" shochtim have already been engaged, no investigator is needed any more.
The parnas Rubinlicht argues the necessity of the item. The root of clandestine slaughter — he says — has not yet been completely eradicated. The suspicion is not only on the young shochtim, but even on the old ones...
After the discussion the item is struck out.
Subsidies: the question — says Mr. Landner (printed "Langrer") — is a painful one in kehilla life. We are powerless against the fact that year in, year out a red line is drawn through this item. Mr. L. is in favour of every institution being entered preliminarily, for outside purposes, at 1 zł.
The parnas Herszlepicz demands that the subsidies for "Yesodei Torah" and "Beis Yaakov" be reduced by 50 percent.
Chairman Landner is categorically against this opinion. For me — he exclaims — the Agudah educational institutions stand as high as Fürstenberg's gymnasium, because from the Agudah cheders a Zionist youth will grow up, and from the gymnasium not; even the bit of Hebrew that some pupils of the gymnasium display is only what they learned earlier at the "Mizrachi" school...
(These words, spoken by a Zionist communal worker, gave the Agudah parnasim great satisfaction.)
In the section [?] (the word is garbled in print) [there is a debate] around the question of maintaining the Talmud Torah. The parnas Goldsztajn is in favour of the kehilla employing 3 teachers of secular subjects instead of the subsidy. The proposal is rejected. The subsidy for "Beis Yaakov" is struck out.
After that the session is broken off.
A local Jew receives an inheritance, — his late brother in America has left him a rich inheritance.

A few weeks ago Mr. Frank received a letter from his sister informing him that their brother in Brooklyn had died, and that before his death he had left instructions that his brother Frank in Będzin should say Kaddish after him.
Mr. Frank took it upon himself to carry out the will, but it was a wonder to him that the brother, who had been a very rich man, the owner of several houses in Brooklyn, had bequeathed him only the saying of Kaddish...
This week the "kashya" [puzzle] was answered. Mr. Frank received a communication from a Brooklyn lawyer that his late brother had left a will in which he divides his estate into 10 parts: one half for his 5 children and the other half for the brothers and sisters, i.e. Mr. Frank receives a tenth of the estate.

Should the Homeowners' Bank Be Liquidated or Not?

[Kielce — economy and institutions.] On Sunday the general meeting of the Cooperative Homeowners' Bank in Kielce took place. The meeting was chaired by Mr. M. Harberg [?]. The activity report was given by Dr. Ch. Y. Ajzenberg. The report shows that when the failures [?] of the Kielce banks began, the Homeowners' Bank, which was also hit by the general crash, owed 100 thousand złoty. But thanks to the energetic work of Dr. Ajzenberg, the bank today owes no more than 3,400 zł., and the assets amount to 8,000 zł., i.e. the bank owes practically nobody anything. However, since the Jewish public in Kielce, which — because of the painful affair of the People's Bank (Folks-Bank) — lost its trust in the cooperative banks, Dr. Ajzenberg proposed liquidating the bank, which [?] is a pity for the Jewish population.
A lengthy discussion then developed, in which Messrs. M. Rozenberg, G. Wygnański [?], A. Rozenblum, Y. Kan, D. Knobel, M. Sztajman, A. Amberg [?], Ch. Wajnryb and A. Berenkipowicz [?] took part.
Some of the speakers came out for the immediate liquidation of the bank, and this, as already mentioned, out of fear that the same story should not repeat itself with this bank as with the People's Bank, about which the Jewish population has much to weep and to tell. And some of those assembled were against liquidation, arguing that in Kielce there is now, apart from the private family banks, not a single public cooperative bank, and in their opinion the Homeowners' Bank should take the place of the liquidated People's Bank.
Mr. Harberg proposes electing a commission of 5 persons, which should acquaint itself with the actual state of the bank and afterwards give a decisive opinion on whether the bank should be liquidated or not.
"Rer." [?] Wielany is for a commission, but on condition that honest, disinterested people in whom the Jewish public has trust should join the commission. However, nobody who owes the bank money may belong to the commission, nor those who directly or indirectly brought about the economic ruin of the People's Bank.
Mr. Harberg's proposal was adopted by a majority of votes.
Elected to the commission were Messrs.: D. Knobel, Y. Goldblum, Ch. B. Balicki, M. Harberg, Y. Kan and A. Rozenblum. Within a month the commission is to come forward with an appropriate proposal on the further fate of the bank, i.e. rehabilitation or liquidation.

At the meeting the question was discussed of reorganising the Keren Hayesod committee, which is to conduct without interruption all current Keren Hayesod affairs in general, and the forthcoming Keren Hayesod campaign of this year in particular, which will be proclaimed in the first days of the month of March by the well-known Zionist leader, the poet Leib Jaffe.
After a detailed discussion a standing Keren Hayesod committee was elected, to which belong the most important and most active activists of all Zionist groupings in Kielce.
Among other things, the question of the preparations for the forthcoming Keren Hayesod campaign was also discussed, which, as is known, will be proclaimed in the first days of the month of March.

Silesian Rabbinical Association Protests against the Legislative Council in Palestine

[Silesia — rabbis; Palestine.] At its last session, which the Upper Silesian association held in the Bielsko (Bielitz) kehilla hall, the Katowice rabbi Chameides greeted the rabbis present, and then eulogised in warm words the late rabbi of Lwów, Rabbi Yitzchak Tsif.
Later a series of important questions were discussed, such as the general Jewish situation in Silesia, and especially the religious-cultural problems in the individual communities.
A longer discussion developed around the kehilla statute. As is known, in both Silesian provinces old Austrian and Prussian kehilla statutes from a hundred years ago are still binding to this day.
The Rabbinical Association therefore considers the simplest and best solution of the question to be the extension of the well-known Piłsudski decree to Silesia as well; although the decree contains some unfavourable provisions, it will thereby unify all the kehillot in Poland.
After granting discharge (absolutorium) to the outgoing[?] board of the association, a new leadership is elected:
Rabbi Chameides (Katowice), Rabbi Kahlberg, Rabbi Eisenberg (Cieszyn) and Rabbi Rybner (Tarnowskie Góry[?]).
The plenum then unanimously adopts a protest resolution against the introduction of a Legislative Council in Eretz Israel.

Not Charity, but Fulfilling a Duty toward an Important Institution. (On the campaign to recruit new members for the Gemilut Hesed fund in Sosnowiec.)

[Sosnowiec — Gemilut Hesed (free-loan) fund; appeal.]
Eight years ago the institution named "Gemilut Hesed" was founded. Although the economic situation of the Jewish population was then much, much better than today, the establishment of this financial institution nevertheless aroused the widest sympathy; the number of members grew, reaching 800, and the income from the monthly payments came to 800 zł. every month, because each and every person realised the necessity of such an institution, which is the bridge of rescue for hundreds of Jewish families.
Unfortunately the enthusiasm did not last long. After the "fat" years came the lean ones; the general economic situation and also the psychosis of fragmentation hit the "Gemilut Hesed" fund hard as well, and the result is that of the 800 monthly payers there remain... 150, from whom barely 150 zł. a month comes in — at a time when, thanks to the actions of the commissarial [government-appointed] kehilla administration, the G. H. fund has been burdened with paying several hundred zł. for the premises and with other expenses.
Even more painful is that among the non-payers are great magnates (gevirim), Jews learned in the Torah, who want to know nothing at all of the verse "And if thy brother be waxen poor... then thou shalt relieve him." If these magnates were to look through the applications of those asking for loans, they would see that these very people years ago gave donations of hundreds of złoty... Nor can the G. H. fund grant loans to everyone, because the "Joint" [?], seeing the cold attitude of the Sosnowiec Jewish population toward the fund, threatens to withdraw its capital — and that would be a new catastrophe for many hundreds of Jewish livelihoods.
In connection with this, the board of the G. H. fund in Sosnowiec has decided to make a last attempt to enlarge the camp of payers and to recruit back the original number of members. For this purpose letters will be sent out to the Jewish population asking them to declare themselves members of the G. H. fund.
Let no one hold back from this holy cause; let everyone realise the great benefit the fund brings to the Jewish community of limited means — we are not asking you for charity, only that you fulfil your duty toward hundreds of fallen [ruined] Jewish merchants and artisans in our town.
Respectfully,
The Board of the
Gemilut Hesed Fund in Sosnowiec.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Trial of 21 Endek Petard-Throwers

[Upper Silesia — trial, antisemitism.]
What's New in Upper Silesia?
Trial of 21 Endek Petard-Throwers.
Before the criminal tribunal of the District Court in Katowice, the trial took place this week of the perpetrators of the attacks on a number of Jewish premises in Katowice, Chropaczów, Lipiny, Piekary and elsewhere.
In the dock sat 21 members of the Endek [National Democratic] party, which has been dissolved in Silesia, headed by a certain Władysław[?] Jakubowski.
On behalf of the Jewish kehilla in Katowice the advocates Dr. Apflender[?], Dr. Weichman, Dr. Kanfrek[?] and the Christian advocate Bay appeared.
After the reading of the indictment the court proceeded to the hearing of the 18 summoned witnesses. The defendants on the whole admit their crimes, but they declare that with the attacks they did not intend to kill the Jews; they did it only as a demonstration.
This statement, however, is weakened by the expert opinion of Eng. Hajczyński[?]. According to the expert opinion it turns out that the bombs were made of such powerful explosives as could have killed people.
Also appearing as witnesses are the Jewish merchants who suffered, Messrs. Laub, Waksman, Fleischer and others, who give exact details of the explosions in their shops. The witness Waksman of Szarlej relates that from the force of the explosion parts of the "shutter" of his shop were found on the other side of the street.
The floor is given to the prosecutor Dr. Stankiewicz, who also touches on the principled aspect of the deeds, which have degraded the prestige of the Polish state, where public security is guaranteed to all citizens without distinction of faith; [he] demands that Jakubowski be punished with 5 years' imprisonment and the others with 4 and 2½ years' imprisonment.
The defence counsel, the Chadek [Christian Democrat] deputy Tempka, makes use of various antisemitic accusations against Jews and says: "I have respect for those who awakened the conscience of the Poles, so that the Jewish invasion of Upper Silesia should be stopped.
In a tense atmosphere the following verdict is announced on Wednesday at 1 p.m.:
The chief defendant Jakubowski is sentenced to 3 years' imprisonment, 7 of the defendants to 2 years' imprisonment, 2 to 2½ years, 5 to one and a half years, the rest to 1 year's imprisonment.
Those sentenced to up to 2 years are released on the basis of the amnesty.
The claim of the Jewish merchants who suffered, in the amount of 6000 zł., was rejected.
After the verdict, Jewish passers-by in the street were "treated" to... blows.
The "Keren Hayesod" campaign proclaimed in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — Zionism; Keren Hayesod; Mizrachi.]
The crisis in the Land of Israel is not a real one — says Rabbi Gold.
In connection with the "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Sosnowiec, the president of the World "Mizrachi" org., Rabbi Ze'ev [?] (Wolf) Gold, and the editor Gerbowski came here.
In honour of the distinguished guests, who arrived last Friday, a festive reception was organised, in which hundreds of people from the various Zionist groupings took part, headed by Rabbi Hager and Dr. Meladysta [?].
In the course of the Sabbath day Rabbi Gold appeared with spirited speeches which enchanted the listeners.
On Saturday morning Rabbi Gold spoke in the "Mizrachi" synagogue. The crush was so great that a large part prayed in the courtyard.
Before the Torah reading the chairman of the local "Mizrachi", Mr. Yitzhak Steinfeld, welcomed the distinguished guest and at the same time expressed, before the whole congregation, the sharpest protest against the kehilla commissioner, who, as a former Zionist, does not permit Rabbi Gold to speak in the synagogue.
This deed must remain a stain of shame on the Sosnowiec kehilla.
The words aroused great bitterness among the many hundreds of worshippers, from whom sharp cries of protest were heard.
Most imposing of all was the "Keren Hayesod" academy, held on Sunday morning in the Municipal Theatre. The organisers were also "meticulous" about punctuality: instead of at 11 o'clock the academy began at 12.30. Thanks to this "punctuality" Rabbi Gold had to cut his lecture short.
At the presidium table sit the town notables. After a choir sang the Polish and the Jewish anthems, Dr. Meladysta [?] gives the opening address, in which he welcomes the "Keren Hayesod" emissaries and the delegates of the Jewish kehilla, of the Merchants' Association, the Small Traders' Association and the House-Owners' Association, for their participation. This is the best proof — says the speaker — that the economic associations too have come to realise that the upbuilding of the Land of Israel is a problem of the whole of Jewry.
Then the floor is given to the long-standing "Keren Hayesod" activist and talented speaker, editor N. Gerbowski, who brings a warm greeting from the Land of Israel, from the work that gives us comfort and hope.
The speaker then depicts the tragedy of a group of homeless people in Tsarist times. If we do not want to remain a homeless people — the speaker exclaims — we must strain all our forces and contribute large sums to the Keren Hayesod.
Before giving the floor to Rabbi Gold, Rabbi Hager delivers a short greeting, in which he points out Rabbi Gold's greatness. The distinguished guest — says Rabbi Hager — does not belong to those rabbis who are occupied only with ruling on questions of "spoons and pots"; he also concerns himself with the Jewish question, the Jewish problem, which must receive its proper solution. Rabbi Gold, the great Torah scholar, has come here on a mission for the redemption of the Land.
A storm of applause breaks out when the chairman announces that the floor goes to Rabbi Gold.
Before beginning his lecture Rabbi Gold says the prayers: 1) to the Master of the Universe, that He "be with the mouths of the emissaries of Your people, the House of Israel", that He teach the emissaries of the people what to say, and 2) that people should be willing to understand him, so that crude hooliganism [?] should have no pretext. (With this "prayer" Rabbi Gold meant to hit at the "malcontents" who had allowed themselves to make interjections during Mr. Gerbowski's lecture.)
The speaker dwells at length [?] on the following important problems of the present moment in the Land of Israel: the economic situation, the political and the spiritual situation. On the economic situation the speaker holds that it is not true, as many think, that the prosperity in the Land of Israel was an inflated, unreal one, whereas the crisis is a natural one, and because of this the public becomes pessimistic and falls into a state of depression. He shows that the crisis is not natural, but is a consequence of external circumstances connected with the political situation, with the fear of war in the country. And here Rabbi Gold comes out sharply against those who came to the Land of Israel not out of conviction but to make easy business, to live lightly [?], feeling no responsibility whatever towards the community, and at the first storm [printed "shtur"] of war the frivolous ones [?] began withdrawing their capital from the bank, which caused the unreal crisis. Rabbi Gold demands spiritual training (hachshara). All immigrants, the capitalist ones too, must be taught the laws of the Land of Israel, so that they be worthy of making aliyah.
As to the Legislative Council, he holds that it must be fought as strongly as possible and stifled before it shows signs of life.
Because of the late hour the speaker has to shorten his lecture and does not speak about the spiritual problem. With strong pathos, with exalted words, he calls out: "Look down from Your holy habitation" — God, blessed be He, look down on Your people Israel and see their deeds for the building of the Land, and send them the true redemption.
The lecture, delivered in a splendid, enchanting language, carried the audience away.
After the chairman appeals that the Keren Hayesod collectors be received cordially, the audience sings "Hatikvah", and with this the academy is closed.
In the evening a banquet took place in the reception hall of the Jewish gymnasium, which went on until late at night.

On Monday [?] evening Rabbi Gold, at the invitation of the local "Mizrachi", appeared with a lecture in Będzin.
The interest was very great. The hall was filled with a varied public (according to "Mizrachi" custom the galleries were reserved for women).
