Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Mishpatim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Mishpatim
—o—
a) "And these are the judgments which thou shalt set before them" (21:1)
"This is what is written (Psalms 99): 'The king's strength also loveth judgment... Thou dost establish equity' — Thou hast established uprightness for Thy beloved ones, for through the judgments Thou gavest them they quarrel with one another and come to judgment." Midrash Rabbah.
Rabbis are taken for this purpose — to make peace among the people. That is the task of rabbis, and for that purpose one elects a rabbi. Meanwhile, however, it turns out that among Jews the greatest disputes arise precisely over electing a rabbi... "The judgments Thou gavest them" — so that there should be peace — "they quarrel with one another": that is exactly where the sharpest fight breaks out. The Dubno Maggid.
• • •
And that is why Jethro was so astonished at Moses: "Why sittest thou thyself alone?" He simply could not understand how among Jews there could be just one rabbi.. A Jewish community needs several rabbis right away, who will tear at one another and blacken the community's face... The same (the Dubno Maggid).
—o—
b) "If thou buy a Hebrew servant" (ibid., 4 [should be 2])
A Warsaw Ger hasid, a householder, once wanted to evict a poor tenant. The Chiddushei HaRim [R' Yitzchak Meir Alter, the Rebbe of Ger] sent for him and asked him: "Can this be?"
The householder began to justify himself: why is he more obliged than anyone else to let the poor man off the rent? Let others collect rent money for him, and he too will give a certain share.
The Chiddushei HaRim answered him:
The Gemara says in Chagigah: "One who is half slave and half free — his master is compelled to make him a free man" (whoever has a slave serving him who is half freed, the owner must free him completely). The question arises: why should the owner be compelled to free him and bear the loss of a servant's value? If it is a mitzvah to free such a one, let money be collected and let him be bought out from his owner. It must be, then, that because it is precisely he who holds the slave, the mitzvah of freeing him lies upon him. So you too: because it is precisely in your house that the poor man lives, the duty lies on you to let him off the rent...
• • •
At one time Jews in Russia were not permitted to own houses and real estate. Later the authorities abolished these decrees, which aroused joy among Jews; only R' Israel Salanter groaned:
"This is a new evil decree! Jews will become landlords. A misery is beginning for Jewish tenants..."
—o—
c) "An ox or an ass" (ibid., 33)
"An ox — but not a man; an ass — but not vessels." Bava Kamma 54.
Why does the Gemara derive "not a man" precisely from "ox", and "not vessels" from "ass"? Why not the other way round?
But the prophet says (Isaiah 1:3): "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib"; from this we see that the ox recognises the person who feeds it, while the ass recognises only the trough, the vessel from which it eats. Therefore the Sages derive "man" from "ox" and "vessels" from "ass".
Doresh Tov.
“I Love My Master…” (From Grandma’s Tales).

[Feuilleton — satire; kehilla and ritual slaughter; Oneg Shabbat — parashat Mishpatim.]
Retold by Ben Amotz.

Saturday afternoon. The Sabbath rest reigns in every corner of Grandma's room; Grandma, the "Tz'enah u-R'enah" in her hand, sits by the warm stove and explains the weekly portion.
— "Ve-im yomar ha-eved": when the servant shall say "Ahavti et adoni" — I love my master — "ve-ratza adonav et ozno": his master shall bore through his ear with an awl...
— Granny dear, what does the verse mean by this? Whose ear is one supposed to pierce with an awl? — one of the grandchildren asks her.
— Health to you, right into your bones! — Granny answers, well pleased. — Our holy Torah is very, very deep; every letter of the Torah is wrapped in a deep veil. If Grandpa were at home now, he would explain to you, little children, why the verse commands boring the ear of the servant who cries "Ahavti et adoni", I love my master. But since your Granny is also no simple Jewish woman — "she knows her way around the small letters" — I will explain the verse to you with a little tale from the old days.
— Maybe Granny means that kehilla strongman?
— Yes, children, there are very many stories about that strongman; especially interesting is the tale of a disrupted funeral of a Jewish victim.
— Granny, don't tell us about funerals, we'll be frightened again at night.
— If so, children, I won't tell about the funeral. Just a merry little tale, about a wedding. Hush![?]
And Grandma tells:
In the town where the strongman "reigned as king" there lived a rabbi. Actually there were several other rabbis in town, but the rabbi I am telling you about, children, was also an ardent national Jew, a man of the people.
— And what did he do that was so special, Granny?
— For instance, today, my children, such rabbis no longer play the important role they did in former times. Because once the English government severely restricted aliyah to the Land of Israel, there were various evil decrees against the Jews, Jewish life with all its goods and property was ownerless, free for all. I remember, when I was still a small child, a Polish woman, a great animal-lover, submitted a bill to ban Jewish ritual slaughter, and various other decrees against Jews. Well, in such bitter times the Jewish people also had rabbis who dared to speak a courageous word; and in this very town, where the kehilla strongman ruled, there lived such a rabbi, who did not want to shout like the strongman's hangers-on[?]:
— Long live the king! Long live our breadgiver!...
This greatly vexed the strongman, and he decided to take revenge on the defiant rabbi.
And the revenge was without mercy, for the kehilla strongman was — so they tell — a great vengeful grudge-bearer. The "people" indeed trembled at his commands; poor folk were afraid to register their children, because the strongman demanded that without his consent the "people", the poor folk, you know, should not multiply...
And everyone who carried on any kind of[?] trade had to register his partners and how much property each one owned...
— What did he do to the rabbi? Tell us, Granny, we want to know.
— Against the rabbi he issued various laws. In that year, children, harsh[?] laws against Jews were indeed issued in various countries... First of all he issued a ban: none of the shochtim in his town was to slaughter any fowl at the rabbi's (Grandpa regarded that ban as a symbol, because in that same year the non-Jewish strongmen banned Jewish ritual slaughter...).
Then a shochet from a neighbouring town violated the ban, and like the anusim [crypto-Jews] of old he came to the rabbi at night and slaughtered the fowl.
— Well, what happened then, Granny?
— People "wept", pleaded — this happened, it seems to me, during the Days of Awe, when the Almighty, as it were, forgives sins — and so on this matter, too, there was a time of grace...
— But you promised, Granny, to tell a merry tale about a wedding?
— That is, my children, almost one and the same story, one link of the chain; the only difference is that the story with the fowl happened, it seems, during the Days of Awe, and the wedding tale — in wintertime, if I'm not mistaken, in the month of Shevat.
A friend of the rabbi was marrying off a daughter. The in-law, a very decent Jew, a great benefactor, wanted at all costs that the rabbi be at his wedding; so he went with this request to the kehilla strongman and said:
— My master, lord of the town, ruler over the synagogue and — to make the distinction — over the slaughterhouse, I, your subject, have come to pay the "R-Kh-Sh"[?] for my daughter's wedding; I'll give as much as your eunuchs demand, only one small request do I ask of you.
— What do you demand? — thundered the strongman's voice.
— I ask that you allow the officiant of the marriage ceremony at my daughter's wedding to be the rabbi, about whom there was a suspicion that he is "half an emissary"...
— Ha-ha-ha, so that's it! You too belong to that gang that wants to overthrow my kingdom[?] — thundered the strongman's voice — hm... a small "re-quest"... hm...
The kehilla strongman pressed an electric button, and at once one of his faithful servants appeared, whom he asked:
— Do you know this man? Do you know what his occupation is?
— Yes, my lord; our "kingdom" has a not-bad income from his business... the shochtim would know better[?] how much our budget gets from him...
— Not important! "With a mighty hand will I rule"... My "enemies" I will crush with all my might. Don't you dare invite the disloyal rabbi to your daughter's wedding — understood?
— Understood — answered the in-law, embittered, and left the strongman's office.
— — — — — — —
— A good week! A good week! — Grandpa calls out. — Old girl, what have you been rambling on about? Eh?
— You're mistaken, Grandpa dear — the grandchildren said to Grandpa — Granny explained to us why the Torah commands boring the ear of the servant who would cry out with one voice[?]: "Ahavti et adoni, I love my master and I don't want to go away from you"...
For the Keren Hayesod Campaign in Będzin. — The Epic of National Capital.

(Welcome to Leib Jaffe on his visit to Będzin.)

Epic and capital, poet and fundraiser — does that not sound, at first, like a glaring, cruel contradiction? Where is the bridge that leads from divine revelation in the soul of a man of genius, from the realm of beauty [?] and Bialik-like [?] fervour, down to the heavy prose of coins, to the jingling arguments whose ring is not always pure, not always aesthetic, and certainly not always good for humanity?

And nevertheless we have built this bridge in Zionism. In the long series of miracles that have occurred in Jewish life since the great revelation of Hess and Pinsker and Dr. Herzl, this miracle is surely not among the smallest. Never in the long Jewish history have we seen such singular emissaries [?] as we have now: men gifted by God, of historic scope, who collect money by conquering the hearts of the people, and under whose eyes this money is transformed, in a reversed process, as in the well-known Greek legend, into life — a great, unique new life in Eretz Israel.

Leib Jaffe stands in the front ranks of these remarkable emissaries of the Jewish renaissance: a people's poet in the best and deepest sense of the word, and the organizer of the Keren Hayesod, the dictator of the Zionist fundraising apparatus.

In a restrained [?] manner he has managed to unite within himself these seemingly contradictory traits and to embody in his person the epic of money; out of the prose of money-chasing he has managed to make poetry, to pour soul-fire into the great creation of the people.

The epic legend of Leib Jaffe is not foreign to us, the Jews of Będzin. We all still remember the "legendary reality [?]" of the year 1929, when with his poetic power he managed to give wings to Jewish Będzin and lift it to an eagle's height. We all became "sons of the prophets" who fell into a mystical ecstasy, and Leib Jaffe himself rightly described it at the time: "Będzin must suffer for 3-4 weeks from Eretz Israel madness" — and so it was. Under [?] Leib Jaffe's magic power we fell into an Eretz Israel frenzy. The results of that "frenzy" are known to you. This year, too, Leib Jaffe comes to us again, accompanied by the well-known essayist and publicist Moshe Gross-Zimmermann of Vienna. Mr. Zimmermann belongs to the young Zionist generation that has thrown itself into Zionist work with full fervour. We greet the distinguished guests with a hearty "Baruchim haba'im" (welcome) and wish the dear comrades that they may again succeed in infecting us all with the Eretz Israel madness, just as in those days.
An Open Letter to an Unknown Jewish Woman

[Będzin — Keren Hayesod; open letter.]
Esteemed lady!
Some time ago one of my friends visited your home and asked your husband for a contribution to the "Keren Hayesod". Your husband was prepared to give it, but when he asked your advice, you exclaimed: "Absolutely not!"
I would not have believed it had I not heard it with my own ears from my friends. God in heaven! How could you utter such words? Do you know against whom that "absolutely not" is directed?
There, in Eretz Israel, a new life is blossoming and growing. People who fled from misery and want, from death and despair, went there and transformed thousands of square kilometres of wasteland and swamps into — blooming valleys, fragrant orange groves, splendid towns. They saved themselves and made possible the aliyah of hundreds and thousands more, who suffer hunger and want in the lands of exile and whom such a fate may threaten tomorrow.
Thousands and hundreds of thousands are waiting impatiently for the day of their aliyah. "Do you not know them? Do you not see them? One need not search far. With an expression of pain on their pale faces and a spark of hope in their eyes they stand at your door and call on you to work with them. Instead of feeling honoured by the opportunity to take part in so great a work, you allow yourself to slam the door in their faces and to shout at them the cruel words: "Absolutely not!". No, esteemed lady, I am convinced that you did not know against whom those words were directed.
I do not have the honour of knowing you personally. But if I am not mistaken, I had the privilege of knowing your grandfather. That snow-white old man still stands before my eyes: the image of God on his brow and God's commandment engraved on the tablets of his heart. One silent ideal lived in his soul: the revival of the people of Israel in the Land of Israel. For that ideal he suffered; that ideal eased his thorny path, filled his heart with pride, with dignity, lent a gleam to his eyes and added to his love for you that endless warmth which was so characteristic of his whole being. He believed that the longing of hundreds of generations still goes on, and that his rock-firm faith in the victory of justice would find its continuation in you. In his daily prayers he joined the prayer for redemption with the prayer for your health and happiness. And now his spirit comes to you and speaks to you: "My child! What was not possible for me to do is possible for you. That for which our people waited whole generations, for which it suffered, for which it prayed, has become reality. I beg you, do not hold back, and help. Make it possible for me to have, through your cooperation, a share in this blessed work."
And you have the courage, you have the audacity to slam the door on this spirit and cry "Absolutely not!". Forgive me, my dear sister — I do not know you, after all, but I know your child and I love it. In the distance clouds are gathering; perhaps a storm will break. We who work for Eretz Israel are building a secure home for your child. The child sees and understands much more than the [warned? / worried?] mother believes. It comes to you in trust, lays its head in your lap and says in tears: Mother, I am afraid, help me! And the mother pushes the little one away from her and says without mercy "Absolutely not".
For my child, as for your child, there are two roads to the future: either the life of oppressed and persecuted people — at best, of tolerated people — or the life of people who are free and proud as children of a nation that knows how to win [?] the respect and esteem of the world thanks to its mighty creations in every field of culture. We turn to you and beg you: help us lead the people out of bondage and into a bright future. And you can, without a shred of understanding, [dismiss?] us with an "Absolutely not!".
I advise you, unknown sister, to distance yourself from the company of cynical people who cannot halt [?] the march [?] of history, and to go our way. It may be a little dearer, a little harder, but certainly finer and more ideal, and certainly better suited to your idealistic soul.
With brotherly greetings,
Yours faithfully,
Dr. E. Alschwanger [?].
Greeting from Prof. Dr. M. Schorr

The chairman of the „Keren Hayesod“ directorate in Poland, Rabbi Prof. Dr. M. Schorr, sent the following greeting in connection with the opening of this year's Keren Hayesod campaign in Będzin:
I send you our blessing on the proclamation of this year's „Keren Hayesod“ campaign in your town under the leadership of our dear comrade L. Jaffe.
I have already heard a great deal about the Jews of Będzin; especially engraved in my memory is your wonderful campaign for the „Keren Hayesod“ in the year 5689 [1928/29], when you rose high in your readiness to sacrifice for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. You then earned the feelings of sympathy of all who are loyal to our banner, and the deepest gratitude of the Jewish Yishuv in our homeland.
The Jews of Poland offer to Eretz Israel not only souls — their children, who go as pioneers (halutzim) before the camp — but they also bring her their wealth with joy, and therefore the contribution to the „Keren Hayesod“ becomes a fixed item among the daily needs of many of our brethren in Poland.
I wish [to say to] you[?], Jews of Będzin, you who have been privileged to be among the best of the Jews, and who through your readiness to sacrifice have been privileged to contribute a significant share to our national work of upbuilding in Eretz Israel:
I know that the sunbeams of success which shone upon you in those days of great efforts have now been darkened; but I believe with perfect faith that the sun of Zion, which is being redeemed[?], and which shines out to you even in these present dark days, will strengthen the spirit of self-sacrifice that lies within you, so that you bring your contributions for our homeland, which is awakening to liberation, and whose gates the „Keren Hayesod“ opens to those who return to her.
I send you my blessing:
May it be God's will that you again be privileged to fulfil the commandment of building the Land in wealth and in honour.
With respect and Zion's greetings,
Rabbi Prof. M. Schorr.
To the Jews of Będzin!

Brother Jews!
Once again our town has the privilege of welcoming Mr. Leib Jaffe of Jerusalem, who will proclaim and lead this year's campaign for the Keren Hayesod.
In the light of the Jewish tragedy we know[?] now more than ever what Eretz Israel means for our people.
In the course of the last few years 30 thousand of our brethren from Germany have found a place of refuge in Eretz Israel. In the last year alone 25 thousand Jews went in from Poland (to Eretz Israel), where they found work, bread and a dignified life.
Eretz Israel has become a source of comfort and hope for our people scattered in all lands.
One could have achieved incomparably much more. Small is our achievement in comparison with the possibilities, in comparison with Jewish want and misery. Jewish masses knock with a cry of despair at the gates of Eretz Israel; Jewish youth strains to get there — that is their only hope and future. Thousands of families are waiting[?] for [—][?].
Great, greater than ever, are the tasks of the Keren Hayesod. It must create the necessary means for immigration (aliyah) and colonisation. New difficulties are being laid in our path. Our only answer is — to increase the efforts, to strengthen the work.
We turn to the Jewry of Będzin, to one of the most important communities in Poland, with our call:
Help build Eretz Israel!
Support the Keren Hayesod, which is fulfilling a historic task with regard to the Jewish people!
Greater than ever must be the number of contributors among us; greater than ever must be the contribution of each one of us. With the contribution to the Keren Hayesod we lay [the foundation of] the future of the liberated Jewish people.

"Jewish Luck"

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satirical poem, the return from America.]
Reb Shloyme Gargel spent
some time in Baltimore —
and there he gathered
(ptoo, no evil eye)
a few fine thousand dollars,
a nice capital.
And from there he decided
to come home to Poland...
His reckoning was:
the dollar is worth 9 złoty,
and all the more 40—50 thousand —
happy is he who has it...
He arrived with a "belly"
and with glasses like "potaytoes" [?],
with talk of "yes" and "no",
of "business" and "how nice it is!".
He did not dawdle long
with the dollars —
his belly [?]
at once began to dry up...
Whatever he took up
went "shlim" [badly] for him.
What used to be straight
has today become crooked. — — —
•
Today one more pauper
has been added in the shtetl — — —
and "Beit Lechem" [the relief society] must every week
give him, too, for a loaf of bread — — —
Meir Grynszpan.
If...

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; local satire, community institutions.]
If the Rescue Committee had money, it would be a fine institution.
If there were peace among the artisans, they would not hold general "zebranies" [meetings] every Monday and Thursday.
If "Ligat ha-Kholim" did not have a maternity clinic, it would not have "won" such sympathy.
If the merchants' association gave out interest-free loans "on condition that they not be repaid", the members would pay their membership dues too...
If the Endek students wanted to restrict themselves in their studies [?] the way they want to separate themselves from Jews, Poland would be in a much better state.

Khatskele Klavnik Makes a Speech about the Shechita Ban

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; parody, the bill banning ritual slaughter.]
Der Kokh-Lefl [The Cooking Ladle] — humour and satire, compiled by Amutslz.
—
[The speech is deliberately written in a garbled, mock-accented Yiddish; some words are uncertain.]
Most esteemed [?], what are these goyish heads after? They want Matshik [Maciek, a gentile] to slaughter animals glatt kosher! I tell you [?], one could after all be ... [?] by the traitors [?].
Do you know [?] what they say? They say that the Jewish shechita is not "humanitarian" and that they must have a "humanitarian" shechita; do you know what this so-called "humanitarian" is? Not to slaughter with a khalef [slaughtering knife] but — to shoot. What do you say to their "righteousness" [?]? It's exactly like with the Jewish manufacturers: they give no work to Jews, they can't bear to watch Jews working hard — they have pity [?]...
True, you did not need ... [?] for the shechita; what do we have ... [?] to worry about? Do you eat meat, then? You only nibble a bone from one Passover to the next and from one Simchat Torah to the other! That is indeed true, but I [?] will not allow Matshik to be the shoykhet and Moysik to be the mashgiach — do you understand now?
A Correct Interpretation of King Solomon's 3 Sayings...

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; a mock gematria commentary.]
King Solomon says:
1) "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing" — if you've found a wife, you've found happiness.
2) "And I find more bitter than death the woman" — I find that the bad wife is worse than death.
3) "But a woman among all those have I not found" — of the thousand wives I have not found a single proper one.
And now let us treat these sayings by mathematical calculation.
What do we find in the 3 sayings?
In the first saying the word "ishah" [woman], in the second "ha-ishah" with a heh at the beginning, and in the third "ve-ishah" with a vav at the beginning. —
ishah
ha-ishah
ve-ishah
Let us set the man, "ish", against the 3 women, and we will also break the word "ish" down into numbers.
By gematria this comes to:
ishah — 306
ha-ishah — 311
ve-ishah — 312
ish — 311
Let us set the man against the 3 women.
306 < 311
311 < 311
312 < 311
1) If the woman is 306 by gematria, she is 5 points lower than the man, 311 — after all it is written explicitly: "and he shall rule over thee" — he must rule over her.
In such a case "whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing" — such a family is happy and lives in peace and tranquillity.
2) If the woman is 311 — with the same rights as the man (also 311), and she wears the trousers — that is already "more bitter than death", that is worse than death.
3) If the woman is — 312 — one point higher than the man, she is a disaster [?] for the husband's years, and she is truly one of the thousand among whom one finds not a single proper one.
Bal Narski Nożyca.
The "Gallery"

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satire, the kehilla and its councillors.]
Why indeed should the "gallery" [the public gallery at kehilla meetings] not be able to voice its opinion? In what way is a Jew from the right, or, say, from the left table, a greater holder of opinions than a gallery-Jew? On the contrary, the true "one who faithfully attends to the needs of the community" is precisely the gallery man.
A parnas [councillor] comes in [?] grandly into the kehilla, sits down at a table and talks. Whether one word sticks to the next or not, everyone has to hear him out, and afterwards he even reads his name in the newspaper — "Councillor X showed shrewdness in his speech"...
But the grey man from the gallery, poor thing, has to stand in the crush a whole evening and keep his mouth shut, even when there is somebody who deserves a piece of his mind.
And besides the plenary sessions, the gallery man is after all a great in-law of the kehilla. He pays for a metryka [civil-registry record], for a circumcision, for a din Torah, he pays tens of groszy for slaughtering a chicken and he gives the hundreds of zł. of burial fees.
And the councillors?
All they know is how to get another little subsidy for their own society, to install another man of their own as an official. From "takers" — as the saying goes — there will never be "givers".
Is it not truly justice, then, that the gallery should decide on the budget items? But where is there justice today?
Yosef.

A Little Story

[Humour — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; joke, matchmaking.]
A Będzin matchmaker arranged a match in which the bride was from Szczekociny and the groom from Sosnowiec.
When the "viewing" [first meeting] was due to take place, the bride's mother, afraid the bride would blurt out some foolishness, instructed her not to say anything herself, but to answer whatever the groom told about himself and his home with: "With us it's the same."
Here is the dialogue:
Groom: — What's new with you?
Bride: — And with you?
Groom: — With us it's not bad.
Bride: — With us it's the same.
Groom: — What kind of flat do you occupy?
Bride: — And you?
Groom: — We have two rooms and a sublokator [subtenant].
Bride: — With us it's the same.
Groom: — And where do you sleep?
Bride: — And you, where do you sleep?
Groom: — Each separately, and I with the subtenant.
Bride: — With us it's the same.
No further conversation took place, because the groom left in the middle without so much as a goodbye...

The Bastard (75)
A Thrilling Tragic Novel by a Prodigy

[Literature — serialised novel; instalment 75.] By Adv. S. Geliszpowski [?].

But as soon as he was out in the street, the great wind swept away with it Benjamindl's words, which had been ringing in his ears, and he forgot them at once.
It was not a suit, not a coat that he had gone to buy, but something better for himself, something without which he could not live.
From old times, when he had still been a young bachelor in the big city, he remembered the old places and dens [spelunki], where one can get anything for money, and there he now hurried with the banknote in his pocket — there, to the people who for money give out such little boxes with a whitish-grey powder that makes you forget everything and everyone.
Like a newborn becomes the man who has such a full little box of the white powder; he is then happy, contented, and sees everything before him in the most beautiful colours.
There is no suffering, there are no troubles, there is nothing bad in the world; everything is beautiful, everything is good and everything is ownerless [hefker]. Let the wife go, let the child go, live and enjoy life, which is short. That is the motto of the lovers of the little boxes with the white powder.
Like a man in a faint he fell into one of the houses, and the first word he uttered was "India".
No one, apart from those who deal in buying and selling cocaine, knows that the word "India" means cocaine. That is the international sign for this poison, which the narcotics users employ.
"How much?" — a limping Chinese man in a long blue robe came up to him.
"Four pieces, Sir Mandarin," Nahum got out, trembling as if in a fever.
"Ten dollars," says the Chinese man, and stretches out his hand for the money.
With a practised eye he examines the hundred-dollar note that Nahum handed him, and, realising that it is good, he gives him as change nine ten-dollar banknotes, and as an extra four not-large little boxes, in which there is the white poison called cocaine.
And it did not take long before Nahum was already hidden in a corner, drawing into himself the white powder, which as it were revived his life, which made him, as he thought, alive again from dead.
And he was not the only one there. There are dozens of them there, the incurably sick narcotics addicts, who sit as if hidden in the corners and draw the white poison into themselves.
From aristocrats down to people of the underworld, they all come here, to "Gras-Bet" [?] Street, to the restaurant of the Chinese Chai-Yung-Hang, where in one of the halls on the first floor the trade in "India" is carried on.
People live there for months on end once they come there. There, in Chai-Yung-Hang's boarding house, they get food and a place to sleep, and when the money runs out one attaches oneself to those who still have something to pay with, who share with them a little of the poison and something to eat; and above all, the food there costs no money, because as soon as one is merely a member of the cocaine-users' association one is no longer lost.
Such a member of the association is also Nahum Rozen, who has long had not a cent to his soul and lives, as they say, on handouts. Before, he shared with others, and now others share with him.
A very comradely, good life exists among the narcomaniacs, who do not let a comrade go further astray as long as they can still help him.
In vain Benjamindl waited for him every day, sure that Nahum had been arrested as an illegal immigrant and deported from the country.
It never occurred to him [lit. he never dreamt] that Nahum was in fact in Chai-Yung-Hang's house, stuffing himself with cocaine for the hundred dollars he had given him to buy himself clothes.
So days, weeks, months ran by, and Nahum did not show himself before his eyes any more.
And once — it was early in the morning — Nahum came out with two more of his comrades from the damp cellar where they used to sleep on old torn rags.
It was still early. Of those who have money and [printed "from"] can get the white powder there was still no one, and the craving for the powder is so strong that they are dying.
Their thirst was roused even more when they caught sight, in the big hall, of the limping Chinese man, who had all the pockets of his blue coat stuffed with the white little boxes.
"Sir Mandarin" — so they called the limping Chinese man — "give one little box, we'll pay later."
"My boss Chai-Yung-Hang me beat, me no white give without money, 'don' sotch' [?] he me said, mandarin 'mura' [?]" — he gave them to understand in his bad English.
But their thirst for the white poison was too strong, and there is then no danger for them when they crave it. So it is no wonder that it did not take long before the Chinese man lay at their feet, bellowing like a slaughtered ox.
From all sides, at his cries, Chai-Yung's people came running, and they barely rescued the limping Chinese man from the hands of Nahum and his comrades.

Sosnowiec: We Want to Be Secure in Our Lives and Property

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism and shechita.]
Sosnowiec
We want to be secure in our lives and property.
A delegation of the Jewish city councillors' caucus at Deputy Madeyski's.
At the invitation of the caucus (koło) of Jewish city councillors, Sejm deputy Dr. Madeyski came to Sosnowiec on Monday, where at the town hall ("ratusz") he received a delegation of the Jewish councillors in the persons of the chairman, Mr. M. Lubelski, the chairman of the Small Traders' Association, H.[?] Kliner, and Dr. S. Lejwerowicz[?].
The chairman of the caucus, Mr. M. Lubelski, after greeting Dr. Madeyski, hands him a memorandum in which all the incidents on antisemitic grounds were recorded, from the brawl at Jabotinsky's lecture up to the latest acts of terror that took place in the Zagłębie area, where dozens of garments of the Jewish population were doused with corrosive (burning) substances.
The floor is given to councillor Mr. Herman Kliner, who touches on the question of anti-Jewish excesses and the decree against Jewish ritual slaughter.
"We," says Mr. Kliner, "have not come to you, Mr. Sejm Deputy, to ask for any favours whatsoever; rather, we demand of you, as the elected Sejm deputy of Zagłębie, that Jewish life and property be secured in accordance with the constitution."
Then Mr. Kliner touched on the shechita question and said: with the decree against shechita not only religious Jewry — the element that has supported the present government from the very beginning — has received a heavy blow, but also the whole of world Jewry, and we shall all create a strong front to ward off this decree.
Deputy Madeyski declared in his reply: "I, as a believing person, hold the view that the foundations of no religion whatsoever may be desecrated. I am not yet clear on this matter: if shechita is a fundamental principle of the Jewish faith, I shall certainly be against the law. But if the rules are only superstitions (zabobony), I cannot yet state my position on the question."
To this Mr. Kliner gave the following reply: "We cannot judge whether the laws of shechita are superstitions or not. Over thousands of years the shechita question has in any case become an important dogma of the Jewish religion, for our whole faith is, after all, something abstract too."
After the discussion, in which Messrs. Lejwerowicz[?] and Lubelski took part, Deputy Dr. Madeyski promised that he would endeavour to deal with the postulates put forward, in accordance with the wish of the delegation.
“And he shall rule over her” led to a divorce...

The "Grievance" of a Kielce Plutocrat against the Mizrachi Leader Rabbi Gold

[Page head: "Life in Kielce" — Friday, 28 Shevat 5696 / 21 February 1936.]
As is known, a few days ago the well-known Zionist leader, the Mizrachi president Rabbi Gold, stayed in Kielce. In his splendid lecture in the hall of the Teatr Polski on the current political, economic and spiritual situation in Palestine (Eretz Israel), Rabbi Gold dwelt at some length on a certain category of panic-mongers and vile usurers who, because of the Italian-Abyssinian war, caused a panic in Palestine and brought about the present passing economic crisis in the country. Rabbi Gold rightly called these [—?], who have never in their lives given a penny for a public Jewish cause, vile creatures who poison Jewish life and who will be removed from it by the Jewish community.
These hundred-percent true words of Rabbi Gold did not much please a certain person present at the lecture, a Kielce upstart war-profiteer plutocrat, a well-known usurer and owner of a large house on Czysta Street. He has strong "grievances" against Rabbi Gold: how did he have the "nerve" to speak in such "drastic" language about those "noble" and "refined" scoundrels[?], usurers and plain scoundrels who "help" build up Palestine by granting "loans" and "interest-free loans" at forty-odd percent to the building contractors and other merchants ruined because of the wars[?]...
Yes, anyone may have complaints and grievances — but someone like that, with closed hands, a heart of stone and ears stopped to the most important needs of Jewish society, a man who gives not a penny to any good cause, a Jew who is still today a great plutocrat and is prepared[?], for the sake of his 5 pennies, to let hundreds and thousands of needy and sick, unfortunate Jews perish from want — such a person has no right to any complaints whatsoever. This usurer should be glad that he is let into Jewish society at all.
Scandalous Disorder at the Kielce Jewish Cemetery! A Fine Plan by the Herszkowicz Brothers

Years ago we already pointed to various instances of desecration of the dead at the Kielce cemetery, facts which ought to have stirred the public conscience of Jewish Kielce.
But to our great shame our outcry was hushed up and everything stayed as it was. Instead of improving the terrible, neglected condition of the Jewish cemetery, it has been neglected even more.
For it is not enough that one does not know where anyone lies, because no markers at all are made on the graves; on top of that a large number of tombstones are set on other people's graves, which are "indicated" by the cemetery "intendant" Jakl Bakałarski, who is better acquainted with the geographical situation of Abyssinia than with the cemetery — but the chaos and the scandalous disorder there are[?] so great that it simply cannot go on like this!
Human and animal filth lies strewn among the graves; the iron bars are regularly stolen from the graves, which are thus prematurely destroyed and broken. Some tombstones are deliberately knocked over by unknown hooligans; gentile youths quite often climb over the cemetery walls and do there whatever their heart desires, and nobody stops them. The purification house (tahara room), where local and outside dead are quite often purified, is in a most scandalous state: the ceiling is rotten through and hangs in the air, and any moment now it will fall down and, God forbid, a catastrophe may happen; even the electric lamps, which were hung up only recently on the cemetery field, are vanishing[?] from day to day, etc. etc.
We no longer want to speak about the bad road leading from the "Kadzielnia" to the cemetery, on which the hearse may overturn at the slightest mishap. That belongs to the Magistrate (municipality), and there is indeed a sacred duty on the kehilla to intercede with the Magistrate so that the road be repaired[?] as soon as possible. We are speaking now only of the internal arrangements that belong directly to Jewish society itself.
True, the kehilla has no money to carry out all the absolutely necessary[?] arrangements at the cemetery; the financial state of the kehilla is catastrophic — but what the kehilla can do and what it must do is: help the brothers Fiszel, Todres and Israelke Herszkowicz carry out their splendid plan.
The Herszkowicz brothers propose that instead of the beth midrash which, according to their father's will, is supposed to be built — and which will not be built anyway, because Jewish society, which is supposed to help build the beth midrash, is now badly impoverished — they be allowed to introduce proper European order at the cemetery, such as: laying out suitable avenues, numbering the tombstones, putting up a small synagogue, a waiting room, a tahara house, planting trees on the field, repairing the walls, installing a telephone, etc. etc.
It would seem that the splendid plan of the Herszkowicz brothers ought to be welcomed by every Jew of Kielce. The kehilla president, Mr. Goldman, is making every effort to have the plan carried out, but there are quite different religious difficulties here, on the principle of "one may not divert charity from one charitable purpose to another"; the matter thus lies in the hands of the Kielce rabbinate, which must decide on all of this.
We wish, however — and this is no doubt the wish of the entire Jewish population of Kielce — that the rabbinate headed by Rabbi Rapaport find a way out of this matter, which in our opinion is not so difficult, and that the rabbinate know that at the Kielce cemetery there reigns, as already said, a most scandalous disorder: it is a profanation of the holy, it is both a desecration of the dead and a desecration of God's name!

"Lechayim Chadashim" ("To a New Life") at a Kielce Cinema

Before a group of Jewish journalists and communal workers, the newest Palestine (Eretz Israel) film "Lechayim Chadashim" ("To a New Life") was screened this week in one of the Kielce cinemas. This film is running, as is known, in Warsaw at the cinema-theatre "Nowości" with great success.
The film, which lasts an hour and a half, leaves an extraordinary impression, and as propaganda for Zionism it works more than hundreds of speeches and articles. One sees the rapid, colossal development of the new Jewish Yishuv and, in contrast to it, the backwardness of Arab life. Every scene is gripping, and one feels like singing along the "Emek song" of the cheerful and carefree pioneers (halutzim).
In general the film puts the viewer in an optimistic mood; one forgets for a while the dark world outside and is filled with striving and hope for the "new life", which is sunny and bright.

From the undersigned craftsmen's guilds we have received the following communiqué:
In connection with the disgraceful attack by the secretary of the G. Ch. [Gemilut Chesed, interest-free loan] fund, Mr. Montag, on our esteemed city councillor Mr. A. D. Balimowski — who had come, as a board member and honorary secretary of the G. Ch. fund, to intercede on behalf of a poor guarantor — an urgent meeting was held[?] on Tuesday evening at the premises of the Central Craftsmen's Association (Kołłątaja 45), at which the following resolutions were adopted:
1) We, the craftsmen's guilds, express our sharpest protest against the base conduct of Mr. Montag toward Mr. A. D. Balimowski, who devotes all his days to the good of the poor Jewish population of Będzin.
At the same time we express our bitter protest against the board of the G. Ch. fund, headed by its chairman, who, instead of branding and reacting properly to such a disgraceful act, took upon himself the role of Mr. Montag's defender.
2) Mr. Montag is to be removed from his post.
And 3) a general meeting is to be convened in the nearest future, at which the entire board shall tender its resignation.
If not, we shall draw the appropriate consequences.
Central Craftsmen's Union, Painters' Guild, Hatmakers' Guild and Barbers' Guild.

9-Month-Old Child Chokes on a Doughnut.
At the home of the Pastek[?] family in Sosnowiec, Szyplecka[?] 31, a tragic accident occurred on Tuesday.
Mrs. Pestak[?] gave a doughnut to her 9-month-old little boy, who was lying in bed, and stepped away for a while. At that moment the child swallowed a piece of the doughnut, which got stuck in his throat[?].
Despite all rescue measures it was not possible to save the child.

Anti-Jewish Demonstration.

[Section:] What's New in Upper Silesia?
Shop windows of Jewish stores smashed — Jewish newspapers torn up.
On Sunday several hundred men gathered in the "Luna Park" in Chorzów and protested against the dissolution of the Endek associations in Upper Silesia.
Afterwards those assembled demonstrated through the streets and in the meantime smashed several shop windows of the Jewish stores. On the way the demonstrators came upon a Jewish newspaper vendor, who was assaulted, and his newspapers were torn up. The police broke up the demonstration and arrested the main leaders.
Hitlerites Wanted to Tear Upper Silesia Away from Poland.

The prosecutor of the Katowice district court has proposed to the investigating judge to conduct an investigation for high treason against the members of the secret German Hitlerite organization which was active in the territory of the Silesian voivodeship.
So far 75 leaders and active participants of this organization have been arrested; its aim was to tear away from the Polish state a part of the Polish territory, and especially — Upper Silesia.
—o—
They Are Fleeing Poland.
Last week the police in Upper Silesia liquidated the secret German political organization which had been carrying on anti-state activity. About 40 persons were arrested.
As the newspapers report, in the course of the last week about 400 members of this combat organization fled from Polish Upper Silesia. They are fleeing to Beuthen.

A Successful “Keren Hayesod” Campaign in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism.]
Last Thursday evening, in honour of the proclamation of the “Keren Hayesod” campaign in Będzin, a festive academy took place at the “Apollo”, which aroused enormous [?] interest among all strata of the Jewish population.
After the “Hakoach” orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems, the academy is opened by the chairman Mr. Fürstenberg, and greetings follow.
On behalf of the K.K.L. (JNF) A. Liwer greets; for the Zionist Organisation — Y. Winadzki; for “Mizrachi” — L. Buchweitz [?]; for the League — Sh. Liwer; for “Hitachdut” — M. Rozinker [?]; for “Et Livnot” — Y. Gelbard.
Then the writer Gross-Zimmermann and Director Leib Jaffe give addresses, calling on the Jewish population to strenuous deeds for the building of the Land.
At the end Mr. Jaffe speaks, rebuking the Jewish people, which does not take account of all that is happening in the lands of exile and does not take its proper share in the building of the Jewish national home.
On Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a large banquet took place in the gymnasium, attended by the notables of the town, Zionist activists from Sosnowiec, donors, and also a larger number of young people, who by their behaviour created [?] the proper mood at the banquet.
The tables were lavishly served with various dishes, fruit and Carmel wine.
With a delay of an hour and a half the banquet is opened by Mr. Fürstenberg, who hands the chairmanship over to Mr. A. Liwer.
“According to the order of the world,” says Mr. Liwer, “the banquet ought to be held after the campaign, but we are changing the order, because we trust that the visit of our honoured guest Mr. Jaffe will give the Keren Hayesod campaign the desired success.”
Dr. Sh. Nussenblatt, the prize-crowned Herzl scholar [?], points out that Director Jaffe already took part in the very first Zionist Congress.
Successful [?] toast-speeches are delivered by Mrs. Ts. Szajn, who appeals to the Jewish woman to take part in the building of Erets Israel, and by Dr. Melarista [?], who turns to Mr. Jaffe asking him to convey a greeting to the builders of Erets Israel: that despite the monstrous decrees on Jewish heads in exile, we are still here.
Editor Gerbowski, the disciple of Leib Jaffe, points to the great achievements of his master and his work for the “Keren Hayesod”.
There also speak the writer M. Gross-Zimmermann, Mr. Rabin (Erets Israel), the chairman of the Zionist Organisation Winadzki, L. Buchweitz [?], Advocate Rechtman, Chairman Fürstenberg, Sabatowski, the League chairman Shmuel Liwer, H. Waszager [?] and others.
The banquet is closed with “Hatikvah”. Then the photographer Goldcwajg takes several pictures and the members of the “Kibbutz” dance a “hora”.
—o—
Very [?] impressive was the visit of Messrs. L. Jaffe and Gross-Zimmermann to the Będzin “Gordonia”. In the parade (report) 400 members took part, uniformed in Gordonia uniforms.
After the singing of “Hatikvah” the guests are greeted by Mr. Sh. Zimmermann on behalf of the organisation, who points to the great achievements of the guests in the field of colonising all strata of the Jewish people on the land of the K.K.L. “We, the youth, cannot help much materially; on the other hand we are devoted with our whole soul to the work of building Erets Israel.”

The Katowice Spring Fairs

[Upper Silesia — economy.]
From 30 May to 14 September 1936 the traditional Katowice fairs will take place in Upper Silesia, organised by the Silesian Society for Exhibitions and Economic Propaganda (Katowice, Staszica [?] 14, tel. 300-71).
The Katowice fairs aim to keep the family workshops in motion, to raise consumption and to increase turnover in many branches of industry.
The fairs take place in the peak trading months, and the merchants and industrialists who take part in them prepare for themselves a ground for enlarging their enterprises.
It is a matter of the highest degree that domestic goods should be exhibited in greater number, in order thereby to acquire a larger clientele. For this reason it is very important that industrialists and merchants take part in the so-called Katowice fairs.

In Defence of the Craftsman!

In many states the craftsman, as the factually most productive [?] element of the population, is specially patronised by the governments.
The craftsman is treated like a stepchild, and that is because, through the pace of technology, the craftsman — the primitive workshop owner — grows ever weaker, and the slightest breeze [?] of burden can sweep him off the economic surface.
All governments have understood this, and in order to preserve the productive element, facilitations were created for the craftsman in running his enterprise.
The Polish government, too, at the beginning, when creating the special tax laws, took the above-mentioned circumstances into account, and with regard to the craftsman the laws were softened.
In the year 1925, when the turnover-tax law was amended, craftsmen working alone or with one assistant were exempted from "tax-ekupkucja" [?; probably a misprint] etc.
When the craftsman was bound by the Industry Law, the tax law gave him the compensation [?] that the holder of a craftsman's card paid only 1 percent of turnover instead of the 2 percent that others paid, and craftsmen working with an assistant were exempted from turnover tax; later a small lump sum (ryczałt) of 20 zł. was assessed for the latter.
Technology and the economic crisis steadily weaken the craftsman, his existence becomes ever more threatened, yet the various allowances have been reduced step by step: the craftsman who works alone must hold a licence (patent), the one who employs an assistant must pay turnover tax, and there is no lump sum any more. The government's protection of the craftsman has been removed.
Now the craftsman who holds a craftsman's card is no longer privileged.
The decree to the Tax Ordinance fixes a uniform percentage rate for the whole of small industry, the craftsmen included, regardless of whether the craftsman holds a card or not — he pays 1.5 percent of his turnover when working on his own account and 2 percent when working for wages.
It is indeed true that the present decree to the Tax Ordinance, in the above-mentioned point, generally grants a certain relief, for example: the cancellation of the communal and the 15 percent surcharge, and also that it exempts enterprises paying turnover tax from the stamp duty on concluding contracts, as well as from the "daning" [?; perhaps danina, levy].
But this is a relief only for the big entrepreneur who deals with such contracts; the small craftsman, however, has nothing to do with these things, and therefore he gains [?] nothing from it. (On a turnover of 20 thousand zł. the craftsman has paid until now, together with the surcharges, 250 zł.; now he will pay 300 zł.)
Nowadays, when the biggest entrepreneurs have in fact been given considerable allowances, the craftsman ought to have received far greater allowances, and not have even the allowances he had until now taken away.
The craftsman, who is now going through a very severe economic crisis — restricted by the various regulations of the Industry Law, receiving no credits, with a narrow sales market — can in no case bear the tax burden.
If in previous years there were certain allowances for the craftsman, these allowances should not merely not have been reduced, but should have been enlarged on a broad scale.
The craftsman who works alone or with one assistant must be free from buying a licence (patent) etc. For the assessment of taxes one should not demand from the craftsman all the regulations that the Tax Ordinance provides for [?], because no craftsman is in a position to state for whom he worked in the course of the year and what turnover he made, and because of this he is assessed according to the estimate of the tax office.
The painful matter of the craftsman ought to have been heard from the Jewish representatives in the Sejm during the debate on the budget of the Finance Ministry; unfortunately it was not heard.
The Jewish representation must unconditionally begin to conduct an energetic intervention in the direction of protecting the craftsman, for otherwise the ruin of the entire community of craftsmen threatens.
Y. R.
Memoirs of the First Zionists in Zagłębie.

[Memoirs — the beginnings of Zionism in Zagłębie; serial, part 2.] By Gershon Stawski.
2.
Kampiński, who all his life had lamented the "exile of the Shekhinah" of the Polish nation, was surely reckoning that Bialik was speaking of Poland's revival, for it never even occurred to him that Bialik was speaking of the revival of the Jewish people — which is the oldest people and has also given the world great men, with so rich a past, which has given the world so much culture and so fine a literature.
Kampiński, however, who as a forwarding agent [customs expediter] had known only the Jewish filth — he knew only how Jews smuggle across the border not only goods but often also "living goods"; he knew that Jews inform on one another, and other such "fine" deeds that one can see in a border town. But how astonished [?] he became when he heard from Bialik such historic praises of the Jewish people, which in the most tragic moments it lived through in exile had still not given up its hope of returning to its fatherland, its hope of becoming once more a free people on an equal footing with all cultured nations.
With great interest he listened to the historic movement of the Hovevei Zion, and that in the last few years our great Western European brethren had joined the movement, such great minds as Dr. Herzl and Dr. Max Nordau [printed "Nardoy"], who organised a world movement under the Zionist banner.
The Jewish spark that had been in Kampiński's heart, almost extinguished, Bialik fanned with his great talent, and the spark kindled the fire and strength and the patriotic national fire that had always burned in him, in his heart, for the Polish nation; and he rose from his seat, took Bialik's hands in both his hands, and with great enthusiasm and shining eyes said on the spot the blessing "Shehecheyanu"... and also said: I thank Almighty God who has granted the man who already stands at [?] the edge of his life the privilege of hearing, in his oldest years, that the people from which his parents stem belongs to the oldest nations in the world and has given the world the greatest men and the finest culture, and strives and hopes to get back its fatherland and to become a cultured people on an equal footing with all cultured nations; and he solemnly declared that he was joining the Zionist movement.
The very next day he visited our Zionist premises, and at the first meeting we elected him chairman of our society, and he fulfilled his duty with the greatest punctuality despite his advanced age.
We called him "Bialik's ger tzedek [righteous convert]", and Bialik was pleased with the whole affair [?] and especially that he had managed to convince — and to make a loyal Zionist out of an assimilationist.
A few years passed; Bialik was no longer in Sosnowiec, he had settled in Odessa, and the time came of the 4th Congress, which was held in London.
In one of Bialik's letters to me, of 9 July 1909, Bialik complains bitterly about the sad situation of the Jewish workers in Eretz Israel and storms against the fact that the Zionists are so indifferent to the sad phenomenon that half the workers have already left Eretz Israel because of hunger and want, and the Zionists do not take account of how hard it was for each worker until we brought him to Eretz Israel; and Bialik therefore proposes to me that we in Sosnowiec too should send a delegate to the 4th Zionist Congress in London and oblige him to join the delegates who will defend the workers' question at the Congress — and our delegate should be Mr. Kampiński (the ger tzedek).

You Will See for Yourselves...

[Sosnowiec — letter to the editor; the relief institutions and the rich.] (A letter to the editors).
Once again Jewish Sosnowiec is being alarmed about the danger that threatens most of our important institutions in our town, such as the Gemilut Hesed [free-loan] fund, the Jewish hospital, the Talmud Torah, Linat ha-Holim [sick-care society], etc., which are threatened with the catastrophe of collapse for lack of financial means.
More than once has Jewish Sosnowiec already been alarmed about this same matter, and it is not the first time that the activists of the above-mentioned [?] institutions appeal to the conscience of the Sosnowiec rich. But unfortunately, to this day this appeal has not found the proper response among the well-to-do section, that they [?] should take an interest in the fate of the institutions in order to maintain their continued [?] existence.
— And what is the reason for this?
— We hold that the main reason is that the strong religious authority is lacking which would enlighten them and make them understand that in such a time the rich must not stand aside and not want to help.
We know from of old that in every age it was the rabbis who took upon themselves the task of admonishing and awakening the conscience of these petrified hearts. And through various moral sermons in the synagogues and batei midrash they did in the end obtain from them some help or other for the good of the community or an institution.
We had, after all, just such a similar case not long ago here in Sosnowiec, which shows us best that no one but rabbis with their moral preaching can influence our rich. We all still remember how many years the town synagogue looked like a real ruin, covered with scaffolding ["rusztowania"], and nobody could be found to have the synagogue painted; but only when Rabbi Hager preached morals in the synagogue on a holiday and appealed to the conscience of our rich did R' Yehoshua Pachter come forward (he does not belong to today's "war rich"), who at his own expense put the synagogue into proper order.
And in the present question too — help for our institutions — our rabbis could have accomplished a great deal, but unfortunately in Sosnowiec the synagogues and batei midrash have been closed to them, and thereby, it goes without saying, they have been deprived of the possibility of carrying out this mission. (As is known, everyone who wants to speak in the synagogue, even rabbis, must first obtain permission for it from the appointed kehilla... and what that means for a rabbi we all understand. It is, after all, something that cannot happen and has not happened anywhere except here in Sosnowiec.)
Because of this the local [?] rich regard the calls for help coldly (we mean those who do not want to know of Jewish need), and thereby they bring the institutions not only to certain collapse but also to a terrible catastrophe for hundreds of poor Jewish families.
And therefore these rich must be stirred [?]: visit the above-mentioned institutions and see how people who only a short while ago were great rich men now, unfortunately, come to these institutions to ask for help.
See for yourselves in what situation the relief institutions find themselves, and then you would surely change your attitude towards them up to now.
Come to the institutions, get to know them more closely — it will do you good.
With respect,
Tzvi Ochsenhändler.

Pseudo-Sport (Once More on Boxing)

[Essay — sport and Jewishness; boxing.] By P. Blumenkranz (Częstochowa).
Although I have already once touched upon the boxing psychosis among Jews and pointed out the un-Jewish character of this sport, I nevertheless feel a need to return to the matter once more and speak out from my heart [?].
A small digression:
I admit and confess that when I see a hunched, worried Jew walking in the street absorbed in his cares, and suddenly some scum comes up to him and strikes him on the head, my blood begins to boil — as it probably does in all other Jews. I feel the blow then on my own shoulders, and at that moment I long to have something of Esau in me. I would like then to possess such big, hairy hands too, and to give that Esau a wallop [?] across the face, to give it to him in his boorish mug, so that he would roll into the gutter!
(I tremble with agitation as I write these words! The maimed [?] faces of dozens of Jews stand before me, and my hand jerks with bitterness, humiliation and rage!)
In these shameful minutes I recall Bialik's cry of woe! Human dignity, trampled and spat upon for hundreds of years, awakens and quivers in its slumber. I feel then the cruelty of our physical weakness, the absence among us of the feeling that it is better to fall than to lead a despicable [?] life ("better to die a heroes' death than to live a life of shame").
I become embittered and despairing; a thought of grief and rage gnaws [?] and cries out in me:
— Why, devil take it, are we so afraid for our cursed life? Why and how is it that we sit hidden, tucked away in the attics, while thuggish boors beat Jews, crack heads, rob goods and chattels, tear out the windows and desecrate everything that is holy?
And I admit that in these minutes I would like to be coarse, hardened, crude, "without the inherited refinement", and to show [?] our tormentors the strength of our fist.
Yes, when I am under the impression of such a mood, I watch the "boxing wars" with interest and even pleasure. My injured feelings are flattered when a Jew lays his opponent down (knock-out [printed "nak-put"] in the foreign tongue) in the first round, when a Jew, hunted like me, mocked like me, deals the muscular, hooligan opponent blow after blow, boldly, with impetus, to the jaw, to the stomach, according to all the rules of boxing.
But this feeling of pleasure lasts only a few counted minutes; it is only a product of bitterness and inner protest.
As soon as I manage to free myself somewhat from this idea and become able to look around at the darkened [?] faces, my heart grows troubled and I feel with all my senses that this way of becoming strong is not our way; that this brutal sport stands in complete contradiction to our whole outlook.
* * *
So I sit at a boxing match! Hundreds of people — if only the Yiddish theatre were so attended [?]! Grown-up Jews and tiny boys, women in wigs and powdered, pretentious girls, Poles with aristocratic manners and others in maciejówka caps [?] and flowered shirts.
Everyone absorbed. Everyone hushed, everyone's eyes shining and moist, nailed with excitement to the two hopping [?] souls in the ring.
And when one of them turns out to be the weaker and would already have wished — were it not for the shame — to stretch out on the boards, voices are heard from the other side, broken voices, squealing, coarse, simply shouting:
— Knock him down! Give it to him in the jaw, in the stomach, finish him off!
In front of me sits a [—] [?] fellow with a fat, two-storey [?] neck. He does not allow himself to sit; he rises up as at a horse race, his eyes bulging with emotion, he makes every movement of the boxers, turns about like a pendulum [?], as if the primeval beast had awakened in him, so that the blood boils in him and he would gladly now fight, just so, at random, with anyone at all. Only to see blood, only that blood be spilled.
Next to me, on the other hand, a little boy stands on tiptoe — his parents took him along — and every minute he pesters [?] his father:
— "Tatusiu, czy on ma silny cios!" [Daddy, has he got a strong punch!] [?]
The little one is sorry that a blow missed. He has complaints to his father that the boxer did not make a "sherm" [?], did not give a [blow] [?] to the left ear
And when the blood is running from the weaker man and he staggers, wanting [?] all the same to last the three minutes in the ring, the crowd protests, cheers on the stronger one. Begs him for mercy [?], shouts to him:
— Lolek, finish him off [Polish "dokończ go"], make an end of it, a left punch! Finish, finish!
* * *
Probably some, or even many, will ask:
— What is the matter with this man? The whole world boxes, crowns champions, spends millions — and he comes along with blockheaded questions.
And others, calmer ones, will ask:
— And the sporting value of boxing is nothing? Who needs [to fight] physical degeneration more than we do? Who needs physical daring more than we do?
So it is like this:
The first questions need no answer — why the world shouts that it wants [?] peace, seeks justice, cares [?] for Jews and the like.
But as for the second category — a few words.
True and certain, one must keep drumming into Jews, again and again, that a pale face is no sign of refinement, that it is foolish to believe that the more pallor from anaemia — the more pedigree, the more [—?] look "silky" [?] and "velvety".
One must [?] keep showing Jews [—?] what damage their physical frailty brings.
But for God's sake, do not abuse this need [?], do not make a fetish out of an idea, for Jews of all people must remember what comes of it when an idea is abused, when one falls into extremes, when one personifies an idea.
* * *
By the way: the whole Jewish sports movement must go in the direction of mass sport, of gymnastics, and not of Rotholc [?] imitators [presumably the Jewish boxer Szapsel Rotholc].
We must be healthy and able to defend ourselves, but not boil the blood and turn the youth into beasts.
We must strive for physical strength. Already in ancient Jewish times it was held that the Divine Presence rests only on a man of stature..
But physical development — straight shoulders, eyes open [—?] — does not mean brawling, does not mean pummelling and bloodying, because Jews cannot bear blood and hate it. They placed the butcher, the murderer and — to make the distinction — the ritual slaughterer under the same planet Mars, except [?] that the slaughterer says a blessing, because if he has to do with blood at all, he already has in him something of the butcher and something of the murderer, even.
For Jews cannot stand blood, no matter how the blood shows itself and for what purpose...
