The White Rooster. (From life at the summer cottage.)

[Story / feuilleton — from life at the summer cottage (dacha).] It has suddenly grown quiet in the village. The few Zagłębie families who spend the summer months here have suddenly vanished [?]. I too have come here to spend a holiday in the sunny stillness and the enchanted calm.
In the middle of summer, when I was here, I saw a kingdom of women:
The little wives were forever on the lookout for a man — someone to pass the time with, someone to dress up for, someone to cook a chicken [?] for. Towards the Sabbath, or on Sunday, a husband would come, here to this wife, there to that one; and if once in a while a guest turned up, a man in the middle of the week, one who had come alone, without a wife, he got all the chickens [?]. The women dressed up for his sake alone, and he thought he was the only successful male in the world.
Now the grass grows green beside Michałek's [Mikhalke's] house undisturbed. And on the sandy patches in the meadows, trodden bare over the summer by the guests from Będzin and Sosnowiec, hens walk about, swallowing little pebbles and scratching with their little feet to find worms.
In the flock of hens, scattered in little groups over the meadow, a white rooster with a red, dressed-up comb bustles noisily about. He clucks [?]. He calls, suddenly raises a cry, an alarm about nothing at all, salutes the hens with an outspread wing. The hens look up to him with great respect, and the white rooster is sure that he is the only rooster in the world.
The master of the house, Michałek himself, who knows what a proper rooster is, actually thinks nothing of this rooster. He calls him the "ploysher" [chatterer], that is, a braggart, a noise-maker and nothing more.
"What's the matter with the rooster?" I ask the peasant. "It seems to me that he's [?] a handsome white rooster, and I see that he entertains the hens in an interesting way,
"Yes," mutters the peasant, looking angrily at the rooster and flinging his cap at him in a temper, "yes, he passes his time in an interesting way, but there's no purpose [takhles] in him."
"What do you mean, a purpose?" I ask?
"Watch closely," the peasant answers, "and you'll see for yourself that I'm right."
So I sit on the veranda, warming myself in the sun, and observe the hens and their handsome white cavalier with the fiery-red comb.
Yes, the first fault I notice in the handsome rooster is that his signals cannot be relied on. He is a bit of a bluffer, as is the way with an uncommonly handsome, spoiled young fellow. His warning cries are always without any cause. He just shouts and raises an alarm. And precisely when a large bird flies past, when the cat appears, when the dog comes chasing through — he neither sees nor hears.
The second fault, I notice, is that he is a lazybones and likes to live on the toil of his sweethearts. He does not scratch up any worms with his little feet, and never calls the hens to some tasty morsel. Only when a hen finds a good little worm does he start shouting, "Sku-ktu-ktik-tut" [?]! as though he were inviting someone to dine with him here, comes running up to the hen and eats it up from her. And she, the little hen who found the fine delicacy, gladly lets him enjoy himself, looks at him with gentle eyes and at once begins again to search and to plough the earth for a living [?],
But then, I find out, he is a romantic hero and the hens love him; they are dying for a glance from him. He crows, he salutes, he is a real noise-maker. True, with him it comes to no purpose; he is very amusing, very handsome, but he has his romantic moods.
I sit and watch and see how all sorts of hens circle around the handsome white rooster — brown, yellow, white, speckled, plumpish and downright fat ones, and slender ones — and he, of all things, sidles up to a scrawny little black hen. He circles around her, keeps paying her "ladies' honours" with his wing, and she, the scrawny black "manzete" [?], keeps moving away from him.
The more she draws away from him, the more he pursues her. Now he grabs her by the little head with his beak and she runs off with shrieks, as though she were being murdered here; he runs after her, and a few hens break into cackling in a somewhat gossipy tone.
The rooster chases the little black hen and she puts up a fight; she gives him a peck and runs away again, but he will not let her go. What matters to him here is his romantic victory. He runs after her with his wing spread and cannot catch her; now he seizes her firmly with his beak by the feathers of her crest, and again she twists herself free of him and runs off to the other side of the cottage.
The rooster is left all worked up, and mutters, disappointed: "Ku-r-ru"
He takes to eating something again, and it looks as if everything is already forgotten. Well then — so nothing came of it [lit. "so it wasn't fiddled"].
I think: good heavens, what is going on here with the romantic caprices between the rooster and the hens?
Here are so many handsome hens swooning over him, and he of all things is mad about the little black hen who does not want him, who does not care a straw for him [lit. "does not have him even in her left sidelock"].
And you, scrawny little black hen, what don't you like about the white "krasavets" [handsome fellow], with whom all the hens want to make a match? Are you looking for a purpose, just like the peasant?
Thinking thus, I see the little black hen come up and the rooster dash after her. She runs away again and he after her, under the house; her shrieks and his angry scolding can be heard.
After that it grows quiet. The rooster appears, gives his feathers a shake and bursts into boastful scolding: Kurrr-rur!
A fat yellow hen, pecking in the sand with her beak, raises her little head, glances at the handsome white dandy and starts arguing peevishly, just out into the world at large, to everyone:
"Gra-gra-gra, gerrr."
The peasant comes up, once again hurls his cap at the rooster and says angrily:
"He's a chatterer and nothing more, I'll slaughter him — and that's the end of it!"
B. Botwinski [?].
Word and Deed.

[Essay — Herzl's yahrzeit, 20 Tammuz; Zionism and the Jewish National Fund.]
(On the day of Herzl's yahrzeit).
Like a flash of lightning through the deep and heavy 2,000-year night of exile, Herzl appeared in the dark sky of the Jewish people, and with the power of his radiance he drove away the darkness.
Mighty was the lightning, and strong was the crash of thunder that accompanied it, so that to this day we hear its rumble [?]. Ever stronger, ever louder we have perceived, and still perceive now, the word "Judenstaat" [the Jewish State], which holds within it the hope and the longing of a [?] nation — the longing that has slumbered in us from the moment we lost our independence as a state.
Thirty-two years have already passed since Herzl departed into eternity and began the life of immortality, which he foresaw at the very beginning of his Zionist work, when he wrote on 15 June 1895:
"I believe that for me life has ceased and world history has begun."
Herzl, raised on Western European culture, was as a jurist acquainted with Roman creation, and as a poet — with Greek creation. The "myth" of ancient Greece was not foreign to him, and he knew that the giants, despite their superhuman strength, could be defeated by killing them in the air. But no sooner had they fallen to the earth than a new spirit entered them, which called them to a new life.
The "myth", a product of the Greek folk imagination, became, thanks to Herzl, a reality among the Jewish people; for Herzl, seeing that in exile we lead a life of "Luftmenschen" [people of air] and are thereby exposed to the danger of perishing, understood that we shall revive only when we come into contact with Mother Earth, and he came out in public with the holy cry
— "The Jewish State" ["Judenstaat"]!
He went to the mighty of the earth and said to them:
"We want to lead the Jewish people, the army of the hungry — the hounded and the persecuted — out of bondage and give them a home, a place of justice, a land of happiness."
When the great ones among the Jewish people heard the tidings, they laughed and mocked him, and, not content with mockery and scorn, they came out publicly against him in order to disrupt his work.
Among the disrupters there was also no lack of those of whom Herzl says:
"There are Jews who live off Judaism and 'those who live for Judaism'", and whom Nordau branded with the name: "Protest Rabbis".
Small was the number of those who listened to his words and his slogans.
From the ranks of the youth and from the benighted ghettos of the East the cadres were formed [?], the beginning of today's army of millions. From there voices made themselves heard — command us, we hear!
But the ruler to whom the land was subject did not allow the gates to be opened to the stream of the wandering [?] masses.
And on top of everything, the distress grew and the persecutions intensified.
A hell of troubles and a sea of suffering opened up anew. Thousands were killed, tens of thousands murderously beaten, and millions chased and driven.
Blood flowed in rivers, and the glow of freedom and redemption was dimmed by the brutal acts of violence of our enemies.
Despair seized those who had rejoiced in the hope.
Fear broke into his own camp, so that some of the most devoted lost their trust and rebelled against the leader.
But he accepted everything with love and turned the nights of rest into days of hard work. He doubled and tripled his toil and exertion for his poor, tormented people.
And so care and self-sacrifice, pain and love broke his aching [?] heart too early.
That, alas, is the fate of the great among the Jews: they die in the middle of the road, like our Mother Rachel long ago, who carried hopes in her womb; like Moses our Teacher, who cast his last glances toward the nearby land which he did not enter.
It was the 20th of Tammuz. Thirty-two years ago!
Short was the life of Herzl. But immensely great was his work. In what does the greatness consist?
Philosophical and philosophizing minds have for generations been conducting an embittered debate: which came first — the word, or the deed?
It is a dilemma. An answer to it we find in Herzl.
In the tohu-vavohu, in the wild chaos that prevailed in Jewish life, there thundered — as has already been mentioned — a word that shook the world and its foundations — "The Jewish State"!
First there was the word, but shortly afterwards comes the deed — the Keren Kayemet LeYisrael [Jewish National Fund].
And if there is anyone today who places the word "Jewish State" higher than the deed whose task it is to realize the word, it is a sign that he has not understood Herzl.
Not to understand is pardonable; that can be forgiven. But whoever consciously fights Herzl's deed, ignoring his resolutions and the Keren Kayemet LeYisrael, not supporting its income — he desecrates the memory of Herzl.
Therefore we call today, on the day of the yahrzeit:
— Back to Herzl!
Yitzhak Buchner.
Zawiercie, 1936.
Questions of the Day — Before the Kehilla Elections

[Opinion column — Zagłębie, kehilla elections.] Before the kehilla elections.
So then, "let us all be merry", for things are beginning to get lively in our little world.
The joyful tidings of new elections to the kehilla (Jewish community council) have reached us in Zagłębie too. And, as can be foreseen, in this field of all fields our towns will not lag behind, for we have no lack of institutions whose activists will carry on the work to perfection, with fire and holy fervour; kehilla elections are quite a fat morsel, and in our lean times people will know how to appreciate such a thing...
In truth it would seem that at the present time things are dark and bitter enough for us; one need not be a grown-up to understand that. Take, for example, our youngest schoolchildren — the kind in whom, in other civilised countries, you recognise in their childish carefreeness joy itself — and among us you will hear from them horror-descriptions of Przytyk, Mińsk Mazowiecki and others.
Children, tiny children, will tell us about the want, the pain and the misery we are living through in Poland at this time; but we ourselves forget, or pretend to forget, everything we see, the whole scroll of shame that is unrolling before our eyes.
At such a time, when everything and everyone is against us, we ought to unite, so as to beat back with joint forces the incessant attacks made upon us; but when people among us begin to talk of unification, they twirl the thumb [split hairs] for so long that the head starts spinning and the main thing is forgotten — unity...
In Sosnowiec too people have begun to talk about unity, about a united bloc; but — would that we were proved liars — you will see how from under the ground, like mushrooms after rain, groups and grouplets, parties and little parties will begin to sprout, and each one, alas, will pull towards itself, for each will hold that only he is worthy of busying himself around such a treasure...
One — because his father was a rabbi and his grandfather a rebbetzin [sic]; a second — because his chain of pedigree stretches all the way back to King David... and a third is simply a "fine Jew", and one's own pedigree is more practical nowadays...
And somehow we are, after all, blessed with double portions, economic and social, and you will surely not wave away the political parties either, such as the Zionist Organisation, "Mizrachi", the Right ["rechte"], and others.
And do you think the philanthropic institutions and mini-institutions will keep silent for you? Well, well, just try to start doing something and you will soon be convinced whether you have to reckon with them or not.
All of this will begin to roar, buzz and dance a round-dance [korohod], so imagine what a spectacle we are going to have.
Yes, poor and petty is our life; we are sinking back into the vermin-swarm of Kabtsansk and Tuneyadevke [Mendele's fictional towns of paupers and idlers]; apparently we feel splendidly well here — but shall we ever crawl out of this swamp?
The nearest future will show us that...
A. Hendel.
What We Do Not Know

[Popular science — curiosities from the world.] By Dr. P. Lagsztajn [Langsztajn?].
There are things going on in the world about which we, simple people, know nothing at all.
Here is a small cutting from those things of which we know nothing whatsoever, as they are reported by the "Prague Fair" [?], which from time to time puts out such interesting items.
We do not know, for example:
That although a man weighs on the whole only about thirteen per cent more than a woman, a man's heart is nevertheless 22 per cent larger than a woman's.
That as early as the year 1789 women began placing advertisements in newspapers saying that they were looking for husbands...
That in America a heavy fortune is being made by the artist Chandler, who holds certificates from many universities stating that he is the best imitator of the voices of animals and birds.
That every year in America at least 20 Black people [orig. "Negroes"] are killed[?] by whites, and the police there pretend not to know.
That when people sing[?] at work one can produce ten per cent more than without singing.
That on a rainy day no fewer than 3,500 umbrellas are forgotten in London's trams and buses.
That the highest railway in the world is in Peru, where it runs at a height of 4,880 metres.
That on the line "Vegtigson Lek"[?], in South America, there is the longest tunnel in the world (22 kilometres long), and that at "Tshao Ving"[?], in China, the railway runs over a bridge which is 144 kilometres in length and is the longest bridge in the world.
That in Sydney (Australia) there is a bridge that hangs almost in the air, for from one point of support to the other there are 502 metres.
Homely Little Letters

[Satirical feuilleton — "Homely Little Letters": Sosnowiec, the kehilla elections.] With God's help, in the week of the portion "And the earth opened her mouth"...
My friend Reb Shloyme, may his light shine.
After inquiring after your good health, I give praise to His dear Name that the present letter will bring you a little pleasure. Enough of tormenting ourselves with the endless lamentations and Job's tidings. As the chapter[?] says: "It is a time of trouble for Jacob, and out of it he shall be saved"; day does not break before it gets good and dark. After Przytyk, Mińsk Mazowiecki and the like we really thought that, God forbid, all the appointed ends had already passed, that the sun had gone completely dark for us, that our fate was already a lost one — but Israel is not widowed! In our darkened skies there has appeared a bright star for which the whole House of Israel has longed for so many years. After the Przytyk verdict we have been allotted — kehilla elections...
And the "joy" among the Jewish population in Sosnowiec and of Dąbrowa is indescribable. Sosnowiec is going about "on little wheels" — not on ordinary wheels, but those of the "kolej" [the railway]. The whole kehilla swarm — and off they ride...
And now the Jewish "riding-wagon" has stopped on Dęblińska Street and held a meeting there, a sort of peace conference, at which the prophecy of "And it shall come to pass in the end of days" was dealt with...
Reb Shloyme, dear heart, do believe me that the Geneva diplomats are fit to be boot-blacks to those who took part in the disarmament conference. The ecstasy grew so great that one of the participants even proposed that a second League of Nations be created in Sosnowiec. The only difference will be that to the League of Nations in Geneva the delegates come decked out in vinegar and honey, with false compliments and criminal intentions, whereas to the Sosnowiec League of Nations "people will come to cry their hearts out", for example, as before the Western Wall...
Just know[?] what speeches there were — true mysteries of mysteries; I swear to you by beard and sidelocks that the greatest diplomats who stand at the helm of the world are not capable of taking their place at the "round table" and delivering such a "profound" speech as was delivered, for example, by the representative of the "Agudah" or of the Zionists... Pearls poured from their mouths; with eyes goggling up at the... ceiling they declared: Gentlemen! — "After all, we want only peace". Enough of tearing at each other's heads, enough of publicly abusing and besmirching one another; let the wings and the angels of peace [perhaps: the wings of the angels of peace] protect us, and peace be upon Israel...
There are also diplomats of the kind who want to wrap peace in a different garb, in a garment of silence: that the fight to obtain the kehilla seats should "take place within the bounds[?] of boxing" — one should not give the opponent a punch right into the heart, but only in the mug [gęba]... In plain language this is interpreted in the sense, for example, that the fight should be conducted among ourselves; one may call the other a thief, a pickpocket, a feeder of treyf and the like, only not inform on him; for firstly, the government offices are already overflowing with Jewish denunciations, and secondly, we are after all in a time of trouble today, so why should one inform on the other? It will be enough to give the opposing side a punch in the ribs on the quiet...
Against the proposal one of the delegates came out — not a townsman, naturally, but a rustic from a suburb — who demanded that one should look in through the smashed window-panes of the Jewish dwellings, and then one would see how on the "coachman's box" [kozioł] of the Jewish riding-wagon there sit several personages in rabbinical garb, who command in which direction the "kolej" is to turn and where it is to stop... But hardly anyone among those assembled listened to the words of a "simple man". The "people" need emotions, they thirst to hear the jingling of the spurs on military boots. And indeed the walls fairly trembled when the representative of "Mizrachi" thundered in his mighty voice:
— Struggle! A struggle for the sake of an idea, not to conquer foreign territories, but a struggle of ideas!...
And just then we, the "popular masses", thought that the struggle was already beginning, especially when the delegate of the League (not, God forbid, of the League of Nations) declared that "on account of the social revolution, which is so near, he withdraws from the peace conference and breaks off all diplomatic relations in general, and in particular in the field of religion"... But at the very gravest hour the idea of peace won sympathy among the majority of those assembled as well, and it was resolved to hand the matter over to a commission of 12. In Geneva there is a commission of 13, and here in Sosnowiec there are only 12, corresponding to the twelve tribes...
Whether the commission will have the strength to bring about a lasting peace, the nearest future will show; meanwhile, do have a good Sabbath, as is wished you by your friend
Ben Amotz.
The main thing "I forgot": Zagłębie Jewry in general, and Będzin in particular, has made a name for itself in the wide world on account of the "statistical" materials which were revealed only recently by the delegate of the Będzin Jewish combatants [ex-servicemen], who "possesses" exact figures on how many Communist leaders are Jews...
— Perhaps your premier, Comrade Blum, would invite him into his government? Make an effort about it; you will be well rewarded by the Będzin combatants...
The above-named.
Jerusalem (From an Excursion) — 6

By Naftali Bialsa[?].
(From an excursion). 6)
Notable sights of New Jerusalem
The New City of Jerusalem on the western side is distinguished by its pulsing life and street traffic, and it keeps on growing and spreading towards the north and towards the south side and further to the west side — such as the outlying colony of teachers and officials, "Beit HaKerem", with the monumental building of the Hebrew teachers' seminary, and further on the outlying colony "Bayit VeGan" and the "Achuzat Bnei Brit", which was built with the help of long-term mortgage loans from the "Bnei Brit" (B'nai B'rith) lodge in Jerusalem. From here one already sees clearly the Mediterranean Sea, although it is still about 50 kilometres away as the crow flies. So pure and transparent is the air in the Land of Israel.
On the north side lies the outlying colony of Romema (where the Arab terrorists have lately been making very many attacks and acts of sabotage).
Here the great water reservoir of Jerusalem has been built. The water is driven here through water pipes from the south side, from King Solomon's Pools, which lie behind Bethlehem, 13 kilometres from Jerusalem, and from Wadi al-Arrub, 23 kilometres from Jerusalem; and for some months now water has been flowing here from the north side, from Ras al-Ayn near Petach Tikva, about 80 kilometres. In this way Jerusalem's water supply is concentrated here, and the city no longer suffers from any shortage of water as it did until now.
The Arab terrorists have lately been damaging the pipes of the water main day after day, and this week they severely wounded 3 Jewish workers there; and in several Jewish quarters, such as Ramat Rachel and others, drinking water has already run short because of this sabotage. Thus the Arabs want to destroy installations which cost gigantic sums of money and which bring immense benefit and good fortune to the whole country — if only to terrorize the Jews.
By the Rechavia quarter stands the Ratisbonne monastery, which was built some 75 years ago by a convert (meshumad) from Strasbourg of the same name, who devoted his whole life and great fortune to the aim of spreading the Catholic faith.
A remarkable historic church is also to be found on the Mount of Olives, to the east of Jerusalem, by the name of "Pater Noster" (the Lord's Prayer; Polish pacierz), which was rebuilt anew 68 years ago. There hang 32 tablets on which the Lord's Prayer is inscribed in 32 languages, among them also in Hebrew and Aramaic.
On the Mount of Olives is "the Christian garden Gat Shemena [Gethsemane]" (oil-press), in which there also grow 8 very old olive trees, of which legend relates that they date from before the Destruction. The Romans at that time, when besieging Jerusalem, cut down the rich forests on the Mount of Olives and hanged the Jews on them in their thousands. Beside this garden there is another such garden, which the Russian Tsar had planted 48 years ago, and he built a large church there.
The oil that is pressed here from the olives of the gardens[?] is very holy and is sold to the pilgrims (olei regel).
Close by is the Kidron Valley, in which stands Yad Avshalom (Absalom's Monument), which had been buried under sand and stones and was only some 12 years ago dug out and freed of the rubbish.
Next to it is a remarkably beautiful burial cave of a priestly family by the name of Beit Hezir [Bnei Hezir], and at the entrance are inscribed in ancient Hebrew letters the names of the priests buried there, from the time of the Second Temple.
Before the entrance there is also the monument of the Prophet Zechariah, who was murdered in the Temple at the command of King Joash. The monument is hewn out of a rock and is 9 metres high, and on its top there is a pyramid.
Close by is the village "HaShiloach" [Silwan], in which is the grave of R' Ovadia of Bartenura, commentator on the Mishnah.

Little Feuilleton: It's Hot...

[Feuilleton — humour.] Heat waves.
Fire from heaven!
Earlier we had Abyssinian rains, and now — Abyssinian heat.
Did the Negus [the exiled Emperor of Abyssinia] not bring these natural traits of his country along with him to Europe?
If so, we have no further reason to be on friendly terms with Mussolini. It is he, after all, who brought us such a guest to Europe.
30 degrees, 35, 40 — it already stands at 42. Let it be 50 already; what, after all, is the difference — 8 or 10 years of prison? A difference there is, though: whether a man is set free while two fresh graves lie in the cemetery, or whether a man is convicted while he stands in an attic and shoots into the clouds.
Learned men say that heaven is arranging special heat-courses in order to prepare sinful mankind for hell. But what are we guilty of here? Why do Jews deserve hell? Does heaven, too, limp where justice is concerned? Why do we deserve such heat, such fire? A little while longer and the Endeks [the antisemitic National Democrats] will start claiming that the heat is nothing other than a Jewish piece of handiwork. Advocate Kowalski will prove it explicitly from the "Talmud".
It is even written explicitly: "By the sweat of your hands shall you eat bread" — very well; but what when no work is to be found and the sweat pours from head to foot? One of the two: either sweat with bread, or, if there is no bread, then what the devil is the sweat for?
And as if all that were still too little, they have also decreed the kehilla elections upon us in the genuine[?] heat.
We groaned that the kehillas are good for nothing — well, so the elections were fixed for such a time, so that, contrariwise, roasted "dozors" [dozory — kehilla board members] should come out.
R' Yaakov.
From the Film World

[Cinema.] Chinese Gold.
That will be the name of the new film in which the leading role will be played by the well-known film actor [the original, by mistake, uses the feminine form] Gary Cooper. The screenplay is being written by the American man of letters and playwright Clifford Odets. The film is being directed by Lewis Milestone (a Jew from Odessa), the creator of the famous film "All Quiet on the Western Front". Together with Gary Cooper plays the English actress Madeleine Carroll. Large masses of Chinese extras take part in the film.

The film actress Gertrude Michael.
Until not long ago this name had no significance whatsoever. Today it is the name of a gifted film actress who is beginning to move up into the front ranks of the Hollywood film stars. The most important film producers and film directors, of the calibre of Rouben Mamoulian, Cecil B. DeMille and Ernst Lubitsch, are now taking an interest in her. Gertrude Michael took her first [steps] in the famous film "Cleopatra", under the direction of the master director Cecil B. DeMille. She played there, incidentally, a small part. She nevertheless distinguished herself, and what especially caught the eye was her beautifully built body, full of grace and suppleness. She is engaged for two further films, "The Last Outpost" and "The Dangerous Beauty", in which she already plays bigger and more responsible parts.
Her further career is suddenly interrupted and disrupted by an automobile accident. Driving her car, Gertrude Michael suddenly ran at a headlong speed into a tree; the car is smashed, and only by some miracle does she get away with several serious injuries. She remains in hospital for a considerable time, and that, naturally, interrupts her work in the film factory. She completes two motion pictures in which she plays together with the well-known actor Herbert Marshall.

A director is already making his 62nd film.
The oldest director in Hollywood today is the famous Cecil B. DeMille. He actually stood at the cradle of the art of film in general. Together with Mary Pickford and Charlie Chaplin he lays the foundation of film production. He is also a co-founder of the film metropolis Hollywood.
Regardless of his years he goes with the current; he makes successful sound films, and now too, as the colour film is arising, the hoary grey-haired director tries his powers. He is now making his 62nd film, which is called "Buffalo Bill". 62 films, among them so-called monumental ones of broad scope — that is no small matter!

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Pinchas

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Pinchas.]
A) "Behold, I give him My covenant of peace" (25:12)
The world thinks — Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk [Kock] used to say — that peace means giving way, yielding, renouncing. Such a peace, however, is not lasting; the true peace is the one that comes after a merciless [?] struggle. The peace that Pinchas brought about by killing the transgressor. "Behold, I give him My covenant of peace" — that is the true peace, the peace that comes after a just and ruthless struggle... Arono shel Yosef.
B) "In that he was zealous with My zeal among them" (ibid., 11)
This was the best proof that the Jews' sin with the daughters of Moab did not come from depravity but only from inflamed lust; for now, when Pinchas took upon himself the vengeance of the Lord of Hosts, nobody stood up against him; all of them, as it were, were seized by remorse and said he was right. Drushei Mahari [?].
—o—
"Their sorrows shall multiply who hasten after another."
The wicked are full of regrets. The wicked who are not bad by nature and sin only because of a momentary outburst of passion are always remorseful and full of sadness. "Their sorrows shall multiply" — their sadness increases — "achar maharu": because they hurried too fast, because they did not reckon what they were about to do... Machazeh Olam [?].
—o—
In the case of Joseph's brothers the Torah, as it were, underlines that after they had committed such a base deed and thrown a brother into a pit — "and they all [?] sat down to eat bread": after the sin they sat down to eat bread calmly, as if nothing had happened...
Of the Golden Calf too it is said that after the ugly work was done "the people sat down to eat" — and that is the very worst: the calm after the sin, the lack of remorse after the transgression. Afikei Yehuda.
C) "And Moses brought their case before the Lord" (27:5)
In another case, when Moses went to ask God about a law, he said to those who asked: "Stand still, and I will hear" — stand and wait; now, with the daughters of Zelophehad, it says "and Moses brought their case before the Lord": he did not tell them to wait, because "do not talk overmuch with a woman", and had he let them talk themselves out they would have gone on talking into the sixth millennium... Imrei Chen.
D) "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right" (ibid., 7)
The commentators take pains to interpret these words in various ways, and yet they remain unexplained.
In truth, however, the law of the daughters of Zelophehad is already found in the preceding chapter. In chapter 26, 33 it says: "And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters; and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Hoglah, etc.", and afterwards, having reckoned the genealogy, the verse says: "Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names". It is therefore clear that "unto these" means those mentioned earlier, and it is plainly said that an inheritance is due to them. This is what God answered: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right" — as Rashi says: "Thus is this passage written before Me" — why, one passage earlier it is explicitly written so...
E) — "And there was not left a man of them" (26:65).
On this the Sages expound: "but not a woman" — the women were not subject to the decree of the wilderness.
And that is why the passage of the daughters of Zelophehad comes after the passage of the counting of the Jews: to show that the Jews [the men] perished [?] because they hated the land — they said "Let us appoint a chief and return to Egypt" — whereas the women loved the Land of Israel and said: "Give us a possession". Toldot Yitzchak.
F) — "That the congregation of the Lord be not as sheep which have no shepherd" (ibid., 17).
Because they consider themselves a "congregation of the Lord", each one of them holding that he speaks with the Almighty, as it were, by himself — therefore "they have no shepherd", therefore it is hard to find a leader for them; each of them is, in his own eyes, even higher than the greatest leader... Leket Amarim.
G) — "And you shall put of your splendour upon him" (ibid., 20).
"...and so we learn: the face of Moses was like the face of the sun and the face of Joshua like the face of the moon... the elders of that generation said: Woe for that shame, woe for that disgrace." Chagigah 15 [?].
Shame is a very good thing. "Whoever feels shame will not quickly sin." But woe to such a shame as comes from the generations growing ever smaller and of ever lesser worth... Be'er Yitzchak.
H) — "And on the Sabbath day two lambs" (28:9).
Why does one not read after the Torah reading, as maftir, the passage "And on the Sabbath day two lambs", just as on Rosh Chodesh one reads as maftir "And in the beginnings of your months", and likewise on all the festivals?
Because in the Sabbath passage there are only two verses, and at the Torah reading one does not read as a passage fewer than three verses. Kol-Bo.
Avot, chapter one.
I) — "Let the poor be members of your household, and do not talk overmuch with the woman... whenever a man talks overmuch with the woman he brings evil upon himself" (5).
There are people who, wishing to rid themselves of charity, send them [the poor] off with such matters to their wives, who by nature have a grudging eye for charity. So the Mishnah says: "Let the poor be members of your household, and do not talk overmuch with the woman" — with such matters do not refer [?] to the wife, for then — "he brings evil upon himself"; for if he hands over to her the monopoly on stinginess, it will later come down on his own head... Siftei Avot.
J) — "Remove yourself from doubt, and do not tithe too much by estimate" (16)
With charity one sometimes buys off sins ("redeem your sin by charity"). It follows that for a doubtful sin one must give a doubtful charity, that is, without measure, for one does not know the worth of the sin... Therefore "remove yourself from doubt" — and you will not need "to tithe by estimate"... The Maggid of Brody [?].
“Der Kokhlefl” (The Stirring Spoon) — The Heat

[Page head:] “Der Kokhlefl” [The Stirring Spoon — also a nickname for a busybody]. Humour and satire. Compiled by “Amutslo”[?].

The Heat.

Oh the heat! Oh, the heat!
Thirty-five! Forty!
Men, women, poor things, sweat —
they sneak, they crawl “open-hearted” [i.e. with shirts open]...

One goes about in a bare shirt,
the sweat pours as if from tubs;
everything is uncovered, everything is revealed —
that of the lean, the fat and the fatter...

A time has come, brothers,
may it not befall us — God protect us!
when every Jew is now
a “Moyshe Groys” [big shot], a real “shvitser” [sweater — and also: braggart]...

No sea of soda water helps,
no “mountain” of cold ices;
all have equal rights —
the bearded and the clean-shaven.

Suffer in silence — what choice has one! —
one barely breathes, one barely pants,
and one sends the warm greetings
both to Krynica and to Sopot...

For “in the sweat of thy face” is written, after all;
you will groan like an old mare —
and your wife with the children
you will keep at the summer cottage?

You curse your years,
which pass under a heavy yoke,
and with great pleasure
you would let yourself be wrung out...

But... well... it’s a lost cause —
lathered up [in sweat] you must sit here...
and by day, with thermometers,
measure the scorching[?] heat!

Yakl ben Flekl.
Who knows?

On the 25th of last month our delegates left for the consultation of the Sosnowiec Jewish organizations, and to this day we do not know where they are.
There is a fear that a “volcano” has carried them off somewhere...
Whoever has any information whatsoever about them is requested, for a reward, to notify the secretariat of the Merchants’ and Industrialists’ Association in Sosnowiec, Kowalska[?] 2.
Khatskele Kalbunik goes on holiday

Listen, lads, I’ve got a piece of news for you, and you won’t like the smell of it. I’ve thought it over: I too ought to go on holiday. Say yourselves — what, is my soul a raisin? All the little squirts may go on holiday and I may not? All the squirts may roast themselves in the sun and I may not? Well, I’ve made up my mind that I’m going too.
I have to tell you the plain truth[?]: it will be very unpleasant for me to leave Zimna [“Cold”] Lane, but I must go. Perhaps you think I have no appetite for eating? Then you are mistaken: appetite I do have, I just have nothing for the appetite. How can I eat, when the fat bellies of Kołłątaja Street eat everything up? Who gobbles up the few strawberries, the berries? Who guzzles the sour cream with the sour milk — the rich; who drinks soda water with syrup? Who stuffs down all the ices? — the fat bellies.
And if I go on holiday, I too shall need the wherewithal — and where shall I get money for it? Nonsense! And all those who do go, have they got money then? They too have the ague[?] [= nothing at all]; one grabs from another, they sign promissory notes, and when it comes to paying they turn the peak of the cap round and say: kiss my... well, and one kisses the other. That is how people live in Zagłębie.
Where am I going? That I can’t tell you yet; I’ll write you a little letter and then you’ll find out.
Keep well and strong, all of you — I’m off on holiday.
Official declarations on a united bloc for the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec

In connection with the initiative to create a united list for the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec, we turned to a number of economic organizations about their attitude to the bloc and received the following official communiqués:

Our organization is ready to join the general Jewish bloc, if 8[?] members (członek) of ours figure on the list.
With greetings,
The board of “Nosei HaMita” [the bier-bearers’ society].
—
We agree (zgadzamy się) to join (dołączyć) the bloc (not of chocolate). We do, however, draw attention (zwracamy uwagę) to the fact that one of our valiant lady members (dzielne członkinie) should figure on the list of candidates (na liście kandydatów).
With deep respect (z głębokim szacunkiem),
The board (zarząd) of “Hakhnasat Kallah” [the society for dowering brides].
—
We take the standpoint that the bloc must be born. One thing must be seen to — that no monster be born. Our organization, however, must get the godfathership (kvatershaft).
The Maternity Clinic.
—
All of us, just as we are — baked, kneaded and plaited — pour ourselves into the general kneading-trough. The bloc must be tasty and crunchy.
Master Bakers’ Association.
—
The bloc must be well mixed [like chopped soup greens]; nothing may be missing, from a parsley root to a carrot. Our organization counts itself into the mixture.
Small Traders’ Association.
—
If it does not come to a bloc, we are all slaughtered. We Jews wander about like sheep without a shepherd. We will not allow our sides to be chopped, and whoever wishes may porge us; with us there are cold lungs and livers [= cool heads]. All the sermons preached on the butcher’s block are superfluous. One condition we set: to hack a butcher (heker) into the list.
Butchers’ Guild.
—
We the undersigned baste ourselves on to the Jewish bloc. A bloc is now according to the latest fashion journal. Let it only have the right cut and not be finished (wykończony) in a botched way (partacko). We press ourselves on to the general front piece (przodek).
Master Tailors’ Guild.

Summer chats

Summer cottages (dachas) — it goes without saying that whoever is not a coward has rented a dacha.
The little wives of Będzin who sit in the “Club” have this year committed a betrayal of all the summer resorts: they are all getting ready to go to Rabka.
Fashion — as you see in the street, ladies’ suits are in fashion; the heat is blazing, after all, so fashion says one should hide the sun with karakul.
The ladies are buying up the men’s cloth; the cloth merchant no longer wants to talk to me at all, and when he does show me a piece of goods and recites its pedigree — the lawyer’s wife (mecenasowa) took some for a suit, the doctor’s wife (doktorowa) — it costs another couple of gulden [= złoty] per metre.
Y–f.

(A song for the Sosnowiec “kile” [= kehilla; in Yiddish “kile” also means a hernia] people, on taking leave of their chairs of blessed memory.)

Oh, one can already hear the echoes,
oh, elections are coming,
oh, how fast they hurry it on,
and already they start shooting at us with arrows.

Oh, oh, oh, oh elections,
meetings in halls,
chattering and boasting,
big bumps on heads,
brawling and beating,
oh, woe, the elections!
— — —
Oh, we cannot rest,
oh help, what is one to do,
from the chairs we shall fly
and cease altogether to bloom.

Refrain:
Oh, oh, oh, oh flying,
flying for whole miles,
oh how it scalds,
let us make an effort —
[yet] we[?] can do nothing at all,
to the chairs we are drawn.
— — —

may no Jew know the like,

In the Tangle of Life.

[Serial novel.] (A novel with dramatic events in Kraków, Zawiercie and New York)

Years ago there lived in Kraków a respected[?] Jew, a great Talmudic scholar, who was called Reb Yosef Dayan [Reb Yosef the religious judge]. Women who lived in his neighbourhood used to come in to him to have their ritual questions decided, although he was not one of the official dayanim of the town.

Reb Yosef also taught a few youths. Among the pupils there was also one, a young lad by the name of Dudl; this Dudl had a fiery head, and while still a bar-mitzvah boy he soon became the best among the already grown-up youths. Dudl knew sixty leaves of Gemara by heart.

Dudl's parents were simple people; they had a business of their own and drew their livelihood from it. Dudl was their only son. Naturally the parents reaped great joy from their gifted son.

In the dayan's house there was one only daughter, Malkele, a pretty girl and a quiet one. Precisely because her father kept praising Dudl so highly, she wanted to talk to him. But she was ashamed simply to start talking to him just like that, and she waited for a suitable opportunity. Once, when her mother was cooking preserves, Malkele said that she wanted to take a little of the preserves in for her father and for Dudl. The mother liked this, and she gave her two little plates of preserves. Malkele went in to her father, into the room where he was studying with the youths, and said:

— Father, Mother gave me two little plates of preserves, one for you and the second for Dudl, who studies so well.

The father looked at her with a loving smile and said:

— Dudl, you see, even the rebbetzin and my daughter are pleased with you, because you study Torah.

Dudl raised his eyes and gave Malkele a look. She returned him a smiling glance; he then said "thank you" to her, and she went away quickly, abashed.

That glance was already enough for both their hearts to begin beating harder. Malkele soon came back to her mother and said:

— Mother, I had no idea at all that Dudl is so handsome!

A little later Malkele came in for the little plates. Again she stole a glance at Dudl, and Dudl looked at her with a smile; she grew bashful and ran away.

From now on Dudl's head was no longer with the Gemara, but with Malkele.

Towards evening the dayan used to dismiss[?] the cheder, and he himself would go off to the kloyz to pray. All the youths would then go home, Dudl too; but now it occurred to Dudl to tell the rebbe that he wanted to stay behind in the cheder in order to go over the Gemara once more. And so he did; the rebbe was pleased with it. When Reb Yosef had gone off to the kloyz, Dudl broke into the study-chant over the Gemara, loudly, at the top of his voice:

— Oy, tanu rabanan [our Rabbis taught].

When Malkele heard his voice, she was drawn to go in; she did indeed slip stealthily into the bet-din room and asked him:

— You haven't gone home?

— No — he answered and looked at her — I want to go over the Gemara.

— Father says that you are the best pupil — Malke went on talking to him.

— Really?

— Yes, and you have such a beautiful voice for studying.

— And you look like a little angel — Dovid answered her.

— Like a little angel! — Malke looked at him.

— Yes, exactly like a little angel; if you wore a white dress, you would be a real little angel.

— I have a white dress!

— Put it on!

— Not today, tomorrow; Mother will ask me why I am suddenly putting on a white dress. Perhaps I am disturbing you in your studying?

— Oh, no, no.

— Do you know what? Perhaps I will dust the holy books, they are simply covered with dust; I'll go and take a rag and dust them.

— Yes, Malkele, do so.

— Mother! — Malkele shouted in to her mother — the books are full of dust, I'm going to take a rag and dust them.

— Quite right, my child, you will have a mitzvah — the mother answered.

That is how it was in the beginning. Something new had entered the lives of both young children.

So a stretch of time went by, but once a thing happened which stirred the young children up utterly.

Dudl noticed that his father had begun coming up to the dayan and whispering in confidence with him. At first he thought that it was about his studies, but from words that he caught he understood that something else was going on here; it somehow seemed to him that a match was being arranged for him. He became agitated, but he said nothing about it.

Once two strange Jews came in to the dayan. The dayan gave them a broad "sholem-aleichem" and spoke about something with them quietly; then they sat down beside Dudl and began asking him difficult questions from the Gemara. Dudl answered them very deftly, and they said:

— A good little head.

And they went away.

Soon he learned from his mother what it was about. It was about a match with the young daughter of a rich Jew from Zawiercie; he is being given a pretty bride, a large dowry and three years' kest [board at the father-in-law's table].

Dudl said that he was not yet up to that, but his mother ordered him not to talk like that any more.

A youth who is a learner must obey father and mother.

In the following week the tenaim [betrothal contract] were already to take place. Dudl, who was then 15 and a half years old, felt as if he were being led to the slaughter. But he was too weak to be able to say anything. The wedding was fixed for half a year later.

"The Jew Is an Enemy of the Polish People, Therefore Strike the Enemy"

[Będzin — antisemitism.]
[Head of the local-news page:] What's New in Zagłębie? — Friday, 20 Tammuz 5696 — piątek 10 lipca 1936.
[Section heading:] Będzin.
[Subheading:] The kehilla president intervenes in the matter with the starosta.
On Wednesday large posters appeared on the fence of the power station in Małobądz, on which the following antisemitic slogans were written in giant letters:
"The Jew is an enemy of the people — so strike the enemy."
"Do not buy from any Jew, because every Jew is a communist."
"The world beats Jews, let us beat them too."
When the kehilla president, Mr. Rubinlicht, received word of this, he turned by telephone to the starosta and conveyed to him the content of the hooligan incitement against Jews.
The starosta declared that he had already been informed of it and that the proper investigation is being conducted.
The police tore the posters down.
Great Interest in the Visit of Dr. Stephen Wise

[Będzin — visit of Dr. Stephen Wise.]
The report in our newspaper that the leader of American Jewry, the well-known fighter for Jewish rights and chairman of the peace delegation in Paris, Dr. Stephen Wise, is coming to Będzin has aroused an extraordinarily great interest throughout Zagłębie and Upper Silesia. The special reception committee is making the necessary preparations so that the reception for Dr. Wise will turn out as impressive as possible.
Dr. Stephen Wise, as is known, will visit only 4 cities in Poland, among which Będzin too has the honour of being counted.
Presidium for the World Jewish Congress

[Będzin — World Jewish Congress.]
On Sunday a plenary session of the committee for the World Jewish Congress took place. The following presidium was elected: chairman — Abraham Liwer; vice-chairmen — Moshe Lewin and Mołczadzki [?]; secretary — Hillel Żabner; Mrs. Lipszyc, Gertler and Gelbard [?].
Because of an Innocent Matter, Musaf Was Not Prayed in the Aleksander Shtibl

[Będzin — religious life.]
Last Sabbath a great scandal took place in the local Aleksander [Hasidic] shtibl, which caused the “congregation” not to pray Musaf with a quorum.
The scandal arose for the following reason: after the Torah reading, Reb Shmuel Zylbersztajn read out a letter in which “our own people” [the Hasidim of the court] are called upon to tax themselves for the benefit of a certain campaign of the Rebbe's court.
Suddenly Reb Yitzchok Rapaport lashed out at the Rebbes' courts, which at such a time of trouble occupy themselves with politics and have nothing in mind but to help see to it that ignoramus rabbis are appointed [?]
The words provoked a storm, the “shtibl” split into two camps, for and against the end of it was that the “moderate” ones ran away and no minyan remained to pray Musaf.
A Hooligan Assault by a Worker on His Employer

[Będzin — crime.]
Two weeks ago a Christian worker at the “Majwing” [?] factory threw up his job because the owners would not raise his wages.
Last Tuesday the worker came to the factory and demanded of Mr. Abram Liwer that he give him a redundancy certificate [a certificate of dismissal owing to staff reduction]. When Mr. Liwer declared that he could not give such a certificate, the worker struck him on the head with an iron file, from which Mr. L. was entirely covered in blood.

[Będzin — a strange incident.]
In the night from Sunday to Monday the maid of the Kamiński family (Piłsudski Street) heard knocking at the door.
— Who is it? — the maid asked.
— Police.
And when the door was opened, a person did indeed come in, dressed as a policeman, who looked around the flat and went away again.

Resolutions of the board of the Merchants' Association.

Sosnowiec — A "peace" conference on Dęblińska Street

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, elections.]
A commission of 12 persons elected. — 6 from the national camp, 6 from the Orthodox one.
As we have already written, the "Koło" [club] of the Jewish town councillors took upon itself the initiative of creating unity among all the political and economic organisations that have a positive attitude to the kehilla elections.
For this purpose the "Koło" called a conference, to which the above-mentioned organisations were asked to delegate their representatives.
The question aroused broad interest; every organisation or grouping delegated several representatives. Individual persons in whom the conference had aroused interest also came.
In a packed hall (Dęblińska 13) Mr. Lubelski, chairman of the "Koło", opens the conference, and after Councillor Mr. Lejzerowicz reads the declaration of the "Koło", in which the aim of the conference is set out, Councillor Aliner takes the floor. He points out the uselessness of any election struggle whatsoever in the Jewish street at the present moment. Among other things Mr. Aliner says the following: "If the election struggle is conducted on the ground of the rabbinate question in our town, there will be no rabbis, and we shall not have an elected kehilla representation either."
Commercial Councillor Mr. Kabak[?] touches on the question of the plague of denunciations. He proposes that a minimum programme be worked out that could lead to a peace.
The representative of the Artisans' Association, Mr. Eksztajn, speaks "plain" words. If we want — he says — the quarrels in Sosnowiec to cease, the rabbinate question must first of all be settled; if not, it is impossible for a unified list to be created.
Mr. Reuven Czapnik is of the opinion that a committee should be created that would play the role of a "League of Nations", before which the local citizens could pour out their bitter hearts.
The committee should also have the task of making peace among all the parties.
The following also speak on the question: Referent Elster, H. Merin, Langer, Jasny, Secemski, Szajer, Jungster, Posłuszny, Landner, Ferstenfeld and others. All agree in principle to the peace proposal of the "Koło", but if, for certain reasons, the "peace" does not come about, the struggle should at least be conducted within our own four cubits [among ourselves], without resorting, as hitherto, to denunciations.
After the discussion, which lasted several hours, the proposal of Mr. G. Stawski was adopted: that a commission of 12 persons be created, 6 from the Orthodox camp and 6 from the national camp. The commission has the task of working out the programme according to which the election struggle is to proceed in a decent manner — possibly even a peace among all the currents.
The retirement pension for Dr. Hercman will be given only as a gift...

[Sosnowiec — town council.]
...will be given only as a gift...
On Monday a session of the town council took place, at which it was resolved to take a loan of 335,000 zł. from the Labour Fund.
The sum will be spent on public works; among other things an elementary school [szkoła powszechna] will be built on... Sucha ["Dry"] Street.
On this matter Councillor Aliner took the floor and described the overcrowding in the "Jewish" elementary schools.
To this the president [of the town] declared that for the new school year the magistrate will rent another premises on Third of May Street for Jewish schoolchildren.
At the session the question of the retirement (emeritus) pension for Dr. Hercman was dealt with again. As is known, the town council in its time, after many debates[?], fixed for Dr. Hercman a retirement pension of 100 zł. a month.
The item was struck out at the voivodeship on the grounds that the pension law does not apply to such officials as Dr. Hercman, but that the town council can give the pension in the form of a "daru łaski" [gift of grace]...
In this sense the town council resolved to give the gift to Dr. Hercman, who, incidentally, also took part in the struggle for Poland's liberation. In 1905 he was exiled to Siberia by the Tsarist authorities.
The gift is granted for the period from 1 April of this year until 31 March 1937.

Life in Kielce — On What Foundations Can a United Election Bloc for the Kielce Kehilla Be Created?

[Kielce — kehilla, elections.] Life in Kielce
Friday, 20 Tammuz 5696 — piątek, 10 lipca 1936

On what foundations can a united election bloc for the Kielce kehilla be created?
The elections to the Kielce kehilla are drawing near. Yesterday the electoral rolls were already laid out for inspection, and very soon the election campaign proper will begin.
Although Jewish nerves are at present worn out to the utmost by the unbearable troubles of the community at large, and although we can hardly believe that in the present, exceedingly bitter time communal workers could be found who would want to occupy themselves with elections, we shall nevertheless have to deal with the elections — and this not merely for the sake of political ambitions, but also in order to uproot once and for all the poisonous sores that have grown on the sick Jewish communal organism, and in order to cleanse the polluted air in Jewish public life.
Reports are reaching us about certain "communal activists" who are already sounding the alarm about Jewish unity and about creating a united election list of all the town's organisations and associations, among them Hasidic shtiblekh. Some of the initiators of this election unity are precisely those of whom the Jewish public would like to be rid for ever. It is these very preachers of unity who are raising heaven and earth about a united election bloc, so that in this way they may "push themselves through" among the community and afterwards go on, as until now, following their disgusting methods in the communal harness.
It is perhaps still a little early to voice a decisive opinion as to how and in what manner the election campaign should be conducted, but what we do want to say in good time, and what must be said quite clearly and plainly, is this: that no Jewish-national grouping whatsoever will venture [?] to unite with such organisations and associations whose candidates are the ones directly to blame for the fatal outcome of the "famous" Kielce town-council elections
We have the greatest respect for the members of this or that party or association; they are our own flesh and blood, and many, very many of them are Zionists, Mizrachists or simply national Jews, and one may unite with them quite boldly. But we shall on no account allow the candidates' list of a united Jewish election bloc to feature such candidates as have brought about the great disgrace of the 20 thousand Jews of Kielce!
One can unite with everyone; one can also conclude a bloc with the non-party Jews, but on condition that they put forward candidates who have, more or less, a communal sense, and first and foremost decent Jews, who incidentally share in bearing the burden of the town's needs, who have an understanding of the most urgent vital interests of the Jewish community — but on no account mere money-Jews, who lock their pockets against Jewish needs, or even men of small means who are, however, plain simpletons and cannot tell day from night.
Only in such a way and on such foundations can one begin to talk about a united Jewish bloc.
Snatched a 500-Złoty Promissory Note and Fled from the Bank

[Kielce — crime.] Snatched a promissory note for 500 złoty and fled from the bank.
This week a certain Christian named Krawczyk came to the Co-operative Bank of Merchants and Industrialists and asked to be shown his promissory note for 500 złoty, which fell due that same day.
When Director Kluska [?] showed him the note, Krawczyk tore it up on the spot and began to run away. The bank employees detained Krawczyk and telephoned for the police, who arrived on the scene. Krawczyk was taken to the police station, where a report was drawn up against him, and he was afterwards handed over to the investigating magistrate. Krawczyk faces a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment.

Dr. Stephen Wise in Kielce

[Kielce — World Jewish Congress.] Dr. Stephen Wise in Kielce.
As is known, the famous Zionist leader and personal friend of the American President Roosevelt, Rabbi Dr. Stephen Wise, is coming to Poland on the business of the World Jewish Congress. 4000 Jews Have the Right to Vote for the Kielce Kehilla

[Kielce — kehilla, elections.] 4000 Jews have the right to vote for the Kielce kehilla.
This week the kehilla administration completed the electoral lists for the forthcoming kehilla elections in Kielce. Some 4000 voters have the right to vote (from the age of 25). On the basis of the election calendar, the election commission yesterday, Thursday, laid out the voters' roll, which every person entitled to vote may check in the kehilla office every day from 8 until 8 in the evening, up to and including the 17th of July (Thursday).

Constituent Meeting of the Election Commission for Carrying Out the Kehilla Elections

[Kielce — kehilla, elections.] Constituent meeting of the election commission for carrying out the kehilla elections.
This week the constituent meeting of the election commission for carrying out the kehilla elections took place. Dr. Rozenberg was elected chairman of the election commission, and Mr. Sz. B. Goldman vice-chairman.
Murdered His Future Brother-in-Law

[Kielce — crime.]
Stanisław Lubek of the village of Zdul[?] (Kielce district) fell in love with the pretty local village girl Marianna Mendak and decided to marry her. Her brother Józef, however, was an outspoken opponent of the match and forbade his sister to keep company with Lubek. Because of this the meetings of the enamoured couple did not take place, as before, in the girl's home, but behind the village. The bride's brother Józef nevertheless found out about it; at a certain hour he met Lubek and warned him not to meet his sister any more. When Lubek answered him that he loved her very much and that he would marry her, Józef Mendak then seized several large stones and with them dealt several heavy blows to Lubek's head. Lubek fell dead on the spot. With the stones he split his head open and knocked his brains out. The murderer of the future brother-in-law has been arrested.
Organizing Meeting on the Elections to the World Jewish Congress

[Kielce — World Jewish Congress.]
On Tuesday a large organizing meeting took place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla [of Kielce] concerning the elections to the World Jewish Congress, which are being held throughout Poland on the 19th of this month.
Representatives of all the local political and economic organizations, the trade unions, the kehilla and a number of communal activists took part in the meeting, which had been convened on the initiative of the Zionist Organization.
The meeting was conducted under the chairmanship of Mr. I. M. Rajzman.
After the report on the district conference in Częstochowa, delivered by Mr. A. A.[?] Rozenblum, and after a short discussion and some instructions on the organizational manner of the elections, a united election committee was elected.
The newly elected committee has already set to work.
Seizures and Executions among the Members of the People's Bank

[Kielce — economy, the People's Bank.]
As we learn, this week the court bailiffs (komorniks) carried out seizures (zajęcia) and even executions among the members of the People's Bank.
These executions and seizures are a result of the negligence of the members, who, despite the repeated warnings, did not want to come to the bank in order to settle amicably the sums assessed on them by the commission for the share capital (pai capital).
The seizures and executions will, it goes without saying, assume a mass character if the members do not themselves come into the bank to settle their obligations of their own free will.
We have already warned about this many times, and we now warn for the last time.
20 Tammuz — the Yahrzeit of Dr. Herzl of Blessed Memory. Herzl and Bialik Memorial Service in the Town Synagogue

[Kielce — Zionism, memorials.]
On the occasion of the 32nd yahrzeit of Dr. Herzl of blessed memory (20 Tammuz) and the second yahrzeit of Chaim Nachman Bialik of blessed memory (21 Tammuz), a solemn memorial service (hazkarah) will take place tomorrow, Saturday, at 10 o'clock in the morning, in the town synagogue.
On Sunday, the 12th of this month, at 8 in the evening, a memorial assembly (akademia) will take place in the Zionist club in memory of the two deceased Zionist leaders.
The Jewish population is asked to take part en masse in the memorial service as well as in the memorial assembly.
Mother Cruelly Murdered Her 3 Children

[Opoczno district — crime.]
On the 1st of this month the 24-year-old Christian woman Zofia Stolarska of the village of Przysucha, Opoczno district, cruelly cut the throats of her 3 children with a rusty knife. First she slaughtered the youngest child, 5 months old, and afterwards — the two older children. After carrying out the bestial murder she cut her own throat with the same knife. In a grave condition she was taken to the hospital in Opoczno.
The cause of the cruel murder was her exceptionally hard material situation.
